Uniform Title: *Kriyākramadyotikā* Author: Aghorāśiva Description:
Transcribed from a 1927 Cidambaram edition in Grantha script supplied by Richard Davis.

Publication Year: 1927 Publication City: South India Publication Country: India
Oṃ tat sat.
May there be auspiciousness.
May there be auspiciousness for the Lord of the Assembly of Consciousness (Citsabheśa), accompanied by Śrī Śivakāmasundarī;
salutations to the Supreme Brahman, the venerable Jñānasambandha Paramācārya.
The *Paddhati* (Manual), titled *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya.
May there be auspiciousness!
I pay homage to Śiva, who is beyond comparison, tranquil, without beginning or end, partless, and stainless; and to Śakti, whose nature consists of knowledge and action. (2)
Commentary: This is the commentary titled *Prabhā*, composed by the illustrious and stainless jewel-like Guru, which illuminates the sequence of ritual action (*Kriyākramadyotikā*).
I salute Śiva, Śakti, Gaṇādhīśa, Guha, and Vāgīśvarī in their proper order;
I also revere Kurvāsas, the sage Paiṅgala, and the other teachers. (2)
He who, having drunk the ocean of nectar arising from the breasts of Gaurī— which originates from the mountain whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon—
performs the playful act of breaking the great trunk of the tree of obstacles; [to him I bow].
I take refuge in that intoxicated elephant, by which the manifestation of consciousness is produced daily for those souls shrouded in impurity. (2) p. 2)

I bow to Śiva, the companion of Ambikā, for the perfect attainment of my own desired goal— he who shines as the creator, protector, and destroyer of all worlds, whose greatness has always been so vast that it lies beyond the reach of both speech and mind. (3)
2. By means of whose mudrās and gestures, and by whose silence, yogins are freed from doubt—
[that Lord] whose smiling and delightful face is the moon-crested one.
I worship Him who dwells at the root of the banyan tree, entering [all beings]. 4.
She who, having pierced the strength of the dense mist of worldly existence, reveals the supreme auspiciousness (śivatva) of men;
May this power of Śiva, possessing the nature of both knowledge and action, be placed at the forefront. [In this work],
the sequence of the essential natures of the categories beginning with Paraśiva is presented within the celestial mansion of the venerable Śaiva Āgama.

I ever bow for the sake of enlightenment to that sun-like teacher named Aghoraśiva, who, having dispelled the entire darkness of ignorance, illuminates all things with great care through the multitude of rays of his own commentary, possessing a soul distinguished by its radiance.
Whose light, having utterly shattered the mass of misdeeds so difficult to cross,
immediately bestows the supreme bliss of the highest good upon those beings who possess devotion.
I bow to my compassionate Guru, named Vāmadeva, the lord of the illustrious city of Padmālaya, who is an ocean of the Śaiva Āgamas.
[7] The knowledge of Śiva beginning with the *Kāmika*, and the primary Saṃhitās beginning with the *Mṛgendra*...
Having thoroughly examined the Saṃhitās and commentaries such as the Śrīraurava and Mataṅga,
as well as the ritual manuals of the venerable Somaśambhu and other former teachers,
according to my own understanding and through the instruction of a true teacher, [I shall compose this]. (8–9)
This brief commentary, titled *Prabhā*, is composed for the sake of awakening the ignorant; it illuminates the unclear meanings of the *Kriyākramadyotikā*.
Those who perceive the faults of others while ignoring their most excellent virtues— [10]

If those who possess virtue deign to forgive my ill-spoken words, then these envious, crooked-minded, and newly arrived wicked men are but messengers who must be rejected; here again is my salutation with joined palms to the virtuous. (11)
In this regard, first of all, here the venerable teacher, for the sake of completing the composition he intends to undertake without obstacle and in accordance with the conduct of the learned,
[offers] the arising of the collection of ritual acts to be described—

The fundamental Śiva, who is endowed with the nature of Śiva characterized by being the agent of all purposes and all things, who is the cause of the destruction of obstacles, who removes what is inauspicious, and who bestows auspiciousness upon individual souls.

With the first verse beginning with "I bow" (*vande*), he pays homage to the partless (*niṣkala*) [Śiva] and the power (*śakti*) that is inseparable from him. Here, the construction of the action and its factors is: "I bow to Śiva" (*śivaṃ vande*).
[The word] "Śiva" refers to the one who is auspicious by virtue of his primordial, established nature as the omniscient and omnipotent Lord.
"Purapatimanagham" is seen in the lexicons; it is the name Tyāgarāja.
There is an alternative reading:
"By virtue of being [the Lord] through yoga, he is Śiva. As it has been said: "Because of his tranquility and because of his state as the creator of all..."

Because he is the supreme cause, Śiva is spoken of in the *Mahātantra* by the knowers of the Tantras as Sadāśiva. When Śiva is pure (*śuddha*), then, according to the venerable *Mataṅga*, his state as Śiva (*śivatva*) would be pure.
Alternatively, "Śiva" means auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*); because of his connection with that, he is Śiva. The suffix *aC* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Thus...

This was composed by the illustrious Vandyaghaṭīya. This is a word that serves as an indicator (*lakṣyapada*). In response to the inquiry "What is its definition?", he says: "Without beginning or end" (*anādinidhanam*).

"Ādi" means origination, and "nidhana" means destruction; that which has neither beginning nor end is so described, meaning it is devoid of both beginning and end. If this were stated thus, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to bound souls (baddhātman), since they too are devoid of beginning and end. Likewise...

In the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, it is stated: "The bonds are without beginning or end, while the individual soul (*jīva*) is proclaimed to be without beginning. To explain its meaning, [the author] says "(niṣkalaṅkam)"—meaning "stainless" (*niṣkalaṅka*). [It is so called because it is] "gone out from" (*niṣkrāntaḥ*) the stain (*kalaṅka*), which is impurity (*mala*);
according to the rule "in the sense of 'gone out from' and so forth, [compounds] with *nis* and others [take] the fifth case," [it forms the compound *niṣkalaṅkaḥ*].

This is a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*). Furthermore, because those [entities] are not established as such due to their connection with beginningless impurity (*anādimala*), that [impurity] is excluded. Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"On account of the connection with beginningless impurity, he is described by me as possessing limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*); because of being liberated from beginningless impurity..."

"By that [reason], he is Śiva, the Omniscient. When this much is stated, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Ananta and others, because, since they are graced by Śiva, they cannot be considered free from blemish (*niṣkalaṅka*). Thus, it is said in the *Śrīmat-tattvaprakāśa*:
"Without first gracing them, Śiva appoints eight as Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśatva*). To exclude that [over-extension], he says:
"Without parts" (*niṣkalam*) means that from which all "parts"—that is, by metaphorical extension, the connection with the aggregate of *kalā* and the other categories—have departed;
the meaning is that He is devoid of the effects and instruments beginning with *kalā*. Likewise...

In the venerable *Mokṣakārikā*, it is stated: "The Lord of the Gods is never associated with the aggregate of the *kalās* and so forth as a bound soul (*paśu*); therefore, He is sung as being without parts (*niṣkala*). Because those [others] possess connection with the *bindu-kalā* and so forth, there would be an obscuration of their nature. Thus, in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"It is said that his body consists of pure *yoni* and is not born of karma.

[This definition] would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) even to Śiva abiding in the state of *adhikāra* (sovereignty) or Śiva abiding in the state of *bhoga* (enjoyment), because those two are devoid of contact with the *māgīya*, *baindava*, *kalā*, and other [powers]. To exclude them, he says:

"Śāntam" (the Peaceful). Here, Śiva, whose entire power has ceased and who abides in dissolution (*laya*), is called "Śānta. Since the state of dissolution itself is the state of peace (*śāntapada*), there is no room for the aforementioned [limited] treasury of meanings.
Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, it is said: "The Lord, Sadāśiva, and Śānta—these three abide here as the Vāmana [form]."
The state of entitlement (*adhikārāvasthā*) is that in which the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has been set in motion;
the state of enjoyment (*bhogāvasthā*) is that in which the power of action is engaged. As they say: "One who is engaged through power... (p. 7).

"And the agent who has entered [into activity] is held to be manifold. As for those [definitions] already mentioned, they suffer from over-extension to liberated souls (*muktātman*), since even they possess the connection with office (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and dissolution (*laya*). Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśva*, it is stated: "In the Sakala and the Niṣkala [levels], and indeed everywhere, the name is the same."

"That is declared to be *sāyujya* (union). Thus it has been stated by the Teachers in the commentary on the *Śrīmatparamokṣanirāsakārikā*: "And thus, if one were to accept that the perfected one (*siddha*) remains in states such as dissolution (*laya*) as previously described, then agency would not be perceived."
On the contrary, [the opponent might argue] that there would be a deficiency compared to Īśvara. To address that, he says: "(Supreme over the universe)" (*viśvādhikam*).

This refers to the Lord who is superior to all things, both conscious and unconscious, within the world. It is only for Him that supremacy over the universe is logically established; as for the liberated souls (*muktātman*), their very nature [is attained] solely through His grace.
"From attainment comes its cessation"—in this manner, [I] praise Śiva;
[I] salute [Him] with prostrations of my body and mind; and [I] praise Śakti—such is the connection [of the words] through the act of lifting up. What are her characteristics?

In the *Viṃśāsā*, it says: "(consisting of knowledge and action)"—that is, she whose nature (*ātman*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) consists of knowledge (*jñāna*), which is vision (*dṛk*), and action (*kriyā*), which is activity (*vyāpāra*); she is thus described.
Having bowed to the gurus, both supreme and subordinate, who have descended through the lineage of the gurus,
this *Kriyākramadyotikā* is clearly composed, beginning with these words.

Now, having performed the salutation to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), he declares his intention to compose [the work] by means of the second verse, beginning with "the gurus" (*gurūn*) and so forth, preceded by prostrations to the supreme, the non-supreme, and the supreme-non-supreme gurus. The "gurus" are Paraśiva and the others who have descended through the lineage of the gurus.
Their lineage (*vaṃśaḥ*) is their progeny (*santānaḥ*); according to Amara, "lineage" means progeny or offspring.

Its sequence (*kramaḥ*) is the uninterrupted succession beginning from Paraśiva to Sadāśiva, and from him to Ananta, and so forth; according to Amara, "succession" (*paripāṭiḥ*) means order (*anukramaḥ*). By that [sequence].
Having approached those who had arrived, the venerable Lord Paraśiva himself indeed took hold [of them] in the *Śrījñānaratnāvalī*; therefore, he is the one with the command (*sadeśa*). (p.
From that Lord, the venerable Ananteśa, who is the self of Sound (nāda), possessing both parts and no parts,
[proceeded] the egg-born Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śrīkaṇṭha-Rudra, and from him the excellent sage Aṅgiras, the deliverer of the Tantras.

"The Guru is named Durvāsanā. Here, the division of the words follows the sequence in which all [elements] have been deposited: *pare*, *apare*, and *parāpare*. Among these, the *pare* are Īśvara and others; the *apare* are the gods, sages, and so forth; and the *parāpare* are Ananta and others. Thus it has been declared.

In the commentary on the venerable Parākhyatantra, many teachers are recognized there according to the distinction between the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (aparā), as well as by the distinctions of the instigator (codaka) and so forth, and likewise by the distinctions of the teacher (guru) and so on. Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are considered the supreme teachers; yet the single supreme reality itself is threefold through its own will.
[The text] stands thus: "Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Umā, Skanda, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—these six;
the higher and lower deities, the sages, and the eight supreme gurus. It specifies the object [of the salutation] with the word "(gurun)" ("the gurus").
They are called *guru*s because they speak and instruct (*gṛṇanti upadiśanti*); [having bowed] to them.
Having bowed down with body, speech, and mind, preceded by an excess of devotion and faith;
then he asks "What [is to be done] from that? [and answers] "The daily [rites], etc. This means the daily rites and so forth. By the word "etc. (ādi),...
The exposition of the occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) [rites] is now being given. Here, the daily (*nitya*) consists of bathing and so forth;

the occasional (*naimittika*) consists of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*); and the optional (*kāmya*) is the rite known as the "consecration by the weapon" (*astrābhiṣeka*), which serves as the means for attaining desired goals such as sons and the like. Likewise:

It is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Bathing, worship, recitation (*japa*), meditation, and fifthly, the fire-oblation (*homa*)—one should always perform these five daily rites. Likewise, it is known that the occasional (*naimittika*) rites are of two kinds: initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*); [and there is also] the optional (*kāmya*) [rite].

That [worship] is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. Three types have been declared for the Ācārya: the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya). For the Sādhaka, the obligatory and optional rites are performed according to the procedure prescribed in his own scripture. For the Samayins and Putrakas, however, it is only the obligatory rite.

Thus it is proclaimed. This [work], the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, refers to "action" (*kriyā*), which means performance or execution; for the *Nānārtharatnamālā* states that "action" (*kriyā*) is used in the senses of movement, doing, and deliberation regarding tasks. Its "sequence" (*krama*) is its orderly progression. Of that...

(11) *dyotikā* means "illuminating"; that is to say, it is that which illuminates the sequence for the performance of daily and other rites. This refers to the phrase "illuminating the sequence of ritual actions" (*kriyākramadyotikā*). Immediately following this [first] action is this [second] action.

Thus, it should be understood that the *Nityādi* [text] is an illuminator of the sequence of rituals (*kriyā*) and their procedures (*karmakrama*). For this very reason, it is indeed useful even when the *Śiva-śāstras* exist. This is so whether the reading is *nityādi* or *nityādir*.

By making "kriyākramadyotikāpada" a qualifier, [the compound] is explained as "that whose beginning consists of eternal rituals," and thus it is stated accordingly; [this is] redundant. (Clearly) by this [word], even though other manuals exist, the utility of this treatise has been indicated. For those others are indeed not clear.

Having composed illuminations for the *Nitya* and other [rites], the meaning is that he reveals the sense not previously stated by them. It is "being made" (*kriyate*), meaning it is "composed" (*viracyate*). By the word "by me," Śiva is meant. And its status as a *paddhati* (manual) should be understood from its being a path of ritual practice (*anuṣṭhāna-mārga*).
The Procedure for the Meditation on Śiva.
(3) Within the five-nāḍī interval prior to the time of dawn?

Having arisen, whether pure or impure, endowed with such purity as is possible, having meditated upon Śiva in the heart-lotus or at the *dvādaśānta* according to the method instructed by the Guru, and having performed recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, [one should enter] into *samādhi*.
Having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva or any other [deity] according to one's preference, even if lacking the capacity [for elaborate rites],

and having then made a formal resolve regarding what is intended to be performed, [one should proceed]; for among the rites to be described— whether daily (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) and so forth— the rule for the occasional and other rites is preceded by the daily rites.

Having begun to describe the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) first, [the author] states therein: "First, having arisen at the time of dawn, the wise man should meditate upon Śiva; then he must perform the necessary acts and maintain purity. Thus, according to the words of the venerable Aghoraśiva, [this is] the preliminary [instruction].

He explains the procedure for the meditation on Śiva with the passage beginning with "at dawn" and ending with "having meditated. He states the time for the meditation on Śiva with the word "at dawn," meaning from the latter part of the night. "At the cutting off of five nāḍīs" refers to five nāḍīs.
Five ghaṭikās. ... [as it is said] in the venerable Kāmika (p.
"Sixty breaths constitute one prāṇa; six prāṇas constitute one ghaṭikā."
Regarding their delimitation—that is, the boundary—it refers to the *brāhmamuhūrta*. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Sūkṣma*: "The end of the night is said to be until the *ābhūta* nāḍī;
knowing this as the morning time, one should commence one's ritual action. [This refers to] the *brāhma*.

For this is the name for that time: "Rising during the stainless *brāhma-muhūrta*, meditation, the necessary purification, cleaning the teeth, bathing, the twilight rituals (*sandhyā*), the offering of water (*tarpaṇa*), and the recitation of mantras (*japa*)—these [should be performed] before the rising of the sun; [this is] the single petal of the camphor [lotus]."

People say: "But when the Lord of Day has risen, one should act accordingly from the beginning. He states the characteristics of one qualified for meditation with the words "or pure" (*śucirvā*). This means a person who is either pure or clean at the time of sleep, being free from contact with those who are untouchable.
"Śuci" [means] pure, unimpaired, as well as [pertaining to] eroticism and the month of Āṣāḍha—so says the Viśva-kośa.
Alternatively, "aśuci" means one who is then possessed of impurity due to touching what is untouchable and so forth;
this qualifying term applies to both the pure and the impure, as appropriate.
14) Therein, for the first [type of person], it is for the purpose of warding off the fault of ignorance;
for the second, it is for the purpose of removing impurity such as touching that which is untouchable.

And this is for the purpose of avoiding the fault of perspiration; for even in the absence of a ritual bath with water (*vāruṇasnāna*), the requirement of purification appropriate to that time remains equally applicable as far as possible. The intended meaning here is that one who has achieved purification according to one's capacity should meditate upon Śiva, since it is heard in scripture that "action must be performed by those who are pure."

Thus [it is said]. Whether pure or impure—meaning endowed with whatever degree of purity is possible—the word "engaged" (*yukta*) should be applied separately to each. He states its further support as "(in the heart-lotus).
We shall demonstrate its essential nature later. As for how one should meditate, he says:

"In the manner instructed by the Guru. Thus [it is said]. He states the object of meditation: "Śiva. This has already been explained. "According to one's capacity" means according to one's wealth. "Recitation" (*japa*) refers to the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīmac-Cintya-viśva-sādhākhya*, having recollected the root mantra upon the tip of the tongue—
"With a serene mind, having remained [there] until before dawn, and having praised with hymns and prostrated," thus it is said.
Recitation (*japa*) is for the purpose of bringing the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) face-to-face.
That is the recitation of the mantra. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"Japa is considered to be the recitation [of the mantra] which brings the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) face-to-face. By this, it is shown that for those lacking the capacity for meditative visualization (*dhyāna*), the attainment of its fruit occurs even through the contemplation of that [deity's] form and so forth.

It is indicated here that one should practice the meditation on Paraśiva and the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra of His wheel (*cakra*), which serves as the means for His worship, according to the instruction. He describes the different types of meditation according to the differences among qualified practitioners with the words "one devoid of the power of *samādhi*. Now, as for *samādhi*:

The final limb of yoga is characterized by the non-appearance of the meditator and the act of meditation, and the appearance of the object of meditation alone. As it has been said: "Samādhi is that in which only the object appears, as if devoid of its own nature. In that state, one who lacks capacity is powerless.
The *Nānārtharatnamālā* states: "Sāmarthya, yogyatā, and śakti [are synonyms].

In the phrase "the form of Sadāśiva and so forth, according to one's preference," the word *sadāśiva* indicates Śiva in his state of enjoyment (*bhogāvasthā*), possessing both the manifest (*sakala*) and unmanifest (*niṣkala*) aspects. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
The Great Lord (Maheśa) residing in the state of authority (adhikārāvasthā), possessing all forms, is understood here.
Likewise, in the venerable Vātulaśuddha, it is said: "Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa..."
The forms are threefold. O Mahāsena, the Śivatattva is proclaimed as being both *niṣkala* (partless) and *sakala* (with parts); it is also called *sādākhya*. One should know Maheśa to be *sakala*;
thus they become threefold. These are the three states.

The venerable teachers have stated that this is appropriate because, like the meditation on the *sandhyās* to be described later, it is to be performed according to the distinction between different types of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*). Thus it was said by the commentator on the *Śrīmat-somaśambhu-paddhati*. Likewise:

"In the *Śrīmad-Bālajñānaratnāvalī*, it is said: 'Having thus understood Śiva— the supreme who pervades all paths and exists in these three states— one should meditate upon Śiva, according to one's qualification, as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.'"
The procedure for the evacuation of waste and purification, etc.

(4) Accompanied by a staff and other requisites, having departed from his home and gone to the place as prescribed, he should perform the necessary rites there: facing north during the two daily twilights, facing south at night,
with the sacred thread over his right shoulder.
One should avoid excrement on ground covered with grass that has been transformed by the great elements, and one should not face the sun or other such objects.

Having discharged [the feces], having wiped the anus with a clod of earth or similar object, and having grasped the penis with the left hand, one should take the aforementioned clay, go to the edge of the water, and perform the cleansing—
either in a single application or in five applications— with clay and water.

Having cleansed the hand with one application of clay after each evacuation of the anus, and having applied clay ten times to the left hand and seven times to both hands together, one should thereafter perform the purification of the feet;
however, in the absence of purity of intention, one should continue the cleansing until it is achieved.
Afterwards, having washed his feet and hands with each [portion] of clay individually and having sipped water twice in another place;
(8) then, having recited the *vyāhṛtis*, which constitute the preliminary rite for the visualization of Śiva and the essential limb of all ritual actions.

Since the discharge of impurities and so forth must be mentioned first, followed by bathing and so forth, and then again the discharge of impurities and so forth— because all ritual activities proceed on that basis—
he first explains the procedure for the discharge of impurities, purification, and so forth, beginning with the words "(the staff, etc. and ending with "having sipped water."
Up to this point. (Accompanied by the staff and so forth): That which has the staff as its first [item] is "staff-and-the-rest" (*daṇḍādi*);
he whose companion is that is thus described. The definition of the staff (*daṇḍa*) is as follows: [p. 18]

In the *Suprabheda*, it is stated that for Brahmins the height should be at the crown of the head (*śirotsedha*), for Kṣatriyas at the forehead (*lalāṭaka*), for Vaiśyas at the bridge of the nose (*nāsikotsedha*), but one should avoid [this measurement] for Śūdras and others. Regarding this, he states a further distinction: "For the Preceptor (*deśika*), it is said to be up to the top of the head; for the Practitioner (*sādhaka*), however, it is the forehead."

"The interval from the ground to the tip of the nose for a *putraka*, and always up to the tip of the nose for *samayins*. Likewise, for *naiṣṭhikas* and householders, one should have it made according to the span of the hand. This excellent bamboo staff (*vaiṇava-daṇḍa*) should indeed be worn at all times."

The meaning of the word "kamaṇḍalu" and so forth is as follows: likewise, O illustrious Ajita, having risen and gone outside, holding a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hand, and having taken earth, wood, cow dung, flowers,
auspicious sesame seeds, salt, *kuśa* grass, and other ritual materials, he should go to the river.
"Flowing to the ocean. Thus, he describes a place suitable for the discharge of excrement and urine with the words "(as sprinkled).
That location is indicated in the *Śrīmat-sahasra*: "One should go to a desired place, avoiding the northeastern direction. By this—
The prohibition against traveling to the region of Ayo is indicated.
Likewise, in the Śrīm... [text missing] ...in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the water of the river-gartas, and in cow-dung ashes... [text missing].

"In a place such as a cremation ground, not far from a single tree or a crossroads, one should not perform the *āvaśyaka* (daily obligatory rite). In that place suitable for the discharge of impurities and the like, [one should perform] the *āvaśyaka*, which consists of the impurities and so forth. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "Having emerged..."

In such expressions as "perform the necessary rite at the place of rest," it is established that the word *avaśyaka* itself denotes "impurity" (*mala*). Furthermore, that word "impurity" (*mala*) in that context should be reflected upon; or rather, [it refers to] both... [text fragment].
Considering that it must necessarily be done, it should be concealed as a qualification of the word "impurity" (*mala*).
To the question, "In what state is the impurity on the trident? he says: "(during the day and at the two twilights).
By the word "day," the period of the day excluding the twilights is expressed. Completely...
"Dhyānāntya" refers to the twilight (*sandhyā*), which is a period consisting of three and three-quarter *nāḍikās*.
This is because it is stated in the *Kṣīrastaraṅgiṇī* that "the twilight is likewise half a watch (*prahara*)," and also because of the designation "yāma."
Regarding the phrase "(saumyāsyaḥ)," the word *saumya* denotes the northern direction, which has Soma as its presiding deity;
furthermore, the word *soma* is a designation for both Kubera and the Moon. [The term] *saumya* [also refers to] a wise man or a brahmin.

In three senses, the term *saumadaivata* refers to Soma. According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*: "Soma [is used] for Kubera, camphor, a species of creeper, and the moon. Thus, *saumya* means "that which has Soma as its deity," formed with the suffix *yañ*. Consequently, *saumyāsya* means "having a face toward the north"; that is, facing north. (At night, one should face south.)
Facing the southern direction; (excluding the transformations of the great elements).

The "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) refer to the five elements beginning with earth; their "transformations" (*vikāra*) are their modifications, meaning the five sounds produced from wood and so forth by those respective elements. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Vātula*:
Sound, which is a modification of the great elements, is traditionally held to be fivefold: that produced from wood, that born of earth, and that which is said to be born of conch.

That which is born from fire is produced from iron; that born from wind is produced from bamboo; and that born from the moon and the sky is produced from earth; therefore, it is a transformation of the elements.
This object of cognition is joined with all [the senses]; sound is traditionally held to be of five kinds.
Thus, according to Amara, *pariṇāma* and *vikāsa* are two [synonyms]. "Devoid of these" means free from them;
that is to say, free from words such as *medinī* (earth), *ādi* (and so forth), *mahābhūta* (great elements), *vikāra* (transformations), *dāruja* (wood-born), and the like.
"(Facing the sun and others)": that which has the sun as its first [member] is described as such; of that—

"Not facing" means not being in front of [the object]. By the inclusion of the word "etc.," it is stated that [the rite] is also "not facing" cows, Brahmins, ascetics, women, and so forth. Thus, in the *Śrīmadbrahmaśambhupaddhati*: "In front of cows, Brahmins, those with sectarian marks, women, and the moon and sun..."
"One should gradually cast off the impurities of the transformations of the great elements.
Thus [it is said]. (In "covered with grass"): "in moments," meaning when it is no longer covered or has become hidden.
Here, by the word "grass" (*tṛṇa*), other types of grass such as *ayāśīya* are indicated. Likewise, in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha*:

"One should void urine and feces after covering the ground with fresh, uncut grass that is not fit for sacrifice. This was said for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of] the earth as a deity (*bhūdevatā*).
Likewise, all the deities and sages, having gone there, spoke their names and likewise said: "Arise, everyone!"

"I shall cast it outside. (Malam) means excrement. According to Amara: "Mala is not feminine; it denotes sin, filth, and dregs. (Visṛjya) means having abandoned. (By means of a clod of earth, etc. Loṣṭa means a clod of earth.
That which has a clod of earth as its beginning is described as such; grass and the like constitute the meaning of the word "beginning. This was stated by the venerable Somaśambhucaraṇas:
"Then one should wipe the anus with grass, parts of the body of a sacrificial animal, or a clod of earth, but not..."
"Never with cow dung, stones, or wood. (The anus: "Vāyu. Regarding the anus, [the Amarakośa] states: "Apāna is the anus; vāyu is wind. (Having wiped: Having performed the cleansing.
(The penis: "Liṅga. Regarding the penis: "Liṅga may mean that which is to be proven, a sign, the male organ, a mark, or a form of a deity."

Thus [ends] the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. With the other [hand], namely the right hand, [he should perform] that which is prescribed in the *Śivāgama*. Its characteristic has been stated in the venerable *Kāmika*:
"For the purpose of purification, one should fetch earth that is pure, free from grit, and soft."
He explains the rule for purification with the words "(near water). "Near water" means in the vicinity of water.
*Antika* means close or near (*antike nikaṭe*).

Thus ends the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. *(Mṛdaṃbhogiḥ)*: "Mṛdaḥ" refers to clods of earth (*mṛttikāḥ*); "ambhāṃsi" refers to waters (*jalāni*); [the compound] is formed with "mṛdaṃgāṃsitaiḥ. *(Ekaprayogeṇa)*: "In one application," meaning at once. *(Sādhanam)*: A sign (*liṅgam*). *(Pañcaprayogeṇa)*: "In five applications," meaning five times. *(Antarā'ntarā)*: From time to time.
At intervals; by each one (*ekaikayā*): that which is one and one is "each one" (*ekaikā*), by that. (The hand:
having cleansed it—that is, having thoroughly washed the hand engaged in the act of purification—having first placed earth from the right hand into the left hand with that [right hand].
Having cleansed the anus with earth and water, one should thereafter wash the left hand with earth and water once; in this manner,
alternating between the cleansing of the anus and the washing of the left hand, one should cleanse the anus five times.

One should purify it; this is what must be understood. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāraṇa*: "Having discarded the grass, roots, and so forth, and having moistened it with water, one should take it with the right hand in the measure of an *āmalaka* fruit and place it in the left;
then, with the left hand, one should rub it again and again" (ten times).
In ten ways: (of both) the right and left hands. (p. 24) (Sevenfold): seven times. (The purification of the buttocks): the buttocks are the fleshy parts of the hips; of those two.
"Purity" refers to that [purity]. According to Amara, "sphicau" means the buttocks (*kaṭiprothau*) in the feminine.
(In the absence of purity of disposition: "Purity of disposition" (*bhāvaśuddhiḥ*) means purity of mind; in its absence or lack thereof.
Thus, it is held that impurity lasts for as long as there is a degree of mental purity.

And the purification of one's being consists precisely in the cessation of loathsomeness. The intent of the stated number is only to establish an addition, not a reduction; for if it were otherwise, there would be the consequence of the injunction regarding the number being rendered meaningless. (As long as purification lasts.)

"Up to the limit of purification. Regarding "yāvat-tāvat," Amara states: "In the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction. "(Vidadhyāt)" means "one should perform. To the question "What then? he says: "(Anyasmin).
In what other place characterized by purity? "(Dviḥ)" means twice. Regarding "(Ācamya)": [the following applies here].
Having first cleansed the mouth with eight mouthfuls of water, one should thereafter sip water silently;
immediately after that, it should be understood that one should rinse [the mouth] with mantras in the manner to be described. Likewise, [this applies] regarding urine, feces, and eating.

And likewise, regarding the consumption of what is forbidden to eat: "One becomes purified by [swallowing] four, eight, sixteen, or thirty-two mouthfuls [of the substance]. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "One [mouthful] in the liṅga, [one] in the anus..."

Five or ten applications of clay on the left hand, and seven on both hands; thereafter, one should perform the purification of the buttocks. Then, elsewhere, one should sip water silently while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savyopavīta).
Having sipped water again with mantras, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth. Thus it is said.
The procedure for cleaning the teeth.

(5) One who desires liberation should take up a tooth-stick eight finger-breadths long— originating from a mango tree or similar source, the thickness of the little finger, moist, with its bark intact, free of joints, and straight. It should not be less than ten finger-breadths in length.
One should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
Having avoided the fingers and other parts derived from trees such as the *piśāca*, *dhava*, *vānīra*, *nimba*, *eraṇḍa*, *kāśa*, *kuśa*, and *yava*,
one should rub [the teeth] with something else.

One should not brush one's teeth on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), on festival days (*parvan*), on the sixth, ninth, and new moon days; rather, one should perform purification by rinsing the mouth twelve times with water using clean leaves.
(5) *Pā*—again.

(22) Next, having described the procedure for the evacuation of excrement and so forth, he describes the procedure for cleaning the teeth with the words beginning "the tooth-stick" (*dantakāṣṭha*) and ending with "having performed" (*vidhāya*).

Thus [ends the section] up to this point. Now, initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is the means for accomplishing the desired goal and has issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, is described in brief; because its purpose is twofold, it is of two kinds: the material (*bhautikī*) and the ultimate (*naiṣṭhikī*).
This is according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-sūtra*. Regarding the ultimate initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*), for one who has been initiated, even if he is like a piece of wood...
He establishes the definition [of the term] as "eight-finger-breadths" (*aṣṭāṅgulim*).
That which has eight fingers (*aṅguli*) as its measure is "eight-finger-breadth" (*aṣṭāṅgulam*).

In this *tatpuruṣa* compound, the suffix *an* is applied according to the rule: "In a *tatpuruṣa*, after a word meaning 'finger' (*aṅguli*), when preceded by a numeral or a word beginning with a vowel."

One desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) should take a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) made from *khadira* or similar wood. Thus it has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "That which arises from *ciribilva*, *karañja*, or *śairīṣa*..."

"Sādira" refers to *arjuna* wood. "Eight finger-breadths for those seeking liberation"—regarding this, he states the characteristic of the [staff] belonging to one who seeks worldly enjoyment (*bhautika*) as "another. "Another" means one who desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). "(Twelve finger-breadths)" means that its measurement is twelve finger-breadths.

As it has been said: "(arising from the mango and so forth). "Mango and so forth" (*cūtādi*) means that of which the mango (*cūta*, i.e., *āmra*) is the first; [the fruit] arising (*saṃbhavam*), i.e., produced, from that. The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *lakṣā* and others.
Likewise, having begun with the words "it is further stated by those very [authorities] for those desiring enjoyment," they say:

"Arising from the *plakṣa*, mango, *kakubha*, *aśoka*, and *jambu* trees, as well as from *campaka*, *apāmārga*, and so forth, and originating from pearls, it should be twelve finger-breadths in length."
(The circumference of the little finger) means as wide as the little finger;

*pariṇāha* means width, according to Amara. (Moist) means not dried. (Covered with skin) means joined or endowed with skin, which is the same as leather. (Without joints) means that which has no joint-knots; thus it is described.

"Granthi, nā, parva, and paruṣī" are synonyms according to Amara. "Ṛju" means straight or not crooked. He mentions trees and such that are unsuitable for cleaning the teeth, saying "piśāca. (The compound *piśācadhavanānīranimbairaṇḍādi* refers to the piśāca tree, dhava, nīpa, nimba, eraṇḍa, and so forth. Furthermore, *piśāca* is a specific type of tree.

*Dhava* is a species of tree; according to Amara, "the *dhava* trees are branches and men. *Vānīra* is *vañjula*, and *nimba* is well known; *eraṇḍa* is *vātari*; [these are] the *piśācadhavana*, *nīra*, and *nimba*.
That which has those [plants] as its first [components] is so described. (Born from the *kāśa*, *kuśa*, and *yājñīya* trees:
*Kāśa* is the *bāṇa* grass; *kuśa* is the *darbha* grass; furthermore, *kāśa* is not feminine; it is the *ikṣugandhā*.
*Poṭagala* is a synonym for *kuśa*, as Amara states: "What is *darbha*? It is *kuśa*. It is a sacrificial tree (*yājñīyavṛkṣa*), meaning a tree fit for sacrificial rites;

thus it is so called because it is born from among the *kāśa*, *kuśa*, and other sacrificial trees. According to Amara, that which is fit for such rites is *yājñiya*. Furthermore, there are sacrificial trees (*yajñavṛkṣāḥ*).
Just as the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, āṣāḍhī, and khadira,
so too the nyagrodha, samī, bilva, cūta, and vaikaṅkata.

"The *āsana* and the *śirīṣa* are proclaimed to be sacrificial trees (*yajñavṛkṣa*). Here, because the *plakṣa*, *khadira*, *cūta*, and *śirīṣa* are specified among the trees suitable for tooth-sticks (*dantakāṣṭha*), the intended meaning is the prohibition of any other sacrificial tree. Regarding the phrase "(the finger, etc.)": [text follows].
What is the meaning of the words "iṣṭa" (sacrificial) and "anirdiṣṭa" (unspecified) and so forth? Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī* it is said:

"That which arises from thorny trees or milky sap trees, or from bricks, charcoal, or ashes—the finger [used for such acts] is not praised; if done through negligence, there is a loss of ascetic merit (*tapas*)."
(Other than that) means other than [spirits such as] piśācas and so forth. [Parigṛhṇīyāt] means one should take hold of it; one should perform the act of grasping.

Now, is it not the case that cleaning the teeth is prescribed for all times? No; he says "on the first day" (*pratipat*). [The phrase] "(on the first day, on the festival days, on the sixth, the ninth, and the new moon)" means: *pratipat* is the first day, *parva* is the festival day, *ṣaṣṭhī* is the sixth, *navamī* is the ninth, and *amāvāsyā* is the new moon; these are so described. On those days, one should "not clean" [the teeth].
One should not purify [it]. To the question of what should then be done, he says: "(of water)"—that is, of liquids.

"(With twelve mouthfuls)"—that is, with twelve fillings of the mouth. Halāyudha states: "A *gaṇḍūṣa* is the filling of the mouth. "(With pure leaves)"—that is, with the leaves of sanctifying trees such as the mango (*cūta*).
The ritual procedure for the Varuṇa-bath.

(6) One should bathe. There, having gone to a river confluence or some other such place, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, one should take earth with the *astra-mantra* from a depth of more than eight finger-breadths, divide it into three parts, and wash [the body] from the navel down to the feet with one part; with the other...

Having smeared all his limbs with water consecrated once with the weapon-mantra, and having entered the water up to his navel, he should form the six-faced mudrā with his face turned toward the east and perform the rites for the mouth and other parts of the body.
Having visualized the radiant weapon-mantra in the heart, one should bathe.

Then the twice-born, having first performed the Brāhmī Sandhyā, should afterwards perform the Astra-Sandhyā. For the sake of that Sandhyā, having sprinkled drops of water on his head with the Astra-mantra, he should offer three handfuls of water as an *arghya* with this very mantra, according to his capacity.

One should recite [the mantra]. Then, taking the remaining portion of the clay, consecrating it with the *saṃhitā* [mantra], and entering water reaching up to the navel, one should divide it three times with the left hand; having consecrated the eastern part once with the *astra-mantra*, the southern with the *brahma-mantras*, and the northern with the root (*mūla*) mantra, [one should use] that which has been consecrated by the *astra*.

Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), having immersed the arm in water with a portion of earth consecrated by the *śiva-mantra* while rotating it, and having contemplated it as being like the sacred bathing place of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*), one should bathe after having fashioned a body [of clay] with earth consecrated by the *bala-mantra* and meditated upon Śiva.
Then, having visualized the Moon and Sun as Śakti and Śiva in the left and right hands respectively,

and having consecrated them with the Saṃhitā-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should sprinkle water upon the head from the navel upwards using the *kumbhaka* mudrā; then, having cast water in the cardinal and intermediate directions with the *astra* mantra, [one should proceed].
Having bathed with fragrant myrobalan and other substances according to the ritual for a universal monarch (cakravartin), and having emerged from the water, [he sits] upon a low throne.

One should conclude the ritual bath (*tīrtha*). Then, having wiped away the water clinging to the limbs with a clean cloth while still wearing wet garments, and having put on two clean garments; (6) (Pra) now, having set forth the procedure for cleaning the teeth:
Now, bathing—which generates the fitness of consciousness for performing virtuous acts such as worship—is described;

for according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, all ritual actions such as worship are rooted in bathing, since no rite exists for one who has not bathed. Therefore, that which brings about its attainment [should be performed] at the outset.
He explains the procedure for the Varuṇa-bath with the passage beginning with "one should bathe" and ending with "having put on [clothes].

"One should bathe" means one should perform the bath. To the question of how that is done, he says "therein. "Therein" means at the time of performing the bath. To the question of where one should perform the bath, he says "at any one of [places such as] a river confluence."

Thus [it is said]. "River-confluence" (*nadīsaṅgama*) refers to the meeting of two rivers or the confluence of a river and the ocean; that which has such a confluence as its beginning is "river-confluence and so forth" (*nadīsaṅgamādi*), and among those, one or another is intended.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes ponds and the like. Thus it was stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"In rivers, limbs of mountains, lakes, ponds, streams, pools," and so forth. Regarding that, he states what must first be done: "(having performed *ācamana*)," etc.

The procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*) will be clarified later. (*Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa*): he is so described because he has performed the *sakalīkaraṇa*—the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs—as it is prescribed and about to be explained. Likewise, there is the placement of mantras along with the limbs (*sāṅganyāsa*) in the venerable *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.

"Karanyāsa is considered to be sakalīkaraṇa. Thus, [the text] prescribes the sequence for taking the earth, dividing it, consecrating it with mantras, and so forth, for the purpose of the clay bath, beginning with the words "With the Astra [mantra]. "[Eight fingers]" means having a measurement of eight finger-breadths.

The phrase "from a pure place" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*: "From a mountain, or from a riverbank, from a sacred field, or from a pure place; from a *brahma* tree, or from beneath *kuśa* grass.
(Adhastāt) means "beneath. (Ekayā) means "with the first portion of earth."
(From the navel to the end of the feet) means starting from the navel and extending down to the feet.

Regarding the sequence for the cleansing bath (*malasnāna*) within the Varuṇa-bath, he says: "with another" (*anyayā*), meaning with a second portion of clay; "once" (*sakṛt*), meaning a single time—according to Amara, *sakṛt* means together or at once; [the clay] "consecrated by the Astra-mantra" (*astrābhimantritayā*).

"Consecrated with the weapon-mantra" (*astrābhijapta*) means, that is to say, permeated by the weapon of Śiva (*śivāstrabhāvita*). "Entirely" (*aśeṣam*). "The limb" (*aṅgam*) refers to the body. "Having smeared" (*ālipya*) means having performed the anointing on all sides. "(Facing east)" (*pūrvāsyaḥ*).
Facing the eastern direction, [the practitioner], having performed the visualization of the face and other features of the Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukhī*)— here, by means of the eyes, ears, and nose—
[should employ] the *Ṣaṇmukhī* mudrā. The definition of this has been stated as follows:

"In the illustrious Siddhāntaśekhara, one should join the fingers. Thus [it is said]. "(Vadanādikam)" means that which has the face as its beginning; by the word "beginning," the ears, eyes, and nose are intended.
"(Pidhāya)" means having covered or concealed them. This is an alternative reading.
The *kāpidhāna* [mudrā] is intended here. Likewise, in the venerable *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"One should firmly bind both ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the pair of nostrils with the two middle fingers."

"One should indeed employ this 'making six-faced' in the rite of bathing. Thus [it is said]. (Radiant,) blazing intensely like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*). [This refers to] the smearing with clay consecrated by the *astra* mantra.

The previous bath is declared to be the "impurity-bath" (*malasnāna*) within the context of the Varuṇa-bath. Regarding this, it has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Having smeared the entire body with [the ash] consecrated by the Astra-mantra and [the breath] made radiant, having closed the eyes with the two *prāṇas* (nostrils), [one should restrain] the vital breaths..."
Having restrained himself in the water, he should remain submerged while recollecting the heart-mantra, which possesses the brilliance of the fire of time;
thus one should perform the bath for removing impurities.

Then, in response to the doubt as to what should be done next, he explains the procedure for the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) of the missiles (*astra*), beginning with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). "Then" (*tataḥ*) means after the ritual bath (*malasnāna*). As for the word "twice-born" (*dvija*):

The term "twice-born" (*dvija*) refers here to initiated persons who have attained the status of the twice-born through the conjunction and generation [of the seed] within the womb of Vāgīśvarī; it does not, however, intend by the word "twice-born" those who are merely endowed with the state of having undergone the *smārta* initiation (*upanayana*), for they are uninitiated [in this sense].
Because there is no authority for the practices established in the Śaiva Tantras, and because, on the contrary, there is a scriptural teaching of transgression [for their performance],
therefore the term "twice-born" (dvija) indicates Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have received Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā). As the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati* has said:
After the Smārta sandhyā-vandana, the triad beginning with the Brāhmaṇa [should perform] the meditation on the Pārameśvara weapon according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures; thus, first.
First: [the Brāhmī, that is, the Vedic].
This refers to the ritual procedure of sprinkling (*ārjana*) composed of mantras such as *āpo hi ṣṭhā* established by the Vedas.
Thus it was stated by the venerable authors of the *Mṛgendra-vṛtti*. Likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*:
"Having sprinkled [the water] with the mantra *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, one should pour water while reciting the Sāvitrī.
(Afterwards: Following the performance of the subtle *saṃdhyāvandana* established by the Vedas;
(*astrasaṃdhyām*)—having raised the weapon-mantra, the *saṃdhyā* is the *astra-saṃdhyā*; that [is what is meant]. Likewise.
"The twilight [sandhyā] during which one releases the weapon-mantra is proclaimed as the 'weapon-sandhyā' (astrasandhyā).

By the use of the particle *eva* ("only/precisely"), the preeminence of the Pārameśvara-sandhyā is established. Likewise, in the venerable Bṛhatkālottara: "Having first performed the Vaidika [sandhyā], one should afterwards perform the Śaiva [sandhyā]."
One should perform [the rite]; likewise, whether one is a *bhautika* or a *naiṣṭhika*, one may or may not first perform the *brāhmī* [initiation].

"But for the Śaiva [tradition], the twilight rite (*saṃdhyā*) occurs only by rule; otherwise, it is a downfall. Thus [it is said]. One should salute [the deity] from whom [the rite] is to be performed. For the sake of that twilight rite: "To the Twilight Rite of the Weapon (*astrasaṃdhyā*). [The offering of] drops of water. (p. 36)

From a drop of water. (Having cast it down) having scattered [it]. (By this very one) by this very weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). Here, it should be understood that a Śūdra, however, should perform the *śaivī* twilight rite (*sandhyā*) after abandoning the *brāhmī* one.
Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*: "The triad beginning with the daily rite (*nitya*) should be performed by all four [castes] without distinction."

"A Śūdra, having abandoned the Vaiśvadeva and the Sandhyā consisting of the three Vedas... and likewise in the *Smṛtikaumudī*: "For a man who is joined with the rite of Āgama-initiation, let there be the very Sandhyā-rite prescribed in the Āgamas—which is not in conflict with the Śruti and Smṛti—for that Śūdra as well."
But there is no entitlement for a Śūdra to the rites prescribed by Śruti or Smṛti, because he lacks authority over the rituals of Śruti and Smṛti; rather, his authority lies solely in the Āgamas.
"Now, having performed the twilight worship of the weapon (*astrasandhyā*), one should perform the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).
By this statement of the venerable Somaśambhu, he describes the sequence of the ritual bath (again).
(The remaining portion of earth: "Remaining" (*śeṣa*) refers to that which is left over from both [portions] already mentioned.
The meaning is that it is the third [part], remaining from the two portions. That is the clay-portion (*mṛdbhāga*). As for the word *saṃhitā*, however—
According to the perspective of the *Dviśatikālottara*, [the mantra] expresses the six ancillaries (anvaṣaṭka) beginning with the Root-mantra and ending with the Weapon-mantra;
according to the perspective of the *Sārddhatriśatika* and other scriptures, it expresses the Root-mantra along with the Brahma-ancillaries.
And so it is stated in the venerable *Kāmika*: "In this scripture, Śiva, together with the Brahma-ancillaries, is designated as the 'Accompanied' (sahita)."

Since this *paddhati* has three hundred and fifty root verses (*mūla*), the *Saṃhitā* itself should be consulted for that [portion]. Thus it was determined by the commentator on the *Somaśambhu-paddhati*. "(Water reaching the navel)" means water of the measure of the navel. "(Having divided)" refers to the division.

The meaning is: having established [the parts] situated in the eastern, southern, and northern directions within the family. (The eastern part) refers to the portion of earth located in the eastern direction. (With the *brahmans*) means with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Īśāna. (The southern part) refers to that situated in the southern direction. (With the root mantra).
With the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva," [one should perform the rite] toward the north, situated in the auspicious direction.

[Reciting it] once—only one time. [Having performed the binding of the directions], with this weapon-mantra (*astra*), for the purpose of pacifying obstacles within the water, [one should cast] earth consecrated by the weapon-mantra in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The meaning is "having scattered.
(From the whirling of the arms) means from the encircling of the arms. (Having seized) thus.

The meaning is that, for the sake of establishing the boundary of the Śiva-tīrtha and for the purpose of consecrating it as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should encircle the bathing water with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) to the extent of the circumference of one's own arm.
[The phrase] "equal to the Śiva-tīrtha" means "equal to that [Śiva-tīrtha]," according to the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.117). Thus says the author of the *Pati*.
Alternatively, "like Śiva’s holy ford" (śivatīrthavat) means being joined with Śiva’s holy ford.
One should consider that by immersing oneself in earth consecrated by the recitation of Śiva-mantras, the water here becomes Śiva’s holy ford.
Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "By means of a portion [of earth] consecrated by the recitation of Śiva..."

Then one should turn back the water; "In this way, O Six-faced One, it becomes the Śiva-tīrtha through ritual bathing"—thus it is said. Here, it should be understood that the contemplation of the Śiva-tīrtha is for the purpose of pacifying the defects arising from contact with fish and other creatures residing in the water. Likewise:
In the illustrious *Suprabheda*, it is stated that water constantly inhabited by fish, frogs, snakes, and other aquatic creatures is especially impure.
"But for the sake of pacifying those defects, one should fashion the Śiva-tīrtha"—thus [it is said regarding] the body (*vigraha*). (p. 39)

(Acting as if making a sacrificial pit: "Having uttered the five Brahmans (*brahmapañcaka*), one should smear [the body] from the head down to the feet for the sake of purifying bodily sins"—this is the meaning. Likewise, in the venerable *Mataṅga*:

"One should touch the head, face, heart, and secret place with the Brahma-mantras in sequence. Likewise, in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "That direction which is called the East has Indra as its lord;
he has been appointed by the Creator (Brahmā) as the leader of all the gods. He is not merely [their leader]..."

He is also the leader of the obstacles; therefore, by his being present here, there shall be the removal of obstacles. In that gentle quarter, Īśāna, born of nectar, resides; when the moon is stirred by Śiva, it flows forth in its entirety. That is the Tīrtha of Nectar.

Because one who has bathed therein becomes immortal; Dharma is the lord of the southern quarter and the remover of all sins. Therefore, whatever impurity (*mṛt*) exists in that direction, its destruction occurs through contact with it. [The author] explains the procedure for the mantra-bath with the word "then" (*tataḥ*).
(Then) p.
40) after bathing. (Soma and Sūrya) means both Soma and Sūrya. (Śakti and Śiva).

"Śakti and Śiva—these two. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. "(Having meditated)" means that here one should contemplate the left hand as being of the nature of the lunar Śakti and the right hand as being of the nature of the solar Śiva; this is the intended meaning. "(With the Saṃhitā ending in vauṣaṭ)" means that which has "vauṣaṭ" at its end.
That [mantra] which ends in *vauṣaṭ* is what is meant by "that" (*sā*), and it is also that which is "joined" (*saṃhitā*); thus it is so described.

The meaning of the word *saṃhitā* has been explained previously. Regarding the phrase "(by means of the *kumbhaka* mudrā)," the definition of this has been stated in the section on the characteristics of mudrās under the *kumbhaka* mudrā.

The two palms should be joined with the thumbs touching the base of the well-joined index fingers, while the little fingers are extended upward; this mudrā is to be employed during bathing and mantra-consecration. (Having consecrated), in this context, one should perform the consecration individually with each of the mantras of the limbs of Brahmā, beginning with the root mantra.
This is the intended meaning. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Kāmika*:

"Having joined the hands, which consist of the sun and the moon, with the jar-mudrā (*ghaṭamudrā*), the consecration (*seka*) should be performed once each time with the mantras beginning with the root-mantra."
And likewise, in the *Śrīcintyaviśvasādākhya*: "One should sprinkle [the disciple] with the hands in the form of the moon and sun,
using the *kumbha-mudrā*, repeatedly with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), as well as with the [mantras of the] Brahmās."

"For the sake of self-protection and for the uninterrupted destruction of obstacles, one should scatter water consecrated with the Astra-mantra in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Based on this statement from the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*,
he says "(in the cardinal and intermediate directions)" to indicate that one should scatter water in the cardinal and intermediate directions for the sake of self-protection.

The quarters (diśaḥ), the cardinal points (kakubhaḥ), the intermediate directions (vidiśaḥ), and the spaces between the directions (digvidiśaḥ)—in these senses, the neuter indeclinable *apadiśam* is used; "the space between two directions is *vidik*, feminine," according to Amara.
He now states what is to be done immediately after the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*).
"Hauṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ," and so forth.
The meaning is that one should perform the consecration with each individual mantra of the *saṃhitā*.

(27) Regarding the term *cakravarti*: by means of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "Universal Monarch" (*cakravartin*), the term refers to the sovereign ruler of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*). His "metaphorical designation" consists of auspicious sounds such as those of conch shells and trumpets;
it is by means of these that [the term is applied]. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*:
One should bathe with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances according to the royal protocol;
seated upon a golden throne or similar seat like a king, one should be bathed with golden jars.
"Having bathed, one should perform the act of immersion with auspicious sounds.

Regarding the phrase "with fragrant *āmalaka*, etc.": *sugandha* refers to fragrant substances, and *āmalaka* refers to the dried *dhātrī* fruit; that which has these two as its beginning is thus described, and [the bathing] is performed with that.

The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to oil and so forth. Thus, it is stated in the *Śrīmadvīratantra*: "Having smeared the entire body with oil and *āmalaka* mixed together. Although it was already mentioned [in the previous verse] that this is done "with the ritual service (*upacāra*) of a universal monarch" (*cakravartin*), the subsequent statement "with fragrant *āmalaka* and so forth" indicates the absolute necessity of using *āmalaka* and the like.

And it demonstrates that this must be performed immediately after the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*). Thus it is recorded in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Thereafter, with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances used for rubbing the body (*udvartana*), the practitioner of mantras, having consecrated them with the *gāyatrī*, [should proceed]."

"One should bathe while recollecting Śiva. (Having emerged) means having performed the emergence and gone to the bank. Regarding the "short palace" (*hrasvaprāsāda*): according to the scripture, "the short is to be known as residing in the *bindu*," it refers to the palace that pervades up to the *bindu*. Some say it is the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). (The sacred bathing place) (*tīrtha*).

A *tīrtha* is that by which one crosses over; the meaning is that one should first contemplate it as the *Śivatīrtha*, that is, as the *Śivatīrtha* thus conceived. (*Upasaṃharet*) means that one should lead it to dissolution in the station of the *bindu* by means of the power of withdrawal (*saṃhāriṇī*). Likewise, in the venerable *Sārddhatriśatikā*:
"One should withdraw the Śiva-tīrtha while meditating with the Saṃhāra-mudrā.
He states what is to be done immediately thereafter with the word "(tataḥ)":
"(Tataḥ)" means after the withdrawal of the Śiva-tīrtha. "(Aṅgalagna-jalam)" means water adhering to the body.

Water. (By one who is not wearing wet clothes) means by one with dry garments. "Two garments" refers to the lower garment and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"In bathing, in the worship of the deity, in sacrifice, and in eating, the wise man [should wear] two washed garments."
"One should wear [a garment] that is unbroken, new, and white. One should not perform rituals while wearing only a single cloth, nor while naked with only a loincloth. (Having put on: having donned.
The ritual procedure for sipping water (ācamana).

(7) Having tied up his topknot, facing either east or north, with his head uncovered and seated, he should [offer] water that is free from bubbles and impurities, looking at it, with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the principle of the Self (ātmatattva); Oṃ hīṃ, svadhā to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva); Oṃ hūṃ, svadhā to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva). Thus.

Having washed each hand individually, having sipped water using the *brahmatīrtha*, having wiped the lips twice at the base of the thumb with the *astra-mantra*, and having wiped [the hands] once downward with the palm;

Having touched with the thumb and ring finger the openings of the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears, as well as the navel, heart, both shoulders, and the head— in right and left order— with the *hṛdaya* mantra,
the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) is performed. (7)

Now, having described the sequence of the Varuṇa-bath, he explains the rule for sipping water (*ācamana*), which is an auxiliary part of all rites, beginning with the words "one whose topknot is tied" (*baddhacūḍaḥ*) and ending with "becomes" (*bhavati*). "One whose topknot is tied" (*baddhacūḍaḥ*): *baddhā* means knotted or bound.
p.
45) He who has a *cūḍā* or *śikhā* [tuft of hair] is so described. According to Amara: "The *śikhā*, the *cūḍā*, and the mass of hair (*keśapāśī*).
(*Prāgāsyaḥ*) means facing the eastern direction. (*Udagāsyaḥ*) means facing the northern direction.
Regarding "direction, place, and time": according to Amara, terms such as *pūrva* (east), *prāk* (east), *udak* (north), and *pratyak* (west) refer to these.

"(Anāvṛtaśirāḥ)" means one whose head (*śiras*)—the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*)—is not covered (*anāvṛtam*), that is, not concealed by a turban; thus he is so described. "(Āsīnaḥ)" means seated (*samupaviṣṭaḥ*).

[Devoid of foam and bubbles: "Phena" means foam (*ḍiṇḍīra*), and "ḍiṇḍīra" means the froth of the ocean; thus says Amara. "Budbuda" means a water-bubble. It is "devoid" (*rahita*)—that is, empty—of both foam and bubbles. (By being) "beheld" (*vīkṣitena*), i.e., looked upon. (Oṃ hām), etc.
The seed-syllables of the principles (tattva) beginning with the Self (ātmatattva), however, are the seed-syllables of the heart, the head, and the crest.
Thus, it is stated in the *Śrīmarāmanāthapaddhati*: "First, one should offer a handful of water [saying] 'svadhā' to the principle of the Self for the heart;
then, looking silently, one should drink that which has reached the heart by means of the Brahma-tīrtha."
"The head is *avaṃ*, preceded by *śi*, and the other two are *svāpū*. Here, the word *svadhā* denotes Sarasvatī. As it has been said: "That which is *svadhā*...

"May it be for one's own sake; may that Sarasvatī be one's own intelligence. Therefore, *svadhā* should be joined as the genus for the sake of the purity of speech according to its meaning. Thus [it is said]. (By means of the *brahmatīrtha*)—that is, by the water located at the base of the thumb. Likewise, it has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"Brahmic [water] is located at the base of the thumb. (Having sipped water:
Here it should be understood that one should sip water without the thumb and the little finger.
Likewise, having placed [the water] on the palm of the right hand with the thumb and little finger released, [one should contemplate it as] the form of Soma during the bright fortnight.

"One should meditate on the black [skin] as consisting of action; with the principles of Self-knowledge and Śiva, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *svadhā*. (The two lips: "The two upper and lower lips are the *uttarāghora* and *radanacchada*;
'the lips (*oṣṭha*) and lower lip (*adhara*) are the *radanacchada*, the covering for the teeth,' according to Amara. (Twice: two times."

"(With the thumb and the ring finger)" means: here, the thumb is the form of Īśāna, and the ring finger is of the nature of the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*). Thus it is said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"The thumb shall always be Īśa, and the ring finger the digit of nectar."
"By that [prāṇa], which is of the nature of nectar, the gods are satisfied with nectar and are free from disease"—[referring to] the cavities of the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears.

The mouth (*mukha*) and the face (*vaktra*), the two nostrils (*nāsike*) and the sense of smell (*ghrāṇe*), the two eyes (*akṣiṇī*) and the organs of sight (*nayane*), and the two ears (*karṇau*) and the organs of hearing (*śrotre*): these are the "mouth, nose, eyes, and ears. Their cavities (*vivarāṇi*), i.e., the hollows (*suṣirāṇi*) or apertures (*bilāni*). Regarding this, Amara states: "Hollow (*suṣira*), cavity (*vivara*), and aperture (*bila*). [Also mentioned are] the navel, the heart, the two shoulders, and the head.

The navel is the depressed region; the heart is the *hṛdaya*; and the two shoulders are the pair of *skandhas*. According to Amara, "the shoulder (*skandha*) is the head of the arm (*bhujaśiras*); *aṃsa* is not feminine. And the head is the *mūrdhan*. These [parts], starting from the right side first (in the order of right and left): the right flank...
The meaning is that one should subsequently touch the left side.
The procedure for domestic bathing for one who is unable [to bathe in water].

(8) Or else, even at home, having bathed as before with clay and other substances, one should bathe with nine, eight, or five jars filled with water purified by a cloth and consecrated with the Śiva-mantra. (8)

Next, having established the procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*), [the author] extends by analogy the rules for bathing at home to those who are unable to bathe at river confluences and the like, from the words "Or else" (*yadvā*) up to "one should bathe" (*snāyāt*). Alternatively, [this refers to] bathing at river confluences and so forth.
If not, it is equal to bathing at the confluence of rivers and the like. [Regarding the phrase] "filled with water filtered through cloth" (*vastrapūtatoyaparipūrṇaiḥ*):
"filtered through cloth" (*vastrapūtāni*) means purified by a cloth (*paṭapavitrāṇi*), that is to say, strained through a cloth (*paṭaparigalitāni*). And those...
"By waters" means by those liquids; "filled with them" means completely filled by them.
"(By nine)" means by those numbering nine. The word "vā" expresses an alternative. "(By jars)" means by vessels made of gold and other materials. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmad-Cintyaviśva*:
"Bathing with a copper vessel from an earthen jar yields a hundredfold merit;
silver yields a hundred times that of copper, and gold a hundred times that of silver.
[This refers to water] prepared with Śiva-mantras, meaning consecrated by the Śiva-mantras.
The ritual procedure for bathing according to the followers of Kapila.

(9) If one is unable to perform the Varuṇa-bath, one should wash the feet or the lower part of the body down to the waist according to one's ability; then, having wiped the remaining unwashed parts of the body with a wet cloth,
one should [perform the rite] with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, as if rising from the big toes of the feet.
Having burned the body along with the external impurities of the limbs,
and having bathed it with pure water flowing from the agitated *śakti*, one should recite the *saṃhitā* once.
49) (Pra) Now, having explained the procedure for the Vāruṇa bath, [it is said]: "But that mortal who is unable to perform the bath should perform the Kāpila bath with a wet garment."

Keeping in mind the statement, "The cleansing of the head and other parts is remembered as the Kāpila [bath]," he demonstrates the method of the Kāpila bath with the passage beginning with "(vāruṇa)" and ending with "(japet).
"(One who is unable to perform the Vāruṇa bath)" refers to the Vāruṇa bath, which is bathing with water. Likewise...
In the *Śrīmṛgendra*, it is stated that "the Vāruṇa [snāna] is the Vāruṇa bath. This means that one is unable to perform that bath—that is, the immersion—due to illness or other reasons;
the sense is that one is incapable of immersing oneself in water from head to foot. (Up to the neck.)
Up to the neck; (below the waist) below the hips; (the feet) the two feet.
The word "vā" expresses an alternative. (The disciple) that which remains after the body has been washed.
(With a wet cloth) with a garment moistened with water. (With fire produced from the big toe) the big toe.
By that fire—the fire which arose, which was produced, from the big toe of his right foot; [it cleanses] merely the external impurities residing in the body. (p.

External impurities residing in the body are those arising from the ears, eyes, and so forth. Likewise, in the venerable *Śivadharmottara*, it is stated: "The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, nails, phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine are recorded as the twelve substrates of impurity."

Thus, the word *mātra* here signifies "entirety" (*kārtsnya*), meaning "as much as exists within the body. Regarding the measure (*parimāṇa*) in both the sense of "entirety" and "determination," Amara states: *mātram kārtsnye 'vadhāraṇe*. "(Having burned") means having performed the act of burning.
"By the pure water flowing from the agitated power":
"agitated" means stirred by the recitation of the root mantra; that which is both this [agitated state] and the power is the crooked power (*kuṭilā-śakti*).
"Flowing from it" means that which has trickled forth from all sides; and that is the pure water, the nectar (*amṛta*). By that [water].
The ritual procedure for the fire-bath (āgneyasnāna).

(Kriyāpāda) (20) Now, as for the procedure for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*): having taken ash that has been perfected according to the ritual manual (*kalpa*), one should consecrate it with the *saṃhitā*. If it is not prepared according to the manual, one should purify it with the mantras of the *nivṛtti*-kalā and others, and then [consecrate it] with the *saṃhitā*.

Having consecrated [the ashes] with the mantra, one performs the impurity-bathing (*malasnāna*) by touching [the body] with the right hand from the head down to the feet while scattering the ash-powder, using the *astrabīja* (weapon-seed syllable) and the *īśāna* [mantra].
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* and other marks to the head with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, to the face with the *aghora*, to the heart with the *vāmadeva*,

to the private parts with the *sadyojāta*, and to the feet and all limbs with the *astra* mantra; then, while recollecting the purification of the ritual hands, one should perform the *uddhūlana* (dusting with ashes).
One should sprinkle the remaining ashes on the head with the Brahma-mantras and the root mantra. Then, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as before.
(20) Now, having explained the procedure for the Kapila-bath, [the author] proceeds to set forth the procedure for the Agni-bath.

He makes his formal declaration with the words beginning with "atha" and ending with "yathā. "Atha" means immediately after one of the aforementioned types of bathing; for otherwise, one has no qualification for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
Thus, in the venerable *Matanga-tantra*: "Having bathed thus in water once, according to one's capacity..."
"Day by day, O best of sages, one shall be entitled to the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), and not otherwise.
This [statement] is not intended as a rule that the bath must invariably be preceded by the water-bath (vāruṇasnāna);
rather, it is an instruction according to one's capacity, depending on one's ability.

It was stated [in the *Kiraṇa* and other texts] in order to indicate whether bathing preceded by water (*jalasnānapūrvakatva*) or not preceded by it (*atadpūrvakatva*) is required; for in the venerable *Kiraṇa* and elsewhere, [initiation is performed] even without bathing with water.
Because the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) is authorized as being performed on alternate days; and because it is clearly stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"The fire-bath (āgneyasnāna), which is another name for the ash-bath, is prescribed as being either constant or superior to the water-bath. And likewise:

In the venerable *Mataṅga*, it was stated immediately after: "For one who repeatedly practices bathing in water, illness may arise; therefore, that is not desired at all times. The [bath] pertaining to fire is said to be desirable.
Thus, for one who is extremely ill or afflicted by disease, the bath in water is simply not appropriate.

It should be understood that while the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) is obligatory for others, it is performed according to one's own capacity. Likewise, in the venerable *Niśvāsottara*: "Having bathed once with water, one should then bathe with ash at the three junctions of the day; thus the afflicted one should always bathe. (The Procedure for the Ash-Bath).
The ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*) consists of smearing [the body] with the *tripuṇḍra* and so forth. As he will state:
"Having remembered the purification of the hands for ritual action, one should smear each limb with the *astramantra* using the *tripuṇḍra* and so forth. Of that—

(53) *Vidhi* means an injunction (*vidhāna*). According to Amarasimha, "the word *vidhi* refers to an injunction as well as to fate. Here, "bathing" (*snāna*) signifies purity itself, and not immersion in water, because such immersion is impossible [in this context]. For example:

This is stated clearly. To explain how that is so, he says, beginning with "the primary ritual" (*kalpa*) and ending with "one should consecrate" (*abhiṣecayet*). Regarding "accomplished by the primary ritual and so forth" (*kalpādisiddham*): *kalpa* means "primary"; as Amara states, "The primary is the first ritual" (*mukhyassyāt prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*). *Ādi* (and so forth) refers to that which follows; thus, "by that which begins with the primary ritual" (*kalpādi*), [it is] accomplished or brought into being.
The meaning of terms such as *amukalpa* and *anukalpa* is as follows: likewise, in the *Śrīmadvallāśabhapaddhati*, it is stated:

"One should perform the *āgneya* [rite] with ashes; it bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men. That ash, when purified by the consecrated [mantra], is of four kinds: the *kalpa*, the *anukalpa*, and so forth."

"Free from conceptual construction and devoid of mental fabrication; each preceding one is superior in quality. Thus the characteristic of the *kalpa* (ritual procedure) was stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"With the dung of a tawny cow that has not touched the ground..."
Or with the hide of a white bull taken from one recently born.
Then, by the wise Vāmadeva, who had established himself in the intermediate space, [the fire] was kindled—
dry, accumulated according to the rules, and possessing many forms.
With a mouth blazing with the fire of Śiva, according to the prescribed rite,
one should collect [the remains] from a pit in a windless place that have been burnt by the Lord.
Thus it is said. Let the characteristics of the primary and secondary substitutes be determined in that very [text].

(Bhasma) means white ash, having abandoned the portion consisting of raw flesh and the like; its measure is one *niṣka* and so forth. (Samādāya) means having taken hold of it in the left hand. Likewise, the ash...
