"One should avoid [ashes] that are smoke-colored, red, or yellow; one should wear white ash, which bestows the fruit of all merit. Likewise, in the venerable *Sūkṣma[-tantra]*, it is said: "One should consecrate the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) in the left hand with the right hand while reciting the mantra."
The wise man should abandon the portion of the Asuras and the thirty-two one-parts of the Rākṣasas.
"A niṣka, half a niṣka, two, and likewise half of two"—

thus is the etymological definition of the word *bhasma* (ash) demonstrated in the venerable *Kāmika*: "That which illuminates [the self], that which makes ash [of impurities], and that which makes auspicious."
Because it consumes all sins, it is celebrated as "ashes" (bhasma).
Thus it is said. If it is unfit (*akalpa*), then it should be accepted after first purifying it; thus he says (p.
"(unfit). The characteristics of what is unfit are indicated in the *Śrīmadajita*.

"Setting aside the previously mentioned procedure, the practice of using ash alone, as prepared by others, is known as 'akalpa'. Here, the word "tu" indicates a distinction from what preceded. [With the mantras of the kalās, beginning with] Nivṛtti... Nivṛtti.
Those whose beginning is [the state of] Nivṛtti and so forth are the Kalās, such as Nivṛtti and the rest; the mantras of these [Kalās] are [referred to] by that [term].
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), Pratiṣṭhā and the others are indicated. Thus, it is stated in the venerable Varuṇapaddhati: "Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vidyā..."
"Śānti and likewise Śāntyatītā—these are the five kalās. (Having purified [them]).
This means that because of its connection with innate purity (*autpattika-śuddhi*), purification is possible through the [five kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti.
Here, one should [apply] the three kinds of ash associated with innate purity, or [apply it] without ritual formalization (*akalpena*).

The state [of being]. Regarding the bath with ashes, he speaks of the "impurity-bath" (with the *astra* mantra). That is, by means of the seed-syllable of Śiva’s weapon, *oṃ haḥ*; thus it was stated by the author of the commentary on the venerable *Sārddhatriśati*.
(By touching with the right hand joined with the dust of ashes) the particles of ash.
The "dust of supernatural powers" (vibhūtipāṃsavaḥ);
that which is joined with them is the right hand, and its touching (sparśana).

By that [rubbing], there is a friction of all the limbs; by this, it should be understood that the obstacles residing in the body are dispelled. Likewise, one should bathe with that sacred ash and with water from the fingernails.
From the utterance of the weapon-mantra comes the bath of impurity and the rubbing of all the limbs.
"And the obstacles residing in the limbs go to destruction by means of the weapon.
Thus [it is said]. Therein, he describes the ritual bath [with the mantra] "(īśānena)":
"(vaktram)" refers to the forehead; "(hṛdayam)" refers to the chest. Regarding "hṛdaya," it is used for both the mind and the chest.
The Garland of Jewels of Various Meanings: The word "guhya" denotes the navel; "pādau" refers to the knees;
"sarvāṅgāni" means the locations beginning with the elbows. Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*, one should know that the *tripuṇḍra* is applied to sixteen locations.
Being composed, [one should apply them] on the head, the forehead, the throat, both shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the heart, the sides of the navel, the back,
and at every station up to the shanks— [thus] with the three *puṇḍra*s (such as the *tripuṇḍra*).
The aggregate of the various types of *tilaka* is the *tripuṇḍra*; those things which have that as their beginning are so described. [The word] *puṇḍra*...
Regarding the varieties of *tilaka* in different regions, the *Nānārtharatnamālā* states: "In [the regions of] Kṛmi and Atimukta.
The definition of this [tripuṇḍra] is as follows: "On the forehead, the heart, and the two arms, it is six finger-breadths in length;
the remainder is said to be one finger-breadth at all the joints; such is the *tripuṇḍra*."
The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the *tilaka* and other such marks. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:

"A householder, being well-composed, should bathe by means of smearing ashes alone, or else [perform purification] starting from the limbs with *tilakas* or *tripuṇḍrakas*. (Regarding the purification of the hand of action: the *karmahasta*).
Regarding the purification of his right hand and left hand as he engages in the act of applying the sacred ashes: likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"That which is inaccessible to the right hand may be taken with the left hand."
Having touched both hands together, one should thoroughly dust the limbs.

Thus [it is said]. To the question "What should one do after that?", he says: "(With the remainder). This means with the remaining ashes (*śeṣabhasmanā*), i.e., the ashes left over from what was worn. "(One should consecrate)" means one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*.
p.
58) This is called the *mantra-snāna* (mantra-bath) within the *āgneya-snāna* (fire-bath). Thus it has been handed down by the venerable Somaśambhu.
Consecration with water using the *sadyojāta* and other mantras constitutes the "mantra-bath";
this same procedure applies to the Varuṇa and Āgneya baths as well.

Thus [it is said]. Now, having described the procedure for the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*), he states that one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the passage beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "one should sip water" (*ācamet*). "Then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the ash-bath.
The procedure for the mental bath.
(22) Mentally reciting the root mantra ending in *nāda*,
one should visualize the body of the deity within the sacrificial fire as bathed by copious streams of nectar flowing from the agitated *śakti*. This is the mental ablution (*mānasa-snāna*).
This is to be applied everywhere.
(22) (Pra) Now, he states the procedure for the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*) with the words beginning with "by the mind" (*manasā*) and ending with "is to be performed" (*vidheyam*).
"Up to the end of sound" (*nādāntam*) means pervaded by the kalā up to the end of *nāda*.
(With streams of abundant nectar flowing from the agitated power: "Agitated" means stirred by the recitation of the root mantra uttered at the end of the *nāda*.

And that power is the crooked power; from it have flowed forth—that is, been emitted—copious streams of nectar, meaning abundant flows of ambrosia. By means of those [streams], she has been consecrated—that is, bathed—[with] her own [nectar]. Thus.
"By means of the stream of nectar from the power agitated by the root mantra,
one should perform the mental bath through sprinkling both externally and internally. Thus,
first, the mental bath is performed by means of the mind, preceded by the recollection of the root mantra as previously described.

Because of immersion in the flood of the Śakti-water, it is designated as the "Śākta bath. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, it is stated that the mental [bath] is the Śākta. "(In all cases)" means at all times when there is a suspicion of impurity. "(It is to be performed)" means it must be done.
The procedure for the divine and other types of ablutions.
(22) However, because the divine [meditations] and so forth are contingent upon specific causes, one should perform them when those respective causes are present.

Now, having explained the procedure for the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*), [the author] states that the divine baths (*divyasnāna*) and others must be performed at their prescribed times because they are occasional (*naimittika*).

From the words "(divya)" up to "vidadhyāt" [it is said]: "(divyādīnām)" means those for which the divine (*divya*) bath of Mahendra is the first; these are the "divyādis. By the word "ādi," the terrestrial (*bhauma*) and other baths are indicated. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, the Vāruṇa and Taijasa [baths are mentioned].
"Terrestrial, aerial, divine, and mental—thus [the baths] are summarized.

And the characteristic of the divine bath is stated in that very same place: "One should sustain a pure rain accompanied by sunlight while reciting *Śiva*. Furthermore, the characteristics of the remaining types of bathing follow from there.
This must be understood as follows: because it is contingent (*naimittikatvāt*), that is, because it is rooted in specific conditions (*nimitta-mūlakatvāt*).

When those respective conditions (*tattannimittopasthāne*) arise—that is, when those various conditions such as heat, rain, and so forth, reach their respective presence or occurrence (*saṃprāptiḥ*)—then [the result follows].

"Vidadhyāt" means "one should perform. By the phrase "upon the occurrence of those respective causes," it is shown that the four stations beginning with the divine (*divya*) are occasional (*naimittika*). And so it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu-pāda: "That group of four beginning with Māhendra is occasional."
It is remembered as follows: the divine bath of Māhendra.
p. 61) The ritual procedure for the sakalīkaraṇa.

(23) Then one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa. Reciting "oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should purify the right and left hands in the order of upward and downward; then, reciting "oṃ hauṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ," one should sprinkle them. Then, with the two thumbs on the palms of the hands, [recite] "oṃ..."
Having performed the placement [of mantras] with "Hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva" (hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ) and "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva" (oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śivamūrtaye namaḥ),
one should place them on the thumbs and index fingers with "Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna" (oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrddhāya namaḥ), and on the other [fingers].

Performing the libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth with the thumbs up to the little fingers: *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevavaktrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ haṃ sadyojātamūrtaye namaḥ* on the palms; *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
*Oṃ vidyādevāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the deity of knowledge); [this is assigned] to the two thumbs;
then with the three middle fingers: *Oṃ hauṃ netrebhyo namaḥ* (Salutation to the eyes), by virtue of the power pervading the entire hand, and by virtue of its pervasiveness in the center.
Having invoked the temple with the two thumbs, [one should place it] on the fingers of the hand, beginning with the little finger:
*oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hīṃ śirase namaḥ*, *oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) with "Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the weapon (*astra*)," having enveloped both [hands] with the armor (*kavaca*),
having joined them together, and having consecrated them with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should proceed].
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart, the seat, and the image with the thumb and ring finger of the right hand;
having bound the fist at the head and performed the placement with the thumb using the *Īśāna* mantra;
[and then] at the regions of the face, heart, genitals, and feet with the *Tatpuruṣa* and *Aghora* [mantras].
Having performed the placement of the *vāmadeva* and *sadyojāta* mantras on the fingers beginning with the index finger joined with the thumb,

having placed the *vidyādeha* mantra at the heart with the thumb and ring finger, and having placed the *netra* mantra on the eyes with the three middle fingers, one should [place] the *prāsāda* as the special presiding deity.

Having invoked [the deity] into the body, one should place the heart, head, and crest mantras at the locations of the heart, head, and crest respectively, using the thumbs, little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers; and [one should place the kavaca mantra] as a neck-veil, extending from the throat to the middle of the breasts.
Having placed the face with the two index fingers and the weapon (*astra*) on the palms of the hands with the two ring fingers,

and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) preceded by three *tāla* slaps with the weapon-mantra, and having veiled [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should display the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

(23) Now, he extends by analogy (*atidiśati*) the procedure for the sequence of the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the words beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*), [instructing that one] "should show" (*darśayet*).

By this much [is concluded]. (Then) after the mental bath (*mānasasnāna*). (The ritual of becoming whole, *sakalīkaraṇa*) consists of the placement of the limbs (*sāṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*). Anticipating the question, "What is the sequence for the ritual of becoming whole?
he first states the method for the placement of the hands: (Oṃ haḥ, to the weapon, phaṭ).
(From top to bottom) means the sequence of the palm and back of the right hand, and then the palm and back of the left hand.
(Having purified) means having burned [the hands] up to the wrists with the weapon-mantra in the form of fire.
This is the meaning. (Having bathed [the hands]) with the *Śakti-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*. This is the procedure for the bathing with nectar (*amṛtāplāvana*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-kriyākaraṇamaṇḍanapaddhati*, it is said: "The Preceptor, having thoroughly purified both the palms and the backs of the two hands with the *Astra-mantra*..."

"By means of the Prāsāda-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the supreme Śakti, there is an immersion in nectar. Likewise, in the venerable *Cintya-niśvāsa-sādākhya*, it says: "Visualizing the two hands endowed with the splendor of the weapon (*astra*) up to the wrists... [referring to] the palms of the right and left hands, which are positioned one above the other.
(With the two thumbs: with the right and left thumbs. (With the two index fingers:
with the right and left index fingers. (From the index finger to the little finger: the index finger... [and so on].

That which has [the thumb] as its beginning is called "beginning with that"; that which has the little finger at its end is called "ending with that. Thus, it refers to [the fingers] beginning with the index finger and ending with the little finger. By the middle fingers—namely, the index, middle, and ring fingers—meaning by those three in number.

By virtue of having power pervading both hands (*sakalahastavyāptaśaktitvena*): he is so called because his power (*śakti*) is pervasive (*vyāpinī*), extending across both hands; the state of being that is its essence (*tattva*), and by means of that.
Herein, because one has rendered the palms of the hands composed of power (*śaktimaya*) through the procedure of burning and flooding.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Brahmās, beginning with Īśāna, upon the fingers starting from the thumb, the body of the Vidyā is also thus placed.

The intended meaning is that, consequently, the nature of Śakti arises within the palms of the hands. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by means of the Śakti pervading the entire hand," the term *sakala* refers to those accompanied by the *kalās*; and these two [palms] are *sakala*.

And the two hands are the *sakalahasta*s; the power (*śakti*) pervading them, consisting of forms such as Īśānī and others, is described in that way; by means of its essential nature (*bhāvatattva*). (In the center) p.

Within the palm of the hand (*karatalāntare*). (By virtue of its pervasiveness: *tasyāḥ* refers to that power (*śakti*) which is the vitality of the body; *vidyā* is its pervasive presiding principle (*adhiṣṭhātā*); the state of being that is its essence (*tattvam*), by means of that.
Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, regarding the hand in the Śākta [tradition]—

(26) "Having placed them on the palms": likewise, in the *Śrīmat Kālottara*, it says, "Then one should install the *Prāsāda* [mantra] upon all the fingers of the hands. (*Prāsāda*) refers to the *Śiva-mantra*. (Having invoked and installed it) upon the fingers of the hand, starting from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā-ādi-kara-śākhāsu*): those for which the little finger is the first.

The "little finger and so forth" refers to those fingers, which are the branches of the hand; as Amara states: "The fingers are the branches of the hand. Among these, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) signifies the ring finger and the others. In response to the inquiry as to what mantras one should place upon them, he says: "(Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart)," and so on.

"Is it not the case that at the end of the *hṛdaya* and the others, there are *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*? At the end of the mantra of Caṇḍeśvara, Hara declared exactly the same.
Thus, according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, the six limbs beginning with the heart are [accompanied by] *svadhā*, *namaḥ*, and *svāhā*.
How is it that all [the mantras] here, which are joined with the six classes beginning with *vaṣaṭ*, are employed ending with *namaḥ*? True; they constitute the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

And they consist of the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning and the word *namaḥ* at the end. As the author of the commentary on the venerable *Dviśatikālottara* has said: "Regarding these [mantras], there is the application of the *praṇava* at the beginning and the salutation (*namaskāra*) at the end; this is stated in the venerable *Niśvāsa* and other scriptures."

"Mantras preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with an ending of salutation (*namaskāra*). However, in the performance of rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), one should recite them joined with the six classes of suffixes such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and so forth; thus it is stated in the section on the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) in the commentary on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*.

"Explained" refers to both the right and left hands. "Having rendered supreme" means having established oneness with Śiva, who consists of the root mantra, for those mantras placed upon the palms of the hands. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Rāmanāthapaddhati*:
Having encircled the limbs with the index finger, one should perform the supreme unification of the possessor of limbs with Śiva. Thus it is said.
Having explained the procedure for the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), he describes the method for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*).

Regarding "the seat and the form" (*āsanamūrtī*): the "seat" is the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*), and the "form" is the form of Śiva consisting of radiant energy (*tejas*) that pervades the entire body from the soles of the feet upward; these two [are referred to].

(Regarding the sequence of fingers beginning with the index finger joined with the thumb: "Joined with the thumb" means that which is joined with the thumb; and that [joined thumb] is also the index finger.
Those which have the thumb as their first [member] are the index finger and the others joined with the thumb;
those are the fingers, and their sequence is the order.
By that [sequence], here, one should place the Tatpuruṣa mantra on the mouth with the index finger joined with the thumb.
One should recite the Aghora mantra at the heart with the middle finger joined with the thumb;
the Vāmadeva mantra at the navel with the ring finger joined with the thumb;
and the Sadyojāta mantra at the knees with the little finger joined with the thumb.

One should understand that "one should place" [is the instruction]. (The *vidyādeha*) refers to the collective form (*samaṣṭirūpa*) of the Brahmās beginning with Īśāna, characterized by five faces and so forth, pervading the entire body; the meaning is "the restraint" (*nigraha*).
(In the eyes) means in the right eye, the left eye, and the forehead-eye. Regarding the phrase "(as the specific presiding deities)": [this is the sense].

However, because Brahmā is to be presided over as a form (*mūrti*), and because he is contained within the Eye, one should invoke Śiva—the presiding deity who subdues Brahmā—as the *prāsāda* [the temple/residence], pervading the entire body. Thus it has been said: [27] *...* [text fragment].
By the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*. (In the body) means in the heart.
(Having resorted to? means by means of the thumb and the ring finger.
The meaning is "having placed [it]. Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-kriyākaraṇamaṇḍanapaddhati*:
"Having placed the root mantra between the heart [and the head] with the thumb and ring finger.
(With the thumb, little finger, ring finger, and middle finger)—together with the thumb.
"They exist" means together with the thumbs; these are the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.

Here, one should place [the mantra] on the heart with the little finger joined with the thumb, on the head with the ring finger joined with the thumb, and on the crown of the head with the middle finger joined with the thumb.
It should be understood that one should place the *śikhā-mantra* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
By the state of being a "neck-covering" (*kaṇṭhaprāvaraṇa*)—that is, by the quality of being a neck-wrap (*kaṇṭhaveṣṭana*). [The phrase] "between the breasts" refers to the right and left breasts.
The middle between those two is its end. (With the two index fingers:

with the right and left index fingers. But surely, since the form has already been perfected here by the deposition of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) together with the heart and other limbs, what further purpose is served by the limb-mantras?

Is it being established? True; however, for the sake of protecting the body of the practitioner, the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) must be deposited. Thus, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated that the heart [mantra] is the protection of the heart, brought forth like a bound bandage.

The *śiras* is that helmet, the wrapping around the head; the *cūlikā* is the protection for the crown of the head, and the *kaṅkaṭa* is the armor for the limbs. When a weapon has been grasped in the hand—
"Bhīkṣaṇa stood like a warrior; he would be unassailable by the base, just as Tārkṣya is by the Serpents. (Accompanied by three claps) "Tālas" refers to the rhythmic movements of the hands;
"trayam" means a triad thereof; "purassaram" means preceded by that, i.e., occurring first. "Tālaḥ" [is the term for the clap].

Regarding the time of death, it is said in the *Nānārtharatnamālā*: "At the time of death, [it occurs] within a *krośa* or an *antara*. This definition is stated in the *Ajita*: "Striking the palm of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand, excluding the thumb—this is the *tāla-mudrā*, which bestows purity. Thus it is described in the section on the characteristics of mudrās.
The *tālākhyā* [mudrā] consists of the three strikes of the hands; it is used in the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making complete) and other such rites.
As for the *mahāmudrā*, it is described in the definition of mudrās as follows: "It is that which, with both palms facing each other, touches from the lotus-feet up to the crown of the head. By this—

It has been stated by the venerable author of the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī* that there is the accomplishment of oneness with Śiva— who consists of the root mantra— of those mantras of the heart and other limbs deposited upon the body.
The procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma).
(24) Afterwards, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the collection of mantras;

(27) (2) Now, having explained the procedure for the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*), he describes the sequence of breath control for the purpose of purifying the internal air within the body.
By the passage beginning with "afterwards" (*paścāt*) and ending with "having performed" (*kṛtvā*): "afterwards" means immediately after the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.

"Prāṇāyāma" refers to *prāṇa*, which are the vital breaths; their *āyāma* is their restraint. Thus, it is said in the venerable *Śivadharmottara*: "Prāṇa is the wind residing in the body; its *āyāma*..."
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of cessation":

here, for the performance of prāṇāyāma consisting of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kuṃbhaka), and exhalation (recaka), one should recite the Śivasaṃhitā three times. This has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and remaining steady through prāṇāyāma, the practitioner of mantra should mentally recite the Śivasaṃhitā three times. Thus it is said.
The rite of immortalization.

(25) From the location of the *bindu*, having drawn [the water] with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* while reciting "oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya vaṣaṭ," and having placed it in the water, one should consecrate the *śivatīrtha* with the root mantra (*mūla*).

Having protected [it] and having enveloped [it], one should render it immortal. (25) Now, beginning with the words "the drop" (*bindu*) and ending with "one should render it immortal," he explains what must be performed prior to the *saṃdhyāvandana* (twilight worship). "From the station of the drop": the "drop" (*bindu*) refers to the *bindu-kalā*.

Its location is the center of the earth; therefore, it is said: "Likewise, in the center of the earth, at a distance of two finger-breadths, there is a circular [point] resembling a lamp, measuring half a mātrā. This definition was stated in the section on the characteristics of mudrās as "by means of the *aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā. Now, the *sṛṇi* (goad) mudrā.
"A fist accompanied by the index finger with its tip bent" means: (having drawn [the nectar])—here, "the nectar" (*amṛta*) is the understood remainder.

Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*: "Having drawn the ambrosia from the point (*bindu*), one should establish it in the water with the heart-mantra. (Having protected) means: having performed the binding of the directions with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
(Wrapping) having encircled with the armor-mantra; (one should render it nectar) one should make it nectar by means of the cow-mudrā.
The meditation on all the twilight rites (sandhyā).
(26) Then, having meditated upon the twilight [devotion], one should pay homage.
Red in color, with red ornaments and garments, wearing matted hair and a sacred thread,
seated upon a swan and a lotus, she is a youthful maiden with four faces and four arms.
One should meditate at dawn upon Brahmī, who is like the desired [goddess] in the starry sky, holding a rosary of passion in her right hand and a staff and water-pot in her left.
She wears white garments, is white in complexion, and is adorned with a forest garland and a sacred thread;
she is seated upon the throne of Garuḍa and the lotus, possessing the bloom of fresh youth.
The rule for the letter *p*.
At midday, one should meditate upon the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, adorned with all ornaments, holding a conch and a discus in her left hands, and a mace and the gesture of fearlessness in her right hands.
She has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, her youth is slightly fading;
she possesses four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
One should meditate on Rudrī, who holds a trident and an akṣa-bead in her right hands, and displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a spear (*śakti*) in her left;
she stands upon a bull and a lotus during the twilight when the sun has half-set and is reddish;
all of them wear black antelope skins and are witnesses to all actions.
The three [vowels] are distinguished by the differences in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the letter *a*; when conjoined, they become fourfold.
On page 73, it is stated that [the fourth] is devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), being thus distinguished by the differences in the limiting adjuncts of the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.

The initiates (samayins) should meditate, in accordance with the respective times, upon Sandhyā— who is indeed the Śakti of Śiva and the witness of all actions— successively in the heart, the bindu, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (26)

Now, since the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) is preceded by meditation, he describes the general meditation for all *samayins* and especially for the *viśiṣṭasamayins* with the passage beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "the *samayins*" (*samayinaḥ*). "Then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after the consecration of the *śivatīrtha*.
He himself will clarify the meaning of the term *sandhyā-vandana*.
(*Vandayet* means) one should salute. Herein, *sandhyā-vandana* refers to that which is performed after the meditation on the *sandhyā*, by standing in the midst of its full orb of radiance.

"It is called 'action' (karman). Likewise, having visualized one's own body as having entered the expanse of that circle of light, whatever action one performs—that is indeed its salutation. Thus it is said.
How so? In response to the inquiry as to how one should worship after meditating, [the author] states that there, in the morning, is the meditation on the dawn twilight (*prābhātika-ra-saṃdhyā*) (p.
Thus: "(Wearing matted hair and a sacred thread)"—here, "matted hair" (*jaṭā*) refers to hair firmly braided together.

"(A water-pot)"—*ka* (water) is taken (*lāti*) or held within (*aṇḍe*, in the middle), hence it is a *kamaṇḍalu*, a small jar (*kuṇḍī*). According to Amara: "The feminine form is *kamaṇḍalu*; it is a *kuṇḍī*. "(Studded with stars)" (*tārakite*).
The stars have appeared in this; it is "studded with stars" (*tārakitam*) therein. The suffix *itac* is used in the sense of "having come into being.

By this, the excellence of the twilight when stars are visible is shown, as well as the three periods of time—superior, middling, and inferior—according to whether the stars have disappeared. Likewise:

In the illustrious *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated: "The morning twilight is remembered as being of three kinds: the superior is when the constellations are visible; the middling is when the stars have not yet disappeared; and the inferior is when the sun has half-risen, like a maiden [blushing]. The remainder is easy to understand.

He states the meditation for the midday *sandhyā*: "(Śukla)" and so forth. "Wearing a forest garland and a sacred thread" (*vanamālopavītinīm*): a *vanamālā* is a garland of *tulasī*, and an *upavīta* is a sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*).
She whose own [ornaments] are a forest garland and a sacred thread is thus described; [he says] "her."
(Seated upon a Garuda-lotus throne: Tārkṣya is Garuḍa; she is seated there upon a lotus throne. (p. 75)

Seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*). Regarding *garutmān*: "Garutmān, Guru, Tārkṣya"—thus says Amara. (Holding the mace and the gesture of fearlessness): regarding the mace, *kaumodakī* is the mace—thus says Amara. And the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) consists of the raised flag at midday; this is named Mādhyandina.

The time is limited to five *muhūrtas*. Thus it is said: "Having performed the midday rite after five *muhūrtas* have passed. Here, it should be understood that the midday [rite] likewise possesses a threefold division. Similarly, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, regarding the midday:
"Likewise, it should be known as consisting of three *ghaṭikās*"; the rest is easily understood.
He describes the meditation on the evening twilight (*sāyāhnasandhyā*) with the words "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). [She is] together with the *abhaya-śakti*;
*abhaya* has already been explained, and *śakti* is the *kāsū*, a particular type of weapon.

According to Amara, *śakti* means both "cough" (*kāsu*) and "capacity" (*sāmarthya*). With the suffix *kan* in its own sense, it becomes *abhayaśaktika*. That which exists together with those two is thus described [as *abhayaśaktikavatī*]. (Regarding *vṛṣābjasthām*: *Vṛṣa* means "bull," as Amara states: "vṛṣabha, ṛṣabha, vṛṣabha, vṛṣa. She is seated upon that lotus (*abja*) situated on the bull.
[She is] seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "the lotus among salt-water lotuses" [refers to this]. [She is] like the sun half-set.

"Half" (*ardha*) means an equal portion; "set" (*astamita*) means having gone to half-setting. He who has that [half-set] Aruṇa—the Sun—is so described. According to Amarasimha: "Aruṇa may refer to the sun, but as a distinct color, it is used in three genders. By this...

The excellence of the twilight when half the solar disc has set is declared to be the highest; that of the twilight after the sun has set is middling; and its inferiority is shown when the stars have appeared. Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
The best [time for] the evening twilight is when half the solar disc has set;
it is middling when the sun has completely set; and it is said to be threefold according as other stars have become visible.
Thus; the rest is clear.

Now, one might ask: "Are there no other specific attributes of the Brāhmī and the others? Anticipating this, he says they exist: "(Wearing black antelope skins). "Dharāḥ" means those who wear; "black antelope skin" refers to the hide of the *eṇa* deer. By the word "all," it is meant that all [the goddesses], beginning with Brāhmī, [possess these attributes].
The intended meaning is that [the goddesses] may also wear garments such as saffron-colored ones, and they may also wear black antelope skins.
Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is stated: "Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) at dawn... (p. 77).

Brahmī has eight eyes; she is red, adorned with red ornaments, wearing red garments, and anointed with red garlands and unguents. Seated upon a swan and a lotus, she is youthful, possesses a sacred thread, wears a black antelope skin, and is the witness of all actions.

"Four-faced," and so forth, beginning thus: "On the right [hands] she holds a discus and the gesture of fearlessness; on the left, a conch and a mace. She wears a black antelope skin, has one [form], two faces, and lotus-eyes, and is seated upon a bull and a lotus."

It is stated that [the three goddesses] are the witnesses of all, wear the sacred thread (*upavītī*), and bear the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), being of the nature of Rudra (*raudrī*). (Of all rites) means of every ritual action. (Witnesses) means observers.
(Three) means endowed with the number three; the meaning is Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī.

"Endowed with sattva and the rest" means that which has *sattva*—the quality of purity (*sattvaguṇa*)—as its first [quality] is "sattva-ādi"; they are joined with that. The meaning of the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) refers to the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Therefore, the assumption of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is secondary; [these are] *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Here, it is *brāhmī*...

The essential meaning is that Vaiṣṇavī is indeed endowed with the quality of *sattva*, Raudrī is accompanied by the quality of *rajas*, and [Ambikā] is possessed of the quality of *tamas*. And so it is said:

The commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* states that because the morning and other junctions (*saṃdhyā*) are characterized by the functions of existence (*sattva*) and so forth, they are the causes of the aforementioned manifestation (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restraint (*niyama*); therefore, the sequence of recitation itself constitutes the sequence [of the junctions]. (The fourth: the Fourth Junction (*turyasaṃdhyā*). (Described according to its qualities.)

She is devoid of qualities such as *sattva*. Regarding the qualities (*guṇas*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. According to Amara: "The quality (*guṇa*) is that which rests upon substance (*dravya*), such as *sattva*, white, twilight, and so forth. The rest is clear. Thus:
she shines forth, divided by the distinctions of Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī.
It is understood that the twilight (sandhyā) is the power (śakti) of Śambhu, the witness of all actions.

Thus, having placed in one's heart the scriptural authority of the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*, [one should understand that] because the Lords of Causes (*kāraṇeśas*)— like the Mantras and Mantreśvaras— are also threefold according to the division of Na, Gu, Śakti, and Śambhu, they have Brahmā and the others as their presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).

He [the author of the *Brahmādikāraṇa*] states that Śiva-Śakti herself, differentiated by divisions and assuming various colors, vehicles, weapons, and forms through those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is Sandhyā.

(Divided by the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts [upādhi] of the causes beginning with Brahmā): those of whom Brahmā is the first are "Brahmādi"; by the word "ādi" (etcetera), Viṣṇu and Rudra are indicated. Those are the causes, and their limiting adjuncts are specific substrata.

"Upādhi" means a condition (*dharma*) or even a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), according to the *Viśva* lexicon. "Bhinnā" means divided by their distinction (*bheda*). "(Of all-doers)" refers to all actions (*nikhilakarman*). "(Witness)" means an observer (*upadraṣṭrī*). "(Sandhyā)" [refers to the twilight].
The deity of the twilight (sandhyā-devatā), according to the specific time—
namely, in accordance with morning, midday, or evening: here, at dawn one should meditate on Brāhmī in the heart,
at midday Vaiṣṇavī between the eyebrows, and in the evening Raudrī in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).

The intended meaning is that they should meditate. In response to the inquiry as to who the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) for this meditation on all the *sandhyās* are, he says: "the initiates" (*samayinaḥ*). Here, by the term *samayin*, both ordinary initiates (*sāmānyasamayin*) and specialized initiates (*viśiṣṭasamayin*) are intended, as these are the designations used in the Tantras. In this context...

Those known as *sāmānyasamayin* (vow-holders of the general level) are those consecrated by the initiation of the vow (*samaya-dīkṣā*) that leads to the state of Rudra. The *viśiṣṭasamayin* (vow-holders of the distinguished level) [are... p. 80.
Furthermore, they have been consecrated by the initiation into the specific *samaya* (observance) characterized by the worship of the feet of Īśvara.

Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Varuṇapaddhati*: "Where there is union with the state of Rudra, and where there is union with the state of Īśvara, and where there is no cutting of the topknot (*śikhā*), that initiation is the twofold *sāmayī*. Of these very [initiates]...

The three meditations on the junctures (*sandhyā*)—beginning with "red ornaments and garments, red," and so forth—occur during the three times of day, such as morning and the others. As the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati* has said: "Now, the meditation on the junctures..."

It is twofold, by way of the division between the *sakala* (with parts) and the *niṣkala* (without parts). Among these, the *sakala* pertains to the domain of the ordinary initiate (*samayin*) and the distinguished initiate (*viśiṣṭasamayin*).

Regarding the domain of the spiritual son (*putraka*) and others, it is *niṣkala* within the self, in the locations such as the heart, the *bindu*, and the supreme station of the *brahmarandhra*, and so forth. Thus he said:

The commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* states here that for those who have taken the initiatory vows (*samayins*), the twilight rite (*sandhyā*) is gross, whereas for those initiated into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣitānām*), it is subtle. Now, one might object: "Is this not the specific pair of fire-offerings (*agnikārya*) belonging to one who previously abided in the stage of the initiatory vows?"
For one initiated here into Nirvāṇa, the three junctions (saṃdhyā) are prescribed.

If it is argued that, according to the statement in the *Śrīmajjñānaratnāvalī*, initiates (*samayins*) perform only one twilight rite (*sandhyā*) and not the three twilights, this is true; such is the view accepted by some teachers.

In this context, however, after describing the three meditations on all the twilight rites (sandhyās) beginning with "clad in red ornaments and garments" for all three periods of time, it is stated: "the initiates (samayins) should meditate," followed by: "but the spiritual sons (putrakas) and others [should meditate on her] as slender as a lotus fiber, red..."

Having uttered "white" and so forth, one should meditate upon these in the previously mentioned locations or at the *dvādaśānta*; thus, separately from the sons and others, even for the fourfold time-periods,
[they are to be visualized] apart from their vehicles, weapons, and forms.
Because the fourfold meditation on the partless *sandhyās* is taught as being concerned solely with colors such as red and white,
the three meditations on the *sandhyās* with parts pertain exclusively to the practitioner of the *samaya*. Otherwise, [it would not be so].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the entire exposition of the three meditations on the junctions (sandhyā) being rendered purposeless.
Meditation on the partless twilight [deity].
(27) But the [goddess] beginning with Putrikā—
slender like a lotus fiber, red, white, or the best among the white;
having the form of the fourth state or black, she who is perceived at midnight.
Thus, one should meditate upon these in the previously mentioned locations or at the dvādaśānta.
Now, having described the meditation on the gross junctions (*sthūla-sandhyā*) for those who have taken the initiatory vows (*samayin*),
[it is said] that according to the *Śrīmac-Cintyaviśvasādākhya-śruti*: "Subtle, resembling a spider's thread, red, white, and black."

The text explains the meditation on the partless (niṣkala) twilight [state] for the three— putraka, sādhaka, and ācārya— who have been initiated into nirvāṇa, by means of the passage beginning with "(putrakādyāḥ)" and ending with "dhyāyīran. Here, "(putrakādyāḥ)" refers to the *putrakas*, those who have received the initiation into nirvāṇa.

Likewise, in the *Śrīmad-Varuṇapaddhati*: "Where there is the severing of the bonds and the crest [of ignorance], and the union with the state of Śiva occurs, that very [initiation] is called 'Nirvāṇa'; however, in the case of a *putraka*, it is so designated because of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Thus [it is stated] by Bhaṭṭa Śivottama, the commentator on this *Kārikāvalī*.

The characteristics of a "spiritual son" (putraka) have also been stated thus: one whose bonds are severed by the initiation for liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā) through a formal agreement, being devoid of further ritual obligations (niradhikāra).
"One who is without consecration is called a *putraka*. Regarding him, it will be stated at the commencement of the procedure for subsequent rites:
"The final sacrifice (*anteṣṭi*) accompanied by the purification of the paths must be performed for the *ācārya*, the *sādhaka*, and the *putra*."
"Those who possess the *samaya* are excluded from that"—meaning those beginning with the *putraka*.
By the word "beginning" (*ādya*), the *sādhaka* and the *deśika* are indicated. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The *deśika*, the one who has died while reciting mantras, the *putraka*, and the *samayin*—these four are the Śaivas."

Thus [it is said]. The word *tu* indicates a distinction from what precedes. (*Mṛṇālatantuvat*) means "like a lotus-fiber" (*bisasūtra*). According to Amara, *mṛṇāla* and *bisa* are synonyms. (*Tanvī*) means "subtle.
Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*, it is described as being subtle, red, and resembling a lotus-fiber.

"White, other than black" means (red), possessing a radiance as crimson as the mass of rays from the rising sun; this is the meditation on the morning twilight (*pūrvāhṇa-sandhyā*). "White" means having a splendor like ten million moons;
this is the meditation on the midday twilight (*madhyāhnika-sandhyā*). "Other than black" means white splendor.
"Amṛtārṇavasavarṇavarṇa" means having a complexion like the ocean of nectar.
This is the meditation for the evening twilight (*sāyantanasandhyā*), which is the *sandhyā* [itself]. "At night" (*niśīthe*) means at midnight (*arddharātre*).

"Arddharātra and niśītha are two [synonyms for midnight]," according to Amara. (It is explained: regarding the qualifier, it is considered; here, because of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, the word *tat* must be supplied—that [night] which is such. (Turyā) means the fourth. (Aspā) means that which has no form (*rūpa*), such as red or other colors; she who is thus described is so called.

It means simply "consisting of light" (*tejomaya*). Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-Siddhāntasārasaṃhitā*, it is said: "At dawn, one should contemplate [the deity] in the heart-lotus within the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*) as resembling the mass of rising suns;
at midday, in the lotus of the eyebrows, as the form of the consciousness of Supreme Śiva, shining like the moon; and in the evening, in the upper [lotus]..."
"In the lotus, the light of the ocean of nectar, the self-arisen sound (nāda), immeasurable, immovable, and unimpaired at midnight—that is the Great Light at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
This is the meditation on the twilight of midnight. He now describes another method of meditation for that same [twilight]:
"Or Kṛṣṇā" means water. "These" refers to the morning twilight and so forth.
"In the previously mentioned places" means in the locations of the heart, the bindu, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The ritual procedure for the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana).
(28) Then, having meditated upon the twilight [deity] appropriate for that specific time according to one's authority,

standing in the midst of its circle of light, having poured water from the right hand into the left hand, and having consecrated it once with the *saṃhitā* mantra, [one should perform the rite] with the *kumbhaka* mudrā.
With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, by performing the application once on the head— [one is] *śitetarā* (the non-white), the other is white (*śvetā*).

(34) Having cast [the water] away, and having again placed consecrated water— empowered by the *saṃhitā* mantra— upon the tips of *kuśa* grass held in the left hand, one should pour that water dripping from below onto the head with the right hand while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. This is the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*).
Then, having contemplated that remaining water held in the right hand as the pure form of Dharma, one should imagine it entering through the left nostril by means of the *pūraka* breath;
then, by means of the *kumbhaka* yoga, having brought about the destruction of sins within, one should visualize that sin as having the appearance of soot.

Having visualized [the impurity] emerging through the right nostril, one should cast it with a flick of the eyebrows onto a blazing, fire-colored vajra-stone using the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
This is the meaning today.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) correctly with the mantra, and having performed the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) as before,

having enveloped oneself with water using the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva situated in the center of the solar disc, or else [meditate upon] the Gāyatrī.
She possesses the luster of molten gold, is the supreme establisher of the samaya,
and holds in her hands the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a rosary, and a water-pot.
Gāyatrī, who is eternally manifest, has four arms and three eyes.

Having meditated thus, one should offer three handfuls [of water] with both hands holding *kuśa* grass, reciting: "Oṃ, may we know that Great Lord; let us meditate on Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva impel us.
Then, having recited the *Gāyatrī* ten or seven times, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ."
Having offered the recitation (*japa*) along with the presentation of three handfuls of water (*añjali*) with the mantra "To Śiva,
svāhā," and having gratified [the deity] with the *saṃhitā* ending in "svāhā," [one should offer] "Oṃ hāṃ, to all mantras, svāhā; Oṃ hāṃ,
to all..."
"p. 87) *Devebhyaḥ svāhā*," [reciting this] with straight kuśa grass held at the tips of the fingers;
then, wearing the sacred thread over the neck (*kaṇṭhopavītī*), [he says]: *Oṃ hāṃ sarvebhya ṛṣibhyo namaḥ*.
Thus, with the joints of the fingers: "Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to all humans," with the bases of the two little fingers; "Oṃ hāṃ, vauṣaṭ to all beings," with the joined bases of the palms.

Then, having performed the *apasavya* (rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder), having broken the *kuśa* grass, and [offering] with water containing sesame seeds: "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all ancestors; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all mothers;
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all kinsmen; Oṃ hāṃ, to all..."
With the words, "Svadhā to the teachers," one should offer libations using the base of the forefinger and the thumb.

(35) Or else, having first gratified the mantras beginning with the root mantra and ending with *svāhā* using the tip of the finger and the *devatīrtha*, one should likewise offer: *oṃ hāṃ ādityebhyaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ vasubhyaḥ svāhā*.
p. 88) Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Viśvedevas; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Sādhyas; oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Maruts; oṃ hāṃ...
"Oṃ svāhā to the Bhṛgus; Oṃ hāṃ svāhā to the Aṅgirases"—with these [mantras], one should satiate the eight classes of gods.
Then, with the sacred thread placed around the neck: *oṃ hāṃ atra ye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ vasiṣṭhāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ hāṃ putrastyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ kratave namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ bhāradvājāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ viśvāmitrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ*...
Salutation to Pracetas; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Ṛcchaka; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Agastya;
Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Dadhīci; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Durvāsas—thus [one worships] the eleven sages at the junctions of the lunar phases (parvasandhis).
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanaka; Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sananda; Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanātana; Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanatkumāra; Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Kapila;
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Pañcaśikha; Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Ṛbhu—thus [are] the seven.
For humans, with the two roots of the little fingers, [one should offer] "Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to all beings," while the palms and roots are joined together. (p. 89)
The five elements;

then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the tips of the roots of *kuśa* grass and sesame-water, [he offers]: *oṃ hāṃ kanyavāhanāya svadhā*, *oṃ hāṃ analāya svadhā*, *oṃ hāṃ somāya*.
Svadhā! Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Yama; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Aryaman;
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Agniṣvātta; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Barhiṣad; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Ājyapa; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Somapa—thus [to] the divine ancestors (devapitṛs).
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Īśa, the father; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Sadāśiva, the grandfather; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Śānta, the great-grandfather—thus [to] the specific ancestors.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the fathers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the grandfathers; Oṃ hāṃ...
Svadhā to the great-grandfathers; Oṃ Hāṃ, svadhā to the great-great-grandfathers; Oṃ Hāṃ, svadhā to the mothers.

"Oṃ hāṃ svadhā to the maternal grandfathers; Oṃ hāṃ svadhā to the maternal great-grandfathers; Oṃ hāṃ svadhā to the maternal great-great-grandfathers; Oṃ hāṃ svadhā to all the ancestors"—thus [he offers] to the ancestral spirits of the deceased (pretapitṛs).

Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the mothers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the maternal grandmothers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the paternal grandmothers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the great-grandmothers; Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to all kinsmen; Oṃ hāṃ, [svadhā] to all...
Svadhā to the teachers; oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the directions;
oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the lords of the directions; oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the perfected ones (siddhas);
oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the mothers; oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the planets; oṃ hāṃ...

Having offered libations with "Svadhā to the constellations" and "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Rākṣasas," he should cast water along with Kuśa grass onto the bank while reciting "Oṃ haḥ, huṃ phaṭ to the Astra. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī),
having offered libations by reciting the mantras of Gaṇapati, Ambikā, and the others, and having discarded the Kuśa grass—
Having sipped water and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should withdraw the *tīrtha* by means of the *hrasvaprāsāda* mantra.
If the practitioner is a twice-born, this should be done after the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* and the subsequent worship (*upasthāna*).

Having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) to Śiva, who is the embodiment of the Sun (*ādityamūrti*), according to the *Saṃhitā*, one should offer [the oblation] after reciting the *Prāsāda* mantra a hundred times, fifty times, twenty-five times, or ten times, according to one's capacity.

Now, having illustrated the meditation on the twilight periods (*sandhyā*) according to the distinction between the types of practitioners beginning with the *samayin*, [the author], in response to the inquiry "How should one pay homage to the twilight period?", states the procedure for that homage with the words beginning with "(tataḥ)" and ending with "(tyaktvā). (Tataḥ) [... (Tyaktvā).

After the meditation on the junctions of time (*sandhyādhyāna*); "according to one's qualification" (*yathādhikāram*) means without transgressing the qualifications of the *samayin*, *putraka*, and so forth; "appropriate to those respective times" (*tattatkālocitām*)—the phrase "those respective times" (*tattatkālāḥ*) refers to the specific periods such as morning and so on; "appropriate for them" (*teṣām ucitā*) means worthy of them.
(Standing in the midst of its circle of light:
Standing in the middle of the circle of light of that twilight— the circle of rays consisting of red and other colors—
he meditates, thinking of his own body as having entered within the circle of the splendor of twilight.
This is the intended meaning.
Regarding the sequence for the mantra-consecration (*mantrābhiṣeka*) in the ritual of the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*),
[the text] says "the right" (*dakṣiṇa*) on page 92. The definition of the *kuṃbhaka* mudrā has been stated in the section on the definitions of mudrās.
(37) The Kuṃbhaka-mudrā: with the two thumbs joined together,
the palm of the right hand placed over the palm of the left hand which holds water, it resembles a half-moon behind [the head].

The two hands, with fingers curved, should be employed during the twilight rituals, at the initiation by mantra (*mantrābhiṣeka*), and so forth. He states the rite to be performed immediately after the initiation by mantra:
"(repeatedly consecrated with the *saṃhitā* mantra). "(That which has flowed down below)" means "below that."
"Fallen" means dropped from the left hand. (Thus) in this manner.
(Wiping) is the rite called *mārjana*. The rite known as *mārjana*, characterized by the sprinkling of drops of water upon the head with *saṃhitā* mantras, is so designated. As it has been said:
The venerable Somaśambhu has declared that sprinkling (mārjana) is performed by pouring water from the left hand onto the head with the right hand,
while reciting the mantras in their proper sequence.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the question of what one should do with the water remaining after the act of sprinkling (*mārjana*), he says: "That" (*tat*). "That" refers to the water held in the left hand; it is the remainder.
The remainder of the cleansing rite (*mārjanakarma*). (Held in the right hand) means it has been transferred from the left hand to the right hand. (Pure) means white in color.
(By means of *kuṃbhaka*) means by performing the *kuṃbhaka* breath-retention. (Within) means inside the body.
(The destruction of evil: "Evils" refers to verbal and other wicked actions;

their "destruction" means their annihilation. Likewise, having drawn that [evil] residing in the heart by means of *pūraka* (inhalation), one should contemplate the *astra* (weapon-mantra) three times.
One should expel the evil of speech, mind, and body through the *recaka* breath.

Thus: (that evil) refers to the unrighteousness residing within the body. (Smoke-colored) means the color of collyrium; that is to say, black. (Issued forth) means gone outside. (Upon a diamond-stone blazing with the color of fire): "blazing" means shining, and it is that very fire.
She whose color and luster are like that [of fire] is "jvaladagnivarṇā"; she is also the "vajraśilā," meaning a diamond-stone.
The meaning is: on that manifested diamond-stone in the direction of the Nairṛta (southwest).
Thus spoke the illustrious author of the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*. Likewise, the illustrious commentator on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati* said:
"One should pour water upon the surface of a diamond-stone; that is the rite of expiation (*aghamarṣaṇa*)."

In this context, the throwing of water should be performed in the south-western direction (nairṛtī). Likewise, in the commentary on the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, it is stated: "Agha is explained as sin; marṣaṇa is its destruction."
She who was spoken of by Śiva as Nairṛtī is known by the name Pāpahāriṇī.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: what is the name of this rite consisting of the casting of a thunderbolt-stone (*vajraśilā*) upon the water composed of sin that has been produced within the body?
Anticipating this, one should draw out the white water in the form of consciousness with the *vāmā* [power] and cause it to be held in a vessel (*kuṃbhayet*).
That which one should cast upon a vajra-stone becomes the Aghamarṣaṇa rite.
Thus, based on the authority of the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, he says: "This is called *aghamarṣaṇa*.
(*Aghamarṣaḥ*) means the pacification of sin (*aghaśamana*). Anticipating the question of what one should do immediately thereafter, [he says]:
"One should sip water for the purpose of purification through the performance of the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite" (p.
95), he says; "(then with the mantra)" means after that—that is, immediately following the *aghamarṣaṇa*. Here...
The venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendra-tantra* has stated that [the rite] is for the sake of purification following the sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Whenever one performs the ritual sipping of water, at those very times one should perform the deposition of mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
One should fashion [images] from water-pots for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra and the mantrin.

Thus, because the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*pratyācamana*) and the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) have been prescribed in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*, it says "one should perform the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the self] complete)" (referring to the phrase "having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* as before").
This is for the purpose of not revealing one's own body with water to people such as those who are uninitiated.

"One should envelop [it] with the Kavaca mantra," he says, using the word "with the Kavaca. Thus it was stated by the venerable author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "[The word] 'self' refers to one's own body.
Satiating with both hands is taught; satiation is traditionally understood as pleasing."
From the *Śrīmatkāmika-śruti*, for the purpose of pleasing all mantras such as the *Gāyatrī-mūla-saṃhitā* and others,
he states the procedure for libation (*tarpaṇa-vidhi*) beginning with the words "(the solar orb)" and "(the Blessed One)."

*Bhaga* is the sixfold set of attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*). As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "The designation *bhaga* refers to the totality of sovereignty, valor, fame, prosperity, knowledge, and dispassion."

Thus it is said. Therefore, it is eternally joined; here the suffix *matup* denotes eternal connection. Regarding the phrase "and the Gāyatrī," the meaning of the word *gāyatrī* here is "she who protects (*trāyate*) the one who sings (*gāyantaṃ*)," as well as the deity Gāyatrī.
He describes her meditation with the words "molten gold" (*taptakāñcana*). [She is] "the establisher of the covenant" (*samayasthāpanīm*).

She who establishes the conduct of the Śaivas; she who is excellent. Regarding "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*), Amara states: "The *samayas* are oaths, conduct, time, established doctrines, and consciousness; in their opposite sense, they mean 'excellent,' 'far,' 'one's own,' and 'supreme'."
*Kuṇḍikām* means a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). The rest is easily understood.
The extraction of the *Gāyatrī* mantra has been demonstrated in the venerable *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*.
Oṃ, let us know that state which belongs to Maheśa, and then that state which belongs to Vāgviśuddha; at the end of that [is the mantra].
[One should meditate] together with the word "dhīmahi."
"May that lead us to the state of Śiva; therefore, may it impel us.
Thus, O child, the Gāyatrī has been described in the *Kālottara*. (Three *añjali*s:
An *añjali* consists of the two hands joined together with palms facing upward. Likewise, Manu [prescribes this] for the *śrāddha*, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), and the marriage ceremony.

In the act of giving (*dāna*), water is given with one [hand]; however, in the act of libation (*tarpaṇa*), water must be given with both hands and not otherwise. According to Amarasimha: "The hollowed palm is a *prasṛti*; those two joined together form the *añjali* [cupped hand]. [This refers to] three of these. (Then) after the libation to Gāyatrī; (having recited) having performed the silent recitation (*japa*).
Endowed with devotion, one should recite the Śivagāyatrī at the three junctions of the day;
having thus recited the mantra and offered the arghya, the dismissal (visarjana) should be performed immediately.

Thus, according to the *Śrīmac-Cintyaviśvasādākhya-śruti*, one should offer the *visarjanārghya* (the water of dismissal) immediately after the recitation of the *gāyatrī*: "To Śiva, Svāhā. Here, because the word *svāhā* signifies nectar (*amṛta*) through the phrase "Svaḥ is heaven," [it is understood as] *sva*.

(39) Heaven (*svarga*) is expressed by the word [“*sva*”]; likewise, even by the syllable “*hā*,” it is [expressed] through the indication of a part (*ekadeśalakṣaṇayā*) as “*āhāra*” (food). Thus, the meaning of the word *svāhā* should be understood as “the food which is nectar (*amṛta*) in heaven.”
"By the offering of three añjalis," "by the offering of three libations," and "to all mantras"—
here, "all mantras" refers to the hundred million mantras categorized according to the divisions of Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava.
"To all gods"— here, "all gods" refers to the eight groups of deities beginning with Āditya.
"By the tip of the hand" means by the *devatīrtha* [the sacred part of the palm]. "With straight *kuśa* grasses" means with the tips of the *kuśa* grasses.

Based on the *Śrīmat Kālottara Śruti*, which states, "The gods have the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*), while the sages have it suspended from the neck (*kaṇṭhalambana*)," he says "(then, with the sacred thread around the neck)" meaning that one should offer libations to the sages while leaving either arm [uncovered] as the sacred thread. (To all the sages...)

"Namaḥ. Here, "all sages" refers to the eleven sages beginning with Atri and Vasiṣṭha. In the word "namaḥ," the syllable *na* denotes *nāka* (the celestial realm), and the syllable *ma* also indicates *bindu* (the point) by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning of the word *namaḥ* is precisely the nectar of the moon (*candrāmṛta*). Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:

[with] "the joints of the fingers," which means by the *ārṣa-tīrtha*. Regarding this, the author of the venerable *Bālajñānaratnāvalī* has stated that the libation to the sages (*ṛṣis*) should be performed with the middle part of the *kuśa* grass.
"To all men"—here, "all men" refers to the seven classes of beings beginning with Sanaka. "(With the bases of the little fingers)" means by the *prājāpatya* tīrtha. "To all beings"—here...
"All beings" refers to the five [elements], beginning with space.

This has been stated in the *Śrīmad-Bālajñānaratnāvalī*: "With the base of the palm joined"—that is to say, by means of the *brahmatīrtha*, which is the region at the base of the palms where they are joined together.
"One should satisfy the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), being well-composed"—

according to this teaching from the venerable *Kālottara-śruti*, he says "having placed [the thread] over the left shoulder" (*apasavyaṃ kṛtvā*) to mean that one should satisfy the ancestors while having the sacred thread suspended over the left arm.

(Regarding the *kuśa* grass: Having broken the ritual acts (*karmān*), that is to say, having placed the *kuśa* grass crosswise by means of both its root and its tip; (regarding "to all the ancestors" [sarvebhyaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ]): here, "all the ancestors" refers to the deities.

"Pitṛviśeṣapitṛpreta-pitaraḥ" [refers to specific ancestors, deceased ancestors, and paternal forefathers]. "(Sarvābhyo mātṛbhyaḥ)" [means] "to all mothers"; here, "all mothers" refers to the mother, paternal grandmother, and so forth. "(Sarvebhyo jñātibhyaḥ)" [means] "to all kinsmen"; here, "kinsmen" refers to those of the same *gotra*. *Sagotra*, *bāndhava*, *jñāti*, *bandhu*, *svasva*, and *jana* are synonymous.
Thus says Amara: "(To all the *ācāryas*).

Here, the *ācāryas* refer to one's own gurus and so forth. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "In the same manner, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), [one honors] the ancestors together with their wives, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers, as well as one's own gurus, the initiators (*udaka*), and the instructors (*bodhaka*)."
"Others... thus [it is said]. (By means of the root of the forefinger and the thumb:

*Pradeśinī* is the forefinger (*tarjanī*), for Amara states that *tarjanī* may be called *pradeśinī*. *Aṅguṣṭhamūla* is the part at the base of the thumb; by those two, namely the root of the forefinger and the thumb...
The meaning is "by means of the *pitṛtīrtha*. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika* (p.
"The *daivika-tīrtha* is at the tips of the fingers, and the *ārṣaka-tīrtha* is at the joints of the fingers. The *tīrtha*...
"The Prājāpatya [tīrtha] is proclaimed at the base of the little finger; the Paitṛka at the base of the forefinger;

and the Brāhmaka from the base of the hand. Here, in the word *svadhā*, the term *sva* denotes the divine (*divya*), and by the term *dhā*, through the indication of a part representing the whole, it means "only nectar" (*sudhā*); such is the meaning of the word *svadhā*.
Likewise, in the *Śrīmad-Bālajñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated regarding the act of giving:
"Since the words *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *namaḥ* have been proclaimed,
nectar is given to these three as well, and that is equal [in effect]."
That which is their food is called *amṛta* (nectar) for those dwellers of heaven;
that which is declared as *svadhā* is the divine *svardivya*, and *sudhā* is dear to the ancestors.
"Salutation to him who is the sky, in whom is the moon, the nectar for men. (Thus one should perform the libation.
One should perform the *tarpaṇa*. Regarding *tarpaṇa*, Amara states: "Satisfaction, satiety, *tarpaṇa*, and *tṛpti* [are synonyms]."
Having thus demonstrated the abbreviated libation (*saṅgrahatarpaṇa*), he states the procedure for the extensive libation (*vistaratarpaṇavidhi*).
Alternatively, he states the libation for the hosts of deities beginning with Āditya, [introducing it] with "in the same manner" (*tathaiva*);
the meaning is "by means of the very tips of the fingers."

102) He states the libation for the sages beginning with Atri with the word “(then)”; he states the libation for human beings beginning with Sanaka with “(Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Sanaka)”; [and the libation] for the elements beginning with space...

He states the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, to all [beings]. He states the libation for the divine ancestors (*devapitṛs*), such as Kavyavāha and others, with: "Then... He states the libation for human beings, such as Sanaka and others, with:
"Oṃ hāṃ, to Sanaka, vaṣaṭ. He states the libation for the elements, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, with: "Oṃ..."

"Hāṃ, to all" (iti). He describes the libation for the divine ancestors beginning with Kavyavāha with the word "Now" (atha). "(Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder)" means wearing it in the *apasavya* manner.
He describes the specific libation for the ancestors beginning with Īśa with: "Oṃ hāṃ, to the father Īśa, svadhā."
He states the libation for the deceased ancestors beginning with the father: "Oṃ hāṃ svadhā to the fathers.

The grandfathers are the progenitors of the fathers. The great-grandfathers are the progenitors of the grandfathers. The great-great-grandfathers are the progenitors of the progenitors of the grandfathers. The maternal grandfathers...
The mothers’ fathers; the great-grandmothers’ fathers (the mothers’ grandfathers);
and the great-great-grandmothers’ fathers (the mothers’ grandfathers’ fathers).

"The grandfather is the father’s father; his father is the great-grandfather. Likewise for the mother’s maternal grandfather and so forth," according to Amara. Regarding the phrase "(the ancestors who were once deceased)": although the state of being a *preta* no longer exists after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, there is no fault in using the term, as it is spoken of by way of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).
He states the libations (*tarpaṇa*) that are to be performed immediately thereafter, beginning with: "Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to the Mothers," and so forth.

Now, he describes the rites to be performed immediately after the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the passage beginning with "(having sipped water)" and ending with "he should offer. Regarding the term "(the sacred site)": the meaning is the nectar drawn from the location of *nāda* situated at the point of the drop (*bindu*). "(He should withdraw)" means [he should withdraw it] into that very place of the drop.

One should perform the *upasthāna* (worshipful salutation). Regarding this, the author of the commentary on the venerable *Sārddhatriśatikālottara* has stated that the *upasthāna* facing the Sun, who is of the nature of Śiva, with handfuls of water is indeed established [as the rule]. And likewise, in the *Mahābhārata*:
Having performed circumambulation and having approached the Sun with devotion according to the Karṇaparvan (p. 104), one should offer [the oblation] to Śiva.
One should offer it.
There is an exemption in the case of the passing of the twilight period.

(Kri) (29) It has been stated that in the event of missing the prescribed time for the *saṃdhyā*, one should recite the *saṃhitā* once. (Pra) Now, with the words beginning with "It has been stated" and ending with "one should recite," he explains the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for performing the rite after the time for *saṃdhyā* has passed. (In the event of missing the prescribed time for *saṃdhyā*)...
The time for the twilight [sandhyā] has been stated as "when the sky is still starred" and so forth; this refers to the period of the *udita-sandhyā* (the risen twilight).

Its *bhraṃśa* is its lapse or passing away; at that [time]. (*Saṃhitām*) means the *Śivaikādaśikā*. Thus, it is said: "At the lapse of the twilight time, one should mutter the *Śivaikādaśikā*. In this regard:

The lapse occurs specifically from the failure to perform the *saṃdhyā* rite, and not from [the omission of] ritual action (*karman*); for there is a scriptural injunction for a separate expiation stating that "if one neglects the *saṃdhyā* even once, one should mutter the *Sadyojāta* mantra a hundred times."
The Worship of the Sun.

(20) Then, situated within the lattice of weapons (*astrapañjara*), mentally abandoning the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth, he [should contemplate] the place of worship which extends as far as the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*).
Having entered and gathered the articles for worship,
one facing east should worship the Sun. Having purified the palms and backs of the hands with "Oṃ Raḥ Astra Phaṭ," one should sprinkle them with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
With the thumbs and index fingers: *oṃ aṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*.
With the little, ring, middle, and thumb fingers: *oṃ aṃ* to the head, *arkāya śirase namaḥ*. *Oṃ aṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaroṃ* to the crest-lock, *jvālinīśikhāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ aṃ*.

*Hrūṃ*, salutation to the armor (*kavaca*); [placing it] on the middle fingers of both palms; *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the two sun-eyes (*bhānu-netra*), [placing it] on the index fingers and thumbs; *Oṃ raḥ*, *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*). Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and having enveloped [the self] with the armor-mantra, having joined both [hands], [one recites] the root-mantra (*mūla*).

Having performed the ritual placement ending with *vauṣaṭ*, and having purified the body with the root mantra of the Sun, one should place the Heart mantra at the heart using the pair of the right thumb and ring finger,
the Head mantra on the head, and the Topknot mantra on the topknot as a covering for the throat.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the armor mantra (*kavaca*) between the breasts with the two index fingers, the eye mantra (*netra*) on the two eyes with the middle and index fingers, and the weapon mantra (*astra*) on the palms of the hands, [one should perform it] in the ten directions.

Having performed the binding of the directions with the *choṭikā* [finger-snapping] and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), and having applied the root-mantra to all limbs with the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), one should contemplate one's own body as being in the form of the sun.

Afterwards, having prepared an *arghya* offering in a copper vessel with water, red flowers, and other ingredients, and having knelt upon the ground and brought it up to his head, he should offer the *darśanārghya* while reciting: "Oṃ srāṃ hrīṃ saḥ | To Sūrya, obeisance. Then, he should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to his capacity.
Then, having purified the arghya vessel with the Astra mantra,

and having filled it with scented water while reciting "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolka," [one should contemplate] there the stream of nectar issuing from the reddish drop throbbing in the center of the forehead.

Having worshipped with the six limbs and the root mantra, having performed protection and encasement with the weapon and armor mantras, having displayed the cow-mudrā with the root mantra, and having sprinkled the ritual substances, oneself, and the ground with that water using the weapon mantra;
Having dispelled the obstacles with the Puṣpakṣepa weapon-mantra, one should then worship the eight-petaled lotus drawn upon the sacrificial ground with a lotus made of copper or other materials.
107) There, on the right side of the door: "Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin.
Thus, Daṇḍin is at the south of the door; he has a protruding belly, a long beard, and holds an ink-pot and a pen.
Holding [a pen] in his two hands, he is the witness of the actions of living beings and records those very deeds. Thus, on his left side: *Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala*.
He is red in color, adorned with fine attire, and equipped with a needle in his hand.
Or Piṅgala on the side, and the door-keeper Daṇḍavat;

Having meditated thus and performed worship, [one should place] in the northeast of the lotus: "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati"—thus [visualizing] the Lord of the Gaṇas, elephant-faced and holding [objects] with four hands.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, to the southeast of that [deity], one should offer obeisance with: *Oṃ aṃ, namaḥ to the gurus*.

[One should visualize them] as being richly adorned with matted hair and a crown, their bodies white with ashes, wearing a yogic cloth and a sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) over the region of the navel.
(43) And one should meditate upon the supreme Guru, peaceful, bearing the mudrā known as *kṛtayoga*.
Having thus meditated and performed worship, [one should offer] in the center: *oṃ aṃ prabhūtāsanāya namaḥ*.

One should worship the white pedestal (śvetapīṭha). In the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should worship while visualizing them in the forms of lions that are white, red, yellow, and green respectively: "Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Vimala; Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Sāra; Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Ārādhya; Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Paramasukha. Thus one should worship.
Above that, [recite] "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the lotus," and thus [visualize] a white lotus.
Upon its filaments, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, [recite]: "Oṃ Rāṃ, obeisance to Dīptā; Oṃ Rīṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣmā;
Oṃ Ruṃ, obeisance to Rujā; Oṃ Rūṃ, obeisance to Bhadrā; Oṃ Reṃ..."
Vibhūtyai namaḥ; Oṃ raiṃ Vimalāyai namaḥ; Oṃ roṃ Amoghāyai namaḥ;
Oṃ rauṃ Vidyutāyai namaḥ—these are in the pericarp, starting from the northeast (īśāna); and Oṃ raḥ Sarvatomukhyai namaḥ. Thus.
Alternatively, the nine Śaktis should be meditated upon as having the form of blazing lamp-flames;
they hold lotuses and chowries in their hands, are red in color, and are adorned on all their limbs.
Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having displayed the *visphura* mudrā, one should worship the sun-throne (*arkāsana*) in the center with: "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to the sun-throne."
Seated upon a white lotus, possessing the luster of a pomegranate flower,
he is a mass of shimmering, great red splendor situated in the center of a circular mandala.
One should meditate upon the Sun-god as having one face and two eyes, wearing red garments, with his two hands holding a lotus with its stalk clearly resting upon his shoulders.

Having meditated thus, one should place the form upon the seat with the mantra: *oṃ khaṃ khaṣolkāyaṃ sūryamūrtaye namaḥ*. Then, having applied the eyes with *oṃ bhāṃ bhānunetrābhyāṃ namaḥ*, and having filled the joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers, one should [place] the throbbing red drop drawn from the forehead into the *añjali*.
Having reflected thus, one should invoke that pervasive presence with the root mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ*.

Having invoked [the deity] with the *upahṛdaya* mantra and the *āvāhanī* mudrā, having established [him] upon a lotus seat with the *sthāpanī* mudrā, having brought [him] into close proximity with the *sannidhānī* mudrā, having bound [him] with the *niṣṭhurā* mudrā, and having displayed the *nityā* mudrā;

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart-mantra and the other mantras upon the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands of the Sun, having established identity with the root mantra, and having performed the protective concealment (*avakuṇṭhana*), [one should proceed].
Having performed the Amṛtamudrā and Mahāmudrā with the root mantra,

and having offered water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) with the Khaṣolkin mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*, and having presented flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice (akṣata), and so forth with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one should recite]: *oṃ khaṃ*.
