Having bathed [the deity] preceded by anointing and other rites with the upahr̥daya mantra, "Oṃ khaṣolkāya namaḥ," and having adorned [him] with red flowers, perfumes, and so forth, one should worship with three handfuls of flowers while reciting, "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ," and after offering the arghya water, [one should display] the lotus mudrā.
And one should display the image-seal (bimbamudrā).
Then, having worshipped the limb of absorption (layāṅga) and having made a request for the sake of worshipping the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga),
one should take the mantras of the heart, head, crest, and armor from the locations such as the Heart of the Sun, and place them upon the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
One should meditate upon the limbs of the Sun as being gentle, red in color, adorned, two-armed, and holding another lotus in their hands.
Having thus meditated upon and worshipped [the deity], one should likewise place the eye, in the form previously described, before the deity,
and the weapon (*astra*) on the four petals starting from the east.
Having meditated upon the weapon [mantra] as resembling a mass of lightning and terrifying with fierce fangs,
and having worshipped it, one should perform the *dhenumudrā* for the heart and other limbs,
the *goviṣāṇamudrā* for the eyes, and the *trāsanīmudrā* for the weapon.
Having displayed [the deity], one should offer the *arghya*.

Thereafter, at the tips of the petals starting from the east: *oṃ saṃ somāya namaḥ*, *oṃ buṃ budhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ bṛṃ bṛhaspataye namaḥ*, *oṃ bhaṃ bhārgavāya namaḥ*; and at the tips of the petals starting from the southeast: *oṃ aṃ aṅgārakāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śaṃ*.
"Oṃ, salutation to Śanaiścara; Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Rāhu; Oṃ kaṃ, salutation to Ketu. And likewise:
"Soma, who has the luster of the kumuda and kunda flowers, and Budha, who has the brilliance of refined gold."
The Guru has the luster of yellow orpiment; Śukra resembles cow's milk.
One should meditate on Mars as red, Saturn as resembling lapis lazuli,
Rāhu as black with palms joined in reverence, and Ketu as resembling a smoky serpent.
All of them assume forms at will, adorned with divine ornaments,
with their left hands resting upon their thighs and their right hands granting fearlessness.
The Moon, holding a white lotus in his hand, and Rāhu and Ketu with palms joined in reverence;
both having half-bodies and hair standing upright, with red heads and red eyes.
Having meditated thus on Śani, who is terrifying with fangs, and Rāhu, whose face is deformed, and having worshipped them, displayed the *namo-mudrā*, offered the *arghya*,
and presented incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), water for drinking, betel, a mirror, an umbrella, and so forth—

(85) Having offered chowries at intervals, accompanied by the offering of water for sipping and respectful oblations (*arghya*), and having recited the root mantra as many times as possible, one should offer the water from the *arghya* vessel to the Sun with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, [and then perform] the tenth part of the limbs (*aṅga*).
Having performed the recitation and the offering,
attended by Daṇḍa and the other [attendants], seated upon a pure throne with four lion legs,
possessing the luster of a ruby through the networks of powers such as Dīpta and others, he is the venerable embodiment of Khaṣolka.
Surrounded by his own limbs, planets, constellations, and other [deities], mounted upon a white lotus, [he holds] a white lotus.
"May Śambhusūrya, who has six arms and a pair of auspicious eyes,
protect you! Having recited this hymn and others, having prostrated before the deity, having worshipped him,
and having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away while ending with "svāhā," one should say, "Forgive me."

Having raised the mantras of the limbs and so forth with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and the *nārāca-mudrā*, and having joined [the deity] with the god using the divine *mudrā* while reciting "Oṃ khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolka, the solar form," one should join him with his root-mantra to Śiva-Sūrya residing in the heart-lotus. (20)

Now, having explained the sequence for the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), [it is said]: "The sun, the self, the sacrifice, the *liṅga*, fire, the guru, and the book—thus is the daily worship of Śiva in the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*) fully described. According to this statement.

Since the worship of the Sun as a support is included as a constant element within the worship of Śiva in the six supports beginning with the *liṅga*, he first describes the procedure for that worship by defining what must be performed prior to it.
From the passage beginning with "tataḥ" up to "upahṛtya. Now, one might object: "In that case, let the worship of him [the Sun] follow immediately after the worship of Śiva.
This is not so, because the Sun, being *sakala* (possessing parts/attributes), must be worshipped first. Thus:
The glorious Aṃśumat is the Sun in his manifest form (sakala), while Śiva himself is the unmanifest (niṣkala);
having first worshipped the deity residing within the body, the wise man should subsequently worship the Lord.

Thus [it is said]. Now, some have remarked that this worship of the Sun should not be performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), because it is an object of desire; that is not so, for one who seeks enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*) should both worship [him] eternally and at once.

Since it is stated thus in the *Śrīmat-Ṣaṭsahasrikā*, the teachers maintain that this must be performed even by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). He describes the ritual duty for one returning home after performing acts such as bathing with the word "Astra": "(situated within the cage of the Astra-mantra)."

The essential meaning is that one should contemplate oneself as being situated within a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) composed of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), that is, as residing in the midst of a chariot made of the weapon-mantra. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kāmika*:
Having warded off obstacles, he— residing in a celestial palace consisting of the path and its stations— should proceed either to a temple of the gods or to his own excellent home.

Thus: "(The principles beginning with Earth). Here, the meaning of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the principles starting from Water up to Māyā. "(Abandoning)" means bypassing them by way of the sequence of the rungs of a ladder. Likewise, in the *Śrīsamanāthapaddhati*:
Leaping over the ladder of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Māyā,
one shall enter the state of Śuddhavidyā, Ātman, and Sadāśiva.
Thus. (Pervading up to the limit of the principle of Pure Knowledge) it pervades the procedure of Pure Knowledge.
(Having brought near) it is to be brought together.

Now, he extends the procedure for the worship of the Sun by means of the passage beginning with "(facing east)" and ending with "one should join. Anticipating the question, "How indeed should one worship the Sun?", [the author] first states:
"In that regard, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands and limbs using the root-mantras and limb-mantras of the Sun."
Having performed the purification of the body according to the state of the Sun and Śambara,

"Having placed in one's heart the scriptural authority of the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, which states: 'One should meditate upon oneself as the supreme Sun-god in the form of the sun,' [this is done] for the sake of attaining that very nature for the worshipper of the Sun."
(p. 116) He explains the method of the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the words: "Oṃ raḥ astrāya phaṭ.
Thus, the extraction of the heart-mantra and other limb-mantras of the Sun is demonstrated.
In the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*,
the heart and the head [are formed] with the preceding vowel accompanied by the anusvāra;
from "to the Sun, the seed of the heart" (*hṛnnīja*) followed by "to the head, obeisance" (*śirase namaḥ*), [the mantra is completed].

Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ; [one should worship] the crest with "Salutation to the flaming crest (jvālinī-śikhā)," and saying "bhāṃ," one should worship the armor with the syllable hūṃ accompanied by the letter ra.
"And one should worship the eyes with the seed-syllable of fire (*raḥ*) accompanied by the *visarga*, as well as the weapon (*astra*).

Thus [it is said]. (He states the sequence for the ritual placement on the limbs: "(On the right thumb)" and so forth; "(With a snap of the fingers)" and so forth. This definition was stated regarding the characteristics of mudrās under the section on "the snap of the fingers" (*choṭikā*).
By means of the tips of the thumb and the index finger, the form consisting of the raising of sound—
which has the nature of dispelling obstacles— should be employed.

Then, in response to the question of what one should do next, he says "afterwards" (*paścāt*), meaning that one should offer the *darśanārghya* (the offering for the vision). Regarding the phrase "red flowers, etc. (*raktapuṣpādi*), the word "etc.
(*ādi*) refers to red sandalwood and so forth. Likewise...

117) "In the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*, it is said: 'Having filled that vessel with water, [one should offer] red sandalwood and rice, or else red flowers and *kuśa* grass. (Thus, having prepared the *arghya*)."

In this context, "with the root mantra" is the understood remainder. Thus it has been explained by the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*. "(Having gone to the earth with his knees)" means having placed both knees upon the ground. Of the Sun...
He describes the procedure for preparing the special *arghya* with the word "Then" (*tataḥ*).
[The phrase] "by the stream of nectar flowing from the throbbing red dot in the middle of the forehead" (*lalāṭamadhyasphuradaruṇabinduviniḥsṛtāmṛtadhārayā*) means:
the middle of the forehead is the space between the eyebrows; in that place, it is throbbing, i.e., shining.
And that *aruṇabindu* is a stream of water in the form of red-colored nectar;
by means of that [stream], the characteristic of the *dhenumudrā* was described by Śrī Bhojadeva as follows:
when the fingers are interlaced with one another, [the thumbs] are placed between the little fingers, the ring fingers, the middle fingers, and the index fingers.

The *dhenumudrā* has the shape of a cow’s udder due to its [two] bonds (*saṃyojana*). He speaks of the purification of the substances, the locus, and the self with the words "by their waters" (*tajjalaiḥ*). "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to the flowers and other materials for worship; "substance" (*dravya*) also means wealth.
"Guṇāśraye" means "in the locus of qualities," according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. "(Ātmānam)" means "one's own head.
[The author] says "on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍile*)" to indicate that the sun should be worshipped as the substratum of the ritual action; this definition will be explained later.
We shall explain.

In that context, he first describes the worship of the door, [saying]: "(There, on the right side of the door)" and so forth. "There" means on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and other such locations. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantras beginning with *daṇḍī* and ending with *arkāsana*, when devoid of the powers (*śakti*) such as *Dīptā* and the rest, is called the "Heart-seed of the Sun. Likewise:

In the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it says: "While reciting the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdbīja*) for the powers (*śaktis*) ending with Vināsana. It states the meditation on the staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*) as "(the staff-bearer)": that by which one is struck is a staff (*daṇḍa*), meaning a club;
he who possesses such a staff as his weapon is the staff-bearer (*daṇḍī*). "(At the southern door)": *dvāḥ* means door (*dvāra*).
"Strīdvārdvāram" means "the female organ," according to Amara. "Of that [organ], the southern part" refers to its right side.
"(Gauraḥ)" means white; according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "gaura" denotes reddish-brown, white, and yellow.
"(Tuṇḍilaḥ)" means stout. The rest is easy to understand. "(On its left side)"...
The meaning is "on the left side of the gate"; however, this does not apply to Daṇḍin, because the northern direction constitutes his right side.

The meaning here is that because the door is "inward-facing" according to the statement, "The door should be known as inward-facing, while the gatekeepers are outward-facing," it is established that the direction associated with the staff is the left side of the door. As was stated previously: "The staff-bearer is on the right of the door."
He states the meditation on Piṅgala: "Piṅgala" [is the subject]. "Pratīhāraḥ" means a door-keeper;

"pratīhāro dvārapālaḥ" according to Amara. The rest is easily understood. Although the half-verse beginning with "raktavarṇaḥ" has been interpolated by some in certain places, it is disregarded [by others].
He describes the meditation on Gaṇapati with the words "(red)": "(tooth)" refers to his own tusk;

"(fruit)" refers to a mango fruit; the rest is clear. "(Of that)" refers to the lotus seat. He describes the meditation on the Guru with the words "(matted locks)": "(above the region of the navel)" [he is] performing the mudrā known as yoga.
The mudrā of consciousness (cinmudrā) is formed above the navel region. The rest is clear. The Prabhūtāsana consists of a white pedestal; likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
"One should worship the Prabhūtāsana, consisting of a white pedestal, in the center."
120) He describes the worship of the lion-throne and the feet with the words "āgneyādi" (beginning from the southeast).
He describes the worship of the nine powers, Dīptā and the others, with the word "tasya" (of that). "Tasya" refers to the lotus.
The extraction of the mantras for the powers (śaktis) beginning with Dīptā has been demonstrated in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*: omitting the letters 'a' and 'i',
and taking the sixth vowel as the final letter, [the mantras consist of] the letter 'ra', the anusvāra, and the vowels in sequence.

"Those which denote 'blazing' and so forth. He describes their visualization with the word "blazing. Regarding that, he states an alternative view with "or else. The meaning of the verse is easy to understand. The definition of the *visphura* mudrā has been stated by Śrī Bhojadeva.

"With the hands facing forward, the fingers are slightly bent, and by the movement of the thumbs, [the hands] flash above the fingertips. The *arkāsana* pervades up to the end of the *māyā-tattva*. He describes the meditation on the Sun (*sūryadhyāna*) as "(white)":
"(with two hands holding a clearly white lotus stalk resting upon the shoulders). The "shoulders" (*aṃsau*) are the tops of the arms.

He whose two hands hold that white (*śveta*) and lustrous (*dhavala*) lotus (*abja*) together with its stalk (*sanāla*), which is attached (*āsakta*), joined (*saṃlagna*), and clearly blossomed (*sphuṭa*); for Amara states: "The words *vyākośa*, *vikaca*, and *sphuṭa* all mean 'blossomed'. He who possesses such a lotus in his two hands.
Thus he is described as "him" (tam). (Bhānum) refers to the Sun; according to Amara, *bhānu* means both "ray" and "maker of day.
The rest is clear: the form of the Sun (*sūryamūrti*) is that which pervades the interior of the principle of Sadāśiva.

And this extraction of the mantra has been performed in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*: "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolka, the solar form. (Having applied [the mudrā] to the eyes). Here, the phrase "with the cow-horn mudrā" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He describes the sequence for the invocation of the Sun with the words "(with flowers)."

*(The añjali gesture:)* the two hollowed palms. *(The phrase "with a throbbing red drop drawn to the forehead" means that the radiance has entered into such a drop.)* One should utter the root mantra as pervading up to the end of the principle of Śakti. As it has been said: "It extends from Māyā to the end of the region of Śakti."
"Of Śiva and the hot-rayed [Sūrya]. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
"The syllable *hā*, together with fire (*ra*) and the bindu (*m*), conjoined with the syllable *hī*;
then the letter *sa* with the visarga (*ḥ*), followed by the word 'to Sūrya'."

"Having uttered the *namaḥ* ending with *śakti*, one should meditate upon the red light situated in the *bindu* as being within the handful of flowers, and then, having established it externally, [place it] within the form.
(Pervading that: "Pervasive of the form whose essence is Khaṣolka.

We shall explain the characteristics of the mudrās beginning with Āvāhinī and ending with Niṣṭhurā in the section concerning the invocation of Śiva. (The Bimba-mudrā. Thus, its characteristic has been stated in the *Mudrā-lakṣaṇa*.

"With palms joined together, the two ring fingers curved at the tips and touching, this is the 'beholding of the sun' [mudrā]. Regarding the phrase "(at the locations from the heart to the end of the hands)": those which have the heart as their beginning are "the heart and so forth" (*hṛdayādi*);
those which have the hand as their end are "the ends of the hands" (*karānta*); and these are both "the heart and so forth" and "the ends of the hands."

And those [mantras] ending with the hands (*karāntāni*), as well as those beginning with the heart (*hṛdayādi*) and ending with the hands (*karāntāni*), and those [mantras] pertaining to those respective locations (*sthānāni*)—thus it is said. (The term *ekatva* means) the non-separateness (*apṛthagbhāvam*) of the limbs, such as the heart, from the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*).
The definition of the *amṛtamudrā* has been stated previously. (Regarding *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya*: *pādya*...

And water for the feet, water for sipping (*ācamana*), water to be offered to the mouth, the *arghya* water to be presented to the head, and likewise the water thus prescribed—[these are offered] with the mantra: "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā. Here, [the mantra is]: "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā."
One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the feet with that [mantra] ending in *svadhā*; water for sipping (*ācamana*) in the mouth with that [mantra] ending in *svāhā*;
and the respectful offering (*arghya*) on the head. As he will state later: "At the feet, [one offers] with the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*."

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) with [the mantra] ending in *svadhā* to the five faces beginning with Īśāna, and likewise water for sipping (*ācamana*) with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā* to the five heads, one offers the respectful offering (*arghya*). Thus [it is said]: "(Anointing, etc.)"; by the word "etc.," rubbing with unguents (*udvartana*) and so forth are intended. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
Having removed the flowers placed upon its limbs while uttering the Astra-mantra,
and having anointed, rubbed with unguents, and wiped it in sequence with the root mantra and the Astra-mantra by name;

Thus. (Having bathed) thus. Here, having visualized the constituent parts of the bath such as the anointing with oil (*abhyaṅga*) and so forth, one should bathe [the deity] with drops of *arghya* water. The definition of the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*) was stated by the illustrious Bhojadeva: "Having formed the two hands into the shape of a lotus, [one places] the two thumbs in the middle."
"One should place them in the form of a pericarp. The definition of the *bimba-mudrā* has been shown previously.

Then, when there is the expectation of what should be done next, he says "(then)" [in the sense] that one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) preceded by the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*). Regarding the phrase "(having worshipped the limbs of dissolution)": here—

One should worship with the heart-mantra and other limb-mantras at the locations of the limbs, beginning with the heart. To the question of *in which places* and *how one should worship*, he says: "(Āgneya-aiśāna). He states that the locations of the limbs, beginning with the heart, are "(saumyāni)"—that is, beautiful or gracious. A "saumya" person is one who is gentle.

The term *budha* refers to a wise man, a Brahmin, or the three [Vedas] when it denotes the deity Soma; it also means "charming" or "gentle," according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. The rest is clear. "(Of the god)" means of the Sun, who is by nature playful (*devanaśīla*). "(In front)" means on the western petal. "(In that manner)" means as follows.

The meaning is "having taken [it] from the locus of the eyes. [It has] the previously mentioned form, its essential nature being proclaimed by the heart and other limbs. He states the meditation on the Sūrya-missile with the word "lightning" (*vidyut*);
the meaning of the verse is easy to understand.

The characteristics of the *goviṣāṇa-mudrā* and the *trāsanī-mudrā* have been observed by the illustrious Bhojadeva: the *goviṣāṇā* is formed by spreading and extending the middle and index fingers of the right hand while the fist remains clenched.
With the right hand in a clenched fist and the index finger extended, one strikes the palm of the left hand; this is called *trāsanī*. (One should worship) means one should offer the *arghya* water.

One might ask: "Is there no covering other than the heart and so forth of the Sun? Anticipating this doubt, he states that there is a covering consisting of the Moon and others with the words "(tadanu)" ("thereafter").
The extraction of the mantras for the Moon and the rest has been demonstrated in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*.

"The seed-syllable of the planets is the first letter of their respective names, conjoined with a bindu. He describes the meditation on Soma and the others with the word "(Soma)": "(Resembling a white water-lily and a jasmine flower)" means that which has a luster like that of both the *kumuda* (the white night-lily) and the *kunda* (the jasmine).

Thus he was addressed. Regarding "white" (*site*): "The *kairava* [lily] and the *ai-rava* [lotus] are white; the *mādhyam* is the *kunda*"—so says Amara. "(Shining with the luster of gold)" (*cāmīkaraprabham*): golden-colored. "(The Guru)" (*gurum*): Bṛhaspati.
"The *guru* refers to the Lord of Speech (*Gīṣpati*), the Father (*Pitṛ*), and so forth"—so says Amara. "(Resembling lapis lazuli)" (*rājāvartanibham*): *rājāvarta* [a type of gem].
"Black-colored" refers to a particular kind of flower; "resembling that" means equal to it. (Regarding the word) "Śani":
he is named Śani, born from the goddess Chāyā out of the Sun, abiding above the entire circle of planets, [influencing] the worlds through variations in his motion, aspect, and disposition.

(126) A specific planet is the cause of the auspicious and inauspicious. According to the *Vaijayantī*: "Śani, Manda, Kheṭaka, Koṇa, Chāyāputra, and Asirkaja [are synonyms]. Regarding (Rāhu): it is that which causes separation (*rahayati*).
"Candrārkau" refers to Rāhu; the remainder [of the verse] states that he is the son of Siṃhikā and has the mouth as his essence.
Kātyāyana, however, says that Rāhu is the eclipser of the moon, while Svarbhānu is the eclipser of the sun (for the purpose of establishing the auspicious time of the eclipse and other such matters).

He is called Rāhu because he has the form of Rāhu. Regarding "Ketu": Ketu is the name of a particular planet residing within the circle of planets, who is the embodied soul of the son born from the union [of the Sun and Moon], and who exists by virtue of drinking nectar and through the grace of Hara. [He is described as] having half a body and hair standing erect.

The two halves of the body are "half-bodies"; those two are also described as having hair standing erect and having upward-facing heads. Here, it should be understood that Rāhu consists of the head alone, while Ketu consists of the body alone. (Fierce with fangs): by means of the fang.

"Karālaḥ" means terrifying; according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "karāla" refers to that which is jagged, high, or terrifying. The definition of the *namo-mudrā* is traditionally taught as the two hands being constantly joined at the fingers.

The two hands are placed at the region of the heart; the binding of all [fingers] should be performed while pressing with the left thumb. This is to be known as the *namaskāra* (salutation) mudrā for all ritual actions.
One should cause [this] to be performed. Thus, with the *upahṛdaya* mantra: "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā. As was stated previously:

"Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khaṣolkā; thus, by means of the *upahṛdaya*. And so it has been declared by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and all else should be offered."

"By Khaṣolkin" means [the mantra consisting of] ten parts; that is, one-tenth. The intended meaning is that if the root-mantra of the Sun has been recited one hundred times, then one should recite it ten times for each of its ancillary limbs (*aṅga*).
He speaks of the hymns and so forth with the words "by Daṇḍyādyaiḥ"; [that is,] "by Daṇḍyādyaiḥ" means Daṇḍin and those who follow him.

By the word *pada*, Piṅgala and others are denoted. (*Seated upon a throne with four lion-feet of pure face*): *Vimala* refers to the one named Vimala; those for whom the lion is the "face" (*mukha*)—meaning the primary element—are so described according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. And he is the one whose feet are those four lions.
It has four lion legs with pure faces; he stands upon that which is both that [lion] and the seat, and thus he is so described. By the word "face" (mukha), [p.

"Sāra" and so forth are understood [as the names of the attendants]. "(Śaktijālaiḥ)" means by the multitudes of powers (*śakti*). "Jāla" means a multitude, a collection, a net, a lattice-window, or a carriage—thus says Amara.
"(Svāṅgasvāṅgagraharkṣapramukhaparivṛtaḥ)" refers to his own limbs (*svāṅga*)... [and so on].
"One's own limbs" refers to parts such as the heart; "one's own limbs" refers to the planets presiding over one's birth sign and so forth;
and "one's own limbs" refers to one's own retinue.
According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, the word *aṅga* is used in the senses of "limb," "proximity," "means," "symbol," and "secondary."
The *grahas* are those denoted by the word *graha*, such as the sun and others; thus says Amara: "The *grahas* are the sun and so forth.

The phrase "headed by the *ṛkṣas*" means the *ṛkṣas* are the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), and those headed by them—meaning those preeminent among them—are the moon, Mars, and so on. And [his] own limbs...

Surrounded and encompassed by those headed by Svāṅga, Graha, and Ṛkṣa— namely, Svāṅga, Svāṅgagraha, and Ṛkṣapramukha— he is thus described: (holding a white lotus with two hands), he is one who has a white lotus (*dhavalāmbuja*) upon his two shoulders— that is, the tops of his arms— and upon his two hands.

(Vaḥ) means "you. (Bhavatāt) means "may he protect. (The rest is clear. Here, the Guru prays for the protection of "you" (*vaḥ*), because he himself is included within "the world" (*loka*) [of those being protected] (p.

The sense is that he requests only his own departure. Although this verse is considered an interpolation, it has been explained [here]. (Parāṅmukhārghyam): the *arghya* water to be offered for the purpose of dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* regarding dismissal: "O son of Gaṅgā..."
"The arghya should be offered with the face turned away"—[meaning] "forgive" or "endure.
We shall explain the characteristics of the Nārāca and Divya mudrās later on.
And the worship of Caṇḍa is splendor.

(22) Then, in the northeastern direction, reciting "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Tejaścaṇḍa," one should meditate upon Caṇḍa as red, with a gaping mouth, and two hands holding a lotus and displaying the gesture of fearlessness; having thus visualized him, worshipped him, offered the remains of the previous offerings (*nirmālya*), and dismissed him, one should also offer the water of respect (*arghya*) and dismiss it.
Alternatively, one should dismiss [the deity] at the conclusion of the worship of Śiva.
(22) Now, having described the method for the worship of Mārtāṇḍa,
he states the procedure for the adoration of his attendant Caṇḍa with the passage beginning with "Then" and ending with "one should dismiss."
Regarding the dismissal of the Sun, he states an alternative with the words "or else" (*yadvā*).
This refers to the worship of the door, which is an ancillary part of the worship of Śiva.

(22) Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should purify the vessel for the general offering (sāmānyārghyapātra) with the Astra-mantra; fill it with pure water using the Hṛdaya-mantra ending in vauṣaṭ; and [then] with the Praṇava.

Having worshipped [the door] sevenfold, having consecrated it with mantras, and having performed the rites of veiling with jewels (*ratnāva-kuṇṭhana*) and making it nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should sprinkle the door with the *astra-mantra*; then, on the upper lintel (*udumbara*) in its southern portion, one should [visualize] Gaṇeśa, pot-bellied (*laṃbodara*) and resembling a dark cloud.
I praise him who holds an axe and a rosary with his two upward-pointing hands, and a spear and a sweetmeat with his lower left and right hands.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," one should [visualize] on its northern side [the goddess] Śuklā, white in color, clad in white garments, and holding a rosary and a book.
And with her right and left hands, she holds the very serene Sarasvatī.

(52) Contemplating thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī," [one should visualize] between those two [deities], Mahāśrī, golden-hued, holding a *śrīphala* fruit and a lotus in her left and right hands respectively, and being bathed by the two elephants holding water-pots.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī," [one should place her] on the right branch of oneself.
Nandikeśvara is red in color, has three eyes, and wears matted hair; with his two hands, right and left, he holds a rosary and a trident.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin," one should [visualize] Gaṅgā on his northern side, seated upon a crocodile-throne, white in form, holding a blue lotus and a full water-pot in her right and left hands respectively.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā," one should [place] Kṛṣṇa, Ṛkṣa, and Mahākāla on the northern branch with their two left and right hands.
Holding a skull and a trident, with a hideous countenance.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla," [one should visualize] on his right side Śyāmā, seated upon a tortoise, holding a water-pot in both her left and right hands.
And one should visualize Yamunā holding a blue lotus.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yamunā," one should inform them [of the need] for protection.

Now, having first explained the procedure for the worship of the Sun among the sixfold supports beginning with the Sun, [the author] speaks of the ritual of the gateway for the protection of that temple in order to describe the worship of Śiva based on the *liṅga*, starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
[Up to the point of] "having informed" (*vijñāpya*). Then, after the worship of the Sun (*sūryārcanānantaram*). "(Having performed the ritual rinsing)" (*ācamya*):

this is for the purpose of terminating the previously mentioned solar contemplation (*saurabhāvanā*). He states the procedure for placing the general *arghya* vessel for the sake of worshipping the door: "the general *arghya* vessel" (*sāmānyārghyapātram*).

With pure water—that is, with water whose form is nectar flowing from droplets—and with the *praṇava*: that which, though repeatedly revolved by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), becomes ever-new moment after moment through excessive devotion; that is the *praṇava*, namely the single-syllabled "Oṃ. Likewise:

"In the *Śrīmat-suprabheda*, all yogins declare that the single-syllable Brahman is 'Oṃ'; it is called the *praṇava* because it expresses [the meaning] in brief. (Having consecrated with this)—here, "seven times" is to be understood. Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-sahasra*:

"Having addressed the *praṇava* seven times, one should display the *dhenumudrā*. Then, in response to the expectation of what follows next, he states the sequence for the worship of the door (*dvāra*) with the word "the door. (The Door)
The western door. In this regard, worship at the western door alone is recommended for a mobile liṅga;

however, for a fixed liṅga, the intent is that worship should be performed according to the respective door. Thus, in the venerable Aṃśumatī, having worshipped the door in the western region of Kheṭaka, the preceptor—

Thus it has been said in the venerable *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*: "Thereafter, one should worship the gatekeepers at the western door. If one asks how, it is because the western door consists of earth (*pārthiva*), because it is composed of Sadyojāta, and because that which consists of earth bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). Likewise...

"One who desires success should invoke [the deity] at the western door for the desired goal. Regarding this, some describe Sadāśiva as facing westward; that is incorrect, because he is the Sadyojāta form and is the cause of creation. Likewise, Īśa is the head...
The eastern face is Aghora, the heart is Vāma,
the secret place is Sadyojāta, and the form is Sādākhya; [these correspond respectively to] the eastern face, the heart, and the feet.

Thus, having contemplated Sadāśiva’s facing eastward according to the manner already described and that which is about to be stated, one should worship the door-keepers at the western gate. Furthermore,
the right and left positions of both one's own self and Sadāśiva are relative to the western gate itself.

And as he will state later: "Having worshipped the gatekeepers as if they were permanent," therein, regarding the gatekeepers, he first mentions the worship of Gaṇapati with the word "of that" (*tasya*). "Of that" refers to the door. "Upon the *udumbara*" means on the lintel situated above; *udumbara* refers to the wooden lintel of a door.

Thus ends the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. Regarding the phrase "on the right side" (*dakṣiṇabhāge*): here, the distinction between right and left must be understood from the perspective of the worshipper. As it was stated by the illustrious Bhojadeva:
"The Nandi, Gaṅgā, Mahākāla, and Yamunā are on the right and left branches of the Self."
He describes his meditation: "(Lambodaram)" means [the one with a protruding belly]. "(Kuṭhāram)" means an axe. "(Īḍe)" means I praise.
The rest is easy to understand.

He describes the worship of Sarasvatī with the words "on its northern side" (referring to page 135). This means on the northern flank of that Gaṇapati. He states her visualization with the word "white."
(With the right and left hands) means with the right and left hands.

According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "savya" refers to the left and right. The rest is clear. He describes the worship of Mahālakṣmī with the words "(of those two)": (of those two), namely Gaṇapati and Sarasvatī.
He describes her meditation with the word "(vāma)": "(śrīphalāmbuje)" means the *śrīphala* and the lotus (*ambuja*).
Regarding *śrīphala*, Amara states: "The *bilva* fruit is the *śrīphala*; [the synonyms for *bilva* are] *śāṇḍilya*, *śailūṣa*, *mālūra*, and *śrīphala*.
*Ambuja* is the lotus; these two [are held by her]. "(saghaṭebhābhyām)" means together with the jar (*ghaṭa*) or pitcher (*kumbha*).
"Moving along" refers to those two elephants together with their jars; "by those two" means by both the jar-bearing elephants.
"(Being flooded)" means being sprinkled;
[this occurs] by both elephants, who hold their frontal globes (*kumbha*) aloft on their trunks (*puṣkara*) on both sides.

The meaning is "being consecrated. The sense of the verse is easy to understand. He states the worship of Nandin with the words "(of himself). To dispel the doubt—"But why is the service of Nandin [performed] in the previously mentioned place?"—he says "(on the right branch)."
The meaning is: on the door-jamb situated at his own right side.
He describes its visualization with the word "red" (*rakta*). "With matted hair" (*jaṭila*) means possessing matted locks (*jaṭāvantam*). The rest is easily understood.

Regarding the propitiation of Gaṅgā, it says "(on its northern side)": that is, on the northern flank of that Nandin. Regarding her visualization, it says "(seated upon a crocodile-throne)": the meaning of the verse is clear.
Regarding the lineage of Mahākāla, it says "(that)": (on its northern branch).

Of that Gaṅgā, the northern branch is the door-branch situated in the northern direction; the meaning is "on her left branch," which refers to one's own left side. He describes the meditation upon her as "(black)" and so forth. "(Vikaṭānanaḥ)" means having a face made formidable by fangs; likewise, she is black.
"Yellow matted hair, terrifying, with a face formidable with fangs"—the rest is clear.

Regarding the image of Yamunā, he says "I [worship] that," which is on the right side (of the deity), specifically on the southern part of Mahākāla. He describes her visualization as "dark-complexioned" (*śyāmām*); this is easy to understand.

This is the meaning of the verse. Here, it has been stated by the venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati* that one should offer the *arghya* to Gaṇapati and the others with their respective mantras; and he will also state this in the ritual for installation (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*).
"In the west, as before, having worshipped and offered the *arghya* to the gatekeepers"— that is,
to these gatekeepers beginning with Gaṇapati. "Having informed them"— that is, by you.
The meaning is that one should pray, "May you remain as protectors of this place of worship with due reverence."
The eradication of obstacles.

(23) Having looked upward with the eyes fixed on the root [of the nose], one should cast flowers toward the celestial beings with the *astra* mantra, "Oṃ aḥ astrāya phaṭ," using the blazing *nārāca* mudrā; then, toward those moving in the intermediate space, one should strike three times with the right heel while reciting the *pāśupata-astra*, "Oṃ huṃ phaṭ."
Having expelled the three kinds of obstacles situated on the ground from the sacrificial hall— (23)—

he then, having prescribed the worship of the gatekeepers, describes the eradication of obstacles for the sake of completing the Śiva-worship without impediment, beginning with the words "placed" (*nyasta*) and so forth.

(With the words ending in) "udvāsya" (having dismissed). "(Nyastamūlena)" means that the root [mantra] has been placed; the root mantra "oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ," which is uttered up to the end of Māyā, has been deposited by means of the thumb and the ring finger.
By that which is so described; likewise, in the *Śrīmac-Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"With the thumb and the ring finger, [one should perform the rite] with 'Oṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva' at the end, and also upon the two eyes."

"Having performed the placement [of mantras] and gazed upon the divine obstacles"—thus [it is said]. By the word "with the eye," the meaning is that one gazes with a divine vision by virtue of having performed the foundational placement (*mūlanyāsa*). Thus it was instructed by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu: "By the casting of the divine gaze, [one perceives] those who move about in the divine realm."

Thus: (the celestial ones) are those that belong to the heavens (*divi*), hence "celestial" (*divyān*). (The sky-goers) are those that go to the sky (*antarikṣa*), which is space; hence "sky-goers" (*antarikṣagān*).
(By three blows with the right heel) refers to the right heel (*dakṣiṇapārṣṇiḥ*).
"The heel of the right foot" refers to the male *pārṣṇi*; "the part below those two" is also *pārṣṇi*, according to Amara.

"Strikes" (*ghātāḥ*) means blows; "by that triad" [of such strikes]. "(Those standing on the ground)": those who stand upon the earth are *bhūmiṣṭhāḥ*; [the word] "them" (*tān*). "(Threefold)": [referring to the three types].
Having dismissed—that is, having expelled—the three types [of obstacles] distinguished as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
The entry into the abode of Śiva and so forth.
(28) Taking hold of a branch on the left side with his right foot leading, he enters within; at the threshold, reciting "Oṃ haḥ,
salutation to the weapon-gatekeeper," he should contemplate the form that will be described hereafter.
Having worshipped him and circumambulated [the site] clockwise, one should worship in the southwest (nairṛta) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site.
[He is] seated upon a swan, pot-bellied, fair-complexioned, with a beard and four faces.
Holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot in his right and left hands respectively.
Having meditated thus and performed worship,
he then describes the sequence for dispelling divine and other obstacles,
and states the entry into the abode of Śiva and what must be done immediately thereafter with the words beginning with "kiṃcit" and so forth.
[Having meditated] up to this point; [then] "leaning slightly on the left branch,
entering within with the right foot foremost"—
this has been designated by the Illustrious One as being for the purpose of following the deities residing in the branches.
By the commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*: [at] the threshold, [specifically] at the lower post of the door (*adhodumbare*).
The house-entrance (*gṛhāvagrahaṇī*), p. 140.

"Dehalī," according to Amara; [this refers to] the Śivāstra. Likewise: "The Śivāstra is in the middle of the threshold, with its seat and so forth as before. [It has] the form that will be described: "Then the weapon is fanged and of tawny luster"—this is the nature that will be described. Here...

It should be understood that the worship of Amara at the threshold is for the purpose of completely dispelling the multitude of obstacles, such as those of the divine class and so forth. Thus it has been demonstrated by the Gurus in the *Śrīmat-Pañcāvaraṇa-stava*:

"I worship the weapon [astra] possessing the brilliance of the fire at the end of the eon, situated beneath the udumbara tree, which wards off the multitudes of obstacles dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and upon the earth. Thus it is said.
Then, as to what one should do next, he says: "In the southwest" (nairṛte). He describes the meditation on Brahmā, the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati):

"Seated upon a swan. "Fair-complexioned" means yellowish-white (*pītavarṇa*). According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "fair" (*gaura*) refers to reddish-brown, white, and yellow. "Possessing a four-faced [form] with a beard" means those four faces which exist together with a beard—that is, facial hair.

He who possesses these is so described; [namely] the staff, the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), the rosary beads (*akṣa*), and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). Here, "staff" refers to the *sruva* ladle, and "beads" refers to [the rosary].
Akṣamālā: The rest is easily understood. (Having worshipped) — thus it connects with what precedes.
The method for gathering the requisites for worship.

(25) For the purpose of bathing, having purified the water-jars with the four purificatory rites and having cleansed the water and cloth with the *astra* mantra, one should fill them with pure water filtered through a cloth using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having gathered all the materials, such as flowers and so forth, for the sake of the sacrifice, [the author] then,

after describing the preparation of the abode of Śiva and other matters, explains the method of collecting the bathing water, the sacred sites, and the ritual implements for worship, beginning with the words "For the purpose of bathing" (*snapanārtham*).
(Upāhṛtya) means up to that point. (Guḍḍukān) refers to the consecration jars (*abhiṣeka-kalaśa*) numbering one hundred and eight, and so forth.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "One hundred, plus eight, or half [of that]."

"Indeed, eight half-portions [of water] should always be offered as *gaḍḍukas* according to the rule and in due order. And as he will say: "Having cast drops of water along with flowers into the vessels containing the bathing water," [this applies] even by means of the *śivakalaśa* that has been established.
"Having bathed," it is said. "Refined by the four purificatory rites" (*catuḥ-saṃskāra-saṃskṛtān*):
the four purificatory rites are the *catuḥ-saṃskārāḥ*, and these here consist of inspection and so forth; they have been refined by those [rites].
Those who possess the excellence of meditative absorption [should perform] those [rites]. Likewise, in the venerable Kāmika:

"The sprinkling of the arena should be done with the root mantra, the sprinkling [of the materials] with the weapon mantra, the striking with the weapon mantra, and the sprinkling [of the site] with the armor mantra."
Thus: (having brought near) means having placed in close proximity.
Purification of the elements.

(26) On the southern side of the deity, having sat upon a seat facing north on a seat made of *bruva* wood and so forth, one should protect the sacrificial hall by means of the enclosures of the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and the armor-encasement (*kavaca-avakuṇṭhana*).
One should perform the act of making [the body] auspicious (*śivīkaraṇa*). Therein, having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*),

one should [visualize the breath] starting from the two big toes up to the bladder as having a dual form, and from there upwards to the abode of Brahmā (*brahmanila*) as having a single form, [proceeding] through the heart, throat, and other centers by means of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels.
Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā in the form of a hollow tube, joined with downward-facing lotus buds, both internally and externally within that very [tube]...
Having visualized the power (*śakti*) whose form is the supreme ether as a stream of the nectar of speech, and having contemplated the blazing syllable *HŪṂ* (the life-force) in the center,
one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kuṃbhaka*), fix the mind upon the syllable *HŪṂ*, and [direct] the breath upward.
One should administer purgation.

By the continuous recitation of "HŪṂ PHAṬ," one should cause the lotus buds to turn upward and their knots to be severed; having turned them back [downward], one should exhale through the right channel (piṅgalā), and then,
by means of the inhalation (pūraka) breath, [one should draw up] the consciousness that has been withdrawn and is resting in the heart-lotus.
Having placed the individual soul (jīva)— which has the form of a shimmering star, consists of the peaceful seed-syllable,

and is manifested from the heart— upon the top of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should contemplate the subtle Person (puruṣa), limited by the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), whose body is the seed-syllable and who resides within the crest of the *hūṃ*.
Having meditated upon [the breath] as having become a single drop (bindu), solitary and free from disease,
and having performed the kumbhaka, one should draw the wind upward by means of the saṃhāramudrā.

By means of a single expulsion (*udghāta*) through the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, one should unite [the self] with Śiva at the *dvādaśānta* for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma, reciting: *oṃ hūṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hūṃ ātmane namaḥ*.

Thus, dissolved in Śiva by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), for the sake of purifying the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), one should cause the principles (*tattva*) to dissolve, in reverse order, into their respective causes up to the point of the *bindu*.
Namely: earth in smell, water in taste, fire in form, air in touch, and space in sound—these are the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) within the *tāmasa* ego;
and those called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are within the *rājasa* ego.

The senses called ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, as well as the mind, are dissolved into the *sāttvika* ego; that [ego] into the intellect (*buddhi*); that into the *guṇas*; the principle of the *guṇas* into *prakṛti*; that into attachment, destiny, and *kalā*;
the principles of the person (*puruṣa*), time, and necessity (*niyati*), along with *kalā*, into *māyā*. Thus they are dissolved.
Having contemplated this, one should meditate that the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) dissolves into the principle of Īśvara; that [Īśvara] into the principle of Sadāśiva;
that into the principle of Śakti; and that into the principle of Śiva. One should further contemplate that even that [Śiva] dissolves into the Bindu, which is of an undisturbed nature.
Alternatively, one should abandon sound and touch in Brahmā; indeed, one should abandon taste in Keśava;
one should abandon form and smell in Rudra; and the intellect and ego in Īśvara.
The knower of reality, having gradually dissolved the mind-bindu into Śivā,
should then purify the gross body; [he visualizes] the yellow mandala of earth.
The *kaṭhina* is marked with a vajra; it is presided over by the presiding deity Sadyojāta through the earthly seed-syllable *ma*, and is purified by Brahmā, the Lord of Causes,
as he expels [the impurities] from the feet.
3. Having turned back.
Having meditated upon the square form of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, which is joined [to the body] from the feet up to the head, one should [recite]: "Oṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ hlāṃ, to the *nivṛtti-kalā*:
haḥ huṃ phaṭ," preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*) within the *suṣumnā*.
Having impelled the vital breath as far as the *dvādaśānta* and having drawn it back, one should exhale through the right channel (*piṅgalā*). Thus, by means of five *udghātas*,
having cast out the qualities of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, [one casts out] the earth.
One should contemplate it as being overcome by its own contrary wind and endowed with that [wind's] form.
Following that, the watery mandala, which has the nature of fluidity, resembles a half-moon, is gentle, white, and marked with the sign of water; it is [generated] from the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Presided over by the seed-syllable Vāmadeva as the presiding lord, and joined with Viṣṇu as the Lord of Causes, it takes the form of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.
Having meditated upon it as before with the syllable *hrīṃ*, one should proceed as previously described by means of the fourfold upward expulsion (*udghāta*).
Having dispelled the four qualities beginning with taste, one should contemplate the water as being overcome by its own opposite, fire, and thus assuming its form.
Then, the Āgneya-maṇḍala— triangular, red, marked with svastikas,

presided over by the lord Aghora with the seed-syllable *hrūṃ* as its mantra, joined with Rudra as the Lord of Causes, and consisting of the form of the Vidyā-kalā (*hrūṃ*)— [is established] by means of the threefold *udghāta*.
Having dispelled the triad of qualities such as form, one should meditate upon that [consciousness] as having that very form, for it has been overcome by water which is its own opposite.
Afterwards, one should draw a hexagonal mandala for Vāyu, marked with six dots, black in color, presided over by the seed-syllable of Vāyu, "yaṃ," and by the Tatpuruṣa face;
it is endowed with Īśvara as the Lord of Causes, and consists of the aspect of the Śāntikala through two upward thrusts (udghāta).
Having removed the two qualities of touch and sound, one should contemplate the wind— its nature overwhelmed by its opposite, earth— assuming the form of that [earth].
Thereafter, in the circle of the sky, one should contemplate the syllable *haum*, which has the form of space, resembles pure crystal, is empty, and is adorned by the power of the *bindu*.

Having meditated upon it as presided over by the sovereign Lord Īśāna, whose seed-syllable is *nabhaḥ*, and as being endowed with Sadāśiva, the Lord of Causes, and consisting of the Śāntyatīta-kalā, one should— just as before—
expel the quality of sound (*śabda-guṇa*) with a single *udghāta* as previously described.
Having abandoned one's own nature characterized by impermanence, non-pervasiveness, impurity, and so forth,
one should meditate upon a nature that has overcome the supreme space (paramākāśa), which is endowed with permanence, pervasiveness, purity, and other such qualities.
Then, having burned the defects of the elements residing in the body with the fire arising from the toe of the foot by means of the Astra-mantra,
one should flood it.
Or rather, one's own body is the seed of the elements such as earth;
it is a sprout produced by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, rooted in passion, hatred, virtue, vice, and delusion, and guarded by the lords of knowledge and ignorance.

The essence of which consists of the principles beginning with *kalā*, whose branches and sub-branches are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), whose sprouts are the perceptions of objects, whose flowers are the manifoldness of states of being (*bhāva-prapañca*),
whose fruit is the determination and volition of the intellect (*buddhi-adhyavasāya-saṃkalpa*), and which is to be enjoyed by the bird that is the *puruṣa*.

Having meditated upon the form of the great banyan tree— with its roots above and branches below, characterized by the essence of the relationship between the enjoyed and the enjoyer— one should [meditate] with the first half of the *pūraka* breath.
Having meditated upon [the tree] as rigid, devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruit, by means of the fivefold utterance of the seed-syllable of the *nivṛtti*-kalā;

and having contemplated it as glossy and endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit, by means of the fourfold utterance of the seed-syllable of the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā during the latter half of the inhalation (*pūraka*).

Having visualized [the body] as dried up, stripped of leaves and the like, and burnt by the fire of Time (Kālāgni) arising from the big toe of the right foot— [this being effected] through the first and second halves of the *kumbhaka* and the three-fold utterance of the seed-syllables of the *vidyā-kalā*— one should then, with the first half of the *recaka* and the two-fold utterance of the seed-syllables of the *śānti-kalā*, [proceed].

Having visualized [the body] as reduced to ashes and dissolved into the ten directions, one should contemplate it as having the form of pure crystal and the nature of space, by means of the second half of the exhalation (*recaka*) and the single utterance of the seed-syllable of the *śāntyatītā* kalā.

Then, having meditated upon the form of the bonds as being entirely empty, one should [purify] one's own exterior and interior by means of the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, through streams of nectar flowing from the downward-facing lotus situated within the crest-lock (*śikhā*), which have entered the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*).
Having bathed the entire body,
[one should visualize] in the heart a lotus in the form of a stalk, petals, and pericarp, joined with the three vowels beginning with *a*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seat (*āsana*), which has descended through the *praṇava* and consists of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*),

one should contemplate the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) within its pericarp as having descended through the *praṇava* with four parts; therein [one should contemplate] that which resides at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*) in the form of a seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Having brought the self, which consists of Śiva, into the state of emanation through the *pūraka* breath using the five-part *praṇava*, and having established it in the form of light, one should consecrate it with a stream of abundant nectar from the agitated power (*śakti*) by reciting the mantra of power ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Now, having described the sequence for bringing the materials for worship, [it is said]: "He who knows the five-fold purification is fit to perform the worship. This is according to the statement of the venerable Vātula-tantra, and also because of the Vedic revelation: "Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva."

Having kept in mind that one should become Śiva through the practice of *sakalīkaraṇa*, supreme contemplation, the focal point (*ālambana*), and so forth, and then worship Śiva both internally and externally, he first focuses on describing the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*). Regarding that—
Since [the ritual] consists of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*), oblation (*havanas*), and meditative absorption (*samādhisamāhāra*),
he first sets forth the procedure for the purification of the elements among those [steps], beginning with the words "of the deity" (*devasya*) and so forth.

(60) [The ritual] ends with the words "one should consecrate. If it is asked what is accomplished here by means of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, it is replied: for those who have taken the pledges (*samayin*), whose powers are manifest and who are established as obstacles and suppressors, their burning away is intended here.
"And for those [initiates], their burning away or cessation is considered to occur at that time. Thus it is said.
For those initiated into nirvāṇa, however, karma spanning many births is burnt by the [mantric] seeds like a seed by fire.
For that by which even the future is obstructed is indeed due to enjoyment.
Thus, even though the karma whose effects have begun is being exhausted day by day through experience during initiation, because latent impressions (*vāsanā*) still persist,
there remains— following those impressions— a state that produces attachment toward objects of enjoyment for the one who is the experiencer.

It has been declared by the Illustrious One that the portion consisting of impurity (*malāṃśaka*), which generates the body and senses as the instruments for that [bondage], and the portion consisting of *māyā*, undergo daily diminution part by part. (p. 151)
By the author of the *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva-vṛtti*: [this refers to] the deity who is to be worshipped. "In the southern quarter" means in the vicinity of Aghora;
for it is not possible for the deity to face north while stationed in the northern quarter, as that would be contrary to the deity's orientation.

"Likewise, one should not worship the God in the east in front of Śambhu, nor in the north where there is a woman's presence, nor in the west since [Śiva's] back is turned; rather, one should worship the God facing him.
Here, by the statement "in the east in front of Śambhu," it is indicated that [the worshipper] should face the east.
This has indeed been established regarding the Supreme Lord. It is not in the west, because it is said "since [it is] behind";
thus, it is logical that it is situated upon the back of the neck of the western part of the God, namely the face of Sadyojāta—this is what was stated.

In the *Śrīmadvālajñānaratnāvalī*: "On a seat such as a *brahmāsana*—where *brahmāsana* means a seat of *darbha* grass, and the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*) refers to tiger skins and so forth; likewise, in the *Śrīmatsūkṣma*, it says: 'The seat is [made of] *darbha* grass, wood, or even the skin of a spotted deer.'"
And: "A tiger skin with its hair intact, or a jeweled woolen rug, is the seat.
According to Amara, *brasī* is the seat for those observing vows (*vratin*).

First, regarding the comfortable seat (*sukhāsana*): it is a seat designated as "well-positioned" among the lotus-posture (*padmāsana*) and others. As it has been said: "The seat of comfort is that which is well-positioned for the sake of spiritual welfare. Now, in a pure house of worship, protected by a wall of weapons—
Having become Śiva within the armor, one should worship Śiva both externally and internally.

Thus, from the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, [the author] states the sequence for protecting the abode of Śiva as "(the rampart of missiles). Then, asking "what should one do next?", he says "(the act of making [everything] Śiva-like).
Now, the act of making [everything] Śiva-like (*śivīkaraṇa*) is the ritual action that serves as the means for achieving the specific purification of the self.

As the venerable author of the *Sarvajñānottaravṛtti* stated: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme process of making [the self] Śiva. In this context, "Śiva-nature" is said to consist of omniscience and omnipotence.
And because of its connection with that which is eternal and unobstructed, the Supreme Lord is designated as Śiva.

Furthermore, that state of Śiva does not manifest with respect to all objects for individual selves, because it is veiled by impurity (*mala*), which is a beginningless succession of impurity. This has also been stated by the Teachers: "Not everywhere simultaneously."
(62) "Śiva shines forth. Therefore, it is said that here Śiva is designated as pure.

One who is possessed of impurities and the like is inauspicious and impure; furthermore, according to the venerable *Kiraṇa-śruti*, "for that [impurity] is indeed [exhausted] through experience. Thus, in the initiation for liberation from an unreal womb (*asadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), there is a complete cessation of the experience of karma whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakāryakarman*).
Since impurity has not been destroyed, it must be removed after initiation through daily rites such as the process of diminishing it and the subsequent acts of consecration as Śiva and worship;
for the self endowed with that degree of purification, there exists a distinction from ordinary purification, which will be described hereafter.

Because it is the cause of purity immediately following bathing and other rites, I shall explain the supreme *śivīkaraṇa*— which effects a specific purification— in both its concise and detailed forms.
It is that by which the non-Śiva is made to become Śiva.
The meaning of the term *śivīkaraṇa* (the act of making [something] Śiva) is as follows; he explains how this is so with the words "(tatra)" (therein).
Regarding that *śivīkaraṇa*, it says "(having performed the karanyāsa)" (having performed the ritual placement of the hands). Here, previously [on page 154]:
If both the karanyāsa and aṅganyāsa were performed, there would be the undesirable consequence of burning the mantras placed in locations such as the heart;
therefore, it has been stated that only karanyāsa should be performed first.
In the *Śrīmad-Bālajñānaratnāvalī*, having raised the doubt as to what should be done thereafter,

[the author] first describes the meditation on that [path], since one must perform the going and coming of the self by way of the *suṣumṇā* channel, beginning with the words "(from the two big toes)" up to "(as far as the bladder)."
The meaning is that the limit extends as far as the *mūlādhāra*.

Likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*: "The lotus of the *vasti*, having four petals, is a treasury of splendors. According to Amarasimha, *vasti* refers to the two [muscles] below the navel (*nābhi*). [This extends] up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*).
"Up to the aperture of Brahmā" means [through] the heart, throat, and so forth. By the word "and so forth," the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā are included.
"Joined with the iḍā and piṅgalā" refers here to the left side of the body.
The *iḍā* channel is on the left, the *piṅgalā* channel is on the right, and the *suṣumnā* channel is in the middle;
likewise [it is stated] in the *Sarvajñānottara*, p. 155.

"That which goes through the left nostril is celebrated as Iḍā; Piṅgalā is to be known in the right, and Suṣumnā is situated in the middle. Thus [it is said]. (In the form of a hollow) means having the shape of a cavity.
According to Amara, "suṣira" and "randhra" are used in three genders. (Having meditated thus) means like a streak of lightning.
The meaning is "having visualized her as radiant. "(Of that very)" means of Suṣumnā herself.
"(The Śakti whose form is the supreme ether)" means she whose form—the supreme ether, the supreme space known as Kuṇḍalinī—is the substratum to be presided over; such is she.
The meaning is that, by means of that [channel], one perceives Śiva-śakti, who presides over the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) of the Self and rains down nectar flowing forth from that [channel].
Thus it has been instructed by the authors of the commentary on the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* (in the middle).
"In the interval within the power situated in the middle of the cavity. Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Outside the end of the cavity, one should place the power whose form is space (*vyomarūpinī*); in its center, however, the syllable *hūṃ*, blazing with the luster of fire. (The syllable *hūṃ*).
The seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā*).
(Jvalantam) blazing, shining like a lamp. He states the rites to be performed immediately thereafter:
(Exhalation): Having first expelled the impure air, the filling of the body with the pure external air according to one's capacity.
(Retention): The abandonment consisting of exhalation and the gathering consisting of the form of filling.
Having abandoned [the breath], one remains in the state of having made [the body] like a pitcher (kumbhī) by means of the restraint of the internal wind.
Thus, in the *Śrīmattantrasāra*: "One should expel the impure wind residing in the body and situated in space; then, having drawn in the pure wind by means of inhalation (*pūraka*)."

"Śanaiḥ śanaiḥ" (very slowly). This has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The filling of the limit of the power of the embodied form by means of the external air is *pūraka* (inhalation); through its practice, one may even draw back [the breath] from a distance. Having abandoned both emission (*tyāga*) and retention (*saṃgrahaṇa*), cessation is known as *kuṃbhaka* (retention). Thus it is said.
(The wind) with the breath held in *kumbhaka*; (upwards) as far as the *dvādaśānta*. (One should exhale):
the meaning is that one should cast the wind residing in the lotus of the heart out through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

157) "(By the continuous recitation of *hūṃ phaṭ*). This means that one should first establish the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā*) ending with *phaṭ*, and then recite that mantra five times without interruption.
Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, one should utter the *śikhā* (the crest-mantra) above the navel, visualizing it in the form of a lamp;
then, by means of that [flame], conjoined with the mind and the vital breath, one should pierce the five knots.

"Uttering that [mantra] ending in *phaṭ* with a long *r*-sound (*surecaka*) one by one for each [of the centers]," thus [it is said]. "(Those with split knots)": those whose knots—that is, the joints of the petals—are split or burst open;
these are located here in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The intended meaning is that the cluster of downward-facing lotus buds is opened by the *pūraka* (inhalation),
restrained by the *kumbhaka* (retention), and turned upward by the *ūrdhvarecaka* (upward exhalation).
Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Samānatantra*:
The lotus indeed blossoms when filled by inhalation;
the lotus becomes an upward-flowing stream when restrained by retention.
Thus, having expelled the breath externally by means of *virecana*,

and having grasped the self situated therein, one should make the body a "drop" (*bindu*) located in the center through the act of emission; then, visualizing the fiery weapon (*astra*), one should burn away the fetters.
Thus, according to the venerable *Kiraṇa-śruti*,
he explains the method of uniting the self with Śiva for the purpose of burning away the body (once again).

"By means of the *pūraka* breath" [is said]. "With consciousness withdrawn" (*saṃhṛtacaitanya*): the meaning is that consciousness (*caitanya*)—the state or activity of the conscious one, consisting of vision and action—is withdrawn; he is so described because he possesses that.
Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Consciousness consists of vision and action."
Regarding the phrase "(resting in the heart-lotus)": here,

it should be noted that the venerable commentators on the *Sarvajñānottara* have stated that the Self, which resides within the subtle body known as the *puryaṣṭaka*, is to be contemplated precisely in the region of the heart.
(Shining with the form of a twinkling star) having the appearance of a brilliantly blazing constellation;
(consisting of the seed-syllable ending in *s*) "ending in *s*" means the letter *ha*; "seed" (*bīja*) means the syllable consisting of the letter *ha* joined with the *bindu*. Thus:
In the venerable *Vātulaśuddhā*, [it is said]:
"The secret sound (*nāda*) is the supreme life-force; the body is the fifth element.
That which ends with the letter *sa* (the *sānta*), ending with the principles (*tattva*), ending with the elements (*bhūta*), and ending with Śiva, is the void (*śūnya*), the imperishable."
*Varṇa*, *bīja*, *arṇa*, *lipi*, *akṣara*, and *mātṛkā*—
these indeed are the names bound together as synonyms for *varṇa*.
Thus it is said; and so the venerable author of the *Kiraṇavṛtti* states:
"And here, the seed is that which was previously mentioned as the originator of mantras, such as the *praṇava* (OM), and so forth."
“(Enveloped by the heart): the meaning is that it has been made into a heart-enclosure (*hṛtsaṃpuṭa*), with the heart-seed-syllable in the middle.

“(Having placed it upon the crest of the syllable *HŪṂ*): the meaning is that, by means of the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one has caused it to mount the tip of the syllable *HŪṂ*. “(The form of the seed-syllable): this refers to the seed-syllable itself.

"Of peaceful nature" means he whose body or form (*vigraha*) is encapsulated by the heart-mantra as previously described. "(Situated within the crest of the *hūṃ* syllable)" means that because it is placed upon the head of the *hūṃ* syllable, it is situated within its crest; thus it has been stated.
By the authors of the commentary on the *Śrī-sarvajñānottara*: "(Constricted by the puryaṣṭaka)" means constricted by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) called the *puryaṣṭaka*;
here, the *puryaṣṭaka* is that which is fixed for each individual soul, beginning from the start of creation.

The subtle body (sūkṣmadeha) is of an uncommon nature, consisting of the thirty principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with kalā; it remains stable until the end of the kalpa or until liberation. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Tattvasaṅgraha*:
This group of principles, beginning with earth and ending with *kalā*, which is determined for each individual soul,
wanders by the power of karma through all the worlds and bodies born therein.
Thus [it is said]. Now, [one might ask]:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the 'city of eight' (puryaṣṭaka)."

Thus it is heard in the venerable *Kālottara*. This is indeed true; for that very reason, that sūtra was explained there by the blessed Rāmakaṇṭha as denoting the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). But how, then, does this [group] constitute the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*)?

There is no contradiction, because [the body] is composed of five groups— namely, the elements (*bhūta*), subtle elements (*tanmātra*), organs of action (*karmendriya*), organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— as well as their cause, which is the *guṇa*, and its fulfiller, the *pradhāna*,
in the form of the group consisting of the five coverings beginning with *kalā*. Thus, there is no inconsistency.

(The word) *puruṣam* means the self (*ātman*). According to Amara, "the self is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the self, and the person (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, the etymological derivation of the word *puruṣa* is cited as follows:
"They call the unmanifest the mind; the body is called the city (*pura*)."
The Puruṣa rests in the city called the Unmanifest; therefore, he is so designated.
Thus: (having become a bindu), by the process of dissolution through the utterance of the mantra, it is the nature of the bindu which is the supreme cause; (it is solitary).

Being liberated by means of the subtle body; likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is said: "Gradually abandoning even the subtle body through the upward movement of the breath (*śikhā-uccāra*), one attains the *bindu* in the form of *nāda*. (Regarding the term *nirāmaya*: *āmaya* has departed.)
He is so described because he possesses afflictions such as ignorance (avidyā) and qualities such as sattva;
his characteristic is that of the *saṃhāramudrā*, as stated in the section on the characteristics of mudrās.
Now, the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā] consists of the four fingers beginning with the little finger placed at the base of the thumb.
"In due order, those consisting of fetters should be demonstrated in the presence of the householder.

[This refers to] the abandonment—that is, the relinquishment—of those causes which have Brahmā as their first; that is, those things beginning with Brahmā which are causes, and their subsequent casting off.
The sequence is as follows: the term "and so forth" (ādi) refers to Viṣṇu and the others. Herein is the sequence of relinquishment (*tyāga*):

the relinquishment of Brahmā in the center of the heart-lotus; the relinquishment of Viṣṇu in the throat-lotus; the relinquishment of Rudra in the palate-lotus; the relinquishment of Maheśvara between the eyebrows; and [the relinquishment] in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
It should be understood as the renunciation of Sadāśiva. (By means of *udghāta*: an upward strike;
*udghāta* [is so called] because of the movement of *udāna*, by which the wind is impelled as far as the *dvādaśānta*).
Likewise, in the venerable Sarvajñānottara,
it is stated that when complete cessation has been achieved, the vital air (vāyu) subsequently flows upward;
this is known as the "upward thrust" (udghāta), which occurs by its own will even for those of lesser capacity.

Thus it is said; likewise, in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "Because it possesses the nature of striking upwards, because it forcefully breaks through the knots, and because of the opening of the knots, it is defined as 'the upward strike' (*udghāta*)."

Thus [he says]. And he will state later: "Having first performed *pūraka*, having impelled the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) through the *suṣumnā* as far as the *dvādaśānta*, and having brought it back, one should expel it through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) by means of five *udghātas*. An *udghāta* is the initial impulse [of the breath].
Thus says Amara. The extraction of the mantra of the Self has been demonstrated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"The syllable *Haṃ*, having the form of a star, is the life-force (*jīva*) enclosed within the heart."
One should place the consciousness, drawn in by the *pūraka* breath, upon the tip of the *hūṃ* syllable.

Thus [it is said]. (For the purpose of experiencing karma that is to be experienced: Karma to be experienced refers to the *prārabdha-karma*—the karma that initiated the present body and was not exhausted by initiation—for the sake of its experience; herein, it is for the sake of taking up [the body] once again.
The intention, however, is not that there is an upward departure according to one's own will for the sake of non-return, as [some might suggest]. Thus,
it is stated in the venerable Kāmika:
The guide should perform the rite of *yojana* for the sake of protection regarding the karma to be experienced;
by virtue of his remaining authority, he assumes embodiment once again.
Thus [it is said]. "In the *dvādaśānta*" means situated in the lotus of the *dvādaśānta*. Likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*, it is stated:
"By means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one [places] oneself at the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhāgra*) at a distance of twelve finger-breadths."
"The wise one should join [it] within the lotus" means that he should cause it to enter without being separated from its own measure of rays.
But surely, since even the Self is all-pervasive, movement is impossible;

therefore, movement here is accepted as occurring by means of the *puryaṣṭaka*. Furthermore, since the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) is also to be purified, and because it is described as something to be abandoned by the qualification "alone," how can this [Self] be so?
Fearing that the Self, being devoid of that [state], might not reach the *dvādaśānta*, he says:
"(In this way)"—that is, in the manner previously described.
By the phrase "the form of the seed" (*bījavigraha*), it is meant that [the body] exists through the function of the seed-mantra (*mantrabīja*), which is to say, by way of *nāda*.
For *nāda* is inseparable even from the absence of the *puryaṣṭaka*. This is what is intended:
the subtle body [is produced] by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Self, presided over by Śiva and Śakti.
It is led forth; as it is stated in the venerable *Samānatantra*: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is led forth by power.

Upon its abandonment, however, through the function of the seed-mantras (*mantrabīja*), having become the *bindu*, one should contemplate the entry of the self into the state of Śiva together with the presiding power of Śiva (*śivaśakti*).
Therefore, entry occurs there. Likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
"The Bindu, having reached Śiva through its nature as Nāda, has attained dissolution (*laya*) by means of Śakti.
[The term] *līnaḥ* means "in the form of pervasion" (*vyāptirūpeṇa*); it has attained identity with that. As it is heard: "Dissolution is fitness for identity with that."
Then, in response to the inquiry "What should one do after that?", he says "(for the purification of the subtle body)"—
that one should purify the subtle body.
Thus, for both paths which possess this sequential mode of production:
Dissolution occurs by way of reversal, extending as far as the principle of Śakti.

As stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*: "The dissolution of the principles (*tattva*) should be performed in the reverse order of their creation. Thus he says "(in the inverse order)" (*pratilomyena*). For the dissolution of an effect occurs within its cause, and not elsewhere.
Having kept this in mind, he describes the sequence of dissolution into one's own causes with the words "in their own" (*sveṣu*).

This means "in their respective causes," that is, in their respective material origins (*upādāna*). "The principles" (*tattvāni*) refers to the thirty-six principles beginning with earth. "Up to the point of the Bindu" (*binduparyantam*) means up to the point of Kuṇḍalinī.
"Laya" means withdrawal; "should lead" means one should cause [it] to reach. Here, the intended meaning is that whatever originates from something must be included within that very thing.
To explain how this is so, he says: "For example" (*tadyathā*). "That" (*tat*) refers to the dissolution into reality (*tattvalayana*). "As" (*yathā*) means according to [the manner].
