It is clearly stated thus: (in the case of) *gandha*, [it refers to] the subtle element (*tanmātra*) of smell; (in the case of) *pṛthivīm*, [it refers to] the principle (*tattva*) of earth. "One should lead it to dissolution" is to be construed with what precedes. This should be applied in the same way everywhere.
[This concerns] the five elements beginning with the non-different (*ananya*).
p.
166) [The gross elements] are produced from the five subtle elements (tanmātra), such as smell and so forth; therefore, their dissolution occurs into those respective causes.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "From the subtle elements arise the five gross elements."

"These tanmātras" means the previously mentioned [subtle elements] beginning with smell. Likewise, in that very same [text]: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these remaining qualities are designated by the term 'tanmātra'."

Thus [it is said]. In the third division of the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), known as the *bhūtādi* (the origin of the elements), which belongs to the *tāmasa* (darkness) aspect—the meaning is this—whence were the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) produced? [The organs] called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; speech, hand, and foot... [pā-]
The anus, the generative organ, speech, the hands, the feet, and the anus and generative organ—these are what is designated by that name;
the meaning is that these are called the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
[This occurs] within the *rajas*-dominated ego (*ahaṃkāra*), known as the *vaikārika*.

In the second chapter concerning the ego-principle (*ahaṃkārika*), it is stated: "From this [ego-principle], speech and the others have arisen—namely, those called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. This means the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*).
According to Amara, the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are those beginning with air (*vāyu*), while the organs of cognition (*dhīndriya*) are those beginning with the mind and the eyes.
This is stated in the first section concerning the *ahaṃkāra* (ego), which is synonymous with *taijasa*, within the *Sāttvikāhaṃkāra*.
From this [sāttvika-ahaṃkāra], the ears and other senses, as well as the mind, emerge together. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
And that [intellect] is declared to be threefold; among these, the first is the taijasa, the second is the vaikārika, and the other is the bhūtādika.
That which has sattva as its predominant portion is here called taijasa;
that which has rajas as its predominant portion is vaikṛta; and that which is excessive in tamas is bhūtādi.
From the taijasa ego arise the mind and the sense organs;
from the vaikṛta ego, however, the five organs of action arise.

"From egoity (ahaṃkāra), the conjunction with the subtle elements (tanmātra) arises from the primary elements (bhūta)," etc. And that egoity: egoity is produced from the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva).

"Likewise, from the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is born; that too becomes threefold. [That] is the intellect (*buddhi*). Intellect is produced from the *guṇas*. Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmat-tattvaprakāśa*: "Intellect arises from the three *guṇas*. The principle of the *guṇas* has manifested from *prakṛti*. Likewise...
"In the venerable *Cintya*, it is said that from *prakṛti*, which is endowed with manifold qualities, the three qualities (*guṇa*) arise;

that is *prakṛti*. From the principle of *kalā*, the principles of *prakṛti*, *rāga*, and *vidyā* come into being. Likewise, in the venerable *Raurava*, it is stated that from the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into existence."
"And the unmanifest" refers to the principle of the person (*puruṣatattva*). Thus it is said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Listen now, O best of sages, to the principle of the person as it truly is:
joined with the five coverings (*kañcuka*), he is intent upon enjoying *prakṛti*."

"A person (puruṣa) is proclaimed as being conjoined with ignorance (avidyā) and the rest. Herein, the individual soul (aṇu), augmented by the five principles beginning with *kalā*, receives the designation of the "principle of the person" (*puṃstattva*). However, in the ultimate sense, it does not possess the status of a [separate] principle.

The intended meaning is that since the Self is eternal, there is no actual origination; therefore, the dissolution of Māyā is merely a figurative expression. From the principle of Māyā, Time, Necessity, and Limited Agency (kalā) manifested.
Likewise, in the venerable *Cintya*,
it is said that from Māyā, who possesses the form of infinite power, Time (Kāla) was born;
and then Māyā indeed gave birth to Niyati.
"That very Māyā, moreover, gave birth to Kalā in due order. Because Māyā is the supreme cause and is eternal, its origination and dissolution do not exist from any source.
Thus, in the venerable *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*, the principle of Māyā [is described].
"The seed of the world is indestructible and of an imperishable nature. Thus [it is said]. He concludes the stated meaning with the word "thus" (*evam*).

Regarding the word "having divided" (*vibhājya*), the word "the principles" (*tattvāni*) is to be supplied as the object. Then, in response to the inquiry "What follows from that?", he says that one should effect the dissolution of the pure principles which impel the principles residing within the subtle body.
(Śuddhavidyā-tattva); that is Īśvara-tattva; that is Sadāśiva-tattva; and that is Śakti-tattva.

And that too is the Śiva-tattva. From the Bindu, the Śiva-tattva emerged; from that, the Śakti-tattva; from that, the Sadāśiva-tattva; from this, the Īśvara-tattva; and from that, the Śuddhavidyā-tattva appeared.
As it is said in the venerable Jñānasiddhi:
By the will of Śiva, the principle of Nāda, which is the primary source of Kuṭilā, arose;
from the midst of Nāda, Bindu emerged, bearing the names of both Śiva and Śakti.

And so forth. (In the "unperturbed form"): he whose form (*rūpa*) is unperturbed (*akṣubdha*), meaning changeless (*nirvikāra*), is the "one of unperturbed form"; this refers to that which is characterized by the portion belonging to the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*).
(In the "drop" [*bindu*]): in the *kuṇḍalinī*. Here, because the drop (*bindu*) is the supreme material cause (*upādāna*), it does not [exist] in its entirety.

It undergoes transformation, however, only partially, according to the analogy of the "ghee-worm" (*ghṛtakīṭa*). Thus, the intended meaning is that within the interval between the modified and the unmodified, there is a dissolution of the *tattvas* into the *bindu*, which is characterized by that part which is unagitated and synonymous with the unmodified. And likewise:
In the venerable Pauṣkara, it is stated that this bindu is not agitated by the Universal Self because of its nature as primordial matter (prakṛti).
In that regard, its undisturbed portion is the power (kalā) of Śāntyatītā.
The division into *laya* and so forth previously described belongs to Śiva with respect to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
that is to be understood as the *bindu*, and it is considered to be *kuṇḍalinī* itself.
Thus, the manner of the dissolution of the principles beginning with earth has been set forth by the venerable gurus in verse:
"Earth in smell, water in taste, fire in form, wind in touch."
In the case of sound, there is space; in egoity (ahaṅkāra), moreover, these subtle elements (tanmātras) reside in the tāmasa aspect;

the organs of action along with the mind reside in the rājasa aspect; together with the organs of perception, they reside in the sāttvika aspect; [the mind] resides in the intellect (buddhi), and that [intellect] resides in the guṇas; and the aggregate of the guṇas goes to dissolution in the unmanifest (avyakta).

That [Māyā] and Rāga, along with Vidya, enter into Kalā; Puruṣatva, Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā enter into Māyā; he [Māyā] enters into Suvidyeśa together with Sadeśa; he [Suvidyeśa] enters into Śakti; she [Śakti] enters into Śiva; and he [Śiva] enters into Bindu.
Thus [it is said].
On this point, some [authorities] in certain places cite the verse beginning with "In the Brāhma [muhūrta], one should abandon sound and touch."
Because it was interpolated, it was disregarded.
Having thus described the procedure for purifying the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*), he now sets forth the method for purifying the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) with the word "then" (*tataḥ*).
The gross body, moreover, is the locus of the conceit of caste, family, and so forth, and consists of earth, water, fire, and—
The combination of air and space, possessing both common and specific forms, is called the elemental body born of the world (*bhuvanaja-bhūta-śarīra*). As it has been said:
"The body is declared to be threefold: the gross (*sthūla*), the subtle (*liṅga*), and the supreme (*para*)."
The gross body is the elemental body, while the subtle body is the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
"The supreme [reality], arisen from the *bindu*, is declared to be threefold.
Thus, one should "purify," that is, effect purification specifically. And therein, for the sake of removing the poison from the principles (*tattva*) residing in the gross and subtle bodies—
Just as in the meditation on Garuḍa, purity consists solely in the contemplation of dissolution for the purpose of removing bondage;
it is not, however, actual withdrawal [of the senses], because that would contradict direct perception and contradict scripture.

Therefore, one should meditate that the five elements, such as earth and the rest, which reside within the external body, are indeed this very reality. The intended meaning is that one should not cultivate the notion of a self (*ātman*) with respect to them. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
Furthermore, the practitioner should not bring about his own death out of a desire for [worldly] results,
nor should he intentionally cast off his body when suffering arises.
Thus it is said. In the Smṛti as well:
"Those worlds called asurya, shrouded in blind darkness—to them they go after death, those people who are slayers of the Self."

Thus, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, it is stated that "the other entity" refers to the five elements (*pañcabhūtāni*). When the question arises as to how this is so, since the gross body is composed of the elements,
one should contemplate the principle of earth (*pṛthivī-tattva*) in reverse order, including its color, nature, signs, and so forth.
He says "one should purify" [referring to] "(pārthivaṃ)" [earth]. "(Pītaṃ)" means golden-colored; by this, the color is determined. "(Kaṭhinaṃ)" means hard.
By this, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is demonstrated. "Marked by a vajra" (*kuliśāṅkita*) means marked with a thunderbolt;

by this, the insignia (*cihna*) is proclaimed. Regarding "hlām": the syllable *hā* is the heart-seed (*hṛdayabīja*), and the syllable *la* is the seed-syllable of earth (*pṛthivībīja*). Likewise, it is taught that for the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), the syllables *la*, *va*, *ra*, and *ha* are [the respective seeds].

In this context, it should be understood that one should employ the letter *la*, conjoined with the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdayabīja*), as the mantra upon the earthly mandala (*pārthivamaṇḍala*). Accordingly, the venerable *Sarvajñānottara* states:
"The heart-seed syllable, mounted upon the seat of the letter *la*, is situated in the center."

By him the mantra was spoken. (By the Adhināyaka) means by the Adhiṣṭhātṛ (the presiding deity). According to the Viśva lexicon: "Nāyaka" refers to a leader, one who is excellent, or even the central gem of a necklace. (By Sadyojāta) means by the one named Sadyojāta. By this, the Lord is fully described. (By Kāraṇeśvara).
By the designation "Lord of Causes" (*kāraṇeśvara*). Thus, in the *Śrīmantravārtika*, it is said: "The Supreme Śiva is known by the names Kamalaja, Keśava, Rudra, and Maheśvara;
these are called the Lords of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*), pervading their respective paths and abiding in their own mantras."
By this, Kāraṇeśvara is described. [It is] the form of the *kalā* of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). Thus it has been declared by the Illustrious One as being presided over by the *kalā* of withdrawal.
The *kalā* was described by this [author] as the commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.
[It is] four-cornered (*caturaśram*), meaning quadrangular. From that [source], the *maṇḍala* was declared; likewise in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

They consist of the elements (*bhūta*) containing the essence of reality (*tattva*), and are endowed with the five marks; they possess the causes of the natural forms of the deities, the constituent parts (*kalā*), and the mandalas, as well as the colors, mantras, qualities, locations, measurements, and so forth.

Thus it is said. In this manner, the other elements (bhūtas) are to be inferred. Now, one might ask: why should the elements such as earth be meditated upon as pervading only a single part of the body?
Anticipating this, [the text] states that one should contemplate them starting from the feet up to the top of the head, according to the scriptural injunction: "It is square."

And because they abide as pervading the external body, they should be meditated upon here as pervading the entire body, and not—as in the case of initiation—by way of pervading only the knees and so forth; thus he says, "beginning from the feet. What follows after that?

Anticipating the question of how this should be done, he says: "Oṃ hām. Furthermore, the extraction of the mantras for the kalās, beginning with *vivṛtti*, is also specified in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati* on page 176.
Reciting her name in the dative case, joined with the seed-syllable of that which is the reality and the form of its digit, and ending with the weapon-mantra appropriate to her class;

Thus: "By the pentad of *udghātas* (means) by the five *udghātas*, which have the form of an upward *recaka*. Five *udghātas* are performed for the destruction of the five qualities of earth. For each *udghāta*, there are three *prāṇāyāmas*, beginning with *pūraka*."
These are indeed established by the facts. As it has been stated in the venerable *Trayodaśaśatika*:
"In this way, fifteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) pertaining to the earth have been declared;
for Vāruṇa, there are twelve," and so forth.

(Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound are its qualities): Smell (*gandha*) consists of fragrant and non-fragrant types; taste (*rasa*) consists of sweet, sour, and so forth; form (*rūpa*) consists of yellow and so forth; touch (*sparśa*) consists of neither-cold-nor-hot types; and sound (*śabda*) consists of clanging and so forth. These—smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—are the qualities (*guṇāḥ*).
Thus they are described;
in this context, one should understand [the terms] such as "the quality of smell" (*gandhaguṇa*) and "the quality of taste" (*rasaguṇa*).
[The phrase] "having their own contrary qualities" refers to that which is contrary to the nature of earth—that is, its enemy.
And that [element] is air; by means of that, there is self-conceit regarding earth and wind, as well as water and fire. (p. 177)
This is the enmity existing among these four due to their mutual relationship as the subduer and the subdued;
whereas earth and water, and wind and fire, possess friendship because they mutually nourish one another;
and between water and wind, as well as between earth and fire, there is no state of enmity.
These [elements] possess a state of neutrality; however, space is friendly toward wind, water, fire, and earth by virtue of providing them with room.
Thus it is stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra:
Space is present in all beings; likewise are water, air, fire, and earth.
Water and fire, earth and air, and water and earth, as well as fire and air, [are likewise found together].
"Those who are neutral are not friends. (Abhibhūtām) means "one whose scent has been taken away.
According to Amara, "one whose scent has been taken away" (*āttagandha*) means "overpowered" (*abhibhūta*). (Tadākārām) means "composed of air.
This refers to that which, having abandoned the nature of solidity and so forth, is overpowered by the nature of the wind.
The intention is that one should cultivate [it].

Having thus described the purification of the earth element (*pṛthivī-bhūta-śuddhi*), [the text] explains the sequence for the purification of the water element (*jala-bhūta-śuddhi*) with the words "thereafter" (*tadanu*). The intrinsic nature of water is its liquid form; likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanātha-paddhati*, the water element is described as liquid.
"Saumya" means gentle.
On page 178, there is a variant reading: "The gentle [form] is a liquid half-moon. Regarding "(hrīm)," it is "hīm."

The seed-syllable of the head is the letter *va*, which is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa. Here, it should be understood that one should employ the water-seed-syllable *va*—conjoined with the Head-mantra—as the mantra within the water-mandala.
Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, [it says]: "situated in the middle of the seat of the letter *va*..."

"The seed-syllable of the head is downward-facing" means: having contemplated [it] as before, one should contemplate it starting from the feet up to the crown of the head. This should be understood for each element. "As previously stated": here, *hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ* is for the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, and *haḥ*.

The phrase "huṃ phaṭ" and so forth should be understood as previously stated, beginning with "preceded by *pūraka*. Regarding the phrase "(the four qualities, taste and so forth)": here, "taste" (*rasa*) is sweet; "form," "touch," and "sound" are the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Among those, form is white, touch is cold, and sound is [unmanifest].

The sound is *jhalajhala*. Here, it should be noted that due to the diminution of the single quality of smell (*gandha*), there is a diminution of the *udghāta* (upward impulse). This is to be inferred similarly in the subsequent cases as well. (Having that form) this consists of fire.
Having set aside the nature of fluidity and so forth, one should contemplate it as being overcome by the nature of fire.
Having described the purification of the water element, he explains the purification of the fire element with the word "Then" (*tataḥ*).

The nature of fire is characterized by burning. (*Hrūm*)—the syllable *Hūṃ* is the crest-mantra (*śikhā-mantra*), and the letter *Ra* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of fire. The seed-syllable of fire, conjoined with the crest-mantra, [is situated] in the fiery mandala.
One should employ it as a mantra. Thus, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said:
"The supreme seed-syllable called Śikhā is mounted upon the seat of the letter Ra. (Regarding the triad of qualities beginning with form:
here, the quality of form is radiant form; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the other qualities are included].

Touch and sound are mentioned: touch is heat; sound is a whistling or hissing sound. [One should] contemplate that which has that form as consisting of water, having abandoned the nature of burning and so forth, and being overwhelmed by the nature of water.

Having explained the purification of the fire element (*vahnibhūtaśuddhi*), he speaks [next] of the purification of the air element (*vāyubhūtaśuddhi*). The nature of air is of the form of movement. "Hyaiṃ": the syllable *hai* is the armor mantra (*kavacamantra*); the letter *ya* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of air.

Having joined the seed-syllable of Vāyu with the seed-syllable of the Armor (kavaca), one should employ it as the mantra within the mandala of Vāyu. Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said that [the deity] is seated upon the seat of the letter Ya.

"The armor has the form of air" means it possesses the two qualities of touch and sound. Here, the quality of touch is of a nature that is neither cold nor hot; the quality of sound is of the nature of the *śaka-śaka* sound.
Having cast off its own nature as consisting of earth (*medinīmaya*) and as having the character of *nalana* and so forth, [it assumes] that form.
One should meditate upon [the body] as being overcome by the intrinsic nature of the earth element.

Having described the purification of the element of air, he teaches the purification of the element of space with the words "thereafter" (*tadanu*). First, the sphere of space (*nabhomaṇḍala*) is circular in shape; thus it is said to be "of the form of the sky" (*vyomākāra*) and perfectly round. "Of the form of the sky" means as the sky is perceived by worldly people.

It has the form of the well-known space (*avakāśa*). It is empty (*śūnya*), consisting of the absence of material substance, having the form of emptiness, but not having the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). [This is] by means of the power of the *bindu* (*binduśakti*), that is, by the power of the curved one (*kuṭilāśakti*). Thus it was explained by the venerable commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.
The intrinsic nature of space is characterized by vacuity; as the venerable author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī* has said:
"Solidity, fluidity, heat, motion, and space are their inherent natures. Thus:
one should employ the letter *ha* joined with the vowel *au* as a mantra within the mandala of names.
Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said that the letter *ha* is seated upon the throne of the vowel *au*.

Regarding the phrase "the pervasive etherial [element]": one might object— since it has been stated that the seeds of the four elements beginning with earth and ending with air consist of the letters from *la* to *ya*, conjoined with the four seed-syllables of the mantras starting with the Heart, how is it that the ether (*ākāśa*) is not mentioned here?
Is it said that one should abandon the *astra* mantra and use only the seed-syllable of space (*nabho-bīja*) as *haum*? True;

the intended meaning here is that it is stated thus because space consists of the *śāntyatīta-kalā*. We shall clarify all of this later, in the section on the purification of the *śāntyatīta-kalā* within the ritual procedure for *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*.
"By Sadāśiva": Sadāśiva is he who is eternally (*sadā*) auspicious (*śiva*); [he is so called] by means of Sarvamaṅgalā, who is the form of his own power. (p.
The meaning is that, because his essential nature is variegated, he is an undivided mass of auspiciousness (*aparicchinna-kalyāṇa-ghana*).
Thus it has been said:
"He who has attained the state of Sadāśiva is Śiva himself directly, though [distinguished] by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)."
He too shall always possess power; deprived of that [power], he is cast out.
Thus [it is said]. (Regarding "sound as a quality"): here, "sound" refers to the sound of an echo, not that which consists of phonemes.

(Regarding "the nature of impermanence, impurity, and so forth"): here, impermanence is precisely the state of being produced without having previously existed and without a material cause. As it has been said:

"The manifest is causal, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite. By the word "etcetera," qualities such as non-pervasiveness are indicated.
(The nature [of the Self] is one that has surpassed the supreme ether, which is endowed with eternity, all-pervasiveness, purity, and so forth.
Eternity means being unconditioned by time, that is to say, being devoid of beginning and end. All-pervasiveness means being unconditioned by space, that is to say, being omnipresent.
As they say:
"That entity whose existence is unconditioned by space and time, they consider to be eternal and all-pervading; such is the eternity and omnipresence of the self."
Thus [it is said on] p. 183).

"Purity" (*śuddhatva*) means whiteness (*sitatva*). Those whose first [qualities] are eternity (*nityatva*), pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and purity (*śuddhatva*) are described as such. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to qualities such as tranquility (*śāntatva*); it is endowed with these.
And that is the supreme ether, called the *bindu*, the supreme void (*paramavyoman*). Thus it is said in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"It is devoid of qualities, beyond all material adjuncts, and free from planets and constellations."
One should contemplate the supreme ether, resembling pure crystal.

Thus it is said: And they declare that within the glorious Triple Gem there is something even more excellent— the imperishable space known as Śiva, which possesses an equality with those who enjoy both worldly experience and liberation.
"Like space is the cause of the elements and so forth for the hosts of luminaries.

Thus, one should not meditate on the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) as possessing attributes such as eternity, because scripture declares it to be an effect of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). As it is heard: "From the subtle elements [arise] the five gross elements."
Thus; that whose essential nature (svarūpa) has been overcome by such [an entity] is described as "thus" (tathoktam).

(184) Having thus explained the purification of the elements, such as earth and so forth, when the question arises as to what should be performed thereafter for one whose power has been exhausted due to the depletion of the *guṇas*:
He says "then" (*tataḥ*) to indicate that one should perform the burning and immersion of the body, which consists of a collection of elements (*bhūtasamudāya*).

"Then" (*tataḥ*) means immediately after such contemplation. "The defects of the elements residing in the commenced body" (*ārabdhaśarīragatabhūtadoṣān*): the "commenced body" (*ārabdhaśarīra*) is the present physical frame resulting from karma that has already begun to bear fruit; [the phrase refers to] those [defects] residing therein.
The defects of the elements such as earth and so forth that have entered [the body],
namely, the defects consisting in the transformation of the impurities known as semen and blood located within the physical body derived from the father and mother;
thus it is stated in the *Śrīmacchivatantrarahasyasāra*:
It is not fitting to remain in a body produced from the impurities of mother and father;
therefore, day after day, one's body is made to consist of mantra.

Thus: "(One should) cause to overflow" means that one should consecrate [the disciple] with streams of nectar using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, in accordance with what will be described later, beginning with "the downward-facing lotus situated at the end of the crest-lock."

(185) Now, raising the objection: "In that case, how [should it be done] for those who are unable to perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*)?", he explains that procedure by way of another method, saying "(yadvā)" (or else). That is to say: "If it were not so."
He describes the body as having the nature of a banyan tree with the words "pṛthivyādi" (earth, etc.).

"Pṛthivyādibhūtabījam" means that which has the seeds of the elements—earth and the others—as its cause; those beginning with earth are the "pṛthivyādīni," and these are the "bhūtāni" (elements), and these very things constitute the "bījam" (seed), the cause of the sprout, for which [the body], thus it is so described.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), water, fire, air, and ether are indicated.

This has been stated with reference to the gross body; therefore, the intended meaning here is that it consists of the transformation of the elements (*bhūta-pariṇāma*) and the seeds of semen and blood.

(With a sprout sprouted by Brahmā and Viṣṇu): He is so described because he is one whose sprout has been produced—that is, brought forth—by both of them; [Brahmā] having the nature of the creator of the world and [Viṣṇu] having the nature of the protector. (With roots of passion, hatred, merit, and demerit): And passion...
Desire and aversion are opposites; likewise, dharma consists of rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, while adharma consists of acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.

And those two, established by tradition and previously performed, are said to be qualities in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in the intellect. In this context, *dharma* is that which holds or maintains the worlds as luminous objects of enjoyment for those belonging to those [worlds]; *adharma* is that which effects the opposite of that. It is not [the self].

It does not sustain the worlds, nor does it produce pleasure; rather, it sustains the non-worlds—the *asāttvika* and *rājasa* states—and among those things to be enjoyed by such beings, it produces displeasure and suffering characterized by delusion (*moha*). Thus is the meaning of the terms *dharma* and *adharma*. Likewise:
In the illustrious *Sūkṣma-svāyambhuva*,

it is said that he who sustains all these worlds and feels supreme affection for the Supreme Person is called "Dharma" by those who know it; Dharma is defined as the opposite of that [which does not sustain the world].
Thus: and *moha* (delusion) is a stain of the mind consisting of the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self;
it is said to be "that whose root is precisely passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and delusion (*moha*). This refers to that [tree of worldly existence].

Because it assumes a body— such as that of a Brāhmaṇa— and possesses sharp faculties, a fixed lifespan, and fixed experience, in accordance with the merit and demerit accumulated in previous births, dharma and adharma constitute the root.
187) Because passion, hatred, and delusion are the causes for the accumulation of karma, they are said to be the root by way of that [karma].
[It is] "protected by the lords of knowledge and ignorance"; and "knowledges" refers to the seventy million great mantras.
And the lords of knowledge (vidyādhipatayaḥ) are the eight great lords of mantra, beginning with Ananta;

[these] are the vidyās and the lords of vidyā. Thus it is said in the venerable Ratnatraya: "Therein, the mantra-arms are first, [followed by] the mantras and the vidyās by name. He who is protected and nourished by them—[him].

(Kalāditattvasāram): Those things of which *kalā* is the first are "those beginning with *kalā*" (*kalādīni*). These, being the *tattvas*, are thus designated; he whose essence (*sāra*)—the stable constituent (*sthirāṃśa*)—is precisely those, is so described.
According to Amara, *sāra* means both strength and the stable constituent. By the word "first" (*ādi*), *prakṛti* and the others are included.

(The subtle elements and the senses are the branches and sub-branches): the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are the subtle elements of sound and so forth; this has been explained previously. And the senses (*indriya*) are the organs of cognition and the organs of action; these themselves are the branches and the great branches.

He who possesses these—the minor branches (*upaśākhā*) and the branches of ritual procedure (*kalpaśākhā*)—is so described; [he is like] a sprout for the examination of objects (*viṣayālocanapallava*). "Objects" refers to sound and the rest; "form" refers to sound... [p. 188] ...and so forth.
According to Amara, "these objects are smell, taste, and touch.
Their "perceptions" (*ālocanāni*) are functions consisting of apprehension. Likewise, in the venerable *Pauṣkara*, it is stated:
"The function of the eye and so forth is solely perception (*ālocanatva*). Those very things are the perceptions of the objects.

"Having sprouts" means that which possesses young shoots (*kisalaya*); this is how it is described. Here, because the coming and going of the perceptions of objects is observed, a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is expressed by treating them as "sprouts. (The flower of the manifold of states of being): "States of being" (*bhāva*) refers to the eight qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-guṇa*), such as virtue (*dharma*) and the rest.
Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The states that are qualities of the intellect—dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya—are *sāttvika*; these same states, when reversed by excluding passion (*rāga*), are *tāmasa*."
Thus, their elaborations (*prapañca*) consist of three hundred clusters—that is, three hundred groups.
This was likewise indicated by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha: "Dharma has ten divisions; knowledge has one hundred and eighty; dispassion [has one hundred]."
Sovereignty consists of sixty-four [powers]; non-dharma consists of ten, and ignorance of half that number.
Non-detachment consists of ten, and lack of sovereignty is divided into twenty-one.

"This [is] the distinction of the suffixes denoting abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*) by means of three hundred [verses]. He is described as such because he possesses those very flowers. Here, "abstract states" (*bhāvāḥ*) are enumerated as flowers because they will exist in the form of fruits at a later time; [the fruit being] the result of understanding, study, reflection, and resolve.

Intellect (*buddhi*) is the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*); its function is determination (*adhyavasāya*), which consists of the ascertainment: "This is indeed silver, not mother-of-pearl. Volition (*saṃkalpa*), on the other hand, is the function of the mind (*manas*) consisting of the investigation of multiple attributes associated with a single alternative.

Likewise, in the venerable Pauṣkara it is said: "Buddhi alone is this [entity], whose nature consists of the determination of objects. In the venerable Tattvaprakāśa it is said: "The mind (manas) has the form of will; its function is volition (saṃkalpa). He is described as such because those two [will and volition] are his fruit. [The word] *phalam* [is used] in the sense of "fruit."
"In wealth, seed, production, enjoyment, and gain"—thus says the Viśvakośa. Here, the object determined by the intellect...

By the statement "the person (puruṣa) perceives," it is described that only those objects which are reflected in the intellect (buddhi) and attended to by the mind (manas) constitute the nature of the fruit. (The phrase "to be enjoyed by the person-bird" means:
the person is the self whose nature is that of the enjoyer; he alone is the bird (vihaṅga), and [the object] is to be enjoyed by him.

"Upabhojyam" (to be enjoyed). Here, the state of being a bird for the person (*puruṣa*) is stated because of the observation of his separation from dwelling and enjoyment. [This refers to] the essence of being both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment;
for the body is the object of enjoyment, as was previously stated: "to be enjoyed by the person-bird."

The *ātman* is the enjoyer and the agent of the act of enjoyment; the state of being both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer is "the condition of being the enjoyed and the enjoyer" (*bhogyabhoktṛtva*). That which has this very thing as its "flavor" (*rasa*)—where *rasa* means fragrance, taste, the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*), aesthetic resonance (*dhvani*), or water—is described as such. According to Mādhava: "Rasa [is used] for fragrance, taste, the sentiment of love, aesthetic resonance, and water."
The meaning is: "the essence connected with the state of being the enjoyed and the enjoyer.

Regarding the statement, "With roots above and branches below," the body is described as being similar to fire by virtue of its being the object of enjoyment; for the body is like the *karabīja* seed.
The state of being a banyan tree is described because of the similarity in the sense of subtle accumulation.
Thus, he states what is to be done immediately after the contemplation of the form of that tree, beginning with the word "first" (prathama).

(Regarding the first half of the *pūraka*): Here, the *pūraka* (inhalation) has a duration of twelve *mātrās*; its half is six *mātrās*. In this same manner, the duration for both *kuṃbhaka* (retention) and *recaka* (exhalation) should also be applied. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
By rotating the kneecaps, a snap of the fingers occurs in succession;
with twelve such measures, there is inhalation (pūraka) and likewise retention (kuṃbhaka).

"And thus is described the exhaling breath (*recaka*), which is the lowest form of *prāṇāyāma*. (Stabdha means) motionless. This is because it is stated that [the earth-element] acts as the support for the earth-retention (*pṛthivī-dhāraṇā*). Herein [is the mantra]: *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ*."
By means of the first half of the *pūraka* [breathing technique] and the earth-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*),

for the sake of the exhaustion of the fivefold objects beginning with smell, one should mentally recite [the mantra] five times while visualizing the body as a banyan tree devoid of sprouts, flowers, and fruit, and motionless.
One should understand that [the word] "one should contemplate" (*cintayet*) is used here.
(Snigdha) refers to a shady tree (*chāyāvṛkṣa*). *Snigdha* means smooth, thick, or shady.
"Nameruṇi" means "all-pervading," according to the Viśva lexicon. He states what one should do immediately after that with the word "(tataḥ)" [then].

"(Bandhakarūpam)" means having the form of the subtle and gross bodies. "(Śūnyam)" means free from the state of being a binder; that is to say, it is like something non-existent. At this juncture, at the end of the twelve [fingers] (dvādaśānte)...
Because it is empty of the nature of being an object of apprehension,

the true nature of the Self becomes non-referential and established solely in pure consciousness; however, according to the venerable [teacher], it does not become merely ceased as it is in states such as fainting.
In the commentary on this aphorism, the author of the *Sārddhatriśatikāvṛtti* has taught that consciousness remains as something solitary and without support at the *dvādaśānta*.
Thus, he describes the procedure for bathing the body— whose defects have been entirely dispelled— with nectar, [beginning with] "vauṣaṭ" (vauṣaḍantamūlena).
Starting from the *mūlādhāra*, [one recites] the *mūla-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the letter *ha*.
The meaning is: by means of the root mantra, preceded by the contemplation of the Self (*ātmanusandhāna*) starting from *kāra* up to *unmanā*, and ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
(With streams of nectar flowing from the downward-facing lotus situated at the end of the crest-lock:

First, the downward-facing lotus situated at the end of the crest-lock is the form of the Supreme Lord’s power that is eternally to be presided over, existing as the support of all things by virtue of being the warp and woof of all entities.

The supreme bindu, whose nature is the highest nectar, resides at the end of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta). Likewise, one should always contemplate the nectar flowing from that which stands at the end of the process (prakriyā). One should visualize the Praṇava as a white lotus, serving as the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), facing downwards.
"One should contemplate that nectar within it, [issuing] from the head pierced by the *suṣumnā*.
Thus, those flowing streams— that is, those aforementioned streams of nectar—
by means of them (having entered the openings of all the channels).
Having raised the doubt as to what follows after [the breath] enters through the seventy thousand channels of the heart,
he describes the method for first preparing the seat for the placement of the Self— which has ascended to the *dvādaśānta*— within the heart, beginning with the word "in the heart" (*hṛdaye*).
The true nature of the heart has been described by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:
"The mind goes out toward objects and dissolves back into that very same [source].
One should know that to be the heart, which is the cause of the mind's stability.

Thus: [by that which is joined with the three measures beginning with 'a']—those whose beginning is the letter 'a' are "those beginning with 'a'" (akārādayaḥ); they are also measures (mātrā), and there is a triad of them.
The letters 'u' and 'm' are the meaning of the word "beginning" (ādi). Here, by the word "om,"...

The essential meaning is that the lotus of the heart, which serves as the seat of the Self— characterized by the pericarp and petals— is brought into being by the union of the three measures (mātrās) of the syllables A, U, and M. For the Self, as the presiding principle, is indeed bodiless.

Based on the Vedic scripture stating, "The liberated self becomes [like space]," one should keep in mind that for the partless Self— whose body and bonds have been consumed— no further action is possible; for it is not logical that consciousness or an instrument could exist for one who is devoid of a body and the like.
He describes the process of descending into the body consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) composed of mantra: "(In its pericarp)" and so forth.
Furthermore, the *puryaṣṭaka* consists of the powers of perception and action. Thus, it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"One should burn away the fettered form with that which touches the state of Sadāśiva."
One should observe that ash being swept away by the wind of Śakti.
Having the form of the solar disc and adorned with the mandalas of the vital functions (vṛtti),
that very body of his is considered to have unmanifest limbs.

Thus: "By the four-part" (*catuṣkalena*): that which has the four parts (*kalā*), beginning with *a* and ending with the *bindu*, as its own constituent portions is "four-part"; by that. According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, the word *kalā* refers simply to a portion, as in "craft" (*śilpa*) and so forth.
Then, he describes the re-deployment (*vinyāsa*) within the heart of the pure Self, according to the aforementioned sequence of the dissolution of the principles (*tatvalaya*).
"In that" means in that *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city). "In the form of a seed" means having the nature of the seed of Śiva.
"Consisting of Śiva" means having become Śiva. Thus it is said in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Then one should draw forth the life-force (*jīva*), which has become Śiva and is free from affliction."
By means of inhalation (pūraka), one should [visualize] the supreme [seed-syllable], consisting of the seed of Śiva, situated within the crest-lock (śikhā).
Thus, by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should place that supreme, stainless seed-syllable of Śiva, consisting of the essence of Śiva, at the end of the crest-lock (śikhā).
Thus: (by the five-fold one).
He who possesses five *kalās*—beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *nāda*—is the "five-fold one" (*pañcakala*); [the action is performed] by him.

(Through the utterance of the Śakti-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*) means through the utterance of the root mantra joined with the word *Śakti* in the dative case; that is to say, *oṃ hauṃ śaktaye vauṣaṭ*. Thus it has been stated by the Illustrious One.
According to the commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*: "In this context,

one should meditate upon the Haṃsa as it floats in the midst of the water— which consists of abundant nectar flowing from the agitation of the partless Power (*niṣkala-śakti*)— and as it returns from there."
According to this scriptural authority (*śruti*), because the Self was previously established [in the vessel] prior to its separation from the body,
the intention is that for that purpose, the immersion in nectar (*amṛtāplāvana*) must be performed once again.
This is the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
Then (27), having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) as before,

and having designated the locations of the heart, navel, and *bindu* as the sites for worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), according to the sequence to be described...

Having mentally worshipped Śiva with all the ritual offerings within the lotus of the inner heart using flowers and other items presented through meditative visualization, [one should worship] in the fire naturally established in the sacrificial pit of the navel.
One should place there the fire of knowledge, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
[one should draw] that fire from the center of the heart-lotus by way of the suṣumṇā path.
One should join that [light], which is tawny with a mass of radiance, at the station of the *dvādaśānta*;
by merely placing it there, one becomes fit for all ritual actions.

Having spoken thus, having installed the fire of knowledge (*jñānānala*), and having worshipped Śiva, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) in the form of nectar flowing from the *bindu* drawn upward by inhalation (*pūraka*); then, having offered it to the deity worshipped within and completed the worship, [one should meditate on] the All-facing One (*sarvatomukha*) in the *bindu*.
Having meditated upon the Lord in the form of a throbbing star and having requested, "I shall worship externally," he receives permission.
(27) (Pra) Now, having proclaimed the procedure for the transformation into Śiva (śivīkaraṇa), [he performs it] for the two bodies, the subtle and the gross.

He states that one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* for the purpose of attaining the state of having a body consisting of mantra, power (*śakti*), and knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of the passage beginning with "thereafter" and ending with "having performed."
Now, that very light-liṅga which resides within the heart is worshipped externally.
Therefore, one should first perform the internal sacrifice; this is what is taught here.

By this statement, he first describes the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) with the passage beginning with "in the heart" (*hṛnnābhi*) and ending with "having obtained permission" (*labdhānujñaḥ*).
As for the rite of worship in the heart, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the navel.
And one should meditate upon Īśvara on the forehead, the granter of boons, facing in all directions.

Thus, based on the venerable *Kālottara-śruti*, he says "the heart" (*hṛt*) with the intention that one should conceive of the heart and other parts as providing the space for worship and so forth. To the inquiry "How should one perform the inner worship?", he says "by the sequence to be described."

Therefore, the intended meaning here is that external worship alone is the primary form, because it is complete with all its constituent parts (aṅgas). In response to the question "With what should one worship?", [the text says]: "The wise man should worship in the heart-lotus, as previously described and in due order."
One should worship by mentally imagining offerings such as perfumes and the like.

Thus, by the statement of the venerable *Suprabheda*, it is said that one should worship with mentally conceived flowers, perfumes, and so forth; this is expressed by the word "bhāva" (state/essence). [Regarding] "in the heart-lotus" (*hṛtpadme*):

In this regard, the true nature of the heart (*hṛd*) has been stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha: "The mind goes out toward objects and dissolves back into that very [place]; know that to be the heart (*hṛdaya*), which is the cause for the mind's abiding. Therein, the *padma* refers to the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*).
The characteristic of that [heart] has been described in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of the plantain tree;
situated in its center is a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp."
The heart is one span (vitasti) in measure, and the lotus is four finger-breadths;
it is situated eight finger-breadths above the navel.
The lotus stalk has nine openings and is covered all over with thorns;
here, its pericarp is equal in size to a thumb-joint and is provided with filaments.
In the pericarp there should be the sun, and in its center the moon;
in the center of the moon there should be fire, and in its center Maheśvara.

"Sadāśiva is [the seat] of Maheśa, and Śiva is even beyond him. (Having worshipped thus: Here, having prepared two *arghya* vessels within the heart-lotus, one should establish the *śivāsana*—the seat of Śiva beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the various *śaktis*—upon the bulb (*kanda*), the stalk (*nāla*), the petals (*pattra*), and the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Having performed the placement [of the deities], one should carry out the ritual actions beginning with the supreme invocation and installation of the two forms, up to the offering of the recitation; thus it was stated by the venerable author of the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*.

He states the procedure for the internal oblation (*antarhavana*) with the word "in the navel" (*nābhi*). [The term] "self-established" (*svatas-siddhe*) means "arisen by nature. This qualification should also be connected to both the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the fire (*anala*).
By this, he demonstrates that the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) of the pit and the fire are not to be performed.
Thus it has been stated by the illustrious commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.
Likewise, in the *Śrīmacchintya*, it is said: "Because the fire has already been established previously, there is no need for the 'mouth of fire' (*agnimukha*).
This refers to the method of depositing the fire of knowledge (*jñānapāvaka*) into the fire situated within the navel-pit (*nābhikuṇḍa*).

He clarifies this with the words "the fire of knowledge" (*jñānānala*). Having joined the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) with the fire of knowledge located at the heart-bindu via the path of the *suṣumnā*,
and having unified it with Śiva residing in the station of the *dvādaśānta*, thereafter—
The intended meaning is that one should not place [the seed-syllable] upon the fire;
and thus the Blessed One, the author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, has said:

In the self-arisen navel-pit (nābhikuṇḍa) which has three ridges, having kindled the fire of one's own nature and discarded the portion consisting of raw flesh-eaters (kravyāda), and having purified it through the rites of inspection (nirīkṣaṇa) and so forth, the seed-syllable of fire is ignited by means of the exhaling breath (recaka).

Having unified [the fire] with the two fires of gnosis located at the heart and between the eyebrows, and having led it to the *dvādaśānta*, one brings that Śiva-fire to the navel by means of inhalation (*pūraka*). (Having thus worshipped Śiva: Here, one should worship the fire in the heart-lotus as the seat-form (*āsana-mūrti*) using the root-mantras.

Likewise, in the illustrious *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is said: "Having invoked the seat and the form, one should contemplate the triad there once" (verse 6), and "having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*)," etc. Here, [one should perform it] with the root mantra according to one's capacity.

The meaning is that one should offer oblations with the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*) in twelve parts. Regarding the phrase "having offered" (*samarpya*), the word "the fruit of the *homa*" (*homaphala*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Anticipating the question "What then?", he says "the worship" (*pūjām*), meaning that one should conclude the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). Here, one should worship with eight flowers.

Having offered the *arghya* for the one who has turned away (*parāṅmukha*), one should perform the conclusion of the worship. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is said: "Then, having offered into the fire, one should restrain the fire."
Having worshipped Brahmā and the others, as well as Śiva residing in the heart, with the eightfold offering (aṣṭapuṣpī),
and having offered the arghya while facing away, one should restrain [the breath].

He teaches the method of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with the words "in the point" (*bindau*). "Facing all directions" (*sarvatomukham*) means endowed with the powers of knowledge and action regarding all objects. "The Lord" (*īśvaram*) refers to Śiva without parts (*niṣkala-śiva*).
As the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* has said:

One should meditate upon that Maheśvara, who has been previously described as having a universal form and worshipped in the fire of Śiva within the heart-lotus, as the Niṣkala-Śiva (the partless Śiva) devoid of the division of limbs consisting of mantras,
yet appearing in the form of the Bindu (the Point) due to being the substratum of the Bindu. Thus...

One should understand that self-purification has been accomplished through the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), internal worship (antaryajana), oblation (havana), and meditative absorption (samādhi). Likewise, it is stated in the venerable Kāraṇa [Tantra]:
"Having cast off the natural state, one should contemplate, 'I am Śiva.'"
One should perform the worship in the heart and arrange the fire-oblation in the navel.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord Īśvara, the omnipresent Master, between the eyebrows.
This is declared to be the purification of the self; now hear about the purification of the place.
Thus [it is said].
Purity of place.

(27) One should perform the purification of the place. Having struck three times with the *astra-mantra*, one should expel obstacles from that location with snapping sounds (*choṭikā*). Then, with the *astra-mantra*, one should [visualize] a wall of blazing fire-colored light all around, and with the *kavaca-mantra*, by rotating the right index finger.

Having visualized three moats with the *dhenumudrā* while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śakti," one should contemplate the net of Śakti above and below, and meditate upon the protection established everywhere. Thus, having performed the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*).

Now, having thus described the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), he extends [the procedure] to the second, the purification of the place (*sthānaśuddhi*), with the words beginning with "the place" and ending with "one should meditate. To explain how one should perform that, he says "with the weapon-mantra" (*astreṇa*). The definition of the *choṭikā* (the snapping gesture) has been stated previously.
(The three moats) are the three excavations (*kheya*). Umāra states that *kheya* means a moat (*parikhā*). (Having visualized above and below.
The intended meaning here is that one should contemplate the place of worship as being woven warp and woof by means of *śakti*.
By this, the state of being composed of *māyā* of the sacrificial pavilion (*pūjā-maṇṭapa*) is removed, and it is brought to the state of being composed of the *bindu*; thus it is fully explained.
By the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*.
The preparation of the *arghya* offering for Śiva.
(29) Then, having washed the arghya vessel made of gold or other materials with the Astra mantra,

and having filled it with pure water consisting of a stream of nectar flowing from the Bindu using the Hṛdaya mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should scatter perfumes, flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth.

Having worshipped that [seat]— which is the body of the five-fold Brahmā-vidyā— again with the Netra-mantra, the Mūla-mantra, and the ancillaries (aṅgas), and having consecrated it with the Saṃhitā-mantra, protected it with the Astra-mantra, and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should cause it to shine forth by means of the Dhenu-mudrā and the Mūla-mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
Then, having sprinkled oneself with that water using the Astra-mantra— (2 [Pra])—
he now explains the preparation of the Śiva-arghya with the passage beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "prarecayet."
p.
205) "(Gold, etc. — by the word "etc. (ādi), silver and so forth are included. Likewise:
"Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or earth, it should be filled with water."
The *arghya* vessel for Śiva should be marked with a lotus, circular in shape, and free from blemishes.

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, according to the venerable *Sūkṣma-śruti*: "There shall be only one vessel for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*)," and according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*: "[The vessel] named Śiva [is used] at the end of the worship, as well as for the water for the feet and the water for sipping."

Keeping in mind that there is only one vessel for the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), and not separate vessels for each, he says: "(the *arghya* vessel)" and "(unbroken rice, etc.).
By the word "etc.," milk and other such items are indicated. Thus it has been said:
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, rice grains, jasmine flowers, sesame seeds,
along with barley and white mustard seeds— this is declared to be the eightfold arghya offering.
Thus: "If the eight components are absent, then one should perform the *śivārghya* with water alone.
Likewise, one should diligently prepare the eight components; in their absence, [it should be] filled with water.
(Having consecrated it with the *saṃhitā-mantra*). Thus.
p.

206) Here, one should consecrate [the object] with the Brahma-mantras and the ancillary mantras (aṅga). As it has been stated in the Śivasūtra: "By means of that form, by the Brahma-mantras, by knowledge, and by the vision."
One should worship with the root mantra, excluding the limbs and the eyes; then one should worship again with the root mantra.
"Then, having consecrated with the limbs of Brahmā" (one should inspire enthusiasm).
Here, by means of the nectar flowing from the station of the *bindu* through the ten channels directed toward the ten fingers of the hands, [the disciple is inspired].
The essential meaning is that by means of the *dhenumudrā* and the utterance of *vauṣaṭ*, its state as supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*) is brought about.
Then, he states the subsequent actions to be performed with the words beginning with "thereafter" (*tataḥ*), ending with "having sprinkled" (*saṃprokṣya*).
By this much [it is explained]. "(With that water)" means with the water of Śiva’s arghya. "(The self)" means one's own head; such is the meaning.
The purification of substances.
(70) (Kriyā 30): Having consecrated the collection of materials for worship, such as flowers and so forth, with the *astra-mantra*;
having sprinkled them with the *kavaca-mantra*; having empowered them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; having encased them with the *kavaca-mantra*;
and having rendered them nectar-like with the *dhenu-mudrā*, [one should offer] drops of *arghya* water into the vessels containing the bathing water.
Having cast [the offering] with flowers, one should consecrate it as nectar (*amṛtīkuryāt*).
207) Having thus performed the purification of the substances, (30) next, having recited the *vyāhṛtis*, one should perform the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*).

He declares the third purification, that of the substances (*dravya-śuddhi*), with the words beginning "flowers, etc. and ending with "having performed" (*vidhāya*). Now, one might object: since it has been stated that "the purification of the self, the locus, the substance, and the mantra has thus been accomplished," the purification of the locus (*sthāna-śuddhi*) must precede the purification of the substances, as the latter is intended to be taught immediately after the former.

If it is asked: "Since each respective definition ought to be stated immediately after its corresponding heading, why has the procedure for preparing the *śivārghya* been mentioned here in this intermediate section?"— it is true that the purification of ritual substances (*dravya-śuddhi*) must be preceded by sprinkling with the water of the *śivārghya*.

There is no fault in this, as its performance occurs subsequent to that [rite]. "Having sprinkled" (*abhyukṣya*) means having touched with the palm of the hand in the shape of a downward-pointing banner.
Having filled small jars with thoroughly purified water.
Having placed [the vessel] for one ghaṭikā, one should gradually pour the arghya water through a leaf.
Thus, according to the venerable Kiraṇa-śruti, one should cause drops of water from the flowers and arghya to fall separately into each of the water-pitchers used for bathing;
this is what he means by saying "(drops of arghya-water)" and "(in the vessels for bathing water)."
"Gaḍḍukān" means in the vessels for water that have been consecrated by the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), as previously stated.

Regarding the word "bhāṇḍa," the *Nānārtharatnamālā* states: "The word *bhāṇḍa* [is used] in the sense of a vessel. Now, one might object: "In this case, [is it not sufficient] through the purification of the substance?"
If it is asked, "What is to be accomplished [by purification], since substances such as flowers and water are pure by their very nature?"—the answer is no;

for the collection of material objects produced from the Māyā of the impure elements is non-Śiva (aśiva), and thus is unfit for the enjoyment of Śiva. Nor does the state of being Śiva (śivatva) arise through connection with Śiva, as if it were something that could pervade [all things].

The word "of him" (tasya) must be stated; for Śiva, like a lotus leaf, is untainted and thus lacks contact with material substances. Therefore, [the purification] of the ritual materials such as flowers used in worship is performed by means of sprinkling with mantras, pouring water over them, consecrating with mantras, veiling, and so forth.

One should perform the purification of substances for the purpose of bringing them to the state of Śakti. Thus, by abandoning their form as Māyā and assuming the nature of the power (Śakti) that is taken up, the substance becomes fit to be enjoyed by Śiva; that is the ritual purification of substances.
Thus [it is said].
Self-worship.

(Kriyā) (32) Having offered a flower upon his own seat with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya namaḥ*, and having projected the form (*mūrti*) into his heart, [he should mark] the forehead with sandalwood paste.
"Having applied [the tilaka]" means having made the forehead mark; one should place a flower on the head with the root mantra.

Having thus performed the worship of oneself and having adopted a silence that is not inconsistent with worship, (32) he now describes the worship of Śiva based on the self, beginning with "Then, the worship of the Sun," and so forth.
From the words "(svāsane)" up to "vidhāya," [the procedure is established].

Now, anticipating the question of what state the worshipper should be in at that time, he says "(pūjā)" and so forth up to "āsthāya" to express the absence of obstacles to the worship and the necessity of remaining silent.
Thus ends [the section]. First, *mauna* (silence) is the refraining from speaking that which is inappropriate for the worship of Śiva;
likewise, in the worship of Śiva, *mauna* is the non-praising of that which is unfit for it.
The purification of the mantra.

(32) Having uttered the mantras in the sequence of short, long, and protracted [vowels], beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should perform the purification of the mantras. (32) (pra) Now, having described the purification of substances, he explains the fourth [type of] purification, that of the mantras.
By the passage beginning with "the mantras" (p. 210) and ending with "one should perform," [it is explained that] they are called *mantras* because one contemplates (*manyante*) by means of them.
Alternatively, mantras are those things characterized by the qualities of *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection).
Thus, *manana* is omniscience, and *trāṇa* is the bestowing of grace upon transmigrating beings;
because they possess the nature of contemplation and protection, they are designated as "mantras."

Thus, although the word "mantra" primarily refers to the *vātya*, it is nevertheless applied here to the expressive [syllables] through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). These, moreover, have the limbs of Brahman as their root. Their extraction is as follows:
among the sixteen syllables devoid of the *ṣaṇḍākṣara*s, the short [vowels]...
The fifth, seventh, ninth, third, and first vowels, together with the letter *sa*,
are said to be the five seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the five Brahmas beginning with Īśāna, respectively. In that group of sixteen vowels, [the syllable] *phu*...

The vowels of the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth [positions], joined with the letter *sa*, are proclaimed as the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the limbs beginning with the heart. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kāraṇa*:
"In the group of sixteen vowels, excluding the neuter ones..."
It is endowed with the collection of the twelve vowels, together with the phoneme known as Nāda.
The syllables of space, fire, and earth, along with the seventh and the ninth,
joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, are called the fivefold Brahman (*brahmapañcaka*).
O twice-born ones, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna are the Brahma-mantras; they should be recited in their proper sequence, ending with the word "namas."
By means of the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth syllables,
as well as the tenth and twelfth, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are prescribed.
The heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye,
and the weapon— these are proclaimed as the six limbs in their proper sequence.
The [mantras] from the heart up to the eye are proclaimed as being joined with the nasal drop (bindu);
the weapon-mantra (astra) ends with the visarga and is endowed with the six classes (jāti).
Having first uttered the Praṇava, followed immediately by the recitation of the mantra,
one should then state the name in the dative case, joined with the word "namas" at the end.
"The utterance of the limbs of Brahmā is honored in all rites.
Thus [it is said]. What is the reading for the extraction of the root mantra (mūlamantra) of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva? *Pā*: "Om hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva."
This is an additional reading.
As demonstrated in the *Śrīmat-kriyākaraṇamaṇḍanapaddhati*,
the sixth [syllable] is with the final nasal (sa), accompanied by the seed-syllable *jaṃ* and *bhāri*, and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
The head-mantras of the deities of the offering are the heart-mantras, joined with the *nīti* [suffix].

Thus, by means of the sequence of short, long, and protracted [vowels]— wherein the short is pronounced as far as the *bindu*, the long as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the protracted as far as the limit of the twelve [finger-breadths] (*dvādaśānta*)—
by that sequence of short, long, and protracted [vowels], here, among the Brahmins...
The short sequence belongs to the limbs (*aṅga*), the long sequence to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and the protracted (*pluta*) sequence likewise [belongs to the root].
Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Sārddhatriśatikā*: "O Six-faced One, the Brahmā-mantras are said to be short, while the limbs are long. Likewise, elsewhere, the root mantra is protracted.
"Situated within the crest-lock."

Now, one might object: "How can there be shortness for the vowels *o* and *ai*—which are the seed-syllables of Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa—within the Brahma-seed, given that diphthongs have no short forms? True;
this is the opinion of some. As the authors of the Śikṣās state regarding the Chāndogas:

"The followers of the Sātyamugri-Āṇāyanīya school recite [the vowel] *go* as short and [the diphthongs] *ai* and *au*. Thus it was stated by the venerable author of the commentary on the *Sārddhatrimśatikā*, p.
Thus it has been said: "Having uttered the mantra ending with the crest of the *nāda* at the point of the *bindu*, one should purify.

And likewise: "The short [vowel] is situated in the *bindu*, the long in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the protracted (*pluta*) should be joined to the station of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*) for the purification of the *Prāsāda* mantra. (Beginning with *Oṃ*...)
"Namontān"— here one should recite the Brahmāṅga and Mūla mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the salutation (*namas*). Likewise,
it is stated in the venerable *Santānasaṃhitā*:
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ and ending with the word of salutation (namas),
one likewise [recites] the limbs of Brahmā, the Prāsāda mantra, and the seed-syllable of Śiva.
Thus, it has already been demonstrated in the preceding ritual for the sakalīkaraṇa that the limbs do not end with the word "go.
What is called "purification of the mantra" (mantra-śuddhi) refers to the removal of the defect characterized by "touch" (sparśa), which arises from being manifested by the words of the māyīya level.
Destruction [of impurity] occurs by resorting to the supreme reality (*paratattva*). As it has been said:
"In this way, the purification of the mantra comes about through resorting to the supreme reality. And likewise:
"Because of the movement between the teeth and the lower lip, and because of the removal of the mantra's impurity."
It is taught that there is no purification of the mantra at all if it is uttered without the final nasal sound (nāda).
Thus it is said. And here, the limbs of Brahmā are Śākta, not Āṇava.
As the venerable author of the *Mataṅgavṛtti* has stated regarding the Brahmās who are limbs of Śiva:

Because it is described as being of the nature of Śakti while existing as the form of Śiva, its actual state is indeed in the station of Sadāśiva. Likewise, the mantra, consisting of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), is eternally presided over by Śiva.
Purification of the Linga.

(33) Thereafter, having worshipped the previously prepared offering with the Gāyatrī, and having offered arghya, incense, and a lamp upon the five heads in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta— using the root mantra ending in *svāhā* along with the common *arghya* and the heart-mantra— one should place the hand over the worship.

Having placed [the vessel] and having repeated the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta, one should remove the worship from the liṅga with the Astra-mantra; then, having placed it in a pure vessel in the northeast for the sake of Caṇḍa using the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should wash the liṅga and its pedestal with the Astra-mantra.

Having sprinkled [the deity] with the general *arghya* water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having worshipped [the deity] in a mobile liṅga by means of the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) or with the seat-mantra, the form-mantra, and the root-mantra, and having offered *arghya*, incense, and so forth, one should remove the worship by means of the *astra-mantra*.
Having bathed [the deity] with pure water, and if the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth are available, having likewise consecrated [it] with that—
interspersed with water, incense, and the eight flowers— so that the head is not empty, one should perform the sprinkling with the root mantra.

Having dried [the image] with a powder of barley and other grains, having performed a thorough purification, and having sprinkled it as desired with fragrant, cool water from a thousand streams using the root mantra five times, the Brahma-mantras, the Aṅga-mantras, and the "Svāhā-ending Vyomavyāpin" mantra, etc., along with the name [of the deity]; then—

Having bathed [the deity] with scented water from the *śivakalaśa* vessel placed there, and subsequently having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water while reciting the Heart-mantra, and having wiped it with a white cloth while reciting the Armor-mantra,
one should install it upon the pedestal. Thus is performed the purification of the self, the locus, the materials, and the mantra-liṅga.

One should worship Śiva. (33) [Prabhā] Now, having illustrated the purification of the mantra, he explains the fifth purification, that of the *liṅga*, with the passage beginning with "tadanu" and ending with "samāropayet. Likewise...
Facing east, one should consecrate [the deity] with all the ritual substances according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, facing north, one should place [the image] upon the pedestal and perform worship.
And at Kāla-liṅga, having placed a cloth upon the bathing altar (snānavedi) facing east, and having worshipped the sixfold raised seat (saḍutthāsana),
[one should recite]: "Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of the gods, the sole leader of all the worlds!"
Rising for the purpose of performing the ritual bath and for the sake of self-protection, one should proceed.
Having made this request, he took up the Śiva-liṅga and placed it upon the bathing altar;
such is the additional reading.
The recitation.

(68) "One should worship you... Thus, having placed in one's heart the statement from the venerable *Kāmika* Tantra— "Having worshipped with the Gāyatrī the worship directed toward the top of the Liṅga, which was previously arranged"— one [should perform] the worship connected to the upper part of the Liṅga, which was performed at the earlier time, by means of the Gāyatrī.

"One should worship," he says, with the words "(previously prepared). If it is a mobile *liṅga*, then one should open the casket, grasp the *liṅga* with both hands, remove the cloth, place it upon the bathing altar, and worship it with the *Gāyatrī*. "(Having turned around)" means:

The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) by touching the head and other parts with the little finger and the rest, in the sequence beginning with *Sadyojāta*. Likewise, in the venerable *Aṃśumatī*, it is said: "In this manner, there is the placement on the faces, the offering of water (*arghya*), and the dismissal of the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*). And here, this is for the lifelong practitioner (*naiṣṭhika*); however, for the householder (*bhautika*), it is according to the sequence beginning with *Īśāna*.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the five heads of the *svarghya* [liṅga] with the thumbs and other fingers; as it is said in the venerable *Sūkṣma*: (p. 217) "Thus..."
Having sprinkled [the deity] with water for the *arghya* offering, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the faces;
one should place the mantras of the five Brahmans, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger.

Thus, by the word *liṅga*, according to the meaning of the verbal root *liṅg* (in the sense of "marking" or "characterizing"), that which marks the world with its functions such as creation, maintenance, and so forth— that is, that which causes wonder— is designated as the supreme splendor of the Lord (*pārameśvaraṃ tejaḥ*). Its locus of manifestation, however, is...
Mountains and the like are designated by the word "liṅga" through figurative usage (upacāra). As the Teachers have said:

"That Śāmbhava splendor by which the world is marked (liṅgita) and adorned with the fivefold duties—that is the primary liṅga; its secondary (bhākta) manifestations constitute the various levels of manifestation."

Thus. (Taking the offering: Here, having grasped the flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger, one should lower the offering from the top of the *liṅga* using the thumb and forefinger while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and then place the flower upon the head of the *liṅga*. Likewise:
One should collect fresh flowers with the ring finger, the little finger, and the middle finger of the glorious Aṃśumatī;
and with the thumb and the forefinger, one should discard the faded garland.
"Thus [it is said].
Having washed the *liṅga* with the *astra-mantra*, which is proclaimed as the *śivāstra*,"
The obstacles, assuming the forms of Rudras, were driven away by him.

"Having washed the pedestal afterwards," according to the scripture of the *Śrīmatsarvajñānottara*, one should consecrate the pedestal of the *liṅga* with the *śivāstra* [mantra] for the purpose of dispelling obstacles; thus he says, "with the *astra*."

Having thus illustrated the general purification of both movable and immovable *liṅgas*, he states that for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the chosen *liṅga* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, the general invocation characterized by the "offering of eight flowers" (*aṣṭapuṣpikārcana*) must be performed; thus he says:
"(In the case of a movable *liṅga*). (In the case of a movable *liṅga*).
Regarding the Bāṇa-liṅga and others: likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*, it is stated:
"The crystalline, the momentary, the stone, the Bāṇa-liṅga, and that which is made of metal—these are declared to be mobile liṅgas. The characteristics of the *Aṣṭapuṣpikā* will be explained later.

Regarding this, some have stated that one should worship with only the eight-fold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) and consecrate [the deity] without the worship of the *gāyatrī* and other such rites; however,
that is incorrect, because the worship of the *gāyatrī* is prescribed even in that context.
p. 219) Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*,
one should worship the previously performed worship with the *Gāyatrī* and with the *ajādi-śambara* mantras.
Having offered the arghya with the general arghya-mantra, one should likewise place the Brahmāṇis.
One should cast the garland from the linga toward the northeast for Caṇḍa with the Heart mantra;
then, having washed the pedestal and the linga with the water of the Arghya vessel using the Astra mantra.
One should consecrate the *liṅga* with the heart-mantra; this is the purification of the *liṅga*.
One should worship Śiva with the [five] limbs, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with Mūrti-Śiva and the others.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the case of a mobile liṅga (calaliṅga), an ablution preceded by the worship of a fixed seat and other rites—as is done for a stationary liṅga—is inappropriate.
As the venerable author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī* stated regarding the worship of an installed liṅga (*iṣṭaliṅga*): "Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth..."

Performing ablutions with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth is impossible; for if such ablutions with *pañcagavya* were performed, there would be the undesirable consequence of mixing them with the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
Therefore, for the purpose of performing the elaborate ablution with *pañcagavya* and other substances, immediately after the purification of the *liṅga*—
"One should worship Śiva with the eight flowers, or with the forms and roots of the seats.
Thus it was said by the venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
Others, however, [hold that this is not so] because of its mobile nature (*calaliṅgatva*),
since the mantras of the seats (*āsana-mantra*), beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, are to be deposited only upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

Some maintain that even when the worship of the complete seat (*samagrāsana*), the placement of the thirty-eight digits (*kalānyāsa*), and so forth have been performed, as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for the fixed linga (*sthiraliṅga*), there is still movement [of the deity].
That is not correct.
When the linga being worshipped moves even slightly upon the touch of the hands or other parts,
one should perform the remaining rites after reciting a hundred of the terrible mantra.
Since this has been stated as a fundamental injunction in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*,
it is not appropriate for movement prior to the dismissal (*visarjana*) during the complete worship of the seats (*āsana*).
Furthermore, [Gaṇapati] is [worshipped] in the northwest and northeast corners in all instances of the Guru-worship.
