Because it is prescribed as something to be performed in the *saṃhitās* and *paddhatis*, and because no dismissal (*visarjana*) is heard of for Gaṇapati and the Guru— who were worshipped at the time of the ritual bath (*snāna*) and during the purification of the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*)— within the midst of their worship; and because there is a dismissal only for the deities worshipped upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Since an expiation has been prescribed for movement [of the deity] previously, movement of those two is inevitable. Therefore,
it should be understood from that very source that the complete worship on the seat must not be performed, and so forth.
Likewise, elsewhere,
the invocation is known to consist of the words "Obeisance" (namas), having the form as its root, lacking limbs and eyes, and consisting of eight flowers;
this is considered appropriate at the time of the bath with water.

"Enough with this much for one's own sake," [referring to] "the water-offering, incense, and so forth. Here, *arghya* refers to the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*). Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it says: "One should worship Śiva with the [five] limbs (*aṅga*)."

"Having offered the special *arghya* with the *pīṭha*, the *mūrti*, *Śiva*, and so forth"—thus [it is said]. He describes the procedure for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with substances such as oil, beginning with the words "(when the five nectars and so forth are available).
Here, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are of two kinds, distinguished by the "nectar of juices" (*rasa-pañcāmṛta*) and the "nectar of fruits" (*phala-pañcāmṛta*).

In that regard, the five nectars of flavor (*rasa-pañcāmṛta*) consist of milk, curd, ghee, sugar, and honey, mixed with scented water. If these are combined with the fruits of the plantain, the jackfruit, and the mango, then it becomes the five nectars of fruit (*phala-pañcāmṛta*). Likewise, there is honey (*madhu*).
One should place curd, clarified butter, and sugar in the middle and the other [sections], using the Brahma-mantras within the squares of the Śarapada-Śivakoṣṭha diagram.

"One should bathe Śiva here with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)—two *kuḍavas*, two *prasthas*, and a quarter [of each]—with the Śiva-mantras at the three times of day. Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhyatantra*:
"In the center is milk, in the east curds, and in the south clarified butter."
Honey should be added to the north, and sugar should be in the west.
One should specifically place plantains, breadfruit, and mangoes, as well as scented water,
starting from the southeast (Agni) and extending to the northeast (Īśāna).
Thus:
"Then, having bathed that [liṅga] with the five nectars, especially with each [substance] individually.
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to oil and so forth. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāraṇa*:
First is the fragrant oil bath, second is the bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
third is the bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the fourth is the bath with clarified butter (ghṛta).
The fifth is bathing with milk; the sixth is bathing with curd;
the seventh is bathing with honey; and the eighth is bathing with sugarcane juice.
The ninth is the essence of fruit, and coconut water is the tenth;
223) the eleventh is scented water, and the twelfth shall be the ritual bathing.
"Food purified by the conch-consecration, incense, and especially a lamp.

(By that as well) means even by the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth. (Separated by water, incense, and eight flowers) means separated by—that is, having an interval created between—water, incense, and the eight flowers.

The meaning is "it is done. In this regard, one should first anoint with oil, offer the eight flowers and so forth, consecrate with water, and thereafter consecrate with another substance. It should be understood that one should perform this for each individual substance. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
From time to time, one should cause incense and a lamp to be offered;
likewise, one should present water, flowers, and the arghya offering.

Thus [it is said]. (Aśūnyamastakam): That whose head—that is, its top or summit—is empty, meaning devoid of flowers, is "empty-headed" (śūnyamastaka); it is so described because it is not that. Likewise, in the *Śrīmatkaraṇa*, it is stated: "One should never fashion a linga with a head that is empty of flowers."

224) Having rubbed [the body] dry and having applied an unguent (*udvartana*), then the great bath (*mahāsnāna*) should be performed with fragrant oils, the nectar [of medicinal herbs], and so forth; having applied an unguent with barley powder, [one should bathe] with scented water.
"Gandhas" refers to fragrant substances such as sandalwood, saffron, and the like. This word "gandha" is used in the masculine gender and in the plural number.
Furthermore: "Gandha, however, [denotes] fragrance, death, mercury, pride, and a small portion."
For it is stated in the lexicon: "That very [word] is recorded as being used in the plural and in the masculine when denoting a substance.
Therefore, *gandhodakam* ("scented water") is a *madhyapadalopa* (elliptical) compound meaning "water joined with scent.
By that [water], [one should act] "having wiped" (*saṃmṛjya*); the meaning is "having rubbed with the armor. Likewise, [with] the *varman* (armor).
"Having wiped with a cloth"— having thus declared the purification of the *liṅga*,

he concludes the stated matter and establishes the rule that one should worship Śiva only after performing the fivefold purification beginning with the self, by means of the passage starting with "thus" and ending with "one should worship."
The worship of Gaṇeśa, Kamalā, and the lineage of gurus.
(34) Then, having meditated upon Gaṇapati situated facing south in the northwestern direction of the *pīṭha*, as previously described, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*.

Having performed worship, and having meditated upon the beloved Śiva-Śakti herself, who stands facing south in the north and possesses the form previously described, one should worship her with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī," and then [worship] in the northeast.
One should worship while remembering Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, as well as Ambikā, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the seven preceptors.

Having worshipped the gurus with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to the gurus beginning with Sadāśiva," having offered the general arghya, and having honored them with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth,
[one should worship] Gaṇeśa, Kamalā, and the sandals of the Lord, [saying]: "Protect me, the teacher of the world."
"Grant permission for me to sacrifice so that the ritual may be successfully accomplished.
Having thus informed the Lord and requested, "I shall perform the worship," he obtained permission. (34) [He thought:
"The sacrifice to the Lord of the Gaṇas should take place first for the sake of ensuring there are no obstacles."

By means of the words of the *Śrīmat Pauṣkara*, he first describes the worship of Gaṇapati and the service to the lineage of Gurus and Lakṣmī, beginning with the passage "Therein... and so forth, [concluding] with "having obtained permission."
By this much [it is concluded]. The meditation upon the seven gurus beginning with Sadāśiva as having a single form has been proclaimed there by the venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
[one should meditate on him] in the northeast corner, endowed with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), with limbs white and pale, and equipped with a yogic belt (*yogapaṭṭa*).

"Meditating upon [the Guru] who wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) over the region of the navel, who has formed the *yogamudrā*, who has two arms, and whose gaze is gentle, one should worship the lineage of Gurus.
This is the manner of requesting Gaṇapati and the others for the sake of the worship of Śiva.
"Enveloped by the words of the illustrious Mṛgendra," it says:
"O Gaṇeśa! O Kamalā! O sandals of the Lord!"—these are vocatives consisting of individual invocations. "(Yajantam)" means one who is intent upon the worship of the Teacher of the World.
(Acting according to what has been provided) means providing the necessary implements according to one's ability.
The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Śiva’s Throne.

(Kriyāpāda 35) One should worship Śiva. Then, in the center below the pedestal of the deity, one should [visualize] her seated upon the tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*), with a body white as the Ocean of Milk.
Upon her head [is she] in the form of a seed-sprout, bestowing boons and fearlessness.

Having meditated thus: "The Śakti Kriyā, who holds a noose and a goad, and whose form is the Foundation (Ādhāra)," and having worshipped her with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," [one should place her] upon the Brahma-stone.
The earth is its bulbous root, the digits of the moon its single stalk, and the contemplator its thorn;
it is a great lotus of agitated Māyā, crowded with many petals.

Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Ananta," one should meditate upon the Lord Ananta, who is pure and situated below by way of pervasion in the center of that [seat];
then, within the Brahma-stone, one should worship Him, the radiant one, upon the Śiva-seat.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta," [one should visualize] those who are the embodiment of his power,
resembling variegated lions, facing one another from behind.
The seats and sandals of Śiva, appearing in the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages.
Meditating on [the deities] in the forms of beautiful lions, white, saffron,
and black, respectively, in the corners starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast, in due order.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya," [one should place] the black-and-white [form] in the eastern part and the white-and-red [form] in the south.
To the west is red and yellow, and in the northern direction it is yellow and black;
these are the four Gāntakas, possessing the powers of Ananta and Īśa.
Alternatively, one may visualize the Gātrakas as resembling crystal, three-eyed, and bearing the heads of Siddhas.
With their arms, heads, and necks rendered motionless, their heads struck by wooden sandals, and their heads positioned at the tips of their forelimbs and feet, they appeared in human form.
Meditating on the qualities of the Buddhas who preside over the gates of Dharma, one should worship them,
having performed the ritual adoration with: *oṃ hāṃ adharmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ajñānāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ avairāgyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ anaiśvaryāya namaḥ*.
Above the pedestal (pīṭha) is the girdle (mekhalā), which has a dark red color below and a white covering above; salutations.
Above that is the pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), which is white in color with a white covering above.

Having worshipped the end of the section in the northeast with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the upper covering," one should [visualize] in its center a bulb (kanda) resembling a ruby and a stalk (nāla) with a luster like that of a sapphire.
The sprout has the luster of coral; the leaf has the radiance of silver;
the filament has the hue of gold and is adorned at its tip with a string of pearls.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the bulb (kanda); Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seed (bīja); Oṃ hāṃ...

Having meditated upon and worshipped the petals as having the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras—saying "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sprout; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the stalk; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the leaves"—one should [worship] the filaments upon its root-pedestal with "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the filaments."
Then, one should worship the pericarp in the center of the elevated portion of the pedestal, which has the luster of molten gold and contains fifty seed-syllables,
together with its sixty-four filaments.
Having visualized the lotus in its fully manifested form with the mantras "Oṃ hāṃ karṇikāyai namaḥ" and "Oṃ hāṃ bījebhyo namaḥ," [one should then recite] "Oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ."
One should worship. Alternatively, one should worship the lotus in its fully manifested form along with the pericarp.
Then, on the filaments from the east to the northeast, one should worship the eight Śiva-śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, who are presided over by the Vidyeśvaras.
At the base of the Śakti-liṅga, within the pericarp, one should meditate upon Śiva-Śakti and Manonmanī;
they shine like the rising sun, possess three eyes and four arms,
are adorned with matted hair and crescent moons on their crowns, and hold chowries.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, their lotus-hands are joined to Śiva;
they hold the mind-transcending spear (Manonmanī-śakti), white as cow’s milk, upon the pericarp.
Having meditated thus: *oṃ hāṃ vāmāyai namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ;
oṃ hāṃ raudryai namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ kālyai namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ kalavikaraṇyai namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ balavikaraṇyai namaḥ; oṃ hāṃ...*
Salutation to Balapramathinī; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī at the northeast of the pericarp; oṃ hāṃ, [salutation] to Manonmanī.
Having worshipped with "Namaḥ," on the circle at the tips of the petals, one should worship with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Solar Orb (Sūryamaṇḍala)," which has a shining yellow form;
its presiding deity is Brahmā, four-faced and yellow, adorned with four staff-like arms.
Equipped with the handle of the sacrificial ladle and the *akṣa* and *kuśa* grass, he stands in the center of the solar disc.

Having meditated thus, one should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc," and then on the circle at the tips of the filaments with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc. Its white-colored presiding deity is Viṣṇu, four-armed and wearing a garland.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
resembling a dark blue cloud, situated in the center of the lunar orb—having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar orb.*
Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] at the tip of the pericarp with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala," [visualizing] its red form and its presiding deity.

One should meditate upon Rudra, who stands in the midst of fire, blue-throated and three-eyed, possessing four arms, holding a trident in his hand, and displaying the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā) and the knowledge of fire.

Meditating thus: "Adorned with all ornaments, wearing the sacred thread of the Naga king," and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala," one should contemplate within the center of the pericarp the Śakti who is crooked in nature and resembles the color of milk-ocean: Oṃ.
Hāṃ, obeisance to Śaktimaṇḍala; and to its presiding deity, Īśvara, seated upon the Śākta-maṇḍala, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, three-eyed, and pure like clear crystal.
The god holds a sword, a trident, an arrow, a rosary, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; he carries a water-pot and bears an excellent lotus.

Having thus visualized [the deity] as being clothed in the skins of a lion and an elephant, arranged in right and left order, one should worship with: *oṃ hāṃ śaktimaṇḍalādhipataye īśvarāya namaḥ*. Above that, the seat—which extends from the earth element up to the limit of the Kuṭilā—is likewise [to be visualized].
Having divided [the space] and worshipped it with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva" (iti saṃpūjya),
(35) on page 233,
anticipating the question of what should be done upon that, he states the procedure for the worship of the seat of Śiva.

From the words "Śivam" up to "having worshipped," [the author] first states the procedure for the worship of the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*) with the word "Of the Deity. He describes its visualization with the word "Below": "Below" refers to the pure, impure, and the differentiated (*sakala*).

In the lower region of the worlds; (seated upon the tortoise-stone): the tortoise-stone is the foundational stone; seated upon it means sitting there. Thus, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "Then, having established the stone, in its center..."
"According to the prescribed rule, the wise one should place there the Śakti, resembling the form of a sprout. Thus [it is said].

"(Having a body white as the Ocean of Milk)"—that which has milk for its water is the *kṣīroda*, the Ocean of Milk; she whose body is white like that is so described. "(Having the form of a seed-sprout)"—[she who has the appearance of a seed and a sprout].
She whose form is like the shape of seeds and sprouts is described as such; that is to say, she whose nature is crooked, because she alone is heard to be compared to a sprout.
For it is heard in the illustrious Kālottara: "That primordial Kuṇḍalinī, joined with the Moon, Fire, and Sun,
is to be known as residing in the region of the heart, situated in the form of a goad."

Thus [it is said]. For, because she is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of these impure sprouts of the world and the material cause (*upādāna*) of the pure ones, it is appropriate to employ a comparison with her own form, since she is the foundation (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the entire universe. The rest is easy to understand. This, then, is the power of the substratum (*ādhāra-śakti*).
She is designated as "Kuṭilā" by the venerable commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, who identifies her as the presiding deity of Śiva-Śakti.
But for what purpose was the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Support Power (*ādhāraśakti*) previously enjoined? It is said: because of the Support Power...
Worship is performed first [with the seat] because it is the support of all;

for since dharma and the other qualities consist of infinite power (*ananta-sāmarthya*), it is impossible for them to exist without a support, and thus [the worship is directed toward] the possessor of power, Ananta, and his seat.
The placement (*nyāsa*) of that which consists of the illusory lotus of a thousand petals is already established by its very nature.
As it is said in the venerable *Samānatantra*:

"First the seed-sprout by means of power, afterwards the seat Ananta; then one should perform [the worship] of Ananta," and so forth. He describes the worship of Ananteśvara with the word "Brahma": [upon the Brahma-stone].

"Above the foundation stone. Now, one might ask: previously, in the passage "seated upon the tortoise-stone," it was said "seated upon the foundation stone," and here in the passage "above the Brahma-stone," it is said "above the foundation stone. How can these two be explained as having the same meaning? True; first of all, the foundation stone— [The text continues: ...is indeed that which supports the entire temple structure. Therefore, whether it is designated as the "tortoise-stone" or the "foundation stone," it refers to the very same architectural element. Consequently, there is no contradiction in the interpretation. Furthermore, the term "Brahma-stone" is merely a specific name for the central foundation stone located at the heart of the temple's base. Thus, "above the Brahma-stone" is synonymous with "upon the foundation stone. This consistency in terminology across different contexts confirms the unity of the underlying meaning.

It is of two kinds, distinguished by the *kūrmaśilā* (tortoise-stone) and the *brahmaśilā* (Brahman-stone). Among these, the *brahmaśilā* is the foundational stone (*ādhāraśilā*) situated upon the *kūrmaśilā* in the position of Brahmā. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Suprabheda*:
"First, having placed the firm *kūrmaśilā*, which is endowed with the portion of Brahmā..."
One should place the Brahmaśilā stone, adorned with the Nandyāvarta design, upon the head [of the image].
Thus it is said in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "First, having meditated upon the Kūrma-śilā, one should install Śakti; and in that called Brahma, Ananta.
Likewise, in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"One should fashion Brahmā and Kūrma from a neuter [stone], and finally [place] the slab.
Similarly, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*: "Having placed the slab in the middle of Brahmā."

He speaks of the meditation on the lotus of the infinite seat (*anantāsana-padmadhyāna*) as follows: "(The earth)" refers to the single stalk ending with the *kalā* [tattva]. "Ending with the *kalā*" means having a single stalk consisting of the twenty-nine principles beginning with water. "(Thorny with objective existents)": objective existents (*bhāva*) are the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*), such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; their essential nature is...

This was stated previously. For that very reason, it is described as having "thorns"—that is, sharp-pointed parts located on the stalk (*nāla*). According to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *kaṇṭaka* refers to a bamboo joint (*drumāṅga*), a bristle (*romāñca*), and a petty enemy (*kṣudrāśatru*). [It is] crowded with many petals (*anekadalasaṃkulam*) [of] illusion (*māyā*).
The meaning is that it is "filled with a thousand descriptions" because it has been spoken of in many ways by various seers.
Regarding the phrase "(of the agitated Māyā and the great calamities)": here, [it refers to] that which consists of the thirty principles beginning with Earth and ending with Kalā.
The lotus on the seat of Ananta is characterized by the aspect of agitation caused by impure *māyā*, in relation to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

It should be understood that it has the form of a bud because it is the cause of limited knowledge and so forth, and because it is characterized by delusion (*moha*). Thus it was stated by the venerable Śrī Somaśambhu: "One should worship [the Lord] mounted upon the *brahmaśilā*, having the form of a white lotus bud as bright as jasmine and the moon" (32).
The seat of Śiva is infinite. Regarding the meditation on Ananta, he says "(situated in the middle of that)":

(pure) means white; (below) means in the lower portion of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); (by pervasion) means by virtue of pervading the entire path of impurity and the path of the worlds (*adhvan*). Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*.
"Śiva is declared the agent in the pure path, while Ananta is the lord in the impure.
Here, Ananta refers to the first of the Vidyeśvaras, and not the serpent-king named Ananta;
for his pervasion extends only as far as the earth, and not upwards. Thus:

In the *Śrīmatpañcāvaraṇastava*, as taught by my gurus, I bow down to the Lord of Mantras residing upon the Brahma-stone through his pervasion of the phenomenal world— the white Ananta seated upon the lotus of Māyā.

Thus, although the abiding of the Vidyeśvaras as the petals of the lotus of the Vidyā-pada is established by implication, it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "It is overspread by the petals of the Vidyeśvaras. (p. 238)
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction, as it is stated that the Infinite One abides here through the pervasion of manifold expansion (*prapañca*).
Thus has it been determined by the venerable author of the commentary on the *Triśatikālottara*.
He now describes the worship of the four feet—Dharma and the others—which constitute the support for the lion-throne, beginning with the word "That" (*tat*).
(Tatsāmarthyarūpān): Those which consist of the power of that Ananta, characterized by the capacity to preside over the qualities of intellect (*buddhi*), the *guṇas*, *dharma*, and so forth.
As it is said in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "The directions are his feet; the limbs are his body."

Regarding the phrase "considered as the directions": it is stated in the commentary on that [text] that the *bhās* (splendors), which are the energies (*śaktis*) presiding over the intermediate directions (*vidiś*), are the feet of that Ananta, while those presiding over the cardinal directions (*diś*) are his limbs (*gātrakas*). He describes their meditation with the word "(vicitra)" [meaning variegated].

(Resembling variegated lions) means like marvelous lions. (Looking at the back) means those who show the back, but do not themselves see it. (In the form of the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages) — here, Dharma and the others [are meant].

It should be understood that, having assumed the forms of the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas, they serve as the feet of Śiva’s throne. Thus it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "The four great feet of the Yugas."
(Sitakāśmīratālādīn): "White" (*sita*) means white; "Kashmirian" (*kāśmīra*) means red; "Tāla" means yellow—by the word *tāla*, realgar (*haritāla*) is meant here. "Kali" means black.
[The compound refers to] those beginning with white, Kashmirian, and Tāla. The rest is easy to understand. [This refers to] Dharma and the others.
The illustrious author of the *Mṛgendravṛtti* has explained that the form of a lion is assumed because of his virility that surpasses all others.

In this regard, the reason why those whose nature consists of infinite capacities (*ananta-sāmarthya*) are denoted by terms such as "dharma" has been stated there by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Śrīmat-kālottara*:
"Dharma and the others, however, are specific infinite capacities, by which [the Lord] sustains and knows everything."

It is said that [the Self] is colored by something and becomes the Lord of all; however, this must not be explained as being due to the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), because of ignorance, since it is impossible for those [qualities] to manifest here.
And it is not the case that animals and fetters are sacrificed here;
rather, he speaks of the worship of the limited entities such as Adharma and so forth with the words "(black and white).
Herein lies the fact that Adharma and the others possess the two colors, black and white.
93. It should be understood that [the state] has arisen through the transference of the splendor of Dharma and the other [qualities]. Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"O Śikhidhvaja, there is likewise non-dharma, ignorance, and lack of dispassion."
The lack of mastery over the four limbs of the body is thus declared.
"Mixed with the colors of the Dharmas and so forth"— the remainder is easy to understand.
Regarding these very [states], he speaks of the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*) with the words "or rather" (*yadvā*). The meaning of the verse is clear.

Following that, having described the worship of the limbs of the Śiva-throne couch (*śivāsanaparyaṅka*), such as the *bhūta-dharma* and others, as well as the limbs of its body, such as the *adharma* and others; of that...
The passage "of the pedestal" extends by analogy the worship of the lower covering, the upper covering, and the intermediate space of the enclosure.
(The lower covering) p.
It is so described because it covers the lower parts.
(Above that) means on the upper portion of the upper girdle. He describes the worship of the bulbous root (*kanda*) and other components that constitute the lotus with the words "(In their center).
He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*) of those [components] with the words "(Rubies...)," which is clear.
The meaning of the verse:
Herein, O Brahmins, the principles (tattvas), the entities (bhāvas), the instruments (karaṇas),
and the genders have been explained in brief regarding both the pure and impure paths.

Thus, according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, one should meditate upon Brahmā, who consists of the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and the element of earth, as the bulbous root (*kanda*). The fifty conceptual cognitions (*bhāvapratyaya*) consisting of Pure Knowledge are to be meditated upon as the seed-syllables (*bīja*). [She] consists of Pure Knowledge.

Purity is to be meditated upon as the sprout; the reality consisting of that [purity], extending up to the *kalā-tattva*, is to be meditated upon as the stalk. This has been stated by the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*:
"In the hollow leaf [of the lotus], in the sunken portion above the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Likewise...
The part above the pedestal is indeed perceived as being concave;
there, in sequence, is the lotus with its petals, filaments, and pericarp.
Thus [it is said]. Anticipating the question, "What are the forms of the petals?", he says: "(having the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras).
Here, for the sake of the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the eight Vidyeśvaras on the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), [the petals are so described].
Since it has been stated that [the Lord] primarily exists as the object of creation in every secondary dissolution (pratisarga),
and since the ancient cities that constitute His abode are heard of as being situated in the eight directions starting from the east, there are eight petals conditioned by those [cities].
"It is to be meditated upon"—thus it has been traditionally taught by that very [author]. (Upon its root-pedestal:
Indeed, the root-pedestal of that petal is the root-base (*mūlapiṇḍikā*), and [the meditation is] upon that.
He states the meditation on the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with the word "heated" (*tapta*). (Having the luster of molten gold.)
"She whose shadow is like molten gold" refers to one whose shadow is like refined, flowing gold.
Regarding the Amarakośa definition: "Chāyā means the wife of the Sun, luster, a reflection, and that which is not sunlight.
(Regarding the phrase "containing the fifty seed-syllables"): here, the fifty seed-syllables are as follows.
It is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara that there are exactly fifty phonemes (*varṇa*). For instance, there are fifty seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*):
twenty-five beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, and sixteen beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*.
"Are they from the letter *ya* to the letter *kṣa*, or not?
"By means of the sixty-four filaments"—here, [the letters] excluding *ma*.
The five groups beginning with *ka*, the semivowels (*antasthā*), and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)—
each joined with the vowel *a* and the bindu, and uttered twice—
are said to constitute the sixty-four filaments in the venerable *Pauṣkara*. As for the pericarp (*karṇikā*), however:
The supreme Kuṇḍalinī herself, who consists of the fifty letters that are the cause and denotators of all things,

and whose form is the supreme space (paramākāśa), is the object of meditation. It has been stated that the lotus, which is the eternal locus of the Supreme Lord and consists of the reality of the Bindu (bindutatva), is likewise to be meditated upon.

This should be understood as being in full bloom by the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*. As the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* has stated: "Its state of being in full bloom and its whiteness manifest precisely its nature of consisting of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); for [it is] his..."
[It possesses] expansiveness and purity because it is the cause of omniscience and so forth.
[The author] states the procedure for the worship of the powers, Vāmā and the others, with the word "thereafter" (*tataḥ*).
Now, one might ask: how is this so in the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva’s throne?

Anticipating the objection that this is merely a description of the worship of the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and others, [the author states] that it is the differentiation of the presiding deities (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Mantramaheśvaras, who have the form of lotus petals. (p. 244)

Regarding whether it is the Śiva-śaktis such as Vāmā and the others that are to be worshipped here, or some others, he says: "(the Śiva-śaktis presiding over the Vidyeśvaras). He describes their visualization: "(shining like the rising sun). He then describes the visualization of Manonmanī.

"White as cow's milk"—thus it is said. Herein, the redness of the powers such as Vāmā and the others is due to their presiding over Ananta and the rest, who are themselves red; whereas the whiteness of Manonmanī is proclaimed because of her association with the presiding presence of Ananta and the others.

The author of the commentary on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati* states the procedure for the worship of the disks of the Sun and other deities with the words, "in the circle at the tips of the petals. These mandalas are not those established in the world, nor do they belong to the *bhuvarloka*; rather—

The substrata for the manifestation of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), and will (*icchā*) are designated as the *ātmatattva*, *vidyātattva*, and *śivatattva* within the transformation of the *bindu*.
Since these [categories] are established in the world as being contained within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Because it is impossible for [the deity] to sit upon the divine lion-throne, and because its presiding lords are not established by worldly consensus,
but rather are specific powers that preside over them— so it has been stated by the Gurus.
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendravṛttidīpikā*, he will state:
"One should meditate on the eye of the Lord as having the luster of the dawn, consisting of [the powers of] vision, action, and will,
and resting upon the triad of mandalas beginning with Fire, which are the nature of the three principles (*tattvas*)."
Thus it is said. Alternatively, the powers of will, knowledge, and action are the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.

Their presiding deities—known as Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śikhā—are indeed specific forms of Śiva characterized by the states of authority (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and dissolution (*laya*). As it has been stated:
In the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra*,
it is said: "Īśvara is indeed the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), Sadāśiva is the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*),
and the supreme Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) is pure, immeasurable, and incomparable."

Thus [it is said]. He describes the worship of the circle of powers (*śaktimaṇḍala*), which constitutes the locus for the manifestation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), with the words "(in the center of the pericarp). He describes the worship of the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana*) with the words "(upon that). "Upon that" means above the circle of powers. "(Pervading from the earth up to the edge of Kuṭilā)" refers to the earth (*kṣiti*).
By the word *kṣiti*, the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) in the form of the Crooked One (*kuṭilā*) is intended.
That which has her as its beginning is "beginning with *kṣiti*" (*kṣityādi*); thus, [the lineage] ends with the Crooked One (*kuṭilā*).

That whose extremities are the circle of powers is "kuṭilāprāntā" (having curved ends); that which is both composed of earth and the other elements and has curved ends is "kṣityādikuṭilāprāntā"; that pervasion which is of such a nature is what is so described.

Here, because the nature of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) and the circle of powers (*śaktimaṇḍala*) as being of the essence of the crooked power (*kuṭilāśakti*) has been established according to the aforementioned method,
this is called the "seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti. Now, by the word "crooked" (*kuṭilā*), [is it not meant that...]?

If it is argued: "Since Mahāmāyā is said to be the eternal substrate of the Supreme Lord, how can the pervasiveness of the Śiva-throne (śivāsana) be described here? For the scripture states that the throne is that which pervades the categories (tattvas) beginning with Earth and ending with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)."
It should be understood that while the seat beginning with Earth and ending with Śuddhavidyā pertains to those seeking worldly enjoyment (*vibhukṣu*),
the seat here described as having a pervasion from Earth up to Mahāmāyā is stated for the sake of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
As the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati* stated regarding the phrase "the seat that pervades the principles from Earth up to Śuddhavidyā," [he identifies] Śuddhavidyā as follows:
This is because of the scriptural statement: "Kuṭilā, Śakti, Parā, Vāgīśvarī, Vidyā, Māyā, and Avidyā are known as the supreme [powers]";
and because it will be stated in the section on *Pratiṣṭhā* that the seat consists of the sequence beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti.
And from the scripture: "The seat (pīṭha) should be conceived as being of such a kind, fashioned from all the paths.

Furthermore, although there are other synonyms for the principle of Śakti (śakti-tattva), the term "principle of Pure Knowledge" (śuddhavidyā-tattva)—which is the name for its final constituent—is employed here in the context of those seeking liberation (bubhukṣu) to refer to the throne of Śiva (śivāsana).

Some say it is for the purpose of making that known. In this manual, because rites are prescribed once each according to the distinction between those seeking enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), both [positions] are indeed approved by the Teacher.

In this regard, it is established that the worship of the mantras of the forms (mūrti) and so forth is performed upon the liṅga, while those of the foundational forms (ādhārarūpa) are performed upon the pedestal (pīṭha). Thus it is stated in the venerable Ratnatraya: "One should install the pedestal-mantras on the pedestal, and the forms and so forth on the body of the liṅga."

(248) Objection: At the time of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the placement (*nyāsa*) of all mantras, beginning with the Foundation Power (*ādhāraśakti*), has already been performed; why then is it performed again every day? True, at that time...
The daily worship of the very mantras that have been installed must be performed for the sake of their satisfaction; otherwise, they become averse. As it is said in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The worship of the mantras must be performed daily for the purpose of ensuring their presence."
Otherwise, they do not grant accomplishment; rather, they create obstacles.
O Guha, if the worship performed over many days is lost,
then the mantras turn away from him and return to their own abode.
Thus [it is said].
The entry into the form of Śiva.
(36) *Kri*: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva.

Having thus visualized the form as consisting of radiant energy (*tejas*), shaped like a staff, with undivided limbs, and pervaded by the supreme point (*parabindu*) which is the essence of the Śiva-tattva, one should place it within the encircling base of the liṅga.
96. (pra) Now, having described the procedure for the worship of the seat of Śiva (*śivāsana-pūjā-vidhi*), [the author proceeds] because the invocation of Śiva (*śivāvāhana*) requires a locus.
The procedure for the installation of the Śiva-form is stated by the passage beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "niveśayet.
The extraction of the mantra for the Śiva-form has been demonstrated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The unborn [syllable] enclosed within the heart [syllable] is indeed declared to be the mantra of the form. [This refers to the form] whose constituent parts are undivided.
Thus [it is said]. The state of having manifest parts is because the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) is so described in the scriptures;
the meaning is that it possesses both natures. (It is "pervaded by the supreme point whose essence is the Śiva-principle.
That which has the Śiva-principle as its essence—that is, its own nature—is *śivatatvātmaka*; and that very [point]...

The "supreme point" (parabindu) means the reality of the supreme point (parabindutattva), which is a synonym for the reality of Śiva (śivatattva). She is so described because her pervasion consists in her being all-pervasive.
Therefore, according to the aforementioned method, among the three realities denoted by terms such as Sadāśiva and the rest, it is the reality of Śiva alone [that is meant].
The Gurus maintain that [the universe] should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Śiva’s form.
Thus it is said in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "From Śakti up to the power of Śakti (Śaktimatī), this is the seat of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*)."
The power residing in the principle of Śiva is the stainless form whose essence is knowledge.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: according to the statement, "One should place the form known as the Īśvara-tattva as the cause of the *liṅga*," it is the Īśvara-tattva itself that is to be meditated upon as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Śiva’s form; why then is it stated here that it is the Śiva-tattva? True, the meditation on the form consists of the Īśvara-tattva.
There is no contradiction here, as [the former] concerns one who desires worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), whereas this [latter] is stated with reference to one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Likewise, it is said in the *Śrīmacchivatantrarahasyasāra*:
"It brings about for the practitioner the state known as the principle of the Lord (*īśatattva*). And so he says:
Having first raised an objection and then provided its resolution, the venerable author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī* asks:
"But how can the form consist of the principles (*tattva*) of Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śakti?
[The reply is: "True; for the Siddhāntas are indeed threefold, as they arise from the upward-facing [face]."

There are the *padārtha-granthas*, the *bīja-granthas*, and the *miśra-granthas*. Among these, in the *padārtha-granthas*, only those words that possess a specific qualification (*sādhikārapada*) are to be meditated upon. In the *bīja-granthas*, only the word "Sarvatīta" (Beyond All) which possesses a specific qualification is to be meditated upon.

It is established in the mixed scriptures (*miśragrantha*) that both [methods] are to be practiced; therefore, there is no fault in this distinction based on differences among listeners in various places. And as for the form (*mūrti*):
It is indeed one's own power (*svaśakti*), consisting of knowledge and action.

And that [power] consists of the five Brahmans, based on the differentiation of its functions. This is because Śiva, due to his stainlessness, lacks connection with a body such as the *baindava* and so forth. Thus, the traditional instruction states: "The seat is the thread of the cause (*kāraṇānta*)."

"The form is of the nature of Śakti," and "The form of the Cause, moreover, consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)," according to the *Śrīman-mohaśūrottara*. "This Śivā, consisting of the five mantras, is the form [of the Lord] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāreṇa*)," according to the *Śrīman-mataṅga*. Enough [of this].
By way of a digression following upon what has been introduced.
(97) The placement of the thirty-eight digits (*kalānyāsa*).

(37) In this form, [one should perform the assignment] upon all the limbs, beginning with the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet: *oṃ hāṃ īśānamūrdhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ*.

(252) Om Hiṃ, salutation to the secret Vāmadeva; Om Haṃ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta—having thus meditated upon [the deity] through the division of the thirty-eight *kalās*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). It is as follows:

One should arrange [the faces] according to the division of their parts for the sake of accomplishing all limbs: Īśāna as the head, Tatpuruṣa as the face, Aghora as the heart, Vāmadeva as the private parts, and Sadyojāta [as the feet].
In the Śaśinī [mudrā], the head is upward-facing; in the Pūrvamūrdhā, it becomes like an armlet;
the Dakṣamūrdhā is desired [as the next]; and the Saumyamūrdhā is Marīcikā.
Jvālinī is the western head; the one called Avyakta is the upward face. Śānti would be the eastern face, and Vidyā would be the southern face.
Pratiṣṭhā shall be its northern face, and Nivṛtti its western face;
Tamisra shall be the heart, and that called Moha shall be the throat.
Compassion (dayā) is on the right shoulder, while completion (niṣṭhā) is on the left shoulder;
death (mṛtyu) is at the navel, illusion (māyā) is called fear (bhayā), and old age (jarā) likewise resides there.
The back is Jarā, the chest is Rajā, and the private parts are Sādhanā;
the right thigh is Rakṣāratī, and the left thigh is Pālyā.
Kāmākhyā is the right knee; the other [the left] is Jānurasayamana. Kriyā is the right shank, and Buddhi is the left shank.
The right buttock should be Kāryā, and the left buttock Dhātrī;
the waist should be Bhrāmaṇī, and the right side Mohinī.
Existence (Bhava) shall be on the left side, and Accomplishment (Siddhi) shall be the right foot;
Prosperity (Ṛddhi) shall be the left foot, and Splendor (Dyuti) shall be the right hand;
Fortune (Lakṣmī) shall be the left hand, and Intelligence (Medhā) shall be the nose.
Kānti shall be the head, and Svadhā shall be the right arm.
Dhṛti shall be the left arm; thus is the Śākta form. Therefore, by means of this Śakti, he is to be known as Sakala (with parts), while Śiva is Viśakala (without parts).
(37) (pra) Now, here begins...
Because the [five] roots and so forth are not possible, the body of the Lord is not of such a nature as that;
rather, His body consists of five mantras which are employed for the fivefold cosmic acts (pañcakṛtya).
"Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta [constitute] the head and so forth"—
thus, according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, the Brahmans beginning with Īśāna serve to establish the body-nature of the Śākta-Śiva form, consisting of its own thirty-eight internal parts.

He states that one should place [the letters] in the locations such as the head and the mouth in the form of a staff-arrangement (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*), preceded by the meditation on the division of the *kalās*: "In this [context]... (p. 254).

By means of [the passage] beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "vinyaset," [it is said]: "(aṣṭatriṃśatkalābhedena)" means by the division—that is, the distribution—of the thirty-eight *kalās*, such as Śaśinī and the others. It is as follows:
The kalās of Īśāna are five; those of Puruṣa are four;
the kalās of Aghora are eight; and those of Vāmadeva are thirteen.
The eight kalās of Sadyojāta are recorded as thirty-eight kalās.

Thus [it is said]. To the inquiry, "In what manner should Śiva be meditated upon through such a ritual placement (*nyāsa*)," he says: "(Then)" and so forth. "(With power)" means with the aggregate of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) beginning with the Moon. "(Complete") (*sakala*):
he who exists together with the digits (*kalā*) which consist of the internal subdivisions of the five mantras; thus, he is "complete" (*sakala*).
Likewise, in the venerable *Matanga*, the Lord is recited as "with parts" (*sakala*), having the five mantras as his body.
Here, this state of being "with parts" consists of the expansion of all powers; through connection with this, even the Lord is called "with parts."
But it is not like the *puruṣa* [of the Sāṃkhya], because of its connection with bodies consisting of the *kalās* and so forth produced by *māyā*.
Thus, even though it is denoted by the word "sakala" (the one-with-parts), there is no state of being a *puruṣa* for such a being here.
The meaning is that [the objection] is invalid because it is not established for the *sakala* [state]. And so it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Even the *sakala* person is not [subject to the *kalās*] due to the absence of the constituents of *māyā*;
because Śiva is here stainless, the dark *kalās* are not to be postulated."

"The digits (kalās) of that [Lord] consist of mantras, and those mantras are of the nature of Śiva. In this context, certain verses beginning with "Īśāna is the head" have been written by some in certain places. Regarding the installation (pratiṣṭhā), [the mantra is]: "Īśāna, of all sciences, [to Śaśinī...]"

Since the *namaḥ* [formula] will be explained specifically as the placement of the *śakti*, and since that very [placement] is prescribed for the *iṣṭaliṅga* in the Śiva-āgamas, the exposition of the sixfold placement (*ṣaḍvidha-nyāsa*) is irrelevant;
rather, it is the placement of the body of knowledge (*vidyādehanyāsa*).
(37) Seated upon the lion-throne of mantras, which has the curved edges of the earth and other elements as its base,
he resembles pure crystal and is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Seated in the lotus posture, five-faced, with three eyes in each face,
possessing large eyes through the powers of vision, action, and will, and endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge.
He has a face that is white like that of Īśāna, a yellow face as Tatpuruṣa,
is endowed with a black face as Aghora, and a northern face that is red in luster.
He has a single face on the west that is very white; he is Sadyojāta in embodied form, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, peaceful, and adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon.
With his excellent lotus-like hands busy holding a spear, a sword, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga staff in the right,
he likewise holds a ḍamaru drum and a citron in those on the left.
Holding a snake-rosary and a blue lotus in five hands;
or alternatively,
holding an axe, a sword, a trident, a thunderbolt, and fire in the right [hands].
In the left [hands], he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a bell, a serpent, and a noose, as well as a goad; or alternatively,
a sword, a shield, a bow, an arrow, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and a human skull-cup.
Holding a water-pot, a rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness— thus bearing these weapons in his multitude of hands, he is the Supreme Lord.

Having intentionally dissolved the manifestation of mere power (śakti) above the form by means of the sublation of the form of the *liṅga*, one should abandon the state of being a *liṅga* through meditative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Having uttered the *prāsāda* mantra— *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*— which pervades up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
[one should contemplate] that which pervades up to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), resembling lightning, and appearing like a garland of water-drops.
Having meditated, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), which has assumed its fully manifested form, upon the rising of the liṅga.
"Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes"— having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllable of omniscience upon the five faces and eyes of the face,
(37) he now states the rule for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the manifest Sadāśiva, whose body is knowledge (*vidyādeha*).

From the words "(earth, etc. up to "having placed," [it is said]: "(the earth, etc., ending with Kuṭilā). This "seat of pervasive extension, beginning with the earth and ending with Kuṭilā," has been explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "(endowed with the thirty-two marks)":
258) This [body] has five long parts, four short, five subtle, and six elevated.
It is praised when it has seven red features, three deep features, and two broad features.

It should be understood that this refers precisely to the characteristics of physiognomy (*sāmudrika-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth. "(Seated in the lotus posture)" means established in the bound lotus posture (*baddha-padmāsana*). Likewise, in the venerable *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*, it is stated:
"Endowed with the thirty-two marks, established in the bound lotus posture. "(Three-eyed)" thus [it is said].

The word *locana* refers to the Vedas, as they are "beheld" (*locyante*) and "investigated" (*vicāryante*) through grammar, Mīmāṃsā, and other sciences, both in terms of their words and their meanings. He is the one whose [nature] is the three *locanas*, the Vedas, acting both as direct expounders and by means of expounding ritual action (*karman*).

Thus it is said: "He who is recognized by all the Vedas. Alternatively, he is so called because he possesses three eyes—eyes that take away darkness. [He is] "endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge."

259) Here, because it possesses the quality of illuminating and the quality of gladdening, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) alone is spoken of as the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*). Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*.
The rest is easy to understand.

(200) If it is objected: "Since it has been stated that [the body] resembles pure crystal, the body of Sadāśiva from head to foot is of a single color; how then can there be a description of different colors, such as yellow and so forth, for the faces of Tatpuruṣa and the others, which lack that [single] color?"—this is true.

There is no fault in this, as the four faces— Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta— are established respectively with yellow, black, red, and snow-white colors, due to their being eclipsed by Indra, Yama, Kubera, and Varuṇa.
Likewise, in the illustrious Parākhyatantra: "One should place the white [element] above as the sky;
in the eastern direction, one should place another, yellow, adorned with the luster of Indra."
The Aghora [face] is in the southern region, black and standing as the end-maker;
and the Vāma [face] is in the north, red, as ruddy as the rays of Kubera.
"Immediately in the western direction is Vimala, with the complexion of Varuṇa.
Thus, the locations for the faces beginning with Tatpuruṣa within the *vidyādeha* are demonstrated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
One should know Tatpuruṣa in the east, beautiful above the heart;
Aghora on the right shoulder, and Guhyaka on the left shoulder;
Sadyojāta in the west, situated above the back of the neck.
Thus: "(With supreme lotus-hands occupied by a spear, sword, trident, and khaṭvāṅga).
Here, as for the *khaṭvāṅga*: it is called *khaṭvā* because it is desired (*khaṭyate*) by those who have desires; it is a bed (*paryaṅka*).
Its "limb" (*aṅga*) is the *khaṭvāṅga*, a specific implement used in yoga.

The specific nature of the *khaṭvāṅga* as a particular implement for yoga has been stated by Puṣpadanta in the verse beginning with "the great bull is the *khaṭvāṅga*" (*mahokṣaḥ khaṭvāṅgam*). The word *vara* means a downward-pointing banner. The word *vyagra* is a synonym for being occupied or engaged.
"Vagra" means "engaged," "busy," or "distressed," according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. (Regarding the *ḍamaru*:
a small kettledrum called a *tuṭyā*. (Regarding the *bījapūraka*: the fruit of the citron tree (*mātuluṅga*).

The remainder is easy to understand. He states the weapons by way of an alternative interpretation (*yadvā*): "(the sword)" (*khaḍgam*). It is called *khaḍga* because it cuts (*khaṇḍati*) or cleaves; it is the "cruel" (*nistriṃśa*) [weapon]. Again, he states another mode:
"(or)" (*athavā*), "(the human skull)" (*nṛkapālakam*). [It is so called] because it protects the head (*kaṃ pālayati*).

There is a skull; that is the cranium of the fifth head of the four-faced one. And that skull was taken up by Īśvara as a sport, not on account of the cause of having slain Brahmā, because that Brahmā remains even today alive and exceedingly robust.

Furthermore, since it is appropriate for the Lord (*īśvara*) to be the destroyer of all, there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) [in this]. This point is demonstrated in the *Mantraśāstra* in the verse: "Bearing the staff, the trident, the boon-granting hand, the skull-bowl, and the sword, [he is] the vessel of Īśāna. [He is so called] because he fights (*āyudhya*) with these weapons (*āyudhaiḥ*).
"Arms" (*āyudhāni*) are those by which beings are slain and cut—namely, the nets of snares;
it is thus stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*. Here, the word "joined" (*yuktāni*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Now, are weapons such as the trident indeed instruments of violence? No;
rather, they are of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and so forth. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Caturviṃśatisahasra*:
"The supreme power (*parā-śakti*), whose form is consciousness, is remembered as the fearless *Sādākhya*."
The trident, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, is firmly established.
By transformation, those very [limbs] become even a khaṭvāṅga with its parts;
it is called *bījapūraka* because of the unfolding (*vivṛti*) of the seeds through their filling.
In the form of a magical drum, that very same [ignorance] is the long double-tongued serpent;
the mind is said to be the blue lotus, and the sense organs are the rosary beads.

Thus, having set aside the form of the *liṅga*, he says "(by the dissolution of the form of the *liṅga*)" to mean that one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) in the form described— having five faces, fifteen eyes, ten arms, and so forth. "(Pervading to the end of the Śiva-tattva)" [is added].
The Śiva-tattva is contemplated as having the form of the limiting adjunct (mūrti-upādhi); it is the supreme bindu-tattva, within which reside knowledge and action.

"Whose form is of the nature of power and whose pervasion is that [power], he is described as such. (Saudāminī-nibham) means resembling lightning; "saudāminī, taṭit, and vidyut" mean lightning—thus says Amara. (Liṅgārohe) means in the length of the *liṅga*; "dairghya, āyāma, and āroha" mean length—thus says Amara. (Vidyā-deham) thus [it is said].
In this context, what is called the *vidyādeha* (body of knowledge) is the power (*śakti*) presiding over the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*).
Thus it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "That body [consists] of five mantras conducive to the fivefold activity.
One should know that the *vidyādeha* faces eastward in the mobile *liṅga*. Likewise...
In the dialogue between Śrī Mallakṣmī and Keśava concerning the daily,
occasional, and occasional rites, Śiva— who presides over all matters— is always facing east, while Lakṣmī, whose body consists of the [sixteen] digits, faces west behind him.
Thus [it is said].
Then, having applied the eye, one should invoke the God of gods, Sadāśiva; for this reason,
based on the statement in the *Śrīmat-Samānatantra*, he describes the placement of the eye (*netranyāsa*) prior to the invocation, beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "having placed."
...up to this point. (The seed of omniscience: That power which consists of vision, action, and will is the seed and cause of omniscience; it is called the "eye. Likewise:
"In the venerable Pauṣkara, it is said: 'Since that which is the seed of omniscience [is located there], therefore the gazing is performed by means of it.

By this very statement, it is declared here that [the gaze] is through the state of being the Netra-mantra. Likewise, indeed, the Netra-mantra is [described] in the venerable Sārddhatriśatikālottara."
Furthermore, because it is not included within the ancillary mantras (*aṅgamantra*), it is taught separately: "The Brahma-mantras, Śiva with his ancillaries, the Netra, and the Pāśupata—
all this extraction of mantras has been briefly told by me for your welfare."
Thus ends the procedure for the invocation of Śiva.

(39) Having filled his joined palms with flowers, while reciting the root mantra— endowed with the [appropriate] kalās, as fierce as the blazing sun, and culminating in dissolution through the process of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā— he [worships] the omnipresent Lord, who is partless, the creator of all, and composed of knowledge and bliss.

Having contemplated the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpaprakāśa*), becoming absorbed in that, [one perceives] by way of the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) from the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*) a light resembling the tawny hue of a sunbeam.

Having brought it down onto the forehead and meditated upon it as resembling ten million moons, whitening the circle of the quarters with the mass of nectar flowing forth, one should imagine it emerging through the path of the flow of the vital breath and entering into the hollowed palms joined in *añjali*.
Having invoked [the deity] into the form of the target with the *āvāhinī* mantra and the heart-mantra (39),

he now sets forth the procedure for the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) and describes the sequence for the invocation of Śiva, beginning with the words "with flowers" and ending with "having invoked."
(With palms joined: The syllable *au* is the digit (*kalā*) of wisdom (*medhā*), endowed with intelligence and other qualities.
Thus, in the venerable *Mantranighaṇṭu*: "The syllable *au* is the end of vision (*darśana*); likewise, the *ulkā* is the primary [digit], and so too is that which follows."
The Anvāhārya oblation is Medhā, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Janārdana.

Thus: "He who is endowed with those measures (mātrās) which are both the *kalās* beginning with *medhā* and whose first is that [syllable]. By the word "first" (*ādi*), the *kalās* beginning with the syllable *ū* are indicated.
As it has been said: "The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu*," and so forth.
266) (*Pracaṇḍamārtāṇḍopamaṃ*): *Pracaṇḍaḥ* means "unassailable. It may refer to a bow; however, *pracaṇḍa* as a masculine noun refers to the white-rayed one (the moon) or a hero.
"Pragalbha-durddharṣa" is a term for one who is bold and invincible, according to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*. He is that very Mārtāṇḍa, the Sun;
he whose comparison is with him is thus described. (By means of the sequence of abandoning the causal origins beginning with Brahmā).
The meaning is: by means of the sequence of abandoning the heart and other locations, which are the abodes of the *kalās* such as *ā*, *i*, etc., that denote Brahmā and the other deities.
"(Ending in dissolution)" (*layāntam*): dissolution is the dissolution of the root mantra; its "end" means up to the limit of the *dvādaśānta*. "(Pervasive)" (*vibhum*): all-encompassing.

"Consisting of knowledge and bliss" (*jñānānandamaya*): here, the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) signifies fullness, while the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is intended to exclude its being insentient (*jaḍa*). "Self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*) means having the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*). In this context, the reading "illuminating both itself and others" (*svaparaprakāśa*) is not correct.
Because it is stated that the manifestation of the other [the object] constitutes its form (*mūrti*). Likewise, in the *Śrīmatkriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*, p.

"Having meditated upon the supreme Śiva as partless and self-luminous"—this means that by means of the state of "I am He," one has become identical with His nature, which is non-dual. "(Shining like a tawny sun)"—*pataṅga* refers to the sun; *pataṅga* denotes both a bird and the sun.

Thus says Amara. He whose luster is tawny like that [of the sun] is so described; [he is located] there (on the forehead), in the place of the *bindu*. (The circle of the quarters whitened by a mass of emerging nectar):
the orb of the directions made pale by a mass of flowing ambrosia.
"By way of the flow of the vital breath" means through the right nostril.
"In the target-form" means in the body of the Vidyā that has arisen for the purpose of being the object of worship;
as it is said: "For the sake of the practitioner's goal, this form of his is remembered."
Regarding the term "āvāhinī" (the inviting mudrā): its definition was stated by the illustrious King Bhoja as follows:
"Having formed the añjali with both hands, the āvāhinī is produced by joining the thumb with the joint of the ring finger."

In this regard, with the body straightened, having filled the hands with flowers in the gesture of reverent salutation (*añjali*) and placed them at the region of the heart, one should contemplate the *pūraka* [inhalation] through the cultivation of *kuṃbhaka* [retention]. (203) p. 268)

Having joined the letter *ha*, the seed-syllable of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), which pervades from the *mūlādhāra* to the navel, with the letter *o* that pervades from the navel to the heart;
and having joined the letter *hau*, which pervades from the heart to the throat, with the letter *ū*; [thus] the letters *hau* and *ū*.

Having joined the aperture of the palate, starting from the throat, with the letter *A*, one should join the point (*bindu*) located between the eyebrows to the *Hauṃ* syllable; the point to the crescent-moon digit (*ardhacandrakalā*) situated on the forehead;
the crescent-moon digit to the obstruction-digit (*nirodhikalā*) situated above it; and the obstruction-digit to...

Having joined that upward-moving resonance (nāda) with the "end of resonance" (nādānta), which pervades up to the end of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) above it, one should contemplate Śakti extending for one finger-breadth above the aperture of Brahmā, and above that, Vyāpinī extending for three finger-breadths.

Having meditated upon *samanā* as pervading four finger-breadths above that, and likewise *unmanā* as pervading four finger-breadths above that, one should contemplate Supreme Śiva— who is non-different from the signified and the signifier— by means of the five-syllable mantra at the end of the temple, beyond the *dvādaśānta*.
Having reflected thus, one should take the handful of flowers as far as the *dvādaśānta*,
and then, by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*), descend them to the center of the brows, [visualizing] Śiva, who resembles ten million moons.
Having visualized [the deity] residing in the heart within the handful of flowers through the practice of *recaka* (exhalation),

and having placed the handful of flowers upon the top of the *liṅga* with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), one should contemplate Sadāśiva’s entry into the lotus of the heart via the path of the *brahmarandhra*.
The sequence of invocation (āvāhana) should be considered.
Now, one might object: "Invocation (āvāhana) is that by which [the deity] is invoked. If the Blessed One is indeed invoked, then there must also be a dismissal (visarjana). In that case—

The quality of being omnipresent would be contradicted [if it were otherwise]. It is not so; rather, here "invocation" (āvāhana) is said to be the manifestation of Śiva himself, who is all-pervading, through mere devotion. As it has been stated:
"The God of gods, Sadāśiva, who is omnipresent and tranquil..."
And that which is the act of bringing [the deity] face-to-face is called āvāhana (invocation).
"But at the conclusion of the worship, that dismissal is performed with [the deity] turned away.
Now, one might object: "Is it not contradictory for [the deity] to be omnipresent and yet present everywhere?
It is not so here, because there is no purpose served by such a [physical] presence; rather, in this context,

"invocation" (*āvāhana*) is precisely the manifestation characterized by the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, which conforms to the faith of the practitioner permeated by the state of the worshipped and the worshipper, and that [manifestation]...

Because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, it is not contradictory that through the specific arrangement of the mantra— which is the signifier— there occurs a particular presence of Śiva, who is the signified. Thus:
Just as the manifestation of fire situated from root to tip occurs within a tree,
so too the manifestation of consciousness in a single place does not contradict its omnipresence.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the venerable Niśvāsa:
"O Goddess of Gods, [the deity] is not invoked by anyone, nor is he installed by anyone; he is not restrained, nor is he brought into proximity."
One should contemplate the supreme Śiva as all-pervading in the form of the mantra;
that is said to be the invocation (āvāhana), and "forgive me" is the dismissal (visarjana).
Thus ends the procedure for the installation and other rites. (p. 271)
(Acting) (40): Having established [him] by means of *sthāpanī*, having brought him near by means of *sannidhānī*,
having restrained him by means of *niṣṭhurā*, and having announced, "Welcome to you, O Great God," and having perceived that the King said, "Welcome, my child."
O Lord, Sovereign of the entire world, remain present within this *liṅga* with a spirit of great affection until the conclusion of the worship.
Having thus made this request, having offered a welcome and the *arghya* water,
and having performed the *kālakarṇika-liṅga-namaskāra-mudrā*;

Now, [the author] speaks regarding the procedure for installation and so forth, from the words "by means of the installation" (*sthāpanyā*) up to "having given" (*datvā*). The characteristics of the installation-mudrā and the others were stated by the illustrious Bhojadeva:
"This very one with the face turned downward is the installation-mudrā," meaning that this is indeed the invocation-mudrā (*āvāhinī*).
"The two hands joined with the thumbs raised are *sannidhānī*; those same hands with the thumbs tucked inside are *sannirodha*. Thus [spoke] the Blessed One, whose compassion is boundless.
The sense is that the Lord remains for the sake of bestowing grace; "establishment" (*sthāpana*) is the steadiness of the mind.

Now, "proximity" (*sannidhi*) is the relationship characterized by the one who is to be graced and the one who grants grace, a state of being oriented toward favor. Furthermore, the Blessed One is constantly intent upon bestowing grace upon me.
"May it be so" is the prayer; "cessation" is what is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*.

(Welcome! "Well-arrived" means a very beautiful arrival. (Child) is the form of address meaning "son. Regarding the word *vatsa*, it is used for a year, the *kuṭaja* tree, a son, and so forth, as well as for the *karṇikā* [the pericarp].
The *Nānārtharatnamālā* states the mantra for offering a welcome and respectful water (*svāgatārghya*) as "O Lord" (*svāmin*).
The meaning of the verse is clear.
The procedure for the ritual placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa).
(42) Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs upon the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands,
having established oneness [with the deity] by means of the root mantra, having protected [the self] with the weapon mantra, having enveloped [itself] with the armor mantra,
and having applied the nectar mudrā;
Having consecrated [the offering] with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and the *mahāmudrā*, one should bind the *pañcamukhīmudrā*. (42)

Having thus set forth the sequence beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), he explains the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs, starting from the heart, by means of the passage beginning with "the heart, etc. and ending with "having bound" (*ābaddhya*).
The phrase "in the places from the heart to the hands" means in the five locations: the heart, the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the chest, and the palms of the hands.
(Oneness) is the non-separation of the limbs and the possessor of limbs. Thus it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the six mantras, one then [attains] oneness."
"One should effect the unification of the limbs with the possessor of the limbs.

Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-Kāmikā-tantra-sāra*: "The realization of the non-difference between the limb and the possessor of the limb [occurs] even though they are distinct. (Having rendered [the self] supreme), the meaning is "having made it pleasing. And likewise:
Immediately thereafter, for the purpose of attaining the state of being beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), one should utter the "Supreme End" (paramāntika) and install the Prāsāda mantra as before.
"And having visualized [the deity] according to the rule, with the previously acquired mudrā.
Thus, the definition of the five-faced mudrā has been stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*.
Having placed the fingers of both hands with their backs touching one another,
and having positioned the two little fingers horizontally, the preceptor should press them down with the two thumbs;
while the middle fingers are held back, the ring fingers should be raised.
"Having formed the five-faced mudrā, this is indeed the mudrā of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the procedure for the water for the feet and other offerings.

(42) Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) at the two feet with the *namaḥ* ending [mantra], water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the five faces beginning with Īśāna with the *svadhā* ending, and likewise the respectful offering (*arghya*) into the five heads with the *svāhā* ending, one should [offer] *dūrvā* grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

And one should offer [the incense] with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* while reciting it with a devoted heart; having offered incense as before, as well as water for sipping (*ācamana*) and the water of honor (*arghya*).

Now follows the procedure for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, beginning with the verse "With a [gracious] heart" (*sahṛdā*) and ending with "having given" (*datvā*). Regarding the phrase "with a [gracious] heart": this means by means of the root mantra preceded by the *hṛdaya*-seed syllable. Thus it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Having uttered [the mantras] preceded by the *hṛdaya* [mantra], one should offer the water for the feet and the other items."

"One should offer" means: "The water for the feet (pādya)" refers to the water given for each foot specifically for the washing of the feet of those who have arrived as guests. Likewise, having placed the pādya at the soles of the feet, one offers it once for each foot.

Here, the purpose of the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), and flowers, as well as the meaning of the four classes of ritual exclamations known as *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ*, are demonstrated.
Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the water for the feet and other offerings for the Blessed One?
Because it is pure by its very nature (*svabhāva-śuddhatvāt*),

the *pādya* is that which brings about one's own worthiness (*arhatva*) for the state of Śiva— the abode— through the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted. For this very reason, the word "namas" is employed therein.
By [saying] "namas," one fixes the mind upon Śiva; through that, Śiva becomes inclined toward grace (*prasāda*),
because the root *cam* has the meaning of eating (*adana*).
The sipping of water (*ācamana*) is the tasting of the supreme essence of Śiva on all sides, which is the state of being of one flavor with Śiva (*śivasamarasībhāva*).

For this very reason, the word *svadhā* is employed here; for *svadhā* is so called because it "holds (*dhatte*) supreme delight within itself (*svasmin*)"—according to the meaning of the term: "the word *svadhā* [is used] in the senses of self-satisfaction, nourishment, gratification, giving, and salutation."

Beyond this, the head is worthy of the highest state; thus, the taking up of the *arghya* (offering water) is the accomplishment of the manifestation of one's own auspicious nature (*śivatva*). For this very reason, the *svāhā* formula is employed here. [The elements] are brought into oneself and manifested therein.
The qualities such as omniscience and so forth.

Thus, when the manifestation of Śiva-nature has occurred, that prior knowledge which discriminates between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is like a flower; hence it is called "the flower" (puṣpa).

The dedication of that [offering] is the ripening into the form of the fruit of destruction, which is the basis for the fruit of Śiva-nature. For this very reason, the *jāti* "vauṣaṭ" is employed here. This is established from the very fact that the word "vauṣaṭ" is derived through the grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) of the root *ṣaca*, preceded by the prefix *vi*, in the sense of "union" (*samavāya*).
The offering of flowers consists in their being inherent in Śiva.

In this context, it should be understood that there are ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) for Śiva, beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of flowers (puṣpadāna). Likewise, in the venerable Siddhāntasārāvalī, [the rites] are listed as:
invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), immobilization (nirodhana), removal of dullness (akuṇṭhana), and the mudrās of the celestial palace (saudha).
The offering of water for the feet, as well as water for sipping, the respectful oblation (arghya), and the gift of flowers—these are considered the twelve consecrations.
Thus [it is said].
The Ritual for the Empowerment of Meditative Cultivation.
(83) Having visualized the limbs of the ritual bath— namely, anointing with oil, rubbing with unguents, and cleansing—

and having bathed [the deity] with drops of water for the *arghya* offering, and having given water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the *arghya*, one should wipe [the deity] dry with a fine cloth. (83)

278) (Pra) Now follows the procedure for the consecration of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanābhiṣeka*), beginning with "anointing" (*abhyaṅga*) and ending with "having wiped clean" (*saṃmṛjya*). [This includes] anointing, rubbing with unguents, cleansing, and so forth; and as for the anointing (*abhyaṅga*):

Anointing with oil (*tailābhyañjana*), rubbing with barley powder and the like (*udvartana*), and scrubbing (*utsādana*)—Amara states that *udvartana* and *utsādana* are two [synonyms]. Bathing (*nirmarjana*) is the sprinkling with turmeric water and so forth.
Those things which have anointing, rubbing, and bathing as their primary components are [referred to by this compound].
Thus it has been stated.
This is the procedure for what is to be performed immediately after the mental ablution.

(44) Having mentally offered with devotion sandalwood, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, śrīpuṣpa flowers, a golden loincloth, girdle, sacred thread, earrings, and other ornaments, as well as variegated garments, along with three handfuls of flowers;
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self (ātmatattva). Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).

Having thus worshipped, adorned [the deity] with garlands of flowers such as *iṇḍa* and others, sounding the bell with the *astra-mantra*, and having offered incense, lamps, water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should display the *manoratha-mudrā*.

Now, with the passage beginning with "sandalwood" and ending with "should show," he describes what is to be done immediately after the mental ablution (*mānasasnāna*). Regarding "girdle" (*mekhalā*): it is called a girdle (*mekhalā*) because it is measured around or fastened to the waist; it is a waist-band (*kāñcī*). [The phrase] "with cords, etc. refers to those made of ropes, circular bands, and so forth.
(Sounding the bell: "In this context, it is called a *ghaṇṭā* because it is struck (*hanyate*) and shaken (*tājyate*).
The definition of the proclamation by the sound of the bell is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:
'The single resonance (*ekanāda*) is praised for the liberation of those who are dispassionate.'"
Thus, the striking of the bell shall produce a double resonance that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"The resonance (nāda) should never be produced below the navel and knees;
however, above the navel, the excellent striking of the bell (ghaṇṭātāḍana) should be performed.
Thus, the definition of the *manoratha-mudrā* is stated in the *Mudrālakṣaṇa*.
