280) Now, for the *manoratha-mudrā*: having intertwined the two little fingers, the two middle fingers, and the two ring fingers, one extends the two index fingers forward.
When the tips are mutually joined and the thumbs are placed at their own roots, the *poṣaṇī* mudrā of Sadāśiva is manifested for one's own benefit.
The sequence of worship for the ancillaries of dissolution (layāṅga).
(85) Then, having worshipped the limbs of Brahmā in the locations of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and having made known one's desires;
(45) (46) now, for the purpose of worshipping the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), the sequence of the worship of the limbs of dissolution—
First, he says with the passage beginning with "thereupon" and ending with "having informed.
The phrase "(in the places of the limbs of dissolution)" means in the limbs of dissolution such as the head, face, and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*: "The limbs of Brahmā [are to be placed] in the limbs of dissolution."
Having worshipped and entreated Śaṅkara, one should perform sacrifice in the place of enjoyment.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa).

(86) Having requested permission for the purpose of the offering to the covering (*āvaraṇapūjā*), and having worshipped Śiva with the root mantra after receiving that permission, one should take Īśāna from his five heads and [place him] on the petal of Īśāna with the mantra: *oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrddhāya namaḥ*.

Having meditated thus: "The three-eyed one, whose cause is the world, who has the luster of crystal, who bears the moon upon his crest, who is gentle and serene, the Lord (Īśāna), with a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands"—one should then invoke him. Taking the face from among the five faces: *Oṃ Heṃ*.
"Salutation to Tatpuruṣa-vaktra"— thus [he worships] on the eastern petal [the form of] Nara, who wears yellow garments and a sacred thread, resembles gold in color,
holds a citron and a rosary, and bears the moon upon his crest.
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship. Taking Aghora from the region of the heart, [one should place him] on the southern petal with: *oṃ huṃ aghorahṛdayāya namaḥ*.
Then [he visualizes him] as three-eyed, with the moon upon his crown, gentle-hearted, adorned with earrings,
with tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair, fanged, and having a distorted face.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with all kinds of scorpions, he holds in his four left hands a khaṭvāṅga,
a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose;
and likewise in his four right hands.
The trident, the battle-axe, the sword, and the staff that crushes enemies.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] who has the luster of a fresh cloud, who is non-terrible (Aghora), and who grants all desires, one should perform the invocation.
Taking Vāmadeva from the secret maṇḍala with "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva," [one should place him] on the northern petal—
Vāma, who is red, glowing with a deep crimson luster, and wearing a garland, garments, and a sacred thread.
He has a prominent nose and a red turban, and holds a sword and a shield in his hands.
Having thus meditated, one should worship:
taking Sadyojāta from the foot and other limbs,
[one worships] on the western petal with "Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta."
Abounding in white garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, with a white turban and white garments, gentle,
adorned with a crescent moon upon his crown, having three eyes shaped like young sprouts, he is Sadyojāta, with a single smiling face.

Having visualized [the deity] with hands granting boons and fearlessness, one should worship. Alternatively, one should worship Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, who have gentle eyes and are respectively brilliant white, yellow, dark as a bumblebee, blood-red, and snow-white, and who possess four faces.

Richly adorned with the beauty of matted locks and crowns, and decorated with serpents and the crescent moon, they hold in their left hands a snake, a rosary, a blue lotus, and a citron, and in their right hands a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting boons, and a spear.
Having reflected thus, one should invoke [the deity].

Having taken the eye from the eyes [of the deity], one should meditate on the eye of the All-pervading Lord— which consists of vision, action, and will— as being reddish in hue in the northern part of Īśāna, reciting: "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes."
It rests upon the triad of mandalas, beginning with fire, which have the nature of the three principles (tattvas).
Endowed with the heart-mantra and other limbs as previously described,
and holding [the implements] in the hands as stated, one should indeed carry a single-faced trident according to the teaching of Yogaśiva.
Having thus meditated, one should invoke [the deity].

Taking the heart, which consists of true being, from the heart [center] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart," [he places it] on the southeast petal; taking the head, characterized by universal sovereignty, from the region of the head with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the head," [he places it] on the northeast petal; [and] to the north of the eye...
Having taken the crest-lock (*śikhā*) characterized by sovereignty not dependent on another from the crest-lock with "Oṃ Hūṃ,

obeisance to the crest-lock," and having taken the armor (*kavaca*) in the form of splendor that cannot be pierced by others from all the limbs at the southwestern petal with "Oṃ Haiṃ, obeisance to the armor," [one places it] at the northwestern petal.

Having taken the weapon in the form of brilliance from his hands, [he places it] on the left side of Tatpuruṣa and the others in the four petals starting from the east, with the mantra: "Oṃ Haḥ, salutation to the Weapon.
Then he visualizes the heart as resembling the moon and the head as having the luster of gold.
(285) [They have] a crest-lock rich with the color of vermilion and armor shining like a bumblebee;
they are seated in the lotus posture, adorned with the crescent moon, and wear a crown of matted hair.
They have three eyes and four arms, and are adorned with all ornaments.
Facing Śiva, they are endowed with the [mudrās of] the spear, the trident, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
Then [he saw] one with four faces, bearing a weapon, fanged, and tawny in luster.
The best of practitioners should meditate on [the deity] as having two arms and one face, granting boons and protection from fear, or alternatively, holding a trident and the gesture of fearlessness.

One should worship these [deities] after consecrating them with the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), ending with the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the presentation of flowers (*puṣpadāna*), performed like those for Śiva; or else, one may perform the worship while merely recollecting the entire set of eight purificatory rites as a collective whole.

One should offer the *arghya* water. One should display the cow (*dhenu*), lotus (*padma*), trident (*triśūla*), and fish-hook (*makara*) mudrās for the Brahmās beginning with Īśāna, and the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra-mudrā*) for their limbs. (46)

(Pratīka: Now, because the *Śrīmatparākhyasaṃhitā* (p. 286) states that "one who is uncovered is not worthy of splendor," since there would be an absence of splendor in the absence of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one might ask: does the worship of the enclosures exist here or not?
In this inquiry, this single covering is the means for accomplishing all desired aims;
it is common to all tantras and supreme among all forms of knowledge.
Thus, according to the *Śrī-sārdhatriśatikā-śruti*,

one might think that the method of worship involving five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*) to be described in the section on the mandala should not be performed, and that worship with only a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa-arcana*) alone is more conducive to spiritual welfare; with this in mind, he states the procedure for that worship.
From the words "(for the purpose of the offering to the obstructions)" up to "one should show," [it is said]:
"having taken Īśāna from the five heads. Here, it should be understood that "taking" means the lighting of one lamp from another. Likewise, in the *Śrīmadvijaya*:
Then, one should bring forth the five Brahmans and their respective limbs from all sides around the Deity— from His faces and those various limbs— like a lamp lit from another lamp.
Thus: (To Īśānamūrdhāya) "Īśāna" means endowed with loftiness; he whose nature is beginningless is that very one.
He who has him as his head (*mūrdhan*) is "Īśānamūrdhā"; to him [is this offering].

Some say that Īśāna is in the center, as stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "One should place Īśa in the center like crystal. That is incorrect, because the application [of the mantras] has been established in this very same location;
for here it is said that from the east [proceed] the three faces beginning with Puruṣa, and that [position] belongs to Īśāna.
The term "crown" (*mūrdhatva*) is used for the sake of indication. Consequently, because it is the crown itself, its application in the northeast—the very place of worship for the head—is logical;
thus it was stated by the author of the commentary on the *Śrīmat Sārddhatriśatikālottara*. He describes the visualization of Īśāna as "(having the luster of crystal)."

Thus, the meaning of the verse is clear. (To Tatpuruṣavaktra: He whose face is like that of Tatpuruṣa is Tatpuruṣavaktra; to him. In each respective city (*pur*)—the body (*tanū*) of those such as the immortals—in that city, by way of being the nature of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
The Tatpuruṣa [face] dwells as the presiding lord; because it manifests knowledge and action and protects [beings] from the nature of birth and so forth, it is therefore called the Tatpuruṣa face.

He describes the meditation on that *tatpuruṣa* with the word "(yellow)": [the phrase] "to the heart of Aghora" (*aghorahṛdayāya*)—by the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*), first of all, existence is expressed according to worldly convention;
and by the word "Aghora," [there is the negation] of the terrible, such as impurity and so forth, belonging to the nature of transmigratory existence, such as passion, hatred, and so forth.

Through the exclusion [of all else], there is the state of being tranquil. Consequently, "Aghorahṛdaya" refers to Him whose heart—His very nature—is non-terrible and tranquil; to Him [the author] says:
"(Tryakṣam)" [meaning] having three eyes. Those which pervade (*aśnuvate*) are the two eyes; thus, there are three eyes.

He whose form dispels darkness is Tryakṣa. Alternatively, "akṣas" refers to worldly dealings (vyavahāra), as they pervade or consume objects by means of these; thus Vaijayantī states: "Akṣa [is used] for a chariot wheel, a die, a legal proceeding, and the Vibhītaka tree. The "treya" refers to the dealings established throughout the three worlds.
He whose [task] was to be carried out by him was the Three-eyed One;
he had tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair— *vabhrūṇi* means tawny— and *bhruvau* means the two eyebrows.
He whose beard, facial diseases, and hair—meaning his head-hair—are [described] in that manner;
regarding this, Amara states: "The word *babhru* may refer to the large mongoose (*nakula*) or to Viṣṇu, and in three genders it means tawny (*piṅgala*).
(*Daṃṣṭrālum*): one who possesses fangs is *daṃṣṭrālu*; the rest is clear.

*(To Vāmadevaguhyāya): He whose secret, extraordinary, and unseen splendor is "left" (*vāma*) is Vāmadevaguhyas; to him. He states the meditation on Vāmadeva with the word "left" (*vāma*). [He describes it as] "the crown of the nose, reddish" (*kaṃ?ganāsāruṇoṣṇīṣam*). Here, the word *uṣṇīṣa* refers to a head-wrapping turban.*

The meaning is "the crown" (*kirīṭam*). Regarding the term *uṣṇīṣa*, Amara states: "In the context of the *pakṣa* [side/section] and *rasa* [flavor], *uṣṇīṣa* refers to both a head-wrap and a crown. The rest is easily understood. (To the Sadyojāta form:
*Sadyas* means that the state of being a manifest form (*mūrtitvam*) occurs merely by the mere desire for creation at the beginning of the world.

To him whose body has become, that is, attained, the state of being the possessor of authority and the whole of the physical form—he is the one whose manifestation is "Sadyojāta" (the newly born); to him [be salutation].
He describes the meditation on Sadyojāta with the words "(white garland)" and so forth; the meaning of this verse is clear.

He describes the meditation on the Brahmās by another alternative with the words "or else" (*yadvā*); the meaning of the meditative verses beginning with "Īśa, Tatpuruṣa," etc., is clear. (From the *vetra* [staffs]...)
[Salutation] to the eyes of the five faces beginning with Īśāna. He describes the visualization of the eyes with the words "(of reddish hue).

[The phrase] "having as its locus the triad of mandalas beginning with fire, which consist of the three principles" means that they consist of the three principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, and these are the mandalas beginning with fire.
The triad of the orbs of Agni, Soma, and Sūrya is its substratum;
the rest is easy to understand.

He describes the worship of the heart and other limbs preceded by the statement of the reality (*tatva*) with the words "the true being" (*sadbhāva*). "Consisting of true being" means existence and so forth; as it is said in the *Śrīmat Kāmikatantrasāra*:
"Existence is its heart. Furthermore, that which is both real (*sat*) and a state of being (*bhāva*) is "true being" (*sadbhāva*).
The meaning is that it has the nature of that [Self], which is the characteristic of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). (The characteristic of being the Lord of All, p.
291) means that its form consists of the eightfold sovereignty through the fivefold activities, beginning with creation.
Likewise, in the *Śrīmacchivatantrarahasyasāra*, it is stated: "Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is eightfold.
Here, the eightfold nature of sovereignty is figurative (*aupacārika*), because it functions as the instigator of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and the rest.

But it does not exist as such [in Śiva], because those qualities belong to the body and the senses, and they are impossible for Śiva, who is devoid of them. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The triad—the effect, its accomplishment, and the sovereignty consisting of aṇimā and so forth—"
The five qualities beginning with attainment (prāpti) have been described as being of the nature of instruments for the yogin.

Thus it is said. For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "The sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting of vision and action belongs to Him; that [sovereignty] is preceded by the Knower.
He should be understood here as the Lord (*Īśvara*). [This refers to the Crest (*śikhā*) whose nature is mastery not dependent on another.]
"Not dependent on another" (ananyādhīna) means that which does not depend on anything else.
That [state] is mastery (*vaśitva*), which is independence (*svātantrya*); she whose crest (*śikhā*) has that as its nature—that [crest] he [addresses].

In this context, the intended meaning is that the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of Īśvara— which is synonymous with mastery (*vaśitva*)— is not manifested through the removal of impurities by means of the activity of another Īśvara, as is the case with liberated souls; rather, it is that very power (*śakti*), whose nature is established as beginningless sovereignty, which is designated as the "flame" (*śikhā*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīmatkāmikatantrasāra*: "His crest-lock (*śikhā*) is sovereignty.

And similarly, in the *Śrīśivatantrarahasyasāra*: "The supreme crest-lock of Śambhu is that submissiveness which is not dependent on another (*ananyādhīnatā*). By others (*paraiḥ*): by other [means]. "Inseparable" (*amedyam*): incapable of being divided.

(Tejorūpam): *Tejas* consists of the rays of the powers of its own vision and action; it is of that nature. Likewise, in that very place, the *tejas* of Śarva is fashioned as an impenetrable armor (*varga*). Thus, [it is called] *kavacam*. It is called *kavaca* because it protects (*pañcati*) the mind of Brahman (*kaṃ*); it is a shield (*varma*). (Pratāparūpam).
It is characterized by the capacity to remove impurities.
Likewise, in the *Śrīśivatantrarahasyasāra*, the majesty of the Lord is proclaimed as His weapon.
It may be said that this [mantra] is capable of destroying the dense [ignorance].

For here, it should be understood that the arrangement of the directions—starting from the east relative to Īśāna—is established solely with respect to the venerable Lord Sadāśiva situated in the center of the pericarp. He now describes the meditation on the limbs, beginning with the Heart: (the Heart).

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: why do the deities of the limbs, such as the heart and so forth, face their own respective directions? Anticipating this, he says "facing Śiva. By this, it is indicated that Īśāna and the others also face toward Śiva.
Likewise, in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
They should be meditated upon and worshipped in their proper sequence, directly in the presence of the Lord.
Thus; the meaning of the verse is clear.
Now, one might ask: "Should one not worship the limbs of Brahmā, having consecrated them with the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) just as one does Śiva?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that one should worship these [limbs] in sequence with their respective mantras, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
p.
294) For these, there is neither veiling nor the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
For each of these, the wise have prescribed a set of eight ritual acts;
bathing, the lamp, and incense are not separate from this, as they are constituent parts thereof.
The meal, however, is prescribed for them and for the Lord [together] at His side;

this is because of the scriptural authority of the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati*. He says "these" (*etān*) with reference to their eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). As to how it is done in cases where one lacks the capacity to perform the eight purificatory rites, he says "or else" (*yadvā*).
"Then one should display the mudrās for the sake of completion according to the ritual procedures"— thus,

from the venerable Mṛgendra-śruti, it is said that "one should display the mudrās of the Brahmāṅgas for the complete fulfillment of the rite of Śiva-worship," [referring to] those beginning with Īśāna.
"(The mudrās known as) the cow, the lotus, the trident, the crocodile, and the sacrificial ladle. Herein, the characteristics of the cow and lotus mudrās have been previously demonstrated.

The characteristics of the trident and other implements have been described in the section on mudrās. For example: "Now, the trident mudrā consists of two hands with the fingers interlaced, such that the two middle fingers, the two little fingers, and the two thumbs are joined together and raised."
It arises from the arrangement of the four fingers— the index, ring, and little fingers— with the thumb [of the other hand];
this Makara-mudrā is also dear to Aghoranātha and is likewise a protective mudrā (sruṅmudrā).
When the two hands are joined together so that the tips of the two index fingers are slightly touching as if to imitate the letter *ma* with the thumb facing outward,
and when the two thumbs are extended as far as those tips, they take the form of fangs.
When the two little fingers are interlaced, this [mudrā] is manifested. Now, for the *sruṅ* mudrā:
having joined the two little fingers so they mutually support one another, having crossed the two ring fingers, and having placed the tips of the two middle fingers together above, facing each other.
Having extended the pair of index fingers and the pair of thumbs so that they are joined upon their respective backs, this [mudrā] is straightened.
"Seals" (*mudrāḥ*) means specific configurations of the hands. In this context, they should be understood as "seals" because they delight the gods (*deva*) and put the asuras to flight (*drāvaṇa*).
As it has been said:
"It brings joy to the gods and likewise puts the asuras to flight;
because of this gladdening and routing, it is therefore proclaimed as 'mudrā'."

Thus [it is said]. The characteristics of the *namaskāra-mudrā* have been shown previously. It should be understood that here one should display the *mudrās* at the location of Śiva’s heart. Likewise, having placed the hand *mudrā* below the two breasts, one should not join them together.
Then, at the place of the mudrā, one should display it in the region of Śambhu’s heart.
Thus [it is said].
The Ritual of the Handful of Flowers (Puṣpāñjali-vidhi).
(47) Immediately thereafter, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Śiva with the root mantra (*mūla*),
and having displayed the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*), one should contemplate the oneness (*aikya*) of all things with Śiva. (87)

Now, for the purpose of fulfilling the power drawn for the sake of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), there is the ritual of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali-vidhi*). (Immediately after that), beginning with "thus" (*ityādi*) and ending with "one should meditate upon" (*bhāvayet*).
The ritual procedure for the offering of food oblations and other gifts.

(86) Then, having offered incense, lamps, water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and the water of honor (*arghya*), and having presented various kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*) and drinking water purified by the four consecrations (*catuḥsaṃskāra*) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*,
and having offered the limbs of Brahmā with their respective mantras— or, in their absence, into a single vessel—

Having offered [the food], having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*), having given hand-rubbing powder, betel, mouth-perfume, and the guest-water (*arghya*), having worshipped again, and having presented incense, lamps, water for sipping, guest-water, and other offerings; (86)

Next, he describes the procedure for offering the *naivedya* and other items with the passage beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "having presented" (*upāhṛtya*). "Various" (*vividham*) means manifold, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*modaka*), boiled rice (*odana*), and so forth.
Amara states: "Various (*vividha*) may mean manifold (*bahuvidha*), of diverse forms (*nānārūpa*), or distinct (*pṛthagvidha*)."
"Water. This definition is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"The water shall be half an *āḍhaka*, or even half of that;
it is said here to be of three types according to the sequence of the highest and so forth."
Likewise, in the venerable *Niśvāsottara*, it is said:
"Water enriched with cardamom, sandalwood, and camphor, and exceedingly cool."
And it was perfumed with fragrant garlands of pāṭalī and utpala flowers and the like.

Thus. (Having said: "Thus. Here, one should offer the *naivedya* to Śiva with the *mṛgī-mudrā*, which consists of the union of the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, together with flowers.
Likewise, in the venerable *Aṃśumatī*:
One should join the middle and ring fingers at the tips of the thumbs;
holding the sacrificial ladle in the hand, one should offer the oblation while reciting the root mantra.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "How is it that the various offerings (naivedya) for the limbs of Brahmā, each with its own mantra and various powers, are to be presented? Anticipating this doubt, one should offer the offering for those [limbs] in separate vessels when possible; otherwise, in a single vessel—according to the scriptural authority of the *Śrīmad-Brahmaśambhu-paddhati*.
Keeping in mind the statement from the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*: "To Śambhu, together with his retinue, [one offers] by means of the root mantra," [one performs the offering] for the limbs of Brahmā.
"One should offer it to Śiva together with his retinue in a single vessel," thus he says; "(in the absence)" means [of such a vessel];
"(in a vessel)" refers to a bowl made of gold or other materials.
The offerings of food (naivedya) and other ritual services (upacāra) should be presented to the Īśāna face alone, and not to the other faces;
for while Tatpuruṣa and the others are the causes for the engagement with other streams (srotas),
the upper face is the cause for the engagement with the Siddhānta stream without any mediation.

One should pay close attention here to the fact that the offerings of food and other services (naivedya-upacāra) must be presented specifically to the face of Īśāna for those who perform the rites prescribed in the Siddhānta scriptures; likewise, it is stated in the venerable Sarvajñānottara:
This [substance], which is to be dried many times with various kinds of food, drink, and edibles,
should be applied to the upward-facing [vessel] according to whatever procedure is prescribed.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding "hand-rubbing, betel, and mouth-perfume": hand-rubbing (*hastodvartana*) is the massaging of the hands with sandalwood powder and the like. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*: "For the sake of accomplishing hand-rubbing, [apply] sandalwood to both hands."
And betel, consisting of one areca nut accompanied by three leaves of the betel vine;
likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*:
One *pūga* for each *pratiprastha*, or twice or thrice that amount;
according to the sequence starting from the lowest grade, the leaf should likewise be three times that size.
"Stone powder should always be given, and likewise conch-shell powder. Thus it is said. And "mouth-perfume" (mukhavāsa) means that which perfumes the mouth, making it fragrant;
the meaning is a substance such as camphor and so forth made into pills. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*:
This mouth-freshener consists of powdered cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and black pepper,
mixed with a little honey and sour gruel.
Thus: hand-rubbing, betel-leaf, and mouth-freshener; (incense, lamp, water for sipping, and the *arghya* offering).

Here it should be understood that one should offer incense to the nostrils for the union with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and a lamp to the three eyes for the union with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Likewise:
In the *Śrīmat-kriyāsārasaṃgraha*, it is stated: "One should offer incense into the nostrils and a lamp into the eyes. Likewise, in the *Śrīmattrayodaśaśatika*, p.
Just as the creative activity of the universe is pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and other principles,
so too is that power of Śiva maintained here under the guise of incense.
The power of knowledge, which resides within itself and consists of its own eightfold nature, is united with Śiva; it is perceived by means of the lamp.
Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for the offering of the purifier (pavitra).

(89) Taking flowers together with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) in his joined palms (*añjali*), he offers the purifier (*pavitra*) while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of all principles (*sarvatattva*).
(49) (225) (pra) Now, it is proclaimed that worship performed without the purifier is of the nature of darkness (*tāmasī*).
The *Śrīmohaśūrottaraśruti* states that one should offer the *pavitra* daily, beginning with the words "dūrvā" and ending with "datvā."
The ritual procedure for the offering of the *ārātrika* lamp.
(Kriyā 50) Having performed the *ārātrika* rite—purified by the four consecrations (*catuḥsaṃskāra*) and ending with "svāhā"—one should rotate it three times above [the head] and then lower it.
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) and the respectful offering (arghya), and having presented sacred ash, a mirror, an umbrella, and chowries,

and having given white garments and palm-leaf fans, one should meditate upon Śiva as being pleased and praised by Ananta and the other [serpents]; then, with the recitation of the temple-mantra endowed with sixteen kalās, one should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Having given the triad, having delighted [the deity] with the Mahāmudrā, and having given the Pañcamukhī;

(50) (Pra) Now follows the ritual procedure for the *ārātrika* offering (*ārātrikārādhanavidhi*), beginning with "the *ārātrika*" and ending with "having given. The procedure for the giving of ashes has been stated in the venerable *Kāmika*.
Then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should apply a mark (*tilaka*) that is white, pure, and fragrant, made from ashes mixed with sand, upon the five parts of the face.

Thus it is said: "By means of the utterance of the temple endowed with the sixteen digits (*kalā*). Here, the sixteen digits refer to the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *unmanā*. Likewise:
"The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu* as well..."
The half-moon, the cessation, the sound, and indeed the end of sound.
Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā;
Vyāpinī resides within Samanā, in that which is designated as the bliss of the limbs of space (vyomāṅgānanda).
"Śiva is endowed with the two [phonemes] *a* and *na*, the two *tha*s, and the eight jars.
Now, one might object: "Is this not the sequence of mantras for the utterance of the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and not concerning the *prāsāda* mantra?
This is not so; for it is intended to express the non-difference between the phonemes *a* and *ha*. And it has been said:
The letter *a* and the letter *ha*, these two, when situated together,
do not undergo any grammatical distinction, just like wind and space.
Thus [it is said].
The procedure for recitation and giving.
(52) Having taken a flower in the hand, having worshipped it with a rosary at the heart, and having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should enclose it with the *astra*,
*kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras— that is, by encapsulating it with the *hṛdaya*, *kavaca*, and *astra* mantras.
Having grasped with his right hand [the deity] protected by weapons and enveloped in armor, while kneeling on the ground with the *sārghya*, *jala*, *japa*, and *udbhava* mudrās, he should recite:
"Oṃ hāṃ! O protector of the most secret of secrets, please accept this offering made by us."
(304) May success be mine through your grace while you remain present!
(PAM) (226) Oṃ Hāṃ! Whatever karma there may be, O Lord, whether always well-done or ill-done—
Therefore, O Śaṅkara, eat and consume that which belongs to me who am established in the state of Śiva.
"Oṃ hāṃ! Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire universe.

Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; He is Śiva, and I am indeed that very Śiva. With these three verses recited from the heart, one should offer the recitation (*japa*), the ritual action (*karman*), and likewise oneself, in due order, into the hand of Śiva which grants boons.
Or, having offered with the heart-mantra alone, one should offer after reciting ten parts of the mantras for the limbs of Brahman.
(52) Now, he describes the procedure for the offering of the recitation (*japa-dāna-vidhi*) with the words beginning with "in the hand" and ending with "one should offer."
(Regarding haste: In the *Śrīcintyaviśva*, it is said: "One should place the flower in the left hand with the right hand;
having placed the cloth upon the right hand, one should perform the recitation especially [there]."
Thus [it is said]. The gathering of flowers here is intended for the purpose of manifesting the *japa* [mantra].
(With a rosary) — this definition has been stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*.
Meru, with its faces turned upward, should be fashioned out of twenty-seven eyes, five-faced and provided with thorns, directly upon the serpent-noose.

Thus. (Having recited: Thus. Here, having placed the rosary on the ring finger, one should draw the collection of beads one by one with the thumb along the path of emanation for enjoyment, and along the upward path for the sake of liberation.
One should perform the recitation while not overstepping Mount Meru by means of any one of these: mental, whispered, or spoken [recitation].
Likewise, in the *Śrīṣaṭsahasra*, it is said:
"One should perform the mental recitation with the thumb and the ring finger."
By means of exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], the fruit shall be multiplied ten millionfold.
"The conjunction of syllables and non-syllables [should be] neither too fast nor too slow.
Likewise, it is said in the *Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī*: "One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of either the mental, the whispered, or the spoken [forms]. And so it has been stated:
For the sake of worldly prosperity, one should draw the thread of the senses by way of creation;
for the sake of liberation, one should draw it slowly by way of the upward path.
"The practitioner must not overstep Mount Meru; if he should overstep it, he shall become a partaker of fault.
Thus [it is said]. (Having encapsulated [the mantra] with the Astra, Kavaca, and Hṛdaya mantras—that is, the Hṛdaya, Kavaca, and Astra mantras. Herein:
Having placed, one above the other, the seed-syllables of the weapon (*astra*), armor (*kavaca*), and heart (*hṛdaya*) upon the flower held in the hand,
the essential meaning is that one should likewise perform the encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) with the heart, armor, and weapon mantras.
Regarding the phrase "with the *udbhava* mudrā," its definition is stated in the section on the characteristics of mudrās.

Now, the *udbhavamudrā* consists of the little fingers being contracted, the index fingers extended, and the other fingers slightly bent. (*Bhūmiṣṭhajānuḥ*) means having the right knee resting on the ground. Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
Having placed his left knee upon the ground, he should offer the recitation to him.
In response to the inquiry as to with what mantra one should offer the recitation (*japa*), he says: "Oṃ hām," and so forth.
"Oṃ" is for the purpose of illuminating the mantra. "Guhyātiguhya" is a term of address.

It is secret, extremely secret, and more secret than the secret. In this context, by the word "secret" (*guhya*), which is a synonym for "mystery," are meant the entities consisting of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti established by such Vedic texts as "This Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth. These [entities] exist transcending those [others].

These are the most secret principles established by the Siddhānta. By the term "most secret" (atiguhya) are meant the Bindu and Vinduva principles; the forms of sound ranging from the various vowels to the end of the consonants; the categories beginning with Māyā and ending with Rāga; all the Vidyeśvaras who dwell within those respective principles; and all individual souls (ātman).
It is said: He who is the presiding lord over all these is the one more secret than the secret;
you are that protector—you alone, and no other, are the guardian of all souls. The meaning is this:
O Śiva, most secret of secrets, you are the protector of all; please accept the recitation performed by us.
O Lord,
while you remain as the protector, by means of which recitation success arises through your grace.

By the word "siddhi" (accomplishment) here, the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, which reside in various stages for the sake of the practitioner, are meant. Even for one desiring liberation, these are performed by means of the offering of oblations to remove obstacles for those seeking liberation.

Whatever action whatsoever is undertaken—both types of action, O God, O Śaṅkara—is expressed by the word *kṣapaya* (destroy) in the sense of the mantra "O Śiva, who abides in the state of Śiva, having united me with the state of Śiva through initiation, consume [my actions]"; this is the meaning of the nature of this mantra. Of this mantra...
The first word denotes the meaning of "destruction" because it is the crest-lock (śikhā),
and the second word is the primary mantra as stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa-tantra*; thus, [the purification] occurs through the application of the crest-lock.
It is prescribed by means of the severing of knots and other such rites;
therefore, its purpose is for the sake of destruction (*kṣapaṇa*). By this [it is shown that] what occurs unintentionally after the time of initiation— (p. 309) [is thus accounted for].

An evil deed performed unintentionally is considered [merely] an action; for regarding the general category of sin committed intentionally, expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) have been prescribed in the specific scriptures (*viśeṣa-śāstra*), and because intentional action is forbidden for one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Therefore, the meaning is: "O Śaṃkara, destroy such karma.
He explains the mantra for self-surrender with the words "Śivo dātā" (Śiva is the giver).
By this verse, the offering of oneself is performed. Of this...
By the first half [of the verse], Śiva, who is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) of the self-offering, is described. (Śiva is the giver.
By the word "Śiva," he is characterized by the state of being Śiva (*śivatva*), which consists of action and eternal, stainless, unsurpassed knowledge of all objects.

The Supreme Lord is so called. He alone is the Giver (*dātā*), the purifier of those possessed of beginningless impurity; from the root *div* meaning "to purify," the form *dātā* is derived as "the Giver. (Śiva is the Enjoyer.
He alone is the protector of all. Regarding the term "Enjoyer" (*bhoktā*), the root *bhuj* signifies both "protecting" and "consuming."
Because it has been stated thus, here (p.
310) (227) the root *bhuji* functions in the sense of protection alone; Śiva exists as the protector alone.
Because worldly transaction is impossible [for one who does not eat], according to the Śruti: "Not eating, another gazes upon [him].
(Śiva is this entire universe): That Śiva exists pervading this entire universe—consisting of the pure, the mixed, and the impure—as its protector and as its purifier.

No one other than this [Self] exists as the purifier and the protector. By the second half [of the verse], the Self is declared to be its giver, its agent, and its instrument—as in "Śiva performs the sacrifice. Having abandoned the natural state, one should contemplate: "I am Śiva."

"Having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva; as long as one has not become equal to Him, one is not capable of propitiation"— by such statements, one who is purified through the previously mentioned methods such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) becomes [qualified] for all ritual bases (adhikaraṇa) enjoined by the scriptures everywhere, [establishing] one's own...
He who sacrifices for the sake of purification and performs worship is the worshipper Śiva.
But I [am distinct] from Śiva, who is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) denoted by the word "I."
The essential nature of the self, which is to be offered therein, is said to be delimited by the previous group of eight (pūrvaṣṭaka).
Thus has the author of the commentary on the Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati explained these three verses.
The method for the worship and other rites of the mantra to be accomplished.

(52) One who worships with mantras for specific desires, having made a request for that purpose and received permission, [should place] the mantras of Gaurī and others in female form on the eastern edge of the right petal of the lotus seat of Śiva, and those in male form on the western side.
One should worship the *mṛtyuñjaya* and other mantras, as well as the mantras of Umā and Maheśvara in their male and female forms,
before the deity. Therein, having offered a seat and a physical form up to the end of one's own path with the *praṇava*,
and having invoked [the deities] with their respective mantras enclosed by the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should perform the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*.

Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, and having recited the mantra a thousand times, or one hundred and eight times, or according to one's capacity, one should offer it to Śiva— who is colored by the desired mantra— after it has been encapsulated by the heart-mantra, protected by the weapon-mantra, and enveloped by the armor-mantra.

Alternatively, at the conclusion of the *āvaraṇa-pūjā*, having propitiated the mantras for specific desires (*kāmyamantra*), and subsequently, at the end of the recitation (*japa*), having performed the recitation of the mantras for specific desires, one should offer [the oblation] as previously described. (52)

Now, [the author] explains the method for the practitioner’s worship of the mantra to be accomplished and so forth, beginning with the words “(kāmyamantra)” and ending with “(nivedayet). “(Strīrūpān)” means those designating female deities; “(puṃrūpān)” means those designating male deities.

"Having the forms of female and male" means those which denote deities possessing both female and male forms. "Of the deity" refers to Aghora-nātha. "In front" means as follows: here, when the mantra to be accomplished (*sādhya-mantra*) is the form of the Goddess, then it is to be worshipped on the eastern part of the southern petal of the lotus-throne of Śiva; however, if it is the form of the God [Aghora], then it is to be worshipped on the western part of the northern petal.
In that case, if there is a male and female form on the western part of the lotus petal,
then the intended meaning is "from the middle of the lotus petal. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*.
On the southern lotus petal, one should place three forms of the male and female deities in the eastern and western sections;
[these are to be placed] in the midst of the light of the Aghora-eye, and nowhere else.
313) Thus, having stated the location for the worship of the *kāmyamantra*, he describes the manner of its adoration with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Regarding the phrase "up to the end of one's own path" (*svādhvāntam*): here, it refers to the limit up to which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *kāmyamantra* extends along the path.

The venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendra-tantra* has stated that one should perform an invocation (*āvāhana*) that is not overly restrictive, explaining: "(to the one) colored by the mantra desired [by the practitioner]" (*kāmyamantrōparaktāya*).
This means: "to the one who is suffused by the mantra favored by the seeker" (*sādhakābhimatamantrōparañjitāya*). Likewise...
In the *Śrīmat-sarvasrotasaṃgraha-sāra*, it is said: "By whatever form the practitioner constantly contemplates [the Lord],
the Lord becomes identical with that very form, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*)."

Thus: "(One should) offer. This means that having stated one's daily desire, one should announce: "Protect this recitation of mine. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The practitioner, having directed his intention toward his desired goal, should consign his recitation [to the deity]. This is the sequence for the propitiation of that mantra.
He states an alternative interpretation with the words "or else" (athavā).
The ritual procedure for the worship of one’s own guru.

(53) Thereafter, having offered a seat— either the *ṣaḍuttha* [seat] or one prepared by a single application— in the south-eastern quarter of the deity's [mandala], and having placed the Guru in the form of the [deity's] form (*mūrti*) there using the *mūrti-mantra*, and having invoked Śiva into that [form] and offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings;
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having meditated upon Śiva, [one should offer salutations]:

"Repeated salutations to the feet of the illustrious Guru, together with his Śakti; repeated salutations to those who are the cause of the eternal manifestation of the consciousness of the self within the virtuous."
One should satisfy [the deity] with hymns of praise and so forth, beginning with these words.

(53) (Pra) Now, having illustrated the sequence for the worship of the *kāmya* mantras, he describes the procedure for the service of one's own guru with the passage beginning with "tadanu" and ending with "toṣayet."

"(The seat by means of a single application)" means that here, while contemplating the mantras of the seats beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti, one should worship while uttering only the mantra of the Śiva-seat. "(Or the sixfold [application])" means:
This definition is stated in the venerable *Vimalāvatī* (p. 315).
Infinity, Dharma, Knowledge, Dispassion,
Sovereignty, and Lotus— this is the sixfold arising seat.

Thus he speaks the hymn: "(To the) venerable ones (together with their powers). This means: to those endowed with the capacity for liberating from bonds. The remainder is easy to understand. Here, "the guru" refers to one's own personal guru, as he will later state: "one's own guru and the seat of knowledge."
The ritual procedure for the worship of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).

(58) Thereafter, in the western direction of the deity, having worshipped the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Yogapīṭha; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the Vidyāpīṭha," [one should proceed].
I bow with my mind, speech, and body to the Lord who bestows all-encompassing wisdom upon the universe, having brought him forth from his seat of knowledge.
Having praised [the deity] with these and other verses;
(54) (pra) Now follows the procedure for the worship of the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), beginning with "thereafter" (*tadanu*) and ending with "having praised" (*stutvā*).
The so-called Yoga-pīṭha is the seat beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti. Likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīmatpañcāvaraṇastava*:
"It is auspicious, consisting of the entire path from the Earth element up to the end of Kuṭilā."
I take refuge in this divine seat of yoga, the throne of Śiva.
Thus it is said: the venerable author of the commentary on the *Sarvajñānottara* has stated that the seat (*pīṭha*) of the body of Yoga belonging to Sadāśiva is its foundational support.
First, the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) consists of the respective *saṃhitās*, such as the venerable *Mṛgendra* and others. Likewise...

In the *Śrīmaj-jñānaratnāvalī*, it says: "One should worship the Vidyāpīṭha, which consists of ten million [verses], or else one's own *Saṃhitā*. It speaks of the hymn as "(sakala)"—meaning it bestows the realization characterized by the manifestation of all knowledge and action (*sarvajñānakriyā*). As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra*,
it is stated that upon the cessation of the authority of the power of darkness (*tamaś-śakti*) and its subsequent withdrawal,
Śiva reveals the infinity of knowledge and action for the individual soul (*aṇu*), who is the ornament of the universe.
Thus, the rest is clear.
The procedure for what is to be performed immediately after the worship of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).

(55) Having offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Deity, (55) the ritual procedure for what is to be done immediately thereafter [is as follows]: beginning with "of the Deity" and ending with "having offered."
The sequence of praise.
(kri) 56) One should please [the deity] with hymns of praise. For example:
"Having paid homage to the Lord of the Gods, who has the moon as his crest-ornament, I bow forever to the god Sadāśiva, who wears a garland of skulls."
I bow always to Sadāśiva, who is Kāleśvara, Mahākāla, Kāla, and the dweller in old age; who is the maker of time and the knower of time.
I bow to Sadāśiva, the doer of all, the giver of all, the omniscient, the unconquered,
who dwells as the self within all beings.
I bow perpetually to that Sadāśiva, the creator of the worlds, who brought forth all beings, including Brahmā and the other gods and asuras.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, the God who is the most excellent, the most venerable, the giver of boons, the supreme, whose vehicle is the bull, and who wears the garland of choice.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, who is full of joy, the giver of joy, most beloved, pleasant to behold, the dear one of Umā, and eternally beautiful.
I bow always to Sadāśiva, the god composed of dharma and adharma, who brings about the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain, and who is the guide to bondage and liberation.
I bow always to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, whose domain consists of the mind, intellect, ego, and the subtle elements and senses.
I bow forever to that subtle Sadāśiva, the supreme syllable Om, whom the great-souled sages devoted to auspicious vows meditate upon.
I bow forever to Sadāśiva, the God who is subtle, all-pervading, eternal, the Lord of the lords of all sciences, and the refuge of all principles.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the self, the moon,
and the sun; mind, intellect, ego, and even supreme primordial nature—
all these follow His will, which undergoes the transformations of existence and non-existence.
To that supreme deity, the highest, the Supreme Self;
Salutations to you, the infinite self, who are greater than the great, more immense than the immense, the master of great illusion and supreme illusion, and subtler even than the subtle.
Salutations to you whose form is awakening; salutations to you, O destroyer of time!
Salutations to you, O lord of the kalās; salutations to you, the impeller of all time!
O Lord of the Universe, who assumes the form of the universe through your parts by means of those very parts;
O Primordial Time, the instigator of all, salutations be unto you!
Victory to you, O preeminent Lord of Heroes, who causes the bursting and splitting of the bonds in Raurava, Jalāndhaka, and Pṛthuskandha, and who utterly consumes the obstructed cities!
Victory to you, O Lord of all the gods, who performed the terrifying decapitation;
victory to you, whose power is renowned, the destroyer of the existence of Manmatha!
Victory to you, O Acyuta, who destroys the body [of Mura], who took away the power of Kālakūṭa;
victory to you, who shatters the force of rivers with the great turbulence of your whirlpools!
O deluder of the sage’s wife in the Jayadāruvana grove!
O you whose great undertaking was the dance of victory, and who were fierce in the agitation of your play!
Victory to you, who terrify the gods and asuras with the fierce intensity of your form;
victory to you, whose elephant-faced head displays a magnificent torrent of blood!
Victory to you, O manifestation of heroic prowess, destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice!
Victory to you, O wondrous Great Liṅga, who are proud of the power of your established form!
Victory to you, O fierce one with white omens who brings down the bodies of Death;
victory to you, O daughter of the mountain, who deludes Kāma and is the abode of all the gods!
Victory to you, O dispeller of the darkness of the web of delusion and the fever of suffering!
Victory to you, the burner of the worlds above and below, from the netherworld to the peak of existence!
Obeisance to you, the omniscient Śrīmatkiraṇa; obeisance to you, the creator of all.
Obeisance to you, whose nature is unimpaired, who consists of pure consciousness.
Salutations to the peaceful radiance whose body transcends all means of valid cognition;
salutations to the inner self, beyond the cause of true consciousness and devoid of both rejection and acquisition.

Salutations to you, the Lord who is without beginning or end, the auspicious one, the Supreme Self; salutations to you whose nature is the ultimate reality, the all-pervading manifestation, the immeasurable soul.
Salutations to You who are distinct from knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge;
salutations to the Brahman of bliss, whose essential nature is pure consciousness alone.
Salutations to You, whose body is knowledge distinct from ignorance;
salutations to You, who are accessible solely through Your own means of valid cognition and who are self-luminous.
Salutations to You, the fulfiller of desires, who always performs the five cosmic acts for Your own selves;
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, as described in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*.
Pervaded by the quality of your grace, the deities sport in heaven.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is pervaded by you;
even sinners [are purified] by the mere remembrance of the power of your lotus feet.
Indeed, those who have destroyed the multitude of their sins become possessors of supernatural powers;
how much more so, then, the steadfast sages who have offered their very minds unto you?
The yogins, freed from all evils and devoid of longing,
are dustless and sorrowless, having indeed transcended the ocean of worldly existence.
For there are other men as well, O Lord of the Gods, who have obtained their desired boons;
I alone am one of little fortune, a partaker of suffering and devoid of happiness.
O Lord, my great sin is like a diamond,
yet your powers are intense for the sake of uprooting saṃsāra.
Having fallen into my power, they have quickly met their death;
therefore, O Blessed One, you yourself should act for my desired end.
In the venerable *Mataṅgapārameśvara*: Victory, victory, O Supreme Lord whose crest is the moon! Victory, victory, O Śiva, accompanied by Ambā, Lord of Śaṅkara!
Victory, victory, O Mṛḍa, Bhīma, wearer of the elephant hide! Victory, victory, conqueror of the cities of Time; be gracious!
Victory, victory to you, O sole Mother of the World, Sovereign! Victory, victory to you, O Mistress who protects her own, the daughter of Vinatā!
Victory, victory to you, O ocean of the nectar of compassion! Victory, victory to you, O Girijā; salutations, be gracious!
Having praised [the deity] in this manner, according to the extent of one's mental capacity,

(56) (pra) now follows the sequence of praise (*stutikrama*) with hymns (*stotra*), beginning with "having praised" (*ityādi*) and ending with "having praised" (*stutvā*). The meaning of the hymn is clear.
The Procedure for Circumambulation and Prostration.
(57) Having performed three circumambulations without making any sound and having prostrated like a staff with the eight limbs of the body, he rose up joyful.
(57) (pra) Now, [the author] demonstrates the procedure for circumambulation and salutation by means of the words beginning with "pradakṣiṇa."
(Standing up) with this [concluding phrase].
(With eight limbs) meaning accompanied by the eight limbs beginning with the head and hands. Likewise, in the glorious and radiant [text].
"The head, the two hands, the two ears, the chin, and the pair of arms—this is the eight-limbed prostration. (Having prostrated).
In this regard, one should perform the salutation three or five times.
"Likewise, having performed prostrations with devotion before Śiva three, five, seven, nine, or twelve times according to the count, the person [should proceed].
This is the rule for those unable to perform the worship at the two times and so forth.

(57) However, one who is unable to perform worship at the two times [dawn and dusk] and so forth should worship Śiva with the *āsana*, *mūrti*, and *mūla-mantra*, and then worship the *brahma*, *netra*, and *aṅga* mantras in the locations of the *bhoga-aṅgas* according to the sequence of the *sandhyā-gaṇa*. (57)
Now, having thus illustrated the sequence of worship—
whether this worship is for the sake of others or for one's own sake, O Janārdana—
it is prescribed to be performed once, twice, or thrice a day.
Thus, since worship at two times and so forth is prescribed in the *Śrīmadajitādishruti*, what [should be done] for one who is unable to do that?
Anticipating the objection that there might be another injunction, he says, from "at two times" (*dvikāla*) up to "one should worship" (*pūjayet*).

Here, worship at a single time is primary and should be performed specifically at midday, because its primacy is explicitly heard in scripture; for it begins with the words, "Having gone to the *savana* at the half-day... (*dinārdhe savanaṃ gataḥ*).
In that meritorious gateway of all mantras, which has the Supreme Lord as its presiding deity,
he who eats the sacrificial offering honored by the gods without first performing that [rite]— [is a sinner].
The day of death for a living being is known to last until its cessation;
the mantras established upon the seat of yoga do not preside over that [cessation].

Thus, at one time, having set aside the worship of the station of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), it should be understood that the performance of the various timely worships occurs through the other [worship] and by means of the eight-flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikārcana*). As it has been said:

"Because the ritual procedure for worship at two times and so forth—performed by including the offering of the eight flowers and other items—is accomplished even by means of worship at a single time. Thus it is said.
p.
225) The procedure for the daily fire-ritual.
(53) Then, having informed Śiva, one should proceed to the fire-chamber for the purpose of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).

One who is not authorized [to enter] should worship Śiva— either with eight flowers, excluding the eye-mantra, consisting of the seat (*āsana*), the form (*mūrti*), and the root-limbs (*mūlāṅga*), according to their respective places, or with all the Brahma-limbs (*brahmāṅga*) together.
Having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, one should conclude the worship.
Even if one is qualified for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), if due to a deficiency of materials or an inability to perform it,
one recites [the mantra] ten times the number of oblations (*homa*) and offers the oblation, one should then conclude the worship.
Then, the officiant responsible for the fire-ritual,

having gathered the necessary materials and requested permission to perform the rite, and having received that permission, shall bring the arghya-vessel and other implements to a sacrificial pit prepared in a direction other than south, southwest, or northwest.
Having approached a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and sat down facing either east or north, one should gaze at it with the eye [of the deity] established by the root-mantra,
and perform sprinkling and striking with the Śiva-mantra.
Sprinkling with the Astra-mantra ending in *kuśair huṃ phaṭ*, and digging, scattering, and filling with the Kavaca-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. (p. 326)
Having performed the leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and smearing with a sword or a *kuśa* blade,

and having prepared three lines oriented toward the east within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using a *kuśa* blade while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should then prepare one line oriented toward the north.
If facing north, having performed the rite in reverse order, having sprinkled with the *kavaca* mantra,

and having visualized the perfection of all consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should place a seat (*viṣṭara*) there with a bundle of *darbha* grass using the heart mantra, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī."
One should duly invoke the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe and the Vidyā,
visualizing her as dark-complexioned, in her menses, and adorned with excellent garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having meditated thus on her with a serene face and three eyes resembling lotus petals,
one should likewise worship the god Vāgīśvara with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvara," offer the *arghya*, and thereafter [use] fuel produced from a forest or similar source.

Having brought the fire into a purified vessel, having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyād), and having consecrated it with the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa), [one should worship it] with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ,
obeisance to the form of Fire (vahnimūrti)."
Having taken up the fire with the mantra and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, having drawn it in through the *iḍā* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*),
and having joined it with the navel-fire and the lunar drop (*vaidava*) by means of retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one unifies them and [exhales] through the *recaka*.

With the Piṅgalā [nāḍī], having placed the fiery seed-syllable, which resembles the flame of a lamp, by means of the udbhava-mudrā while reciting "Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire," using the *saṃhitā* [mantra].

Having worshipped [it] and contemplated it as the supreme power (*vīrya*) of the Lord, or visualizing it being cast by Vāgīśvara into the channel within the womb of Vāgīśvarī, one should project it toward oneself with the root mantra, collect it, and [unite it] with the Goddess.

Having offered the garments, purification, and sipping of water with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, having worshipped with the Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, and having offered five oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), [one should worship] in the east, south, west, and north directions with: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. *Oṃ*...

Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra; Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta," and having requested protection for the infant from Agni, one should give the fire the name "Oṃ Hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations," and then dismiss the two parents.
Then, having worshipped Śiva in the heart-lotus of the fire as before, at the time of the food offering (naivedya),
one should perform oblations with sesame seeds and other materials according to one's capacity, using the root mantra and the Brahma-aṅgas, each for one-tenth of the total number.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having paid homage to that ash, having worshipped with the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),
having offered the *arghya* for the one facing away, having raised [the deity] residing in the fire and joined it with the image (*mūrti*),
and having dismissed Śiva as independent, [one recites]: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ*.

Having offered four oblations with "svassvāhā" and "oṃ bhūrbhuvassvassvāhā," having presented the *bali* offering to Brahmā and the other deities, and having bowed to the fire, one should consume the sacrificial remains (*huta*) and say, "I shall now cease. Then, [one should worship] the fire with "oṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ śivāgnaye namaḥ."
That which is to be released; one should release even Brahmā and the others in reverse order.

Now, having thus explained the sequence of worshipping Śiva with the five bases, beginning with the Sun— as prescribed by such scriptural passages as "Next, the worship of the Sun"— [the author] now sets forth the procedure for the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*), characterized by the worship of the sixth base, the Fire.
The [rite] named Līlāvatī, performed according to the method prescribed in the Śivāgama, is summarized by the passage beginning with "śrute" and ending with "visṛjet" on page 329.

Now, anticipating the objection that "should not the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) be performed by everyone as well?", he says "no" with the word "(that)": "(he who is) unqualified for that. This means one who lacks the qualification (*anadhikārī*) for that fire-ritual; and such a person includes the *parahaṃsa* ascetics and others. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
For those who are Parahaṃsa ascetics and for those who are ascetics of the renunciation (saṃnyāsa) order,
eligibility for the fire-rituals of these two [orders] is not prescribed.
Thus. (Or, having worshipped with all the limbs of Brahmā in their respective places.
Here, the meaning is that one should worship in those various locations according to the sequence beginning with the east (*savādikrama*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīmad-aṃśumatī*:
Having performed the worship of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga-yajana), the wise one should present the [offering] with the face turned away;
having worshipped from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, he should apply it in reverse order.
(226) One should join the limbs, from the weapons up to the heart, with their respective mantras;
having worshipped the weapon-mantra in the four directions, as well as [the deities] beginning with Soma and ending with Indra.
Having worshipped the eye in the front, the armor in the region of the wind (northwest),
the crest-lock in the southwest, and the head in the region of Īśāna (northeast).
"In the southeast, one should worship the Heart-mantra along with the constituent parts of dissolution.
Thus [it is said]. That which is called the "Parāṅmukha-arghya" (the arghya for turning away) is the arghya to be offered at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*).

Likewise, in the venerable *Sarvajñānottara*, regarding the dismissal (*visarjana*), it is said: "The *arghya* for the son of Gaṅgā (Śiva) is to be offered with his face turned away. We shall demonstrate the nature of this further on.

One might ask: "What should he do who is entitled to the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) but lacks its means and is thus incapable of it? To this he says: "(The fire-rite). Anticipating the question, "Of what kind is one entitled to that, and where should he go?", he says: "(Now)" (*atha*). One entitled to the fire-rite is the teacher (*deśika*) and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Śrīmatsārasaṃgraha*,
it is stated that the qualification for performing fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) follows immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
for without that [consecration], teachers have no authority in initiation and other such rites.
Thus it is said: "By offering oblations in this very manner, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth.
Regarding the phrase "in another [direction]": the meaning is in the direction of Agni (the southeast), and so forth.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

331) "For the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma), one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hasta) to the southeast of the Vedic hermitage, or to the northeast or the east. Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the sacrificial pit.

We shall now demonstrate it. First, regarding the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*): its measurement is a square area prepared to be three finger-breadths high with sand and other materials. Thus, while the characteristics of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) have been declared in the venerable *Kāraṇa-tantra*, the sacrificial mound is now being described.
[One should prepare a site] one cubit wide with dry sand originating from a pure location.
It should be three finger-breadths in height, level, and neither depressed nor protruding.
Thus [it is said]. He states the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "or in the pit" (*kuṇḍe vā*). Regarding the phrase "in reverse order" (*viparyayeṇa*):
it should be understood that if one is facing north, one should then produce three lines with their tips pointing north and one line with its tip pointing east.
He states the invocation of Vāgīśvarī with the word "therein" (*tatra*). He states the placement of the fire (*vahnivinyāsa*) with the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*).
The definition of Saṃhāriṇī was stated previously. [The phrase] "resembling the flame of a lamp" (*pradīpakalikopama*) [is explained as follows].
In this context, the word *kalikā* denotes a cluster of blossoms; as Amara states: "A cluster of blossoms (*stavaka*) may be called *mucchaka*, *stavaka*, or *kalikā*.
(*Parameśvaravīryam*) refers to the semen (*śukla*) of the Supreme Lord. According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*: "The word *vīrya* [is used] in the senses of prowess and semen. In this case—

The intended meaning is that if there were no contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that "this is the virility of the Supreme Lord," then the introduction of the channel within the womb of Vāgīśvarī would be impossible.
By means of this [contemplation], the fiery seed-syllable becomes like the flame of a lamp.
Having placed [the fire] in the sacrificial pit, one should worship the five Brahmans within the fire.
"Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations with the root-mantra of the five [deities].
Keeping this statement of the venerable Somaśambhu in mind,
for the sake of accomplishing the five purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, one should perform worship with the root-mantra by means of the Brahmās.
And he says that one should perform the *homa* [offering] with [the mantras] beginning with *Sadyojāta*.
One should consecrate the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) and other implements by sprinkling them with the *arghya* water.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
By a single sprinkling alone, the consecration of the *sruk* ladle is accomplished;
in this same manner, it should be performed for the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) using the water from the *arghya* vessel.

Thus [it is said]. He describes the invocation of Śiva with the words "then" (*tataḥ*). "[Having worshipped Śiva as before]"—here, one should perform the worship up to the end of the *pavitra* rite. Likewise, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Then, one should worship him together with his seat (*āsana*) as before, within the fire-lotus of the heart."

Having worshipped Śiva—along with his limbs (*sāṅga*), his substratum (*āśraya*), and his limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), together with the ritual offerings (*sopacāra*) up to the purification (*pavitrānta*)—one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) by means of the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), saying: "O Blessed One, I satiate you. Thus [it is said] "(according to one's capacity)" (*yathāśakti*); by this, the number ten and so forth is indicated.

Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*: "One hundred, fifty, or half of that again—twenty or even ten—one should satisfy the limbs [of Śiva] with a tenth part [of the remainder] from the [libation] for Śiva. And: "[Having saluted that ash]. Here, having ignited the *darbha* grass in the Śiva-fire, one should [use] the ash which has manifested the nature of Śiva.

The meaning is: having applied a *tilaka* on the forehead. Some, however, [state that] after dismissing Śiva and the Śiva-fire, one should cast a single blade of grass from the surrounding layer (*paristaraṇa*) into the fire.
They say that one should kindle it and make a tilaka-mark from its ashes;

however, that view is not favored by the Gurus. For he will state immediately thereafter: "having dismissed Śiva without further regard. Thus also said the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*.

Regarding the instruction "one should worship the ashes," it means that prior to the dismissal (*visarjana*) of Śiva, one should perform the application of ashes— made manifest by fire through a flaming blade of *darbha* grass— upon the head, forehead, and other parts of the body. The dismissal of Śiva residing within the fire is expressed by the phrase "(with the eight flowers)."

"(Agni-stham)" means the collection of mantras residing in the fire of Śiva. "(Having dismissed Śiva without further expectation)"—here it should be understood that one should establish Śiva within one's own heart-lotus; for it is there that the manifestation and dissolution of the mantras occur. Thus...
"In the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*, it is said: 'Having taken up the ashes, one should worship them and unite the deity within oneself.
He states the dismissal of the Śiva-fire with "Oṃ Hraum," and so forth, ending with "having dismissed the fire.
The meaning is that one should establish [the fire] within one's own heart. The manner of dismissal is such that the fire may never again remain in its original location or elsewhere.
Having joined it to the fire of knowledge within the heart-bindu, one should dismiss it.

Thus [he should release them]. The meaning is that one should also establish Brahmā and the others within one's own heart. As it was stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu: "With the breath-inhalation (*pūraka*) and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaṇu*), [one should place] the radiant ones situated in the periphery; with supreme purity, in one's own [heart]."
One should place that within the heart-lotus. Thus [it is said].
The procedure for the inner and outer offerings.

(Kriyā) (60) Then, having prepared two mandalas in the area to one's own right, [one should place] in the first mandala, in the directions starting from the east and ending with the north: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Rudras;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Mothers; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Gaṇas; Oṃ hāṃ...
Homage to the Yakṣas in the corners beginning with the northeast (īśāna):
oṃ hāṃ, homage to the houses; oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Asuras; oṃ hāṃ... [p. 336]
Homage to the Rākṣasas. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Nāgas. In the center of the maṇḍala, in the northeast, southeast, and southwest: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Nakṣatras;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Rāśis; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the Viśvedevas. Between the northwest and the west.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," and having offered the bali and arghya ending in "svāhā," one should worship in the second maṇḍala, in the directions from the east to the northeast, with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; Oṃ hāṃ, [obeisance to Nirṛti]..."
Homage to Ṛti: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna in the northeast;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā in the southwest; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu in the center. Oṃ.
Having worshipped with "Hāṃ, obeisance to Nīlalohita," and having offered the *balī* and *arghya*, [one recites] outside:
"Oṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to the crows and others who violate the covenant; Oṃ Hāṃ."
One should offer the bali with the mantra: "Svāhā to Agni and the others! Om Hāṃ, svāhā to all the deities of the domestic site (gṛhavāstu)!"; then one should dismiss them all.
Or alternatively, one may offer the bali in this concise manner.
Oṃ hāṃ!
Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes,
and whoever among them are gentle and dwell in gentle abodes— [to them all, salutation].
The Mothers of fierce form, those who are the lords of the Gaṇas,
and others who have become obstacles, dwelling in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
May you all, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering;
may you quickly grant us success and always protect me from fears.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation, one should place the bali-mantras within one's own heart.

Next, having described the procedure for the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*), one should cause the inner offering (*antarbali*) and the outer offering (*bahirbali*) to be given with food mixed with water, ending with the word *svāhā*. Likewise:

In the *Śrīmad-Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated: "Having offered the *bali* to Rudra and the others with food mixed with water, ending with the word *svāhā*. (Regarding the two mandalas: Here, one should draw one mandala in the southeast corner of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and one mandala in the west, both being square, and another in the east.
Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*,
having prepared two mandalas in the southeast and then in the west,
one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Indra in the east, starting from the east in due order.

(229) Thus, he states the sequence for the worship of the deities of the internal *bali* with the word "first," and he states the procedure for the worship of the deities of the external *bali* with the word "second. In this context, the deities of the internal and external *bali*,
such as Rudra and others, are residents of the principle (*tattva*) of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
"Because worship is not prescribed for those who dwell on the impure path," so it has been stated by the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati* (p.
The offering of bali to Rudra and others is called the "internal bali" (antarbali), while the offering of bali to Indra and others is called the "external bali" (bahirbali).
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"Having dismissed the fire, one should remember [the deities] at two mandalas by the side of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)."
One should offer the inner and outer oblations with the heart-mantra, using the names [of the deities] ending in "svāhā."
Thus [it is said]. And he will state in the ritual for the *pavitra* (purifier): "To the Rudras and others who eat the inner oblation, and to the Indras and others who eat the outer oblation."
He speaks of the bali offering for the crows and others with the word "outside" (*bahiḥ*). "Outside" means on the exterior of both mandalas.
Regarding "for the crows and others," by the word "others" (*ādi*), dogs, spirits, and so forth are included. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Having dismissed them and gone outside, one should cast an offering upon a circle of cow-dung for the dogs, the lords of spirits, the fallen, the hungry ghosts, the crows, and so forth.
Thus [it is said]: "(From Agni and the others). By the word "and the others" (*ādi*), the Sun and so forth are intended. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
With the heart-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should worship Agni, Soma, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati in the eight directions beginning with the east and ending with the southeast.

[He offers to] Prajāpati, and all the gods, and all [beings] by name, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Then, on the other alternative, he performs the abbreviated bali offering (or, if not so). If it is not thus, the meaning of the verse of the mantra beginning with "ye rudrāḥ" [is as follows].
This is easily understood.
The ritual procedure immediately following the bali offering.

(62) Then, having performed the offering of hymns, sandalwood paste, and so forth, and having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should go into the presence of Śiva with water and the *arghya* offering in hand, and say: "Whatever has been done and whatever I shall do— all that is your good deed."
"You alone are the protector of the universe here; there is no other auspicious lord for me."
Having thus made this request, one should perform the worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites with the root mantra ending in *svāhā* (p.
Then, the fruit of merit should be offered into the hand of Śiva, who grants boons, along with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the *udbhava-mudrā*.
One should report [the rite] with the knees placed on the ground.

(62) Now, he states the subsequent duties with the passage beginning with "Then" and ending with "should report. The meaning of the text beginning with "That which has been performed" is clear. (The phrase is: "The fruit of merit."
It is called a "fruit" (phala) because it bears fruit (phalati), that is, it comes into being.
(230) The ritual for concluding the worship of Śiva.
(62) Then, having worshipped with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), having shown the five faces,

and having worshipped with the root mantra (*mūla*) according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta, one should offer the *arghya*. Having offered the *arghya* from the weapon (*astra*) to Īśāna in reverse order from the worship, one should [recite] the mantras for specific desires (*kāmyamantra*) within their respective limits.
Having joined [the deities] with the *nārāca-mudrā* and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), having raised them by scattering flowers, and having withdrawn them,
one should join them to the [central] form with the divine mudrā and the form-mantra (*mūrti-mantra*). Then,
having worshipped with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should say, "Forgive me."
Just as [stated on] p. 342):
