"O Master, you have been troubled by me, your lowly servant, whose mind is defiled."
"Whatever [fault] has been committed through even a slight fragment of devotion, may You, being pleased, forgive that.
Then, having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and having worshipped [the deity].

Now, he describes the procedure for concluding the worship of Śiva with the words beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "having worshipped" (*abhyarcya*). Regarding the term "arghya": at the time of dismissal (*visarjana*), the *arghya* should be offered in the sequence starting from Sadyojāta and so forth;
the meaning is that it is the *arghya* offered with the face turned away (*parāṅmukha*). Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*:

"Then the *arghya* [offering] facing away, from Sadyojāta up to Śiva, and from the *astra* [mantra] up to the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. Here, the *arghya* facing away is not to be given for the purpose of dismissal (*visarjana*);
rather, it is at the conclusion of the worship, with the thought, "This is our worship."
The sense is that one should offer [the water] as a means of cessation. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"The supreme *arghya* is for the sake of measuring those [deities] during worship, not for their dismissal.
And likewise:
In the *Śrīmatkāmika*, it is stated: "In the case of a mobile liṅga, [the rite] is dependent [on external supports], whereas on altars (*sthaṇḍila*) and the like, it is independent.
However, the dismissal (*visarjana*) must be performed everywhere according to the prescribed path."
Anticipating the question of where the conjunction of the *kāmya* mantras occurs, he says:

"(In their respective limits). Here, one should contemplate those [mantras] as dissolved at the end of that path (*adhvan*) wherein the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *sādhya* mantras extends; however, their dissolution into the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) is not to be performed.
This has been declared by the illustrious author of the *Mṛgendravṛtti*. Regarding the definition of mudrās, the characteristic of the *nārāca-mudrā* is thus illustrated:
the *nārāca-mudrā* is accomplished and honored by the casting of the two index fingers while the tips of the two thumbs are joined like flowers.
"It becomes that which causes the mantras to arise"—this means the mantras residing in the place of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*). Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, it is stated:
"In this way, having withdrawn those individual souls (*aṇu*) from the manifest lingas and so forth..."
One should place those situated in the abode of enjoyment within the form; one should not withdraw them.
Thus. (Raising [the hands])—this means having meditated on them as risen like lightning.
Likewise, in the *Śrī Kālottara*: "Having meditated on them as risen like lightning, [one effects] their dissolution into their own places."
"One should lead [it]"—thus it is said. Regarding the characteristics of the divine mudrā (*divyamudrā*), it is stated in the *Mudrālakṣaṇa*:

"The divine mudrā consists of two flowers held by the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers; at the conclusion of the worship of the deity, its nature is that of a circular movement (*bhramaṇa*) in a suitable form. As for the mantras of the seats (*āsana*):

One should join [the deity] to the pedestal with the Śivāsana mantra. Likewise, according to the venerable Kāmika: "With the Astra-mantra and the Saṃhāra-mudrā, one should join all those deities who reside in the enclosures and have been offered up, together with the Liṅga."
"One should indeed join the mantras honored on their seats with the pedestal.

Then, [the author] asks what one should do next and says: "Forgive me" (*kṣamasva*). Anticipating the question of how that is to be said, he says: "In this way" (*yathā*). This is the meaning of the verse beginning with "O Lord" (*svāmin*).

This is easy to understand. He states what must be done immediately thereafter with the word "Then" (*tataḥ*). In this regard, if it is a mobile *liṅga*, then while reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should take the *liṅga* from its lotus-seat, wrap it in a variegated cloth, place it inside a casket, and meditate upon Bhīmarudra.
Having requested protection, one should perform the covering;
likewise, O illustrious Aṃsumatī, having recollected the Śiva-mantra and taken hold of the liṅga.
The preceptor,
having wrapped it in a multicolored cloth, should place it within the middle of the casket.
"Then, having joined the *apidhāna*, one should proceed with the *bhīmarudra*.
Thus ends the procedure for the dismissal of the preceptor and others.

(Kriyā) (63) Having worshipped one’s own guru, the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), the gurus, Mahālakṣmī, and Gaṇapati stationed at the door, one should dismiss them. (Pra) Now, by means of the words beginning with "sva," he extends the rule for the dismissal of one's own preceptor and the others.

[One should] release [the offering] with these words. Here, it should be understood that one should cause the mantra of one's own guru, the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), and so forth, to enter into oneself. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is said:
"Having offered the general *arghya* water to the guru and the others while facing away from them..."
"Having brought [the deity] into one's own self by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of Caṇḍeśvara.

(64) In the northeastern direction, upon a pure ground, having worshipped with "Oṃ ca caṇḍāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ" and "Oṃ caṇḍamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," [one should meditate on] Caṇḍa, who is born from Rudra-Agni, resembling collyrium, and terrifying.
Fierce, with four faces and four arms, he holds a trident and an axe.
With great flames issuing from his mouth and twelve red eyes,
he is adorned with a crown of matted hair and the crescent moon, and wears a garland of serpents as an ornament.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, along with a rosary and a water-pot;
he is seated upon a white lotus throne and is the destroyer of the suffering of those prostrate in devotion.

(132) Having meditated thus, and having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) with "Oṃ hāṃ, homage to those with fierce eyes, huṃ phaṇ," and having invoked [the deity] with "Oṃ, svāhā to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, huṃ phaṭ," [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍahṛdaya, huṃ phaṇ; Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍaśiras, huṃ phaṇ."

Having performed the ritual of complete protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the limbs [of the mantra] as follows: *oṃ caṇḍaśikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, *oṃ caṇḍakavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, *oṃ caṇḍāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, one should perform the worship.
Alternatively, having worshipped with the [mantras] of the seat, the image, and the root, or with the root alone,
and having presented the *arghya*, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth, [one should discard] the previously placed *nirmālya*.
Having offered the arghya and honored you,
may these foods to be licked and sucked, drinks, betel, garlands, and ointments— indeed,
even the remnants of offerings— be granted to you by the command of Śiva.
Having made this request, and having recited [the mantra] according to one's ability and offered [the oblation], [one should say]:
"O Caṇḍa, by your command, all this ritual section has been performed by me;
whatever was done deficiently or in excess through delusion, may that become complete."
Having thus made this request, having offered the *arghya* with the face turned away, having raised the limbs,

and having united [the deity] with the form-mantra (*mūrti-mantra*) within the image, one should place [the deity] in one's own heart by means of the root-mantra recited during inhalation (*pūraka*) and the gesture of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-mudrā*). (64)
Now, having thus correctly described the worship of the Śiva-liṅga,

[the author] states the worship of Caṇḍeśvara in order to ward off defects arising from omissions or excesses in that [worship], beginning with the words "In the northeast" and ending with "one should place."

He describes the meditation on Caṇḍeśvara with the word “(Rudra)” [p. 348]. “Born from Rudrāgni” means Rudrāgni, that is, the fire of Rudra; or else, it refers to the wrath of Rudra, from which Caṇḍa emerged out of anger.

Thus [it is stated] in the Śruti. Therefore, "prabhava" means that whose birth (janma) is "prakarṣṭa," i.e., excellent; he is thus described. This has been stated by the venerable commentator on the Somaśambhupaddhati. The rest is easy to understand. [This concludes] the extraction of the Caṇḍāsana-mūrti and the root-mantras.
It has been shown in the venerable *Kāmika* that on the seat of Anu,

one should place the word for Caṇḍāsana ending in the fourth case and followed by the word "namas"; likewise, on the seat of Dīpa, one should place the word for Caṇḍamūrti preceded by "pūrva" and also ending in "namas."
This [mantra] ending in the dative case is called the *mūrtimantra*,
together with the words "to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara," followed by *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
"Oṃ caṇḍapūrvaka huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the one beginning with Dhruva. Thus he states an alternative for the worship of Caṇḍa with the words "or else" (*yadi vā*).
That which is called *nirmālya* is that which has been used by the Supreme Lord and cast away while preceded by mantra.
It is called a garland (*mālya*).
Likewise, (p. 349) [it is said:]
Garland that has been discarded is considered *nirmālya*; it is not [merely] that which remains on a *liṅga* or other such objects.
It is not [to be taken] unless it was previously offered when possible, nor is it that which has been excluded by mantras.
That which is given to Caṇḍeśvara with the accompaniment of mantras and then cast away is indeed consumed by the Lord; that is proclaimed as *nirmālya*.

Thus [it is said]. *Arghya* refers to the special *arghya*. "The special *arghya* for Caṇḍeśa" has been stated by the commentator on the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*. He describes the manner of the announcement with the word "(leehya)": "(leehya-śoṣyānna-pānādi)"—that which is to be licked (*leehya*) such as honey and so forth, and that which is to be sucked (*śoṣya*).
Coconut water and so forth; "food" (anna) means that which is to be eaten, and "drink" (pāna) means that which is to be drunk.

That of which the first [items] are food to be licked (lehya), food to be sucked (coṣya), food to be eaten (anna), and drink (pāna) is described as such. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), food to be chewed (bhakṣya) is expressed. This has been stated:
Food is fivefold: that which is to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked.
Chewing refers to fruits and the like; eating refers to cooked grain; drinking refers to elixirs (*rasāyana*).
"Licked" (*lehya*) refers to honey and the like; "to be sucked dry" (*śoṣya*) refers to coconut water and the like.
The rest is clear. Again, he states another prayer with the word "(all)" (*sarvam*).
"(The section on ritual action)" (*kriyākāṇḍam*) refers to the category of rites for the worship of Śiva.
"Kāṇḍa is not feminine; it refers to a staff, an arrow, a bamboo, a section, an occasion, and water," so says Amara.
The rest is easy to understand. He describes the sequence for the dismissal of Caṇḍeśvara with the words "turned away.
On this point, some do not desire the worship of Caṇḍeśvara in a private ritual performed for one's own sake.

That [position] is not pleasing. In the Śaivasiddhānta, there is a rule that Caṇḍeśvara must always and everywhere be worshipped. Furthermore, the prohibition against the worship of Caṇḍa pertains specifically to the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa Tantras. Thus, it is stated in the venerable Kālottara:
Whether fixed or movable, made of gems, wood, or stone, or fashioned from iron or variegated materials— whether the arrow is stationary or the controller is fierce—
it belongs to the Siddhānta and other Tantras, neither to the Left (Vāma) nor to the Right (Dakṣiṇa).
Thus [it is said].
The ritual procedure for the dismissal of Śiva and the other deities.
(65) Then, one should likewise dismiss Śiva and the others who have been worshipped upon the sacrificial ground.

Then, having raised the mantras residing in the arghya vessel, withdrawn them, and placed them within the heart-lotus, one should remove the withered floral offerings (*nirmālya*), purify the ground with cow dung,
and sprinkle it with water. (65)
By means of the passage beginning with "on the sacrificial ground" (*sthaṇḍile*) and ending with "he should dismiss" (*visarjayet*), he extends the previously stated rule to other cases as well.
Next, he describes what must be done immediately thereafter, beginning with the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "he should sprinkle" (*prokṣayet*).
The procedure for the recitation of the Aghora mantra.

(66) Then, having washed his feet and sipped water, having bathed with pure ashes and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*), he should recite the Aghora mantra twenty-one times for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the entire worship.
(234) Thus, in [this work] composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara, on page 352.
The procedure for the worship of Śiva in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* is completed.

(66) Now, he states with the words beginning with "thereafter" that one should recite the Aghora mantra for the purpose of pacifying all defects of deficiency or excess and for the sake of obtaining the fruit of the worship: "one should recite."
By this much [it is concluded].
The ritual procedure for the worship of Kapila.
(Kriyā) (67) Then, having worshipped Kapilā: "O Surabhi, born from the churning of the nectar of immortality, sustainer of the world!
Accept this morsel; this is my supreme vow."
Thus, having offered the morsel (grāsa).

(67) (Pra) Now, the procedure for the worship of Kapilā (kapilārcanāvidhi): from "then" (tataḥ) and so forth, ending with "having offered" (datvā). [The instruction] "having fully worshipped Kapilā" (kapilāṃ saṃpūjya) means: here, *oṃ kapile nande namaḥ*, *oṃ kapile bhadre namaḥ*, *oṃ*...
One should worship with: "O Kapilā of virtuous character, obeisance! Oṃ, to Kapilā the fragrant one, obeisance! Oṃ, to Kapilā of beautiful mind, obeisance!

Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*: "One should address a tawny cow (*kapilā*) with names such as 'Tawny One' (*kapilā*), 'Auspicious One' (*puṇyā*), 'Joy' (*nandā*), and so forth; saying, 'O Tawny One, O Joy, salutations,' together with the *sāvitrī* mantra."
"Bhadra, Suśīlā, Surabhi, and likewise Sumanas.

Thus [the text] states. He declares the mantra for offering the morsel: "Amṛta" (nectar). "Grāsa" means a mouthful; as Amara says: "Grāsa is used in the sense of a mouthful (kabala). The rest is easily understood.
The Procedure for Studying the Śivasaṃhitā.
(68) Having performed his recitation (*svādhyāya*) and other duties until the time of midday, (pra) then,
whoever studies the *Śivasaṃhitā* day after day according to the prescribed rule destroys all sins, just as the sun destroys the darkness.

Based on this scriptural authority, [the text] prescribes that one should study the *Śivasaṃhitā* every day with the passage beginning with "(at midday)" and ending with "having performed" (kṛtvā), as indicated by the phrase "(one's own recitation and so forth).
In this context, "recitation" (*svādhyāya*) means any desired scripture of Śiva among the *saṃhitās*;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *purāṇas* and other such texts are to be understood as subjects for study. The term "(having done)" (*kṛtvā*) means "having studied.
Thus it has been written by the venerable author of the *Matanga-vṛtti*:
By the mere recitation of mantras and likewise by the study of their sacred texts,
they are liberated from evil deeds as well as from meritorious actions.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*, it says: "One should perform the desired study (*svādhyāya*).
The meaning is that one should perform what has been studied. This is stated in its commentary as well.

(235) In this regard, it should be understood that the four castes who have received Śiva-initiation possess the qualification for the study of the Śiva-āgamas. Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-siddhāntabodha*, it is stated: "The Siddhānta known as Āgamānta [is for] the Śūdra caste, and the Purāṇa [is for them]."
The occupations of Śūdras shall be declared according to the meanings of the scriptures as stated in the Vedas.
Thus it is said; likewise in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "Having attained which, all men...
And so he says on page 355:
The venerable Nīlakaṇṭha Ācārya, in the section beginning with "Because of the inconsistency of the Lord" (Brahmasūtra 2.2.37), states:

"We, however, do not perceive any difference between the Vedāgamas and the Śaivāgamas. If there is an absolute non-difference between the Siddhānta-Śaiva Āgamas and the Veda, for what purpose then was both created?

If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: there is indeed this distinction between the two; the Veda has the three higher castes as its qualified practitioners (*adhikāra*), whereas the Āgama has all four castes as its qualified practitioners. This too has been stated in the *Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya*:
"The Veda concerns the three higher castes, while the other concerns everyone."
The sequence for the study of the Śiva Āgamas has been extensively elucidated in the venerable Kāmika and other scriptures;
it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity.
The Midday Ritual.
(69) At the time of midday as well, one should perform the bathing, twilight rites, worship of Śiva, and so forth, just as before.
Alternatively, one should worship with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*) at the time of the previous worship, or at that specific time, according to the count of the three times. (69) (p. 356)

Now follows the midday ritual, beginning with "at midday" and ending with "one should worship. The determination of the midday time has been clarified previously in the passage: "At midday, one should meditate on the Goddess."
The procedure for consuming alms-food received from a lineage.

(70) Afterwards, having well-smeared the dining area and adorned it with lines of four, three, two, or one made with cow-dung or ashes, the instructor and the others should sit down in order, facing east, south, west, or north, or all may sit independently.

Or, having previously sat in a single row with those of his own caste who are refined and purifiers of the assembly, he should [offer] in vessels of gold, silver, copper, or iron; or, in their absence, in a vessel purified sevenfold with ashes.

Having consecrated [the food] seven times with the Aghora mantra, they should eat from a bell-metal vessel or from forbidden leaves such as those of the plantain tree, with their hands placed between their knees.
Either sitting in the bound hero’s posture (baddhavīrāsana) or avoiding conversation that is inconsistent with the meal,
he should eat with his left hand resting upon the alms-bowl.

Then, having sprinkled the food placed in the vessel with the Astra-mantra, and having consecrated it seven times with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having offered it to Śiva and the others in separate vessels according to one's capacity, and having sprinkled it with water and cast a small portion of the food upon the ground,
With water poured from the little finger of the right hand, [one should offer it] with the mantra: *oṃ nāgakūrmakṛkaradevadattadhanañjaye-bhya upaprāṇavāyubhyaḥ svāhā*.
Having offered the food remaining on the ground to the Nāgas and others,

and having consumed the remaining water with the mantra "Thou art the under-layer of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*), or else, having sprinkled it around with the Īśāna-mantra and consumed it with the Puruṣa-mantra, one should meditate upon the fire within the stomach as blazing with the Astra-mantra, and [recite] "Oṃ, for Prāṇa."
Svāhā! Om, to apāna, svāhā! Om, to samāna, svāhā!
Om, to dadāna, svāhā! Om, to vyāna, svāhā! Thus, by one established upon the earth.
Having offered the oblations to the vital breaths with the bowl, one should eat as desired.
In that interval, if flies, fingernails, hair, or the like have fallen [into the food], one should discard a small portion of the meal, wash one's hands, touch ashes, and then eat.
[One should likewise avoid] garlic, onions, leeks, bottle-gourd, snails, fish, meat, and rock salt...
One should avoid salt and other substances given by a horse, a donkey, or an elephant, as well as those prohibited by general scriptural injunctions.

While eating, one should not take up salt or clarified butter. One should not drink water after the meal is finished, nor should one drink the remainder of what has already been drunk with a mouthful turned away. Furthermore, one should not look upon a person of the lowest caste.

Having eaten a measured amount, and at the end, having sipped water with the right hand while it is still unwashed, reciting "amṛtāpidhānam asi" either with the Taittirīya or the Ṛgveda formula, and having washed his hands and so forth and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana),
[he should consume] what has fallen from the thumb held in his own right fist.
p.
359) With water, one should sprinkle the big toe of the right foot, reciting either *oṃ hāṃ kālāgnirudrāya svāhā* or *oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya svāhā*. Then, with ashes...

Having purified oneself and performed the sakalīkaraṇa, having bound the paridhāna-mudrā, and having recited the Vāmadeva mantra nine times, one should cleanse the mouth with betel leaf and other such items.
When eating at another's house, one should eat after first performing the japa of the Śiva-gāyatrī in front of the food.

Now, having explained the midday ritual (*mādhyāhnikavidhi*), [the author] describes, from the words "afterwards" (*paścāt*) up to "he should eat" (*bhuñjīta*), the rule for the consumption of alms-food (*sāntānika-bhikṣā*) by the Śaiva teachers (*deśika*) and others for the sake of maintaining the body. Of what kind are the teachers and so forth?
Anticipating the question of what kind [of food], with whom, and in what vessel one should feed [the guests] when space is available, he says: "prepared with cow-dung" (*gomayakalpite*). This means:
on a square mandala made of cow-dung. Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-Ṣaṭsahasra*:
"But one cubit is the *vedāśrama*," as stated in the *Śrīmatkiraṇa*: "It consists of four, three, two, or one line, extending from the Guru down to the end of the *samaya*. (p. 360)

He states that the mandala is adorned with four or more lines, corresponding respectively to the four [categories] beginning with the Śruti and ending with the Samayin—namely, "by means of four, three, two, or one line.
(Deśikādayaḥ) refers to the Deśika, Sādhaka, Putra, and Samayin. (Savarṇaiḥ) means "of the same color."

By those who are "of the same caste" (*savarṇaiḥ*), meaning those of a single caste; by those who are "well-restrained" (*saṃvṛtaiḥ*), meaning those perfected by the purificatory rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Likewise, [it is said]: "One should not share a dwelling with one who is uninitiated, nor eat in the same row. By those who are "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvanaiḥ*), meaning those who sanctify the row.
In this context, "in the presence of" (*saṃhati*) is the understood remainder. "Possibility" (*saṃbhave*) refers to the availability of materials.

Regarding "in vessels of gold, silver, copper, and iron," here the vessels of gold and so forth are assigned respectively to the Guru and the others. Thus it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
The vessel for the Guru should be made of gold; for the Sādhaka, it should be of silver;
for the Putraka, it is said to be of copper; and for those seeking the Samaya, it is made of iron.
361) Thus: (in the absence) means in the event of the lack of vessels made of gold and so forth as prescribed in the sequence of the lineage of teachers;
(on leaves such as those of the plantain tree) means on leaves of the *raṃbhā* (plantain), the lotus (*padma*), and so forth. Likewise...
In the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*, [it is stated that offerings may be made] upon leaves of the *palāśa*, *kadalī*, mango, lotus, and so forth—
provided they are not prohibited, are unmixed, and have their tips tied together.

Thus it is said; the colors of the *aśvattha* and other such trees are forbidden. Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "A vessel for food should not be made from *aśvattha*, *eraṇḍa*, *bhallātaka*, *nyagrodha*, *arka*, *vibhītaka*, *śāka*, *udumbara*, *sajja*, and so forth."
Thus [it is said]. Those who eat should provide the food. As for how one should eat, he says:
"With the knee" and "bound in the vīrāsana posture. This definition is stated in the venerable *Suprabheda*:
"The left foot, having passed over, should be placed upon the right."
The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is prescribed as being especially suitable at the time of eating.
Thus [it is said]. The instruction to "avoid talk not conducive to eating" refers to persons other than one's teacher (ācārya).
Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"However, the triad beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka) should eat while observing silence;
the Lord (prabhu), that is, the teacher (ācārya), may eat according to his own desire. Thus it is said.
Having done what should one eat? To this he says: "(Then).
That is, immediately after remaining in such a state. The extraction of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra is demonstrated in the venerable Kāmika: "Om juṃ sa—this very mantra is called Mṛtyuñjida."

(To Śiva and the others) means to Śiva, Agni, and the Guru. The fruit of the offering to the triad beginning with Śiva is described in the venerable *Śivadharmottara* [as superior] to agriculture, usury, trade, anger, untruth, and the acquisition of wealth through such means.
The sins of men increase through the five defects of the slaughterhouse:
sweeping, anointing, water, fire, and grinding.
These five slaughterhouses of householders constantly lead to the increase of sin.
"By means of worshiping Śiva, the fire, and the Guru, one is not tainted by these sins.
363) In this regard, one should eat what remains after the offering to one's own chosen *liṅga* and so forth; however, one should not eat that which has been offered [to the deity].
This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). For this very reason, it is stated here that [the offerings] should be placed in separate vessels according to one's capacity.

Thus, the venerable author of the commentary on the *Somaśambhupaddhati* says regarding the injunction "one should not eat without having offered [the food]": for the sake of the locus of one’s chosen *liṅga*, the fire, and the Guru...

The intention is that one should supply the word "to Śiva" [at the beginning] and eat only what remains after that offering. The phrase "(a little food)" indicates a quantity of about half a morsel. Likewise, in the venerable *Aṃśumatī*:
On the left side of oneself, upon a mandala smeared with cow dung on the ground,
one should offer a portion measuring half a morsel to the Nāgas and other beings.

Thus, "one should offer the oblation" refers to the digestive fire (*audarya*), that is, the gastric fire (*jāṭhara*). In that [fire], which has risen within the belly, it should be understood that starting with the self (*ātman*), all [the elements] become satisfied by the offerings of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The Self resides in the *prāṇa*; the sources of the elements are situated in the *apāna*."
The gods are established in the udāna, and likewise the ancestors in the samāna.
The Nāgas residing in the Vyāna wind, as well as those dwelling in Pātāla,
are situated at the tips of the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger, extending from the palm of the right hand.
Situated within the flames of the fire located inside the cavity of the mouth,
one should satisfy these [deities] with individual oblations, touching them with the teeth.
"One should offer the remainder, mixed with ghee and condiments, to Īśāna.

Thus [it is said]. If one asks what should be done if there is a visible hair or other such thing in the rice within the eating vessel, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). "In the interval" (*tatrāntare*) means at that time of eating. "Hair and so forth" (*keśādi*)... [refers to]...
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), husks and so forth are meant. Likewise, in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"In food, however, husks, hair, rags, charcoal, and even nails, as well as all reptiles, bedbugs, and flies [are to be avoided] in the rice."
"Lice, bees, and gadflies are purified by being thrown into ashes. Thus [it is said].
365) In response to the desire to know which things are unfit to be eaten here, he says: "garlic" and so forth—(garlic, onion, leek, bottle-gourd, fish, meat, and rock salt).

(Regarding salt given by hand with salt, etc.): garlic (*laśuna*), white-stalked [garlic] (*śvetanāla*), and onion (*palaṇḍu*)—for "onion" (*palaṇḍu*) is "white-stalked" (*sukandaka*), according to Amara; and *gṛñjana* (red-stalked), *gṛñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, and *rasonaka*.

Thus says Amara. "Alābu" refers to the bottle-gourd; "tuṃbara-phala" is the fruit of the Tuṃbara tree; "śaṃbūka" is a freshwater shell; "matsya" is fish; "māṃsa" is meat; and "saindhava-lavaṇa" is rock salt.
That which has these as its "ādi" (beginning/first items) is so described. By the word "ādi" (etcetera),...

The *bimba*, the *udumbara* fruit, and so forth are thus described. Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśva*: "The *udumbara*, the *alābu*, the *sauvīra*, the *kumārikā*, the *vṛntāka*, the *kataka*, the *chatrāka*, and likewise the *bimbikā*."
Thus: (prohibited by general scriptures). General scriptures (*sāmānya-śāstra*) refer to the Vedas, the *Smṛtis*, and so forth; "prohibited by them" means not enjoined by them. In this context—

The intention is that even the Vedas and other such texts are accepted as general scriptures (*sāmānya-śāstra*) when it comes to the instruction of *dharma*. Likewise, in the *Śrī Mohaśūrottara*, it is stated: "The Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth are the Āgamas that reveal *dharma*. Furthermore, [it distinguishes between] the general and the particular, namely the Śaiva and the Vaiśeṣika.
Regarding the word "speech" (*vacaḥ*): likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*:
"The realization of the means of dharma arises solely from the sacred tradition (*samnāya*);
for since the *smṛti* is rooted in that [tradition], it [arises] from those two alone, and not from anything else."
And these, such as a mere skull, nails, skin, and sesame seeds—
one should avoid these in succession on the eighth lunar day and other such occasions.
Regarding the meaning of these words, Bṛhaspati states that on both fortnights, one should not eat coconut on the eighth day;
and on the ninth day, one should avoid the bottle-gourd, the smoky gourd, and the round gourd.
One should always avoid paṭola in one's food on the tenth day;
one should avoid niṣpāva on the eleventh day, and one should abandon sarṣapa on the twelfth day.
"On the thirteenth day, by way of prohibition, one should not eat sesame seeds in either manner.
Beyond this, nothing is written for fear of excessive detail.

By the instruction "while eating," it is shown that salt should be taken only before one has finished eating. "(One should not take)" means one should not take it. "(One should not drink water after food)"—by this it is indicated that one may drink at the conclusion of the meal. Likewise...
In the illustrious Āgneya Purāṇa, it is stated: Having eaten a little less than that, one should drink liquid water at the end of the meal;
by drinking salted buttermilk until satisfied, one shall become healthy.
Thus [it is said]. (With his face turned away: One by whom the face (*vaktra*) is turned away—that is, split open—is so described.
(The "lowest caste" [*antyajāti*]: refers to castes such as actors (*naṭa*) and fishermen (*kaivarta*). Likewise:
"The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, and the *varaṭa*."
The Kaivarta, the Meda, and the Bhilla—these are remembered as the seven types of Antyajas.
Thus [it is said]. He states what is to be done immediately after eating at the end:
"The Self, indeed, is in the right foot; it is the all-pervading one, higher than the highest. (p. 368)
I consecrate him who is established at the tip of the thumb.

Having kept this statement in mind, he states another alternative with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). He then explains what one should do after that with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). The definition of the *parighā* mudrā has been stated in the *Śrīmad-aṃśumatī*.
Having placed the little finger of the left hand at the navel region,
one should join that very finger with the thumb of the right hand. Then, having extended both hands, one should place the face upon the right thumb.
This is declared to be the Parigha [mudrā], which destroys the consumption of impure food.
Thus [it is said]. (Repeating: Thus. The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] preceded by touching the navel.
Now, raising the doubt as to whether or not one may eat the food of others, he says (regarding "others"): "One should eat it after first performing the penance-recitation."
The method of meditative absorption for ascetics.
(72) But one who is dispassionate, as described on page 369, should remain established in meditative absorption until midday.
The Liṅga consists of the light of knowledge, blazing like the autumnal moon.

One should fix the mind and the vital breath there, situated in the middle of the eyebrows; absorbed in that, the yogi, becoming one with it, should lead the consciousness into emptiness through intense concentration.
When the mind has perished, the supreme bliss of consciousness shines forth by itself;
this indeed is described as Samādhi, the abode of the powers such as Aṇimā and the rest.
Thus.

(72) (Pra) Now, having described the procedure for the meal of those related by spiritual lineage (*sāntānika*), he speaks in response to the inquiry as to what should be done by the ascetics until midday.
From the words "atha" up to "iti," he explains the method for the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with the word "jñāna.
The meaning of the verse is clear.
The procedure for wandering for alms.
(72) Immediately thereafter, having performed the midday rites and having gone for alms according to the rule, he should eat.

One who is restricted to eating alms-food should not eat the food of a single person anywhere. One should not accept food that is afflicted by requests and the like, which is called "that obtained through suppression.
Between that obtained from a lineage (*sāntānikā*) and that obtained by begging from house to house (*mādhūkarī*), the *mādhūkarī* is superior. That too—

The alms-gathering known as *kaṇānna* is of two kinds. Among them, the *kaṇabhikṣā* (gleaning of grain) should be performed only in the forenoon; the second, however, at the conclusion of the second *savana*. Now, the procedure for that:
having bathed himself with ashes, having changed his loincloth and upper garment there, and having sipped water (*samācānta*), [he should proceed].
A vessel made of copper or other materials upon which mantras have been placed, or one fashioned from leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other trees,

washed with the *astra-mantra*, consecrated with the four purificatory rites (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*), empowered seven times with the *aghora-mantra*, empowered with the *kavaca-mantra*, and covered with a cloth.
Having taken [the staff] in the right hand, having consecrated it seven times with the Astra-mantra, and having taken a staff equal in size to oneself—
or a parasol— in the left hand, one should, wearing sandals,
meditate upon Śiva and the Guru, and having made a formal request, [obtain] the permission if [the Guru] is present.

Having undertaken this, and having maintained a silence that is not contradictory [to his vows], he should [eat] in pure houses, avoiding those of outcasts, barbers, the accused, artisans, those who live off the property of Brahmins or gods, and the homes of prostitutes.
While muttering the *bhikṣā-mantra*,
he should not perform prostrations, spit, touch [impure things], follow wrong paths, pluck leaves, revile others, become angry, or engage in disputes.
Having entered a house for the sake of alms, he should say, "Give alms," and having eaten...
Gazing at the tip of his own big toe, he should remain standing until the time when the cows have finished their crying and the flow of milk has ceased;

then he may enter the interior of the house. While walking, if called back, he should not return. There, he should collect alms that are free from defects such as iron or bronze vessels. While wandering for alms—
Having transcended the eating of alms-food, and having thus wandered for sufficient alms, he went to his monastery while recollecting the welfare of the world.

Now, [the author] states what should be done after the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by means of the passage beginning with "immediately" (*anantaram*) and ending with "he should eat" (*bhuñjīta*).
Now I shall describe the procedure for wandering for alms (*bhikṣāṭana-vidhi*), as it is to be performed by ascetics (*yatins*).
In that manner, I shall explain it to you; listen, O Lord of the lords of Brahmins.

"Having performed all that is to be done, one should stand facing the sun"—according to this venerable *Mataṅga-śruti*, one should perform the bath, twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), ritual adoration (*pūjā*), and so forth even at midday;
thus he says "(mādhyandinaṃ)". That which occurs at midday (*madhyandina*) is "mādhyandina".

Now, one might raise the objection: "Should one who subsists on alms eat food from a single house? Anticipating this, he says "no" with the words "(bhikṣā)" [and] "(bhikṣābhojane niyataḥ). "Bhojanam" means food, that which is eaten or consumed by living beings.
The meaning is that there is a restriction regarding alms-food. "Kvacid api" means nowhere stated; that is to say, not in any [scriptural] tradition.
Likewise,
one should practice the *mādhūkarī* mode of begging for alms even from the families of barbarians;
however, one must not eat food from a single source, even if it comes from the family of Bṛhaspati.
Thus [it is said]. Here, eating a single meal at one time is permitted, but not always.
As it was stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu: "One should, however, always avoid [eating] food from a single [source].
Now, if it has been requested by another, then why [should it be] from only one?
Anticipating the objection that one might [grasp it], he says "no," [stating] "(it is) a prayer" and so forth;
that is, "(a prayer and the like, which is afflicted)"— here, [an action] set in motion either by oneself or by another.

The meaning of the word "beginning with strength" (*balam-ādi*) is as follows. Likewise, in the venerable *Pauṣkara*: "Either by oneself or by another. [This refers to] that which is called "opposition" (*virodha*), designated as "suppression" (*nigraha*). According to Amara, "suppression" (*nigraha*) is indeed "obstruction" (*nirodha*). The intention here is that "alms for obstruction" (*nirodha-bhikṣā*) means "downward" (*adhas*). Thus it has been said:

The venerable Somaśambhu stated that one should avoid the lowest form of alms, known as *nirodha-bhikṣā*, which is to be accomplished through the pressure of requests and the like. One should reject this inferior alms-gathering.

Thus [it is said]. When there arises the desire to know which among the types of alms—such as *sāntānika* and so forth—is the primary form of begging (*bhikṣā*), he says: "The *sāntānika* [is primary]. [This refers to] that which is not requested from *santānikrā* and *mādhukarī*. Now, *sāntānika* is the alms obtained from a lineage (*santāna*) such as disciples and the like. Likewise...
In the *Śrīmadbrahmaśambhupaddhati*, it is stated that in the Śaiva tradition, the lineage (*santāna*) is that which has been declared;
whatever substance is received through the mouth [of the guru] is indeed remembered as the "lineage-begging" (*sāntānikī bhikṣā*).
(Thus, p. 374.
And "unasked" (ayācita) refers to alms not requested. This definition was stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
Whatever is given with faith for the sake of bringing [the guest] and for his honor—
ranging from food to land— that is alms (bhikṣā) received unasked.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the term *ayācita* (unasked), the alms known as *svayaṃ-dattā* (self-given), as described in the venerable *Pauṣkara* and other scriptures, is also implied. Accordingly, it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Alms are declared to be of four kinds for the noble-souled *sādhus*."
The honey-gathering, that which is self-given, the offspring-providing, and that which is accompanied by the "not-me" (ayānvita).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, the definition of *mādhūkarī* (the honey-gathering mode of begging) is stated in that very same source: "Begging from house to house until one's needs are met is known as *mādhūkarī*. From those who have passed beyond the state of being a *sāntānikā* (one seeking progeny), [he receives] the *mādhūkarī* alms;
therein, he distributes the *mādhūkarī* alms (she also...). By whom?
He states that there is a twofold division according to the manner [of practice] with the words, "known as the alms-gathering of grains" (*kaṇānnabhikṣā*).

Here, by the word *kaṇa*, rice grains are meant. He states the time for that alms-gathering with the word "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means in those two. "Only in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhna eva*) means...
This characteristic has been stated in the venerable *Sūkṣma-tantra*:
beginning from the rising of the sun, there are two nāḍīs for each element.
"It should be understood as 'forenoon'. (The second [term]) means "alms-food.
When there is an expectation as to when that should be received, he says "(the second).
(At the conclusion of the second *savana*); the second *savana* refers to the midday bath and so forth.
The conclusion is its completion therein; likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"One should practice the *mādhūkarī* alms-round when half the day has passed, at the [third] pressing."

Now, regarding the statement that one should eat after wandering for alms according to the prescribed rule, since there is a desire to know how that is so, he explains that rule with the passage beginning with "atha" and ending with "gatvā. (The rule for that) refers to the rule for the *mādhūkara* [alms-gathering] practice; the words "is stated" (*ucyate*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. In this regard, first:
In response to the inquiry, "What are the characteristics of a bhikṣu who should undertake the mendicant's life? [the author] says:
"(Having bathed himself with ashes)," and so forth. "(One whose loincloth and upper garment have been exchanged)" means one by whom the loincloth and upper garment have been exchanged or swapped.
The meaning is that, having discarded the loincloth and upper garment previously worn, he puts on another loincloth and upper garment. As it has been said:

Having bathed with pure ashes at the feet of the venerable Somaśambhu, and having changed his loincloth for an upper garment, he sips water; "having sipped water" (*samācāntaḥ*) means that the ritual rinsing of the mouth has been properly performed. To which vessel he should take alms, he says:
"Of copper" (*tāmra*) means "copper and so forth, having abandoned [other metals]. Here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to iron and other such materials.

"A vessel made from the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other trees" refers to a container fashioned from the foliage of the *palāśa*, *rasāla*, and similar species. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*:
One should use leaves of the *palāśa*, *madhupa*, *kadaṃba*, mango, and so forth; however, one should avoid those of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *piśāca*, *akṣa*, *kesara*, and similar trees.
Thus, the characteristics of the vessel are stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The alms-bowl must necessarily be made of copper or even iron;
it should be eight finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in width."
Thus [it is said]. (Equal to oneself) means one's own measure. (p.
377) Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:

"Having washed [the staff] with water from the heart [mantra], one should take up a staff of appropriate length. (The term *sopānatkaḥ* means "one who is together with sandals"; *pāduka* is a sandal. Amara states: "A *pādu* is a sandal. Now, [it is said]: "One should practice the *mādhūkarī* mode of livelihood even from among the families of barbarians (*mleccha*)."

Fearing that, according to the Śruti, one might go to the houses of all for the sake of *mādhūkarī* alms, he says "no," [stating] "fallen" (*patita*). [The phrase is: "(Excluding the houses of the fallen, barbers, the accused, artisans, those of censurable conduct, those who live off the property of Brahmins or gods, and courtesans). And "fallen" (*patita*)...

One who has fallen away from the conduct of his own stage of life (*āśrama*); likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Bṛhannāradīya*: "He who has fallen from the conduct of his own stage of life is designated as 'outcast' (*patita*). Furthermore, a barber is well-known [as such]. An "accused" (*abhiśasta*) is a village leader (*grāmaṇī*). Thus it has been determined.
By the author of the commentary on the *Śrīmat-sarvajñānottara*: "A craftsman" means an artisan; "despised" means censured; and "one who subsists on the property of Brahmins or deities.

A Brahmin is one who enjoys wealth as his deity; a *līlāvadhū* is a woman skilled in jesting, playful sport, conversation, and affection. Likewise, in the illustrious *Mṛgendra*, it is said that where women are clever at jesting and the like, one should not accept food obtained through begging.

The wives of those who have fallen from their caste, those whose husbands have been executed, those accused of crimes, those who live by performing music, those who live by serving Brahmins or gods, and those who live by dancing—his houses are to be avoided by him in every way. To which houses, then, should he go for alms? He says: "In pure houses" (*śuddhagṛheṣu*). "Pure" means those possessing virtuous conduct.
The four castes beginning with the Brahmins; their houses; in those [houses]. Likewise, in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*:
"The alms of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, excluding those who are accused and so forth."
But those Śūdras who do not drink intoxicants and are endowed with purity and proper conduct, [should be honored].
"From those very people alone one should seek alms, and never from others.
Thus [it is said]. "(Aṭet)" means "one should wander" or "one should practice.
Regarding what should not be done at the time of wandering for alms, he says: "In that [regard]"— that is,
during the wandering for alms— one should avoid bowing down,
spitting, touching [impure things], taking bypaths, covering oneself, reviling, anger, and quarreling.

Prostration (*praṇāma*) and salutation (*namaskāra*), spitting (*niṣṭhīva*) and the spewing of saliva from the mouth, contact (*sparśa*)— that is, touching anyone at all— and traveling by a wrong path (*unmārgasaṃpādana*) or walking on an improper road,
reviling (*kutsana*) and censuring (*nindā*), anger (*kopa*) and wrath (*krodha*), or [the state of] not obtaining alms or [seeking them] for that purpose.

Being restrained, one should not become angry; it should be understood that one must not harbor anger toward those people who run along the paths, nor toward others who speak unpleasant words. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Having failed to obtain alms, one should not become angry, nor should one remain restrained for too long."
"Vivāda" means legal dispute; according to Amara, "vivāda" is "vyavahāra. These [terms] are indicated in the neuter gender in the general sense. (One should not do so) (one should not perform).
In what manner and for how long [should one act] in the houses?

"Or he may stay," he says, "for the sake of alms. (This refers to the period ending with the time of the cow's milking. Here, for as long as the cow, through its union with the calf, continues to yield milk, for that long [he may stay].
The intended meaning is that one should wait. Thus it has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"One should wait for that length of time until the cow [is reunited] with her calf."
The sage obtains the full measure of the drop; thereafter, he may proceed elsewhere.

Thus [it is said]: "(Hand, bronze, etc.)". By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the ladle (*darvī*) is expressed. Likewise, it is stated by those very same authorities that one should not take it with a ladle, nor with the hand, nor with bronze: "one should not take it with those. "(Sufficiently)" means up to the point of satiety. Likewise, in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*, it says: "having begged..."
"Either until the bowl is full or until one is satisfied"— Amara states that *kāma*, *prakāma*, and *paryāpta* mean "to one's heart's content."
The procedure for what is to be done after wandering for alms.

(73) One should go to [the temple] where offerings such as withered garlands have been placed; one should bathe together with the alms-bowl. Having placed the alms-bowl in a clean spot, having sipped water for purification (*ācamya*) and performed the ritual dusting (*uddhūlya*), [one should proceed].

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, having sprinkled [the food] with the Astra-mantra, having rendered it nectar-like (amṛtīkṛtya) with the three-syllabled mantra, having mentally divided it into three portions, and having offered it to the deity and to one's own mouth, one should eat for the sake of self-protection as previously described.
But one who worships at a single time, having first entered meditative absorption as before,
should raise that resonance from the *kanda* and cause it to issue forth from the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*),
possessing the brilliance of fire that illuminates all the quarters of space with its excellent radiance.
There, the one of great splendor beholds the entire network of mantras;
by him are empowered the mantras born of various divisions, such as the peaceful, the fierce, and so forth.
What wonder is there that those whose minds are absorbed in that state achieve success,
even if they remain there with their consciousness concentrated for only a moment?
At that moment, there occurs a trembling; that indeed is the direct experience.
Within that void, situated at the tip of the flame, is the partless, supreme Śiva.
Having himself become accessible through meditation, he stands like a wish-fulfilling gem;
thus, worship performed everywhere during the twilight hours is dear to Śiva.
Having spoken thus and having worshipped [the deity] at all times,

(73) (pra) next, after describing the procedure for wandering for alms, he states what is to be done immediately thereafter with the passage beginning with "nirmālya" and ending with "bhuñjīta. (One whose limbs have been consecrated).
"With his body smeared" (meaning: having applied it). "Having placed" is the intended meaning. "With the three-syllabled" refers to the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra. As it has been said:
"The rite that is to be performed should be consecrated with the three-syllabled [mantra]."
Then it quickly becomes nectar; that which was dug up becomes the end of death.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the intended meaning is that after eating, one should perform the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) and other rites until sunset. This was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Then, having performed the evening twilight rite (*sandhyā*) through the yoga of private recitation (*svādhyāya*)."
The evening ritual.

(74) Afterwards, at the time of evening, having performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), and having carried out the worship, recitation, meditation, and absorption according to one's ability; (74) (pra) this is the evening ritual. [The section] beginning with "afterwards" and ending with "having performed."
The ritual for lying down.
(75) At the time of sleep, having ascended the bed and meditated upon Śiva as the imperishable Self, one should sleep.
(75) [The root text marked by this sign is not found in some manuscripts.]
Nor is even a commentary on it found.
(285) (Pra) Now, the procedure for sleeping: from "at the time of sleep" (*svāpakāle*) and so forth, up to "one should sleep" (*supyāt*).
The definition of the time for sleep is stated in the venerable *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*:
"In the middle of the night between the eastern and western [halves], there are ten nāḍīs."
"It is called the time of sleep" means [the state of] "lying down. Its definition has been described in the venerable *Kiraṇa* (p.
One should sleep on a bed with the head toward the east or toward the south;
that bed should be four cubits in length and half of that in width.
"And its pillow should be equal [in length], twelve *aṅgulas* wide;
upon it shall sleep the householder who [desires this]. Having done what should he sleep? He says:
"Śiva. [The word] "Akṣara" refers to the Self (*ātman*), which is free from defects such as decay caused by either intrinsic or adventitious conditions.

He whose own nature (*svarūpa*) is such is described as "thus"; that is to say, he is "without parts" (*niṣkala*). Alternatively, [he is] the one whose self is the Imperishable (*akṣara*) or whose self is Sound (*nāda*). Thus, it is said in the venerable *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"That which flows forth from the Imperishable is eternal; it is not subject to decay like the primary phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth."
Thus,
within the body, the unmanifest sound (avyaktadhvani) issues forth spontaneously as the imperishable syllable (akṣara). This subtle body of mine is designated as Nāda.

"And thus it has been said: 'The marvelous [state] has been revealed for the removal of the bonds of the bound soul. Furthermore, this refers to Śiva known as Sadāśiva in the state of enjoyment (*bhoga-avastha*), who is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
As it is stated: 'He is the one entitled to authority (*adhikārī*), the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and, by way of metaphorical designation, the one absorbed in dissolution (*layī*)."
Likewise, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are differentiated according to the distinction of their functions; or else,
[he perceives] within himself that which consists of the syllables, that which is distinguished by the syllables, and that which has the form of five faces and so forth.

He who grasps that [state] is the one known as Īśvara—meaning the form possessed of all attributes (*sakalarūpa*)—because he presides over the *sadāśivatattva* during the stage of authority (*adhikārāvasthā*), and is thus another synonym for Sadāśiva.
As it has been said: "The Blessed One, Sadāśiva, is to be celebrated by the word 'Īśa'."

The Gurus maintain that these three states are appropriate because they are to be performed according to the distinction of the practitioner's capacity, similar to the meditations on the junctions (*sandhyā*) already mentioned. In this context, one should not employ the phrase "the syllable, the self" (*akṣaram ātmānam*) as separate words. This has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"Having lain down in yogic sleep while contemplating the Imperishable Self"—thus [he] should sleep;
he should perform the act of sleeping.
The Ritual for Midnight.
(76) Having risen even at midnight and recollected the fourth twilight, one who has performed meditative concentration may sleep again.
Having risen in the morning and recollected Śiva, one should perform the prescribed rites;
may there be auspiciousness.
Thus, for one who daily worships the Cause with devotion,
no sin arises, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Nor does the world, under the influence of its accumulated karma, attain [liberation] at the end of the body;
for this common sacrifice is eternally conducive to prosperity.
Having bathed the Liṅga daily with milk mixed with white sugar,
one should offer milk-rice as an oblation and smear it with agallochum and sandalwood paste.
For one who worships Śiva in this manner with the very word *vyomavyāpin*,
portents shall perish as well as the terrible afflictions caused by the planets.
Freed from all diseases, he prospers in union with Śiva;
[this is] the compendium of the meaning of the Vidyāpāda according to the Śrīmataṅga and other scriptures.
He who, by means of their utterances, fashioned the one named Sarvavidyeśinī,
and he who, by means of the words of Śiva, fashioned the essential nature of the Purifier.
By that renowned Guru, known by the name Parameśvara,
the procedure for the daily rites has been composed in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*. (76)
Thus ends the procedure for the daily rites (*nityakarman*) in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.

Now follows the procedure for midnight (*ardharātravidhi*), beginning with "at midnight" (*niśīthe*) and ending with "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). [Objection: But surely, according to the scriptural injunction, "One should perform the twilight worship and the adoration of Śiva as before, even at midnight, using water and other materials brought during the day," [midnight worship is required].

If it is asked, "Since the performance of the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and other rites is already enjoined, how can there be an injunction here for the recollection of the twilight?"— it is true that one should perform the evening rite when midnight has arrived.
Having sipped water and performed the ritual purification with ashes, one should sleep while meditating upon the Lord as before.

Thus, having kept in mind the meaning demonstrated in the latter half of the *Brahmaśambhupaddhati-kārikā*, there is no contradiction in stating here, "having remembered the fourth twilight (*turyā saṃdhyā*).
Immediately thereafter, he states what is to be done by means of the two words "(having slept again).
Then, he explains that one should perform the entire ritual section as prescribed every day, beginning with the word "in the morning" and ending with "may it be auspicious."

Now, with two and a half verses beginning with “(The Śrīmataṅga),” he states both the conclusion of what has been explained and the introduction of what is yet to be explained. By the words “(And the nature of the pavitra),” the introduction of the subject matter to be explained is made. By the words “(By the name of the Supreme Lord),”...

In this context, it should be understood that "Parameśvara" is another name for Aghoraśivācārya; as he will state later: "He who is renowned on the circle of the earth by the other great name Parameśvara. The rest is easy to understand.
This procedure for daily rites has been explained by the Guru, who is like a stainless jewel,
according to the meanings set forth in the Śivadarśana and as prescribed in the Kriyākramadyotikā.
Thus ends [the work] composed by Nirmalamaṇi Guru, the son of Ācārya Tyāgarāja, who was born in the lineage of the presiding devotee residing in the illustrious Kamalālaya.
The procedure for daily rites is completed in the *Prabhāsa*, known as the *Sphuṭārthaprakāśikā*, which is a commentary on the *Kriyākramadyotikā*.
May there be auspiciousness.
The Ritual of the Purifier (Pavitra-vidhi).
The procedure for collecting the implements required for the purificatory rite.

(Kriyā) (2) Now follows the procedure for the *pavitra* [purification]. Having prepared the *pavitra* ornaments as prescribed at the stated time, and having arranged the sacrificial materials—using vessels that are new, made of clay or copper and the like, and thoroughly purified—and having gathered fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass, flowers, *dūrvā*, and so forth; (77)

Having bowed to the jewel among teachers known as Aghoraśiva, who was born from the ocean of the lineage of virtuous Brahmins and who is always to be cherished in the hearts of the meritorious, shining with the splendor of his fame; (p. 390)

I shall explain, according to my limited vision, the supreme and most purifying ritual procedure for fulfilling the daily obligatory rites— a method that shatters the fragmentation caused by the omission of duties arising over the course of a year.

Now, having thus described the sequence of the rules for the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) to be performed day by day, he undertakes to describe the sequence of the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇakarman*), which is to be performed every year and constitutes an obligatory subsidiary (*nityāṅga*). (Now...)

(The Ritual of the Pavitra). [This refers to] after the description of the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). The word "it is said here" (*atrocyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Now, one might ask: how is the *pavitra* included within the rites known as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and expiatory (*prāyaścitta*)? To this it is replied: this *pavitra* rite is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the obligatory rites.

It is not, first of all, obligatory (*nitya*). For instance, although the installation of the thread (*sūtrāropaṇa*) must be performed every year, it is not performed every day; thus, because it possesses a distinction from that which is daily obligatory, it is not obligatory.
Nor is it occasional (*naimittika*), because it is restricted to being occasional only in the case of these two: initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
As it has been said: "Initiation and consecration are of two kinds, both being occasional."

Furthermore, because the expiation for the non-performance of occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is not observed anywhere [in the scriptures]. Now, if it is argued that these are called "occasional" because they have fixed times, we say no;
for even initiation and the like, which do not have fixed times, are considered occasional.
Because the definition stated [for *naimittika*] is over-narrow (*avyāpti*) with respect to [the *pavitra* rite],

and because it would lead to the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of [the term] to obligatory rites such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*), which must be performed at fixed times such as morning; nor is it optional (*kāmya*), because it is purificatory (*pavitra*).

Because it is not dependent upon desire; however, that which is characterized by [such] desire is an obstacle. As it has been said: "Even for the sake of attaining powers such as *aṇimā*, that [desire] is sought after in detail. Nor is there any need for expiation (*prāyaścitta*);
for that merely produces the state of non-production of sprouts from actions consisting of the performance of what is other than what is prescribed.
But that [previous rite] was not preceded by this; rather, this [present rite] generates both of those. As it has been said:
"One is released from the annual [debt] through the fulfillment of the injunction for the completion of duties. Therefore, [this is] the *pavitra*.
It is indeed a part of the daily rite (*nitya*).
Thus it is declared in the venerable *Kālottara*:
"Therefore, they say that the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) is indeed a part of the daily rite. That [offering] is of two kinds.

[The rites] are daily (*daivasika*) and annual (*vārṣika*). It is established that the annual is more important than the daily. This has been explained in detail in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhatīṭīkā* and other works; it should be understood from those very sources.

In this regard, there are four types of qualified practitioners, beginning with the *deśika*. This has been declared in the venerable *Kāmika* [Tantra] for the purpose of destroying the sins accumulated over a year.
One who does not perform the expiation due to transgressing the ritual procedure [is at fault].
The teacher incurs a loss of accomplishment and becomes a partaker of faults;

the spiritual son (putraka) would become a partaker of liberation through a single birth due to this binding. However, the initiate (samayin), even while remaining within the rules of conduct, does not suffer thus, because he possesses the purificatory thread (pavitraka).
It must be accomplished with effort by whatever means possible.
Thus, it is not the case that this effect is produced by anyone; enough with excessive elaboration.

Now, he first explains that the implements required for performing the *pavitra* rite must be gathered, using the passage beginning with "(at the stated time)" and ending with "(having gathered them).
He states "at the stated time" to indicate at what time one should install the *pavitra*s.

This is what is meant: during any one of the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada, on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of the bright or dark fortnight, one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa). However, one who desires worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should perform it only during the bright fortnights within those three months.
One should act thus. Likewise, in the venerable *Kāmika*,
it is proclaimed that the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are the superior, middling, and inferior [periods],
or else the months of Aśvinī and Kṛttikā are so described.

"On the fourteenth or the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the *pavitraka* [should be offered]," and "for a householder during the bright fortnight, for an ascetic (*yati*) during both fortnights."

In this context, Āṣāḍha is the month marking the end of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) according to the solar reckoning, and its zodiacal sign is Gemini (*mithuna*); this has been stated by the venerable commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*, and should be understood from that very source, as it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity.

One should perform the *pavitrārohaṇa* in a pure month, avoiding a month in which Jupiter or Venus is eclipsed (*mūḍha*) or in conjunction with the sun. When there is no heliacal rising of Jupiter or Venus even within a period of three months, then [the rite of] the *pavitra*—

Because it is a permanent constituent part [of the ritual], it must certainly be performed. Likewise, in the *Śrīmatsiddhāntaśekhara* it is said: "Even when the Sun, Jupiter, or the Guru has set, or even during the three months [of the intercalary period] when there is no [lunar] rising, one should nevertheless perform the Pavitraka rite because it is occasional (*naimittika*). (As stated, the Pavitras—)
"Having completed [the rite]," it is said. Here, [one should prepare] threads such as fine silk (*dukūla*) in numbers such as one hundred and eight, provided with an equal number of ten knots.
The sacred threads (*pavitra*) are equal in their intervals and measure the length of the top of the *liṅga*, or they may be four finger-breadths long;
they are known as *tattva-pavitra*, ring-shaped, and adorned with eighteen knots. One *pavitra* is ring-shaped and named *Gaṅgāvatāraka*.
And one should perform it accordingly. Thus, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"Having made a thread of nine strands—whether of fine silk, woven silk, linen, or even cotton—with nine threads using the *Sadyojāta* [mantra]."
Having washed it with pure water and likewise with sandalwood water,
one should dry it with many forms and perform [the rite] with the heart-mantra like a ball.
Thus, in the venerable Cintya-viśva-sādākhya, it is said:
"A purificatory thread (pavitraka) may consist of one hundred and eight threads;
likewise, three, half of that, ten, or seven."
Thus, the wise one should increase the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) on the glorious crown by means of threads in nine ways;
it is said that there are three inferior types, namely those consisting of nine, sixteen, and twenty [threads].
Twenty-five, thirty-two, and thirty-six are the three middling [collections];
fifty, seventy, and ninety are the three superior [collections].
O Maheśvarī, one should adopt one of these according to one's capacity.
The first three [types] should be made of metal and measured eight fingers long by twelve fingers wide.
Having fashioned it there like a bracelet with ten knots at equal intervals,
this is the fourth *śaktisūtra*, named the Gaṅgāvatāraka.
It should be made the length of an arm, or one should make it as auspicious as possible;
having placed four knots there at intervals of two finger-breadths.
Then, leaving a space of one *tāla* interval, one should fashion four knots;
in this manner, on both sides, there should be sixteen [knots] consisting of *kalās*.
"At the end, one should again fashion two knots consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
Likewise, it is stated in the venerable *Sūkṣma*:
"One should fashion the Gaṅgāvatāraka [cord] provided with eighteen knots."

One should prepare a fragrant *pavitra* adorned with eight threads and a single knot for the doors, the door-keepers, and so forth; likewise, according to the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, [it is prepared] for the planets, the world-protectors, Lakṣmī, and all the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇa*).
At the gatekeepers, however, the circumference should be made at four finger-breadths.
"A purifying thread (*pavitra*) made of nine strands should be prepared for both the Guru and oneself;
it should have a single knot, be enriched with nine threads, and be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
One should make that fragrant *pavitra*, or else one devoid of measurement. Thus [it is said].
The procedure for the preliminary rites preceding the worship of the pavilion.
(2) On the seventh or thirteenth lunar day, having performed the two daily rites (*nityāhnika*),
having decorated the sacrificial hall with flower garlands and [fragrant] powders (*kṣamābhiḥ*) in the evening,
and having performed the occasional twilight rite (*naimittikī saṃdhyā*) and the special libation (*viśeṣatarpaṇa*), one should examine [the site].

[Having performed the examination,] on the ground that has been taken possession of, [on the ground, eternal] in the middle between the directions of Śakra and Agni, having worshipped the Sun as described for the "eternal" [rite], and without dismissing him [having worshipped him]. (78) (Pra) Now, in order to describe the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the *pavitra* [thread]:

He states what must be performed prior to that with the passage beginning with "(on the seventh)" and ending with "(without releasing)" on page 398. Regarding the phrase "(on the seventh or the thirteenth)": here, if [it were] on the eighth...

When the *pavitrārohaṇa* is performed, one should carry out the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) on the seventh lunar day; if it is on the fourteenth, then the intention is that the *adhivāsa* should be performed on the thirteenth. However, when the offering of the *pavitra* together with the *adhivāsa* must be performed on a single day, then in that case—

The full fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) should be observed. As it has been said: "O Śambhu, if all the rites are to be performed on a single day and that day possesses the full lunar tithi, then the Pavitraropaṇa and other ceremonies for Śambhu are intended to be performed on that one day."

Thus it is said: when the fourteenth lunar day (*tithi*) extends across two days, then the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitra-samarpaṇa*) should be performed on the fourteenth day joined with the latter part of the day (*paraghasra*).
Likewise, in the *Śrīsiddhāntaśekhara*, regarding the rite of the sacred thread, it is stated that the fourteenth day joined with the latter part of the day [is to be used].
"The eighth [lunar day] may also be auspicious. Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"When there is a *khaṇḍatithi* (a partial lunar day), then one should offer the perfumed thread and the sacred thread (*pavitra*) during the two parts of that lunar day."
Since the *pavitra* rite is performed at a time subsequent to Viṣṇu’s sleep,
its commencement takes place on the fourteenth day, rather than on the pure eighth day (*śuddhāṣṭamī*) associated with the *mithuna* period.
It should be performed. And it has been said:
"Except for the pure eighth day, when there is a conjunction [of tithis], it should be performed on the white and black fourteenth and eighth days of the months of Karkaṭaka, Siṃha, and Bhādrapada."
Thus [it is said]. (The occasional rite) is that which is to be performed on account of the occasion of the *pavitrārohaṇa*.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is stated:
"The twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) that is to be performed during the *pavitrārohaṇa* is due to that very occasion."
Therefore, it is called "indicative" (naimittikī) because it arises from the indicative cause (naimittika-nimitta).

Thus: the meaning is that having performed the obligatory (nityā) twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should thereafter perform the occasional (naimittikī) twilight devotion. For, according to the maxim "it is the time that enjoins the rite, not the rite that enjoins the time," it is precisely at the evening hour, immediately following the obligatory twilight devotion, [that the latter is to be performed].
For the purpose of the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *pavitra*, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) must be performed once again.
By the power of this very procedure, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is also accomplished; nevertheless, the specific mention [of it] again is for the sake of [indicating] a particularity.
In order to illuminate the extensive propitiatory rites (*tarpaṇa*) taught in the *Śrīmanmṛgendra* and other scriptures,
it is said that after they have sipped water (*ācamana*) once more, [the practitioner should offer] the most excellent quality with the tips of the hands.
The five beginning with Brahmā, as well as all the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras.
Meditating upon all the presiding deities within the maṇḍala of the end of time,
one should satisfy them by means of their names in the dative case, ending with the word *svāhā*.
Then [he saw] Sanaka and the others, as well as Bhṛgu and the others, together with the lords of their lineages and pravaras— the sages with sacred threads suspended from their necks.
One should offer to the spirits (bhūtas) and others through the path of the little finger at the joints of the fingers;
likewise, one should offer to the paternal ancestors together with their wives through the left-hand path.
One should likewise honor those preceded by *pra*, as well as gurus, those who provide water, those who awaken [the mind],
brothers, friends, teachers, maternal grandfathers, and maternal uncles;
one should address those of middle rank with their names ending in *svadhā* and conclude with a prostration.
Thus it has been explained by the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.
(Having examined) means: having performed the purification of the ground by means of the removal of obstacles (*śalyoddhāra*) and so forth.
The sequence for the worship of the doors, door-keepers, and so forth.

(3) Having performed ritual sipping (*ācamana*) and having effected the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), with the ordinary *arghya* water accompanied by the *praṇava* in hand—[the *arghya* with the *praṇava* on top]—and having sprinkled the doors with the *astra-mantra*, [one should worship] in the east with: "Oṃ hyaiṃ [hāṃ], obeisance to the door of the Śāntikalā"; Oṃ hrūṃ [hāṃ]... [in the south].

Having worshipped with "Oṃ vidyākalādvārāya namaḥ" in the south, "Oṃ hlāṃ [hāṃ] nivṛttikalādvārāya namaḥ" in the west, and "Oṃ hnīṃ [hāṃ] pratiṣṭhākalādvārāya namaḥ" in the north, in that same manner...
On the two branches [of the tree], situated to his right and left—beginning from the east—[one should worship]: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla*;
*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgin*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka*. *Oṃ*...
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Devī;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍa"—thus, having worshipped two at each door (preceded by the visualization to be described hereafter), [one worships] at the two side-vases.
Having worshipped the gatekeepers in the sequence of right and left (p.
and having likewise worshipped the gatekeepers in the west as usual,
Having dispelled the obstacles and secured the other doors with the weapon-mantra,
one enters within by the western door; having placed the weapon-mantra for protection upon the udumbara tree, one proceeds clockwise.
Having offered a flower to the southwest with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (Vāstvadhipati)," and having worshipped him,
one should protect the sacrificial hall with the enclosures of the weapon-mantra (astra-prākāra) and the armor-mantra (kavaca).

Having protected [the site], he sits to the south of the mandala upon a black antelope skin or similar seat facing north; then, beginning with the words "having sipped water" (*ācamya*) and ending with "having sat down" (*upaviśya*), he describes the sequence for the worship of the door and its guardians.
The procedure for the preliminary rites involving the performance of the *śivahasta* (the hand of Śiva).

(8) Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) as previously described, preceded by the ritual placement of the digits (*kalānyāsa*), one who has completed the internal sacrifice, oblation, and meditation, [performs] the three claps (*stālatraya*) and so forth at the abode.
Having protected [the site] and prepared the special arghya water consisting of milk and the other eight ingredients, [he should sprinkle] with that water. (p. 403)

Having sprinkled one's own head with water containing *kuśa* grass, having sprinkled the collection of sacrificial materials with water and *kuśa* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*, having sprinkled them again with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having consecrated them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should consecrate the sacrificial pit with the *vakuṇṭha* mantra and render it immortal.
Then, having applied a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste, having worshipped oneself, and having performed the purification of the mantra; (70)

Regarding the performance of the *praśivahasta* [mudrā], he describes the preliminary rites with the passage beginning with "purification of the elements" (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and ending with "having performed" (*vidhāya*).
The forming of the Śiva-hand gesture, its placement upon [the disciple], and so forth.
(5) Having first applied sandalwood paste and, by means of the *mantras* associated with the seat, the image, and so forth,
having consecrated the *Śivahasta* and meditated upon it as being of the nature of radiant energy (*tejas*), one should place the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) upon one's own head.
Having taken [the weapon] over which the Astra-mantra has been recited seven times,
he describes the making of the *praśiva-hasta* (the hand of Śiva), its elevation (*adhiropaṇa*), and so forth, with the passage beginning with "candana" and ending with "ādāya."
The contemplation of Śiva.
