(6) "I am Śiva, the primordial omniscient one; I hold the preeminence in this sacrifice"—thus is he whose nonduality of the crest-lock (*śikhādvaita*) has been cultivated [i.e., whose nonduality with Śiva has been realized]. (72) (Pra) Now, he explains the contemplation of Śiva (*śivabhāvanā*) beginning with the words "Śiva" and so forth, concluding with "nonduality with Śiva" (*śivādvaita*).
By this much [it is explained]. (Ādisarvajñaḥ): He is both the "first" (ādi) and the "omniscient" (sarvajña) among all the gurus, such as Ananta and others; thus he is the Ādisarvajña.
As they have said:
He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time.
The consecration of the pavilion.
(7) Having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and having set out the scattered offerings (*vikira*),
he should consecrate them seven times with the Astra-mantra. Then, standing in the southwest facing northeast, he should [offer] with the *pañcagavya* and the *arghya*.

Having sprinkled the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) with water and purified it by means of the fourfold rites beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and the purificatory acts extending up to the crossroads (*tuṣpathānta*),
(73) he then extends the procedure for the purification of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) by means of the verse beginning with "the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*).

By the words "having consecrated" (*saṃskṛtya*) up to "having prepared the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavyaṃ saṃsādhya*), one should understand that this is to be performed according to the procedure to be described hereafter in the rite of initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*). This is how it should be noted.
The ritual procedure to be performed immediately after the consecration of the pavilion.
In that [mandala], having dispersed the transformative modifications (*vikāra*) that have become blazing weapons with the *astra-mantra*,

having gathered them together with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, and having assigned them to the *vardhanī* and the seats in the northeast, one should worship the Lord of the Site (*vāstunātha*) in the southwest.

In the west, having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī," the wise one should meditate upon her as dark-hued, facing the door, raining down floods of flowers and jewels, and manifesting in the form of a pavilion; having invoked her, he should sacrifice and remember her within the pavilion.
One should meditate [upon her]. (68) He states what is to be done immediately thereafter with the passage beginning with "in that" and ending with "one should meditate."
(253) The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī along with their Accessories.

(9) Then, in the northeast, in a jar filled with all kinds of grains and water, its mouth adorned with mango sprouts, containing a *niṣka* measure of gold, facing west, and having become an embodied form, one should place the movable seat.

Having offered [the oblation] and having fully worshipped the Blessed Lord Śiva, who is complete with all his limbs and free from the obstruction of veils, one should likewise [worship] the Vardhanī vessel to His right with "Oṃ."
To the weapon-posture: *oṃ oṃ* *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. To the weapon-form: *oṃ oṃ* *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ ślīṃ* (or *śrīṃ*) *paśūṃ huṃ phaṭ* to the weapon; *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *[-śūṃ huṃ phaṭ]*.
Namaḥ oṃ hṛdayāya oṃ oṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; oṃ ślīṃ (śrīṃ) śirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ [and so forth, according to the Pāśupata system]; oṃ paṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; oṃ śūṃ kavacāya.
Having worshipped the Pāśupata weapon with the mantra: "Oṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ; Oṃ huṃ to the eyes, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ;

Oṃ phaṭ to the weapon, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," and having adorned both [the deity and the weapon] with white garments and other ornaments, [one should proceed] to the interior portion of the directions within the pavilion.
Having meditated upon the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their vehicles and weapons, [one should place them] in the jars in the directions starting from the east—
between Mahākāla and Sūrya— with: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye*...
In the western pitcher of Gaṇeśa: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti [facing toward Indra]; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. In the northern [pitcher] of Skanda: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu.
p.
407) [Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera, to the east of Caṇḍeśa; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna, in that very place [of him].

Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā" to the south of that pitcher, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu" to the north of that pitcher, and [the mantra for Nairṛta] to the east of that pitcher,
[one should worship].
O Śakra, O Cakrin! For the pacification of obstacles in your own quarter,
you must remain alert until the conclusion of the sacrifice, by the command of Śiva.

In this sequence, one should cause all the world-protectors (lokapālas) to hear the command of Śiva; then, taking the *vardhanī* vessel, one should [pour] an unbroken stream of water reaching the tip of the *kumbha*.

Recalling the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should circumambulate from the northeast (*īśa*) to the east (*īśa*)— [from the northeast to the end of the east]— and having first established the *kumbha* vessel in its own place in the east and afterwards the *vardhanī* vessel, one should perform the *sthirāsana* upon the *kumbha*.

Having fully worshipped Śiva, and having worshipped the *astra* (weapon-mantra) in the *vardhanī* vessel, one should perform the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* with the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ hrauṃ [hauṃ] obeisance to Śiva and Śakti" [or "obeisance to Śakti and Śiva"] using the *liṅgamudrā*, and then [worship] the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*).
Having offered the sword, performed the recitation of the root mantra ten times its usual measure,
and presented the weapon-mantra (*astra*) into the *vardhanī* vessel, [the ritual concludes] here with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Then...

Having requested, "O Blessed One, you must remain until the end of the first watch," and having prepared the water for the rite of cessation (nirodhārghya), having offered that water for the rite of cessation with the Aghora mantra,
and having placed that vessel right there without moving it—
One should contemplate the sacrificial hall as having all obstacles completely dispelled by the weapons scattered from the *vardhanī* seat;
(75) (254) (pra) then, the worship of the Śiva-vessel and the *vardhanī*.

He speaks of that together with the worship of the World-Protectors who are its retinue by means of the passage beginning with "(then in the northeast)" and ending with "one should meditate. "(Until the avabhṛtha)" means until the end of the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Amara states: "In a sacrifice, the *avabhṛtha* is the conclusion of the initiation."
The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Gaṇeśa.
(20) Having worshipped Gaṇapati in the eastern jar located at the end of the northwest [direction],

and having requested, "May there be no obstacle," (76) (7) Now follows the procedure for the worship of Gaṇeśa for the sake of removing obstacles, beginning with the words "In the northwest" and so forth.
Thus ends the request.
The ritual procedure for the worship of the chosen *liṅga*.
(22) Having worshipped and petitioned the Guru at the western jar located in the northeast,

and having received his permission, one who knows [the ritual] should worship Śiva in his own chosen *liṅga* with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, according to one's means, for the purpose of the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*).
Having fully worshipped up to the end of the *pūjā*—
from "(pra) iṣṭaliṅgapūjāvidhiḥ" (the ritual procedure for worshipping the chosen *liṅga*) and so forth, ending with "saṃpūjya" (having fully worshipped).
The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Lord of the Maṇḍala.

(22) In the Brahma-sthāna, in a maṇḍala arising from the *latāliṅga* and so forth, or in a maṇḍala fashioned with fragrant substances, one should worship Śiva— the Lord of the Path (*adhvapati*), the Supreme Cause— up until the worship of one's own chosen *liṅga*, or up until the recitation (*japa*).
Alternatively, having propitiated [having fully propitiated] (77),

he now describes the ritual procedure for the worship of the Lord of the Maṇḍala with the passage beginning with "Brahmā" and ending with "having propitiated. Regarding the phrase "in the station of Brahmā":
410) We shall explain this essential nature in the ritual procedure for initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*).
Regarding the phrase "in the mandala arising from the *latāliṅga*," here is the definition of the *latāliṅgodbhava*:
It has been declared in the *Śrīmad-Siddhāntasārāvalī* that for a devotee, there are twenty kinds of external [worship]: the white path of the lunar squares (śaśipada) in the directions,
the Lingas on both sides possessing the luster of the faces of Brahmā (Ja), Indra (Ra), and Īśa (Ma), and those marked by pairs of white [squares].

In the corners, there are creepers with four squares; the path is green with sixty-four squares; and there is a lotus with the lunar digits and other elements in the mandala arising from the entwined liṅgas.

Thus [ends the worship up to one's own chosen liṅga]. Here, it should be remembered that what was previously established—that the worship concludes with the worship of the limbs of enjoyment—must be kept in mind.
The procedure for going to the place of the fire.
(23) Having requested permission for the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) and received it, he takes the vessel of honorific water (*arghyapātra*).

Circumambulating clockwise with all the ritual materials, he gazes upon the implements of sacrifice with divine vision and approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), placing the center of the pit before him.
One should sit facing the north.
411) Now, with the words beginning "the fire-rite" (*agnikārya*), he extends the procedure for going to that place by way of analogy to the fire-rite itself.
(Seated) up to this point. (For the purpose of the fire-rite) for the sake of generating the Śiva-fire.
(Having entreated) having prayed, "I shall perform the fire-rite.
(The arghya vessel) the common arghya vessel. Thus it has been stated in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*.
"Having requested the common [portion] for the sake of *hīṃ*, one should take the *arghya* for the Fire-eater (*havirbhuja*).
(With the ritual materials) "along with the implements. This is an adverbial phrase. Thus it was stated by the illustrious author of the *Somaśambhupaddhati*. (The implements for the sacrifice).
This is the substance for accomplishing the sacrificial rite of Śiva; it is situated on the left and right sides. As it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Having been established there according to the rule, [one offers] the arghya, perfumes, ghee, and so forth."
Having placed the sacrificial fuel, darbha grass, sesame seeds, and so forth, on the left and the right.
Thus [he spoke]. (With divine vision: with the eye of another. (Approaching the sacrificial pit:
Thus. On this point, the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) are taught in the venerable *Mohaśūrottara*.
One should dig one cubit deep horizontally, together with a girdle;
the neck outside the excavation shall be one finger-breadth wide—this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
The girdle should be made of three strands, consisting of nine parts of finger-breadths;
its length should be twelve finger-breadths, while the navel should be one-third of that in width.
It is one finger-breadth high and likewise enters within;
it is joined with two bulbous parts (kumbhas) like the leaf of an aśvattha tree.
The Aṅguṣṭhamekhalā is joined in the middle like the support of clarified butter;
Dakṣasthā is in the east and south, while Jalasthā is in the west and north.
Thus;
the *kuṇḍalābhi* is a specific part situated at the front of the *hotṛ*.
The ritual procedure for the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
(28) Therein, with the ring finger and the thumb joined at their bases, one should gaze at the fire-pit with a steady eye; then, with the Śiva-mantra,
one should perform the sprinkling and the striking.
(413) Sprinkling with kuśa grass using the weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and digging and scattering [the earth] using the armor mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having performed filling, leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and smearing with a sword or a blade of *kuśa* grass,
[in the center of the pit and] in the east, south, north, and west;

Having placed the mantras of the Kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā, having conceptualized [the pit] as consisting of the Kalās, and having encircled it with the three-stranded cord using the Astra-mantra, one should worship it with "Oṃ hāṃ,
obeisance to the pit consisting of the Kalās," [and then draw lines] extending eastward and northward.

Or else, one should form four lines together with a horizontal line on both sides; then, using three *kuśa* blades in the shape of tridents, one performs the "vajrification" (*vajrīkaraṇa*), and with two *kuśa* blades having their tips pointing east and north, one performs the "deposition of the crossroads" (*catuṣpathanyāsa*) with the *astra-mantra*. (90)
Now, having explained the procedure for going to the fire-site: an oblation offered either in an unprepared place or in an unconsecrated fire becomes fruitless.
Therefore, the preceptor should perform the consecrations of the sacrificial pit and other elements with mantras.

By the venerable Ajita’s statement, "p. 414)," he first describes the procedure for the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the passage beginning with "(tatra)" and ending with "(astreṇa). In that context, "(tatra)" means in that sacrificial pit.
(With the root [mantra] placed): that in which the root—the root-mantra—is placed is thus described;
by that [mantra]. (The inspection): the first consecration is called "inspection" (*vīkṣaṇa*). (Sprinkling and striking):
sprinkling is the second consecration called "sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇa*); and striking (*tāḍana*).

The third consecration for you is called *tāḍana*. *Prokṣaṇa* is performed with water mixed with *arghya*, using the palm of the hand turned upward in the shape of a banner (*patākā*). *Tāḍana* is performed with a fist from which the index finger is extended. The fourth consecration is called *abhyukṣaṇa*.
Sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) is performed with the palm of the hand in the shape of a banner, turned downwards.
The word "with *kuśa* grasses" should also be connected to the act of sprinkling. Thus it has been explained by the illustrious commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.
(digging, scattering, filling, leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and plastering) p.
Digging and excavating is the fifth consecration;
scattering and leveling is the sixth consecration; filling and making complete is the seventh consecration;
smoothing and arranging for evenness is the eighth consecration; and thorough sweeping is [the ninth].
The removal of dust is the eleventh consecration (*saṃskāra*), and the proper drying after anointing is the twelfth consecration [performed] with the sword (*khaḍga*) as the weapon.
Here, for the sake of removing defects such as bone-fragments and the like, digging and so forth should be performed mentally.

The term "bhāva" refers to [the directions] from the center of the pit (kuṇḍa) to the east, south, north, and west; specifically, the center of the pit, the space between the girdles (mekhalā), the eastern girdle, the southern girdle,
the northern girdle, and the western girdle.

The western girdle, the center, and the east, south, north, and west among them—having thus conceived [them]. This is the thirteenth consecration, called the conceptualization of the form of the *kalās*.
Having thus encircled [them].
The fourteenth consecration is called "the donning of the triple thread" (*trisūtrīparidhāna*).
"(Having worshipped)" refers to the fifteenth consecration, called "the worship consisting of the *kalās*. "(Extending eastward)"...
"Facing east" is the meaning. "(Extending north)" means facing north.

"With *kuśa* grass" is the ellipsis to be supplied here. In this regard, if the preceptor faces east, he should draw three lines facing east and one line with its tip pointing north; if he faces north, then—

The intended meaning is that one should draw three lines facing upward and one line facing eastward. As was stated previously regarding the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*): "Having prepared three lines facing east with *kuśa* grass, one should also prepare a single line facing northward."

"If [the practitioner] faces north, it should be prepared in the reverse manner. In that regard, it should be understood that the four lines consist of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Maheśvara. Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*, it is said: "There are three lines facing east, and one line facing north."
Or else, this procedure should be performed in reverse; the lines should be drawn as having the nature of the gods.
p.
417) "Known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśa"—this is the sixteenth sacrament, called the arrangement of the four lines. (In both cases).

The meaning is "at the root and the tip. (Vajrīkaraṇa): The seventeenth consecration is known as Vajrīkaraṇa. Here, one should perform two Vajrīkaraṇa consecrations—the arrangement of four lines—with the Heart Mantra.
Other rites not mentioned here are also said to be performed "with the heart.
As it has been stated: "Whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, all that is indeed done with the heart.
Alternatively, one may perform them with the Astra-mantra. (The Nyāsa of the Crossroads)
The eighteenth consecration is called the "Placement at the Crossroads.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*, it is said:
"Having gazed with a gracious eye and having sprinkled [the disciple] with the Śiva-mantra..."
The wise one should strike and sprinkle [the disciple] with the armor-mantra (varman) ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
One should perform the excavation with the Astra-mantra, the extraction of earth with the Hṛdaya-mantra, the filling with the Samatā-mantra,
the sprinkling with the Kavaca-mantra, and then the treading with the Heti-mantra.
One should perform the cleansing and the smearing with the *kavaca* mantra.
The digits (*kalā*), beginning with *Śāntyatītā*, should be deposited in the center and starting from the east, respectively.
One should wrap [the sacrificial ground] with a protective covering consisting of three threads;
then, having joined the salutation "Obeisance to the pit composed of parts (kalāmaya)," one should perform the worship.
Three lines should be drawn facing eastward, and one line facing northward;
the transformation into a vajra is performed with the weapon-mantra using three kusha-grass blades in the shape of a vajra.
The heart-shaped [altar] should be made at the crossroads with two *kuśa* blades beginning from the northeast toward Soma and Indra;
thus, the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) have been briefly described.
Thus [ends] the invocation of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara.
(Kriyāpāda 25) Within the sacrificial pit, one should prepare a protective covering (*akṣapāṭa*) with *kuśa* grass rising up on all sides.
Having covered it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should place a seat in the form of a tuft of grass (kūrca) in the center, saying:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī" (or "to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara"). Having visualized the Goddess upon that, one should invoke the Goddess—the Vidyā—into it.

The wise one who, according to the prescribed rule, meditates upon the Mother of the Universe— Śyāmā, who is not yet menstruating— (p. 419) having meditated upon Śyāmā, who is not yet menstruating, [he attains success].
[She was] adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments.

Having meditated thus: "She with a serene face and three eyes resembling lotus petals," [one should recite: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī. [Thus, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī; thus, one should worship Vāgīśvara and his consort Vāgīśvarī.]
In the same way, one should worship Vāgīśvara with perfumes and other offerings, reciting: *oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ*.
(32) Now, anticipating the question of what should be done once the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) has been consecrated in this manner:

He describes the invocation of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara preceded by the arrangement of the seat and the gaming board with the passage beginning with "(of the *kuṇḍa*)" and ending with "(having worshipped). "(Samantāt)" means on all sides.
"(Utthitaiḥ)" means placed or arranged. "(Akṣapāṭam)" refers to a curtain or screen.
In this regard, for that purpose, let four blades of *kuśa* grass be spread all around above the necks of the fire-pits situated within [the mandala] of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. Likewise,
it is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should place the *kuśa* grass with the armor-mantra (*varma*) above the throat for the protection of the eyes.
Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
"One should [place] the *kuśa* grass all around above the throat with the armor-mantra, having their tips pointing east and north."
"akṣapāṭam" means a seat made of *darbha* grass.
According to Amara, "viṣṭara" refers to a tree, a handful of *darbha* grass, or a seat such as a stool; [it is used here for] that [seat].
Regarding the seat (*viṣṭara*), he states the meditation on Vāgīśvarī with the word "the Goddess" (*devīm*). "The Vidyā" means that which is called Vidyā;

as it has been said: "The supreme Vidyā is Vāgīśvarī. "According to rule" (*vidhivat*) means by the sequence prescribed in the scriptures. "The Mother of the Universe" (*viśvamātaram*) means she who is the cause of the entire world. "Dark-hued" (*śyāmām*).
Of dark complexion; (meaning "in her season") refers to one who has bathed after her menses. Likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīcintya*:
"He who meditates specifically upon her in her youth, having bathed after her menses, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus."
Thus [it is said]. The rest is easily understood. The meditation on Vāgīśvara is described in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Ten-armed, white, gentle, five-faced, with fifteen eyes..."
Likewise, O God, the Lord is in the form of Nāda, together with the Goddess who is the nature of Bindu.
"May you two both be present for the generation of fire"—
having thus invoked them with the Heart-mantra and worshipped them, one should contemplate their union.
Thus [it is said].
The fire-nyāsa.
(26) Having brought fire from a forest, a sun-crystal, the house of a twice-born, the house of a vaiśya, one’s own house, or the house of a brahmin, into either an earthen vessel or a copper vessel,
[one should place it] in the southeast, the northeast, or the southwest.
Having set it aside, and having expelled the portion for the flesh-eaters toward the southwest with the Astra-mantra,
one should purify it with the four rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa), etc., saying "Oṃ."

Having grasped the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) with the inhalation (*pūraka*) while reciting "Hāṃ [Haṃ] Haṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire," and having united it with the heart-fire (*hṛdayāgni*), the navel-fire (*nābhyagni*),
and the bindu-fire (*bindvāgni*) through retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one should expel it with the exhalation (*recaka*) while reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ."
Having projected [the mantra] "HĀṂ HRŪṂ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire" (vahnicaitanya) into the fire situated in the vessel,

having worshipped it with the *saṃhitā*, protected it, and veiled it, one should take it up after making it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* with the *prāsāda* mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and circumambulate it three times clockwise above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having rotated [the wheel] (p.

422) and meditated on it as the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should visualize the two parents with their heads directed toward the northeast (or, according to another reading, "directed toward the Lord").
Or, having visualized it being cast by Vāgīśvara into the central channel within the womb of Vāgīśvarī,
one should [visualize it] facing oneself from the root-mantra located at the knees on the ground.
One should cast [the image] resembling oneself at the root of the knee.
(32) Now, he explains the fire-assignment (*vahni-nyāsa*) with the passage beginning with "from the fire-drill" (*araṇeḥ*) and ending with "one should cast.
"From the fire-drill" (*araṇeḥ*) means from wood such as that of the *aśvattha* tree which serves as the source of fire. "Fire" (*vahnim*) refers to that which carries [the heat].

He is called *vahni* because he carries (*prāpayati*) the oblation; [he is placed] in that [vessel], namely, a fresh earthenware bowl (*mṛtpātra*). The extraction of the mantra for the form of Vahni is performed according to the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*: "Then, enclosing [the seed-syllable] with the *hṛdaya*-mantra, while uttering the self-seed-syllable, one says: 'Salutation to the form of Vahni (*vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*)'."

“(The elemental fire)” means the fire of the elements; “(by the navel-fire)” means by the digestive fire; “(by the bindu-fire)” means by the fire of the *bindu*. “Having joined” means having unified the triad of fires: the elemental, the gastric, and the *bindu* fires.
Thus it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Having unified the three fires—the gastric, the cranial, and the elemental" (p. 423). (Circumambulation)
In a clockwise direction. (Having whirled it around: This is for the purpose of agitating the womb of Vāgīśvarī; such is the intended meaning.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"For the sake of agitating the womb, one should whirl that [the vessel] three times above the *kuṇḍa* while reciting the heart-mantra."

(Śivabīja) means the white seed of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). The implication here is that if fire were not the seed of Śiva, its entry into the channel of the womb of Vāgīśvarī would be logically untenable. (Pitarau) refers to the father and the mother; "pitarau" [is the dual form] referring to Vāgīśvarī [as the mother].
"Vāgīśvarau" means [the two lords of speech]. "Pitā mātrā" is a *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning father and mother].
"(In the navel-channel of Vāgīśvarī)" means in the womb of Vāgīśvarī.
"(With knees placed on the ground)" means with both knees resting upon the surface of the earth.
Likewise, in the venerable Mataṅga, it is said:
"Having meditated upon oneself as being like Śiva, one should meditate on the fire as a seed-syllable;
having slowly rotated it three times with the Sadyojāta mantra."
Having gone to the ground on his knees.
The procedure to be performed after the placement of the fire (vahnivinyāsa).
(27) Then, having gathered [the fire] at the navel region, having visualized the covering of the lower garment,

having offered drops of water from the heart for the sake of purification and sipping water, having covered it with the armor-mantra and fuel, and having kindled it with the weapon-mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ garbhāgnaye*.

Having worshipped the fire of the womb with "[-oṃ hāṃ garbhā-] namaḥ," and having tied a darbha-bracelet consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra onto the hand of the Goddess for the protection of the embryo, [on the hand of the Goddess]. (23)

Next, [the author] states what is to be performed immediately after the placement of the fires (*vahni-vinyāsa*) with the passage beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "having bound" (*badhvā*). Regarding the phrase "in the region of the navel" (*nābhideśe*):
the "navel" (*nābhi*) is a specific part in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a lotus. Thus, in the *Śrīmatkāmika*:
The navel should be fashioned in the middle of the pit with a measurement of one and a half [units];
its height should be one-fourth of that, so that it takes the form of a lotus.
Thus, in its place; having performed the sweeping (*samūhana*), when the fire has been scattered toward the navel region—
that is,
having gathered together that which was spread out all around— [this refers to] the undergarment (*paridhāna*).
Of clothing: *saṃvṛti* means covering. Regarding *astrajaptadarbhakaṅkaṇam*:
here, it is called *kaṅkaṇa* because it "makes a pleasant sound" (*kaṇati*) or "moves" (*sarati*); it is a hand ornament.
Or, *pratisara* is *kaṅkaṇa*; it is an armlet. *Kaṅkaṇa* may be a *pratisara*.

Thus say the lexicographers. (In the hand of the Goddess: Vāgīśvarī is in the right hand. Likewise, in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*, it is said that the weapon-bracelet (*astrakaṅkaṇa*) is made of *darbha* grass over which the weapon-mantra has been recited seven times.
One should bind it on the right hand while recollecting the Astra-mantra.
"For the sake of protecting the one containing the fire" refers to the ritual procedure for the sacraments beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*).

(28) Having worshipped with the *sadyojāta* [mantra] for the sake of conception (*garbhādhāna*), and having offered three oblations of sesame seeds with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], [one should proceed] for the sake of the *puṃsavana* rite. (p.
In the third month, having worshipped with the Vāmadeva mantra, having offered three oblations with the head-mantra, and having sprinkled drops of water,
one should worship with the Aghora mantra in the sixth month for the purpose of opening the mother's hair-parting (sīmanta).
Having offered three oblations with the *śikhā* [mantra], and having performed the visualization of the faces and limbs as well as the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) by means of the *śikhā* itself,
and having worshipped the person for the sake of birth during the tenth month, and having offered three oblations with the *kavaca* [mantra], when [the child] is born...
For the purpose of bathing to remove the impurities of the womb—
[having kindled the fire with darbha grass and other materials]—
and having removed the darbha-grass bracelet from the hand of the Goddess, [the gold binding].
Having meditated on it as "the work of the Goddess" (*devyākṛta*), having worshipped it with the heart-mantra,
having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astrāmbhas*) for the immediate cessation of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*),
having struck it with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the weapon-mantra, and having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
For the purpose of protecting the fire,
having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing toward the northeast upon the eastern and other girdles using the Astra-mantra,
and having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhis) and sacrificial seats (viṣṭaras) upon them, [of the faces...]
p.

427) For the removal of saliva and for the nourishment of the fire, one should offer five fuel-sticks smeared with ghee into the fire using a sword at both the base and the tip, [in the directions] east, west, south, and north—
In the intermediate directions: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ anantāya [īśvarāya] namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped those stationed at the perimeter (*paridhisthāna*), [one should worship] upon the seats (*viṣṭara*) in the directions starting from the east with *oṃ*...

Hāṃ, obeisance to Indra; [on the seat, Indra and others in the eight directions: Oṃ hāṃ Indra—] Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; Oṃ hāṃ...
Hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera [and Soma]; Om Hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, directed toward the upper portion in the northeast; Om Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā in the northeast; Om Hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu.

Aiming toward the lower region in the southwest, having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ Viṣṇave namaḥ" and offered the arghya, and having warded off the host of obstacles, one should proclaim the command of Śiva: "Protect the child! [having warded off the host of obstacles, "protect the child"].

Then, having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles together with *kuśa* grass— with their faces upward and downward respectively [or: having grasped them with the *kuśa* blades held upward and the faces downward]— by means of the *astra-mantra*.

Having sprinkled [it] thoroughly, having sprinkled it with the *kavaca* mantra and performed the *avakuṇṭhana* (enclosing) rite, having heated it over the fire and whirled it around, having touched its tip with the tip of a *kuśa* blade and whirled it around again, and having touched its middle with the middle [of the blade] and whirled it around again;

Having touched the root with the root [mantra], and having rotated [the thread] over the parts of those two [threads] touched by the *kuśa* grass, one should [visualize] the three principles known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, along with the triad of Rudras— the presiding lords named Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā— respectively.
Having sequentially assigned [the mantras] *om hūṃ [haṃ] hīṃ hāṃ* along with the *Śambaras*,
and having placed *Śakti* in the *sruc* ladle and *Śambhu* in the *sruva* spoon,
one should place [the offering] upon *kuśa* grass on the left side of oneself, over which a cord has been wound three times around the neck, using the root mantra.
Having established it at the base, one should worship it with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).

Then, having brought cow-derived clarified butter (gavyamājya), purified it through the rites of inspection and so forth, contemplated one's own body as consisting of Brahman, and taken hold of it, one should swirl it three times above the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and heat it within the range of the fire.
Having placed [the vessel] in the southeast (āgneyī), and having taken a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a blade of darbha grass, one should offer it by reciting: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*.
Furthermore, having offered [the oblation] consisting of Viṣṇu, and having meditated upon his own body as the *sthāpaka* (the installer),

he should place it over the fire in the northeast; then, having offered a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave svāhā," he should thereafter [offer the oblation and] perform the heating (*adhiśravaṇa*) of his own form.

Having contemplated [the deity] as consisting of Rudra and having held [it] at the navel, one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting "oṃ hrūṃ [hrāṃ] rudrāya svāhā"; then, having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*),
[one should prepare] a [wick] made from two tips of *darbha* grass, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length.

Having grasped the middle portion of the *pavitraka*— consisting of two tips of *darbha* grass fashioned to a length of one *deśa*— between the thumb and ring finger at its central knot, one should cause the clarified butter (*ājya*) to overflow three times toward the fire with the *astra-mantra*.

In the same manner, having performed a ritual immersion facing oneself with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, having untied that sacred thread (*pavitra-granthi*) and cast it into the fire, and having thrown a burning blade of *darbha* grass consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra* into the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the *astra-mantra*;
Having purified it, one should cast that too into the fire with a cloth;
having performed the *nīrājana* rite over it with another blazing blade of *darbha* while reciting the *kavaca* mantra, one should cast it into the fire.
Having ignited that firebrand as well with another blazing weapon,
one should cast it into the fire.

Then, having placed two blades of kuśa grass with a knot in their middle, measuring a span (prādeśa), into the midst of the ghee while reciting the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should visualize the two fortnights— the bright and the dark— in the order of one's own right and left hands.

Having visualized the three channels— Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā— in the right, left, and middle portions respectively, and having taken clarified butter from the right side with the *sruva* ladle, one should recite: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*.

Thus, for the fire in the right eye; having taken clarified butter from the left portion—[for a householder, "Oṃ Hāṃ Soma"—] saying "Oṃ Hāṃ Somāya Svāhā," [having taken from the middle portion] into the left eye of the fire;
and having taken [from the middle], saying "Oṃ Hāṃ Agnīṣomābhyām."

Having offered a little with "Svāhā" into the fire's middle eye, and with "Oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" into the fire's mouth, one should cast the remaining clarified butter into the respective portions of the ājyabhāgas with "Hā," during the bright fortnight.
p.
431) But in the dark fortnight: *oṃ* [in the light fortnight: *oṃ hāṃ somāya*] *hāṃ somāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ somāgnibhyāṃ svāhā*, *oṃ*.

Saying "Hāṃ, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā," one takes clarified butter from the left, right, and middle portions; having offered it as before into the left, right, and middle eyes of Agni— and [into the mouth of Agni]— and having consecrated the clarified butter with the *saṃhitā* mantra...

Having protected it with the *saṃhitā-mantra*, having veiled it, having rendered it nectar-like with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) using the *dhenu-mudrā*, and having worshipped it with the root mantra— [having veiled it and having applied the *dhenu-mudrā* seal].
By casting drops of clarified butter (ājya) with the heart-mantra, one should perform the purification of the remaining clarified butter. Thereafter, [one should offer]:
*oṃ haṃ [hāṃ] sadyojātāya svāhā*, *oṃ hiṃ [hīṃ] vāmadevāya svāhā*, *oṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā*, *oṃ [devāya svāhā oṃ heṃ-] heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā*.
Svāhā! Oṃ Hoṃ! To Īśāna, Svāhā!—with each of these offerings of clarified butter, one should perform the libation for the faces of Agni [the support of the faces]. Oṃ Haṃ Hiṃ [Hīṃ]!
To Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva, Svāhā! Oṃ Hiṃ Huṃ!
"Vāmadeva-aghora-bhyām svāhā, oṃ huṃ heṃ aghora-tatpuruṣa-bhyām svāhā, oṃ heṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣa-īśāna-bhyām svāhā. (p. 432) Thus [it is said].
The connection of the faces is: *oṃ haṃ hiṃ [hīṃ] huṃ heṃ hoṃ sadyojāta-vāmadeva-aghora-tatpuruṣa-īśānebhyas svāhā* (or *...-īśānābhyāṃ svāhā*).
Thus, from the southeast (*agni*) to the northwest (*vāyu*), and from the southwest (*nirṛti*) to the northeast (*īśāna*).

Having offered the oblation of clarified butter, one should perform the unification with the mouth of Agni. Then, for the purpose of naming, having worshipped [the deity] with Īśa and offered three oblations with the Astra-mantra, [one should address him as]: "O Śivāgni, you..."
Having given him the name Hutāśana (98),
then, having introduced the arrangement of the fire (*vahni-vinyāsa*),
and having honored the incidental sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* with perfumes and other offerings, [one should worship] with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
Having offered three oblations with the *hṛdaya* [mantra], and so forth, according to the venerable *Kiraṇa-śruti*,

one should worship with the *brahmans* beginning with Sadyojāta; then, he says that one should perform each consecration (*pratisaṃskāra*) with three oblations using these [mantras] beginning with the *hṛdaya*— [namely, for] *garbhādhāna*.
By means of [the passage] beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "ityantena."

433) Therein, he first states the ritual procedure for the sacrament of conception (*garbhādhāna*) with the words "for the sake of conception" (*garbhādhānāya*). With the words "by means of Sadyojāta," [he indicates] that here—
It has been stated in the venerable *Ṣaṭsahasrikā* that worship should be performed preceded by the recollection of Śiva in His form [as the Yoni]:
"Having cast the seed-mantra into the Yoni like a seed, while recollecting Śiva as the Immediate Mantra (Sadyomantra)..."
With the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should offer five oblations to the heart.
"The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed in this manner. Thus, in the case of the rites for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana) and others as well,
worship preceded by the recollection of Śiva in the form of Vāmadeva and so forth must be performed.
This should be understood according to the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*.
He states the *puṃsavana* sacrament with the words "the *puṃsavana*.

For the purpose of the *puṃsavana*— that is, for the sake of [the fetus] becoming male and not female, meaning for the sake of ensuring it is a male— the term *puṃsavana* is used because by means of this, a male (*pumān*) is brought forth (*sūyate*).
But at the *puṃsavana* rite, one should pour a drop of water onto a blade of *darbha* grass while intending,
"May it be living," and should say, "Become a male."

Thus, according to the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti*, one should drop a drop of water from the *arghya* with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, saying "Bhava," for the purpose of infusing consciousness into the fire while it is still within the womb; thus he says "(the drop of water)."
He states the *saṃskāra* of *sīmantonnayana*:

"The *sīmā*"—that is, the boundary, limit, or demarcation of the parts [of the womb]—its "end" (*anta*) is its completion; for the purpose of the ritual imagination, it serves as the occasion (*nimitta*) for the "raising" (*unnayana*) of that end.

(The visualization of the limbs of the speaker): One should consider that by this ritual act, the body of Śivāgni is produced here through the conceptualization of its constituent parts, such as the head, face, neck, thighs, and feet.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"One should first demarcate the boundary of the woman's body with a blade of *darbha* grass" (and also the expiation), which means the complete removal [of the impurity].
Thus it has been stated by the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*:

for the purpose of conceiving the faces and limbs [of the deity] and for the sake of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should offer oblations three times each with the *śikhā* mantra. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *śikhā* [mantra], one should offer oblations three times for the sake of purifying the faces and limbs;
likewise, one should perform three oblations for the purpose of opening the faces and for expiation (*niṣkṛti*).
Thus it is said; some maintain that one should offer oblations fifteen times for the sake of expiation.
He speaks of the *jātakarma* sacrament (for the sake of birth): "having kindled" means having inflamed the fire with *darbha* grass and other materials. Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"having ignited the fire with *darbha* grass and so forth, [one performs the rite for] the newborn child who is the son of Śiva."

*(Darbhakaṅkaṇam)*: A bracelet made of *darbha* grass. According to Amara, *kaṅkaṇa* means a bracelet or an ornament for the hand. *(Svarṇabandhanam)*: A golden fillet. Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:

"Having meditated on [the goddess] adorned with golden bands"—this means [on the goddesses] in the middle girdles starting from the east; that is to say, in the middle girdles beginning with the eastern one. Likewise, in the venerable *Suprabheda*:
If there is a single girdle-altar, one should spread [the grass] upon the girdle;
on the sacrificial mound, the spreading is said to be outside the sandy area.

"In those with two girdles, in the second, and in the middle one with three girdles"—this refers to the *darbha* grass used for strewing (*paristaraṇa*). Regarding the enclosures and seats (*paridhi-viṣṭarān*): "enclosures" (*paridhi*) are the branches used for strewing around the sacrificial pit; as Amara states, "enclosures are the branches of a tree fit for sacrifice. And the "seats" (*viṣṭara*)...

The handfuls of *darbha* grass are for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat (*viṣṭara*). Regarding the characteristics of the enclosing sticks, it is stated in the venerable *Kāmika*: "The enclosing sticks should be straight, fresh, produced from the same wood as the sacrificial fuel for that fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), free from blemishes, cut evenly, and equal in size."
The characteristics of the *viṣṭara* (seat) are stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Those produced in pure locations, soft, straight, and auspicious,
and avoided [those from] cremation grounds, anthills, and crossroads."
p. 437) With those very [blades], a seat (*viṣṭara*) should be made, consisting of thirty blades of *darbha* grass, equal [in length],
measuring one cubit (*hasta*), and likewise having a braided or woven binding.
Thus [it is said]. (For the removal of saliva: *Lālā* refers to that which flows from the mouth, meaning the water within the teeth;

*sṛṇikā*, *syandinī*, and *lālā* are synonyms according to Amara. For the purpose of its removal—that is, for its clearing away—he describes the worship of the deities of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), beginning with the word "in front" (*pūrva*).
He describes the worship of the presiding deities of the seats with the words "(on the seats).
"(In the northeast)" means to the south of Īśāna. "(In the southwest)" means to the north of Nirṛti. "(The child)" refers to the infant Agni.
The presiding deities of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seat (*viṣṭara*) should be known as facing the fire.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"In sequence, starting from the east and ending with the north, [are the positions] of the enclosing sticks."
From Indra to Īśāna, [worship them] in order according to their positions on the seats.
"One should worship [the deities] facing the fire in their own directions with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Thus it is said. Now, he extends by analogy the ritual purification (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, beginning with the word "then" (*tataḥ*). [The phrase] "the *sruk* and *sruva*" refers to the *sruk* and...
And those two are the *sruva* and the *sruc*. It is called *sruva* because one pours clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and other substances downward with it;
it is an implement for sacrifice. The definition of these two has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:
"From trees such as the *brahmāśvattha*, *śamī*, *parṇa*, *śiṃśapā*, and so forth..."
The handle of the *sruva* ladle is one thumb-joint long, and its length is one cubit.
A depression with a width of half a cow’s footprint and a depth of one *karṣa* is for the sake of prosperity;
its opposite—being excessive, deficient, maimed, or distorted—is considered unfavorable for the body.
The Aya has six limbs, the Ti eight limbs, the Ra four, and the Va one neck;
it has five faces like mountains, hands, and a small, wide protrusion.

The width at the base of the altar-platform (vedī) and so forth is three parts; it is established with a circular rim (avaṭa) consisting of one part. The girdle (mekhalā) is half a part, and the remainder is adorned with various patterns, leaves, and other ornaments.
The altar-platforms attached to the side-projections (gaṇḍikā) at the corners extend for a measure equal to half the length of the main platform.
It rises from a kalaśa that has been fashioned from half a bhāga of the six-fold staff.
439) The *sruc* [ladle] has the shape of a cupped hand (*añjali*), the *sruva* [spoon] the shape of a cow's ear, and the *praṇālā* [channel-ladle] the shape of a water-spout.
Thus it is said. By the phrase "having heated them," it should be understood that the wooden nature of the *sruc* and *sruva* is thereby excluded.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*,
for the purpose of removing the state of being mere wood, these two— the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles— have been purified by means of gazing and other rites, and then heated.

Thus [it is said]. "(At the tip)" means the tips of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. "Touching the tip" is for the purpose of conceptualizing the principle (*tattva*) of Śiva. "(By the middle)" means by the middle of the *darbha* grass. "(The middle)" refers to the middles of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

The touching of the center is for the placement of the *vidyā-tattva*, while the touching of the base is for the placement of the *ātma-tattva*; thus it has been explained by the venerable commentator on the *Kiraṇa*. (Oṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hāṃ śambaraiḥ).
By means of the seed-mantras of the crest (śikhā), the head (śiras), and the heart (hṛdaya). Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is said:
"One should place the three principles (tattva) within those [locations] by means of the heart, the head, and the Jvālinī seed-mantras.
Herein: *Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ śivatattvāya*; *Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ śivatattvādhipataye*.
"Salutation to Rudra"— in this manner, one should also perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the principles of knowledge (vidyātattva) and so forth.
This sequence is to be understood as intended for those who seek worldly enjoyment (bhukti).

However, for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), the venerable commentator on the *Mṛgendra-tantra* has demonstrated that one should touch the base, middle, and tip of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles through the pervasion of the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. "(On the left side)" means on the right flank.

Likewise, in the *Śrīmat-suprabheda*, it says: "Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles upon *darbha* grass, [place them] on the right"—meaning they should be established with their faces turned downwards (*adhomukhau*). Similarly, in the *Śrīman-mṛgendra*: "Having performed [the rite], they should be placed facing downwards upon a seat of *kuśa* grass to the left."

Thus it is said. In this regard, in the absence of the aforementioned *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should fashion them from *palāśa* leaves and the like. Likewise, in the venerable *Kiraṇa-tantra*: "In the absence [of the proper vessels], one should also use *palāśa* and *udumbara* leaves for the *sruva*."
Or even with the petals of the *kiṃśuka* tree.

Having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he explains the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the word "Now" (*atha*). "(Gavyam)" means a product of the cow. "(Āvartya)" means having whirled it around.
This is called the purificatory rite known as *paryagnikaraṇa*. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should indeed cause it to circle three times around the sacrificial pit; that is *paryagnikaraṇa*. (Having heated it...)

Having performed the consecration known as *tāpana* (heating). Here, the consecration known as *tāpana* is performed by means of the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*. It should be understood that the same applies to the subsequent [consecrations] as well.
Thus it has been said:
Assuming his own form composed of Brahman and taking [the offering] from the tip of the *kuśa* grass,
he should offer a drop to Brahmā with the heart-mantra ending in *svāhā*.
That is declared to be the heating (tāpana); furthermore, it is itself composed of Viṣṇu.
Then, having placed ghee in the northeast corner, one should offer it as an oblation to Viṣṇu.
Thus is known the act of placing [the vessel] on the fire; having likewise held the clarified butter at the navel, Rudra should offer that to Rudra—this is declared to be the "removal" (udvāsana).

"In some places, this triad is proclaimed by means of the *hṛdaya*, *śiras*, and *cūlikā* [mantras] along with the *aṇu* [mantra]. (It is fashioned from two tips of *darbha* grass, each a span in length. A span in length.

"Prādeśa-pramāṇa" means the measure of a *prādeśa*. A *prādeśa* is a hand with the thumb extended and the other fingers contracted. Regarding the terms *prādeśa*, *tāla*, and *gokarṇa*, Amara states that these [measurements] are defined by the extension of the fingers beginning with the index finger (*tarjanī*) up to the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*). Furthermore, "that" refers to the two tips of the *darbha* grass.
The meaning is "two blades of *darbha* grass with unbroken roots and tips"; it is fashioned from those.
(*Madhyagranthipavitrakam*) means that which has a knot in the middle; that is, a *brahmagranthi* in its center, and it is a purifier (*pavitraka*). (With the thumb and ring finger...)

"Having grasped [it]"— here it should be understood that one should grasp the base portion with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand, and the tip portion with the thumb and ring finger of the other [right] hand.
Likewise, in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Kusha grass with unbroken tips and roots, measuring a span (prādeśa) in length, should be used for the consecration with clarified butter; others do not bestow great auspiciousness.

"Having formed two blades of *kuśa* grass into a *brahmagranthi* knot in the middle, one should grasp their roots and tips with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands. Thus it is said: "(one should) leap," meaning one should perform a leap.
p.

443) Here, immediately after performing the *utplava* rite, one should untie the knots of those two blades of *darbha* grass and cast them into the fire. (In the same manner) means that here [the ritual is performed] with another such pair of *darbha* blades.
It should be understood that one should perform the *saṃplavana* (sprinkling). Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*:

"Having taken two blades of *darbha* grass, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length and joined at the middle knot, one should perform the *utplava* (upward sprinkling) toward the fire with the ring finger and the thumb."
Having loosened that knot with a blade, one should cast it into the fire;
likewise, with such a darbha grass, [one should do so] facing oneself with the heart-mantra.
Having performed the immersion as before, one should likewise cast it into the fire. Thus [it is said].
*Utplava* is the threefold upward surging toward the flames of fire;
*saṃplavana* is the upward lifting. *Utplava* is the upward movement of subtle forms of obstacles; [the same applies to] those very obstacles.
"In every way, downward movement is called 'submergence' (*saṃplavana*)," as stated in the venerable *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*: "(The incanted and burnt darbha-twig)" (p.

Here, by the word *ulmuka*, a firebrand (*alāta*) is meant; as Amara states: "A charcoal, a firebrand, [and] an *ulmuka*. Regarding the phrase "(having purified)": here, it should be understood that the clarified butter (*ājya*) has been rendered completely pure by the casting of the darbha grass—previously consecrated with the Heart-mantra and burnt—with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*). Likewise...
It has been declared by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"One should purify [the site] by casting the weapon of burnt darbha grass obtained from the heart. (Having performed the *nīrājana* consecration:
Having performed the *nīrājana* consecration, [one should proceed] from right to left around oneself.

"By way of the left and right sequence. (Having made this resolve) means having meditated upon [the oblation] as having entered the clarified butter. "(From the left side)" means from the portion of fire situated within the piṅgalā nāḍī. "(Clarified butter)" refers to the ghee consisting of light.
(In the right eye: in the fire of the right eye; (from the left side:
from the lunar portion situated in the *iḍā* channel; (the clarified butter: nectar-like ghee; (in the left eye:
in the moon of the left eye; (from the center).
From the central portion consisting of Agni and Soma located within the *suṣumnā*,
[there arises] the clarified butter (*ājya*), which is the essence of both; likewise, from the middle eye, there is the corresponding eye on the forehead.

Regarding the light [deity] (*jyotiṣi*), that is, in the mouth of fire (*agnivaktre*), which has a blazing face consisting of both Soma and Agni—this has been established by the illustrious author of the *Jñānaratnāvalī* with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā!
One should offer this oblation by taking clarified butter from the left portion. Likewise...
In the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, it is stated:
"Having said 'svāhā' to Sviṣṭakṛt, one should offer ghee in three portions into the blazing mouth [of the fire];
and having uttered 'ha', one should also offer the remainder in three portions of ghee."
"In those respective *ājyabhāga* offerings" means: those various *ājyabhāgas* are "those respective *ājyabhāgas*"; [the locative case] refers to them.
The meaning is that in whichever portion the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) was drawn, it is in that respective portion.
It should be understood that the oblations to Agni and the others are for the purpose of opening the eyes here.
Thus it was stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"For the opening of the eyes, [one should recite] 'of Agni' three times over the face. (In the bright fortnight) this refers to the first half;
(in the dark fortnight) to the latter half. Regarding the two halves, Amara states: "The two halves are the first and the latter, namely the bright and the dark."
446) Considering that the moon wanes during the dark fortnight,
the Blessed One taught that the Soma should first be gratified for the purpose of its replenishment.
By the author of the *Mṛgendravṛtti*.

In this context, it should be noted that there are eighteen consecrations (saṃskāras) for the clarified butter (ājya), beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and ending with the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa). Likewise, in the venerable Jñānaratnāvalī, it is stated:
"The four [rites] beginning with inspection, as well as its threefold circumambulation in the fire."
Heating, placing on the fire, lifting up, as well as overflowing and submerging;
The purification of the ghee consists of eighteen rites: the *pūtanī*, the *nīrājana*, the *udyota*, the *mantra*, the *dyotana*, the *mantraṇa*, the *rakṣā*, the *kuṇṭhana*, and the *rocyaka*.
It should be purified by mantras; then it will become that very nectar. Thus [it is said].

Having thus illustrated the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskṛti*), [the author] extends by analogy the rules for the sprinkling (*abhighāra*), the joining (*sandhāna*), and the unification (*ekīkaraṇa*) [of the breaths], starting with the words "(tadanu)" (thereafter). (Abhighāram) means "kindling" (*dīpana*).

Likewise, in the venerable *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*, the "sprinkling of the mouth" (*vaktrābhighāra*) is described as the "illumination of the mouths. Alternatively, what is called "sprinkling" (*abhidhāra*) is the offering of individual oblations (*āhuti*) to each of those mouths; while what is called "joining" (*sandhāna*) is by means of a collective recitation.
The offering of a single oblation to the two faces is called the "unification of the faces.
This consists of an uninterrupted stream of ghee-oblations, proceeding from Agni to Vāyu, then from Nirṛti to Īśāna, by means of a single utterance of the five faces.

Having visualized the inclusion of all the remaining faces within the mouth of each respective desired face, one should visualize the upward-facing mouth as having the dimensions of the sacrificial pit with its mouth wide open.
And it is said: "The sprinkling of the fires' mouths and the meditation on their unification of faces [should be performed];
one should offer clarified butter into the western mouth of the fire-eater with the Sadyojāta mantra."
Having offered oblations with the left [hand] into the north-facing [mouth] by means of Bahurūpin,
and with the male [deity] into the east-facing [mouth], and with the Īśāna mantra into the upward-facing [mouth].
p. 448) With each individual oblation of clarified butter, or with three, the sprinkling is performed;
the joining of the faces is described as being like five oblations of clarified butter.
One should offer clarified butter into the mouths of the two [deities] Ajā and Vāmā using the *sruva* ladle;
one should likewise offer clarified butter into the pair of mouths of the two [deities] Vāma and Aghora.
One should offer clarified butter into the two faces of Ghoratattva and Puruṣa;
one should offer clarified butter into the two faces of Puruṣa and Īśa.
And one should offer clarified butter into the mouth of Aiśa, which is the designator of Śiva;
it is considered that there should be either one oblation at the junction of the mouths, or three.
The union of faces has been described, and now the unification of the mouths is explained:
one should pour a stream of clarified butter from the five faces, beginning with Sadyojāta.
Starting from the southeast corner and extending to the northwest corner;
and starting from the southwest corner and extending to the northeast corner.
"One should effect the unification of the mouth with an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter.
In this interval, as an incidental point, [the rite is performed] by the offering of each individual oblation.
"One should perform the 'kindling of the tongue' (jihvādīpana)," so said some who take pleasure in detail; thus it was stated by the illustrious commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*.

He states the purificatory rite of naming for Agni with the word "tataḥ" (then). The intended meaning here is that Agni has been rendered pure by these five purificatory rites beginning with *garbhadhāna* according to the Pārameśvara [Tantra]; otherwise, the invocation of Śiva and so forth would be untenable.
Likewise, in the venerable Sarvajñānottara it is said:
"How could one who is not Śiva ever perform the rites of Śiva?
For that purpose, Śiva must be diligently established as the sacrificial fire."
The procedure for the rites to be performed immediately following the sacraments beginning with conception (garbhādhāna).

(23) Having worshipped Vāgīśī and Vāgīśa with the heart-mantra, having dismissed them, and having fashioned the mouth of the fire-pit according to the desired measurement, for the sake of completing the consecrations up to the crest-jewel on the central tongue—
One should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
For example, having filled the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) with clarified butter, [one should hold it] face-down over the *puṣkara* [of the *sruc*].
Having turned the *sruva* ladle face down and having placed a flower at its tip, one should take hold of those two [ends] with the left and right hands joined like a conch shell, and then,
with the right hand again, grasp them firmly together.
Having taken [the vessel], rising with both feet together— [having risen straight up with his body from the navel]— with his body raised upward from the navel, extending it horizontally,
fixing his gaze on the tip of the sacrificial ladle, he should recite the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Having brought [the ladle] from the base of the left breast to the root of the *sruva* [ladle], one should pour the entire clarified butter into the fire with a steady stream the measure of a barley grain. Having thus performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sit down. (95)

Now, having described the ritual procedure for the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, [the author] sets forth those rites to be performed immediately thereafter, starting from the words "with the heart" (*hṛdayena*) and ending with "having sat down" (*upaviśya*).
Regarding the word "having dismissed" (*visṛjya*): here, according to the scripture, one should satisfy the Goddess and then withdraw her.
Some say that one should dismiss [the deities] immediately after the offering of oblations. (The measurement of the sacrificial pit) refers to the dimensions of the pit.
(As desired) means according to one's wish. In this context—
Just as with the unification of the Īśāna face, so too for the other faces: the oblation is for the Mūrti in the Īśāna face, while *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis] are in the Puruṣa face;
likewise, expiation and the like are in the Ghora face, as they are in the performance of cruel rites.
For the purpose of the fire-sacrifice (homa) for subjugation and attraction, one should perform the oblation with the Vāmadeva mantra;
this daily ritual procedure is beneficial at this western face.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Śrīmad-Bṛhat-Kālottara*, the intended meaning is that one should conceive of the unity of the faces with one another in accordance with the specific ritual action (*kṛtya*). Alternatively: "Having meditated upon the five faces of the Fire-god, by whichever [face] whatever rite is desired..."
One should turn its face upward, and in that position, the face should be directed upwards.
"Having internalized the other faces, that [central face] is of the same measure as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Having understood this statement, one should contemplate the internalization of the other faces within the Īśāna face, and thus consider that the bestowal of the fruits of those respective faces occurs through the Īśāna face.

Because the scripture states that "she alone, by virtue of her manifold forms, bestows the fruits of all desires," it is established that she holds primacy upon the tongue of Īśāna, which is known as Bahurūpā.

In that very context, he extends the rule for the *pūrṇāhuti* offering by saying "(in the middle)" (*madhya*), meaning "on the middle tongue" (*madhyajihvāyām*). This refers to the tongue of Īśāna, which is designated as *bahurūpā*.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā,
the exceedingly red Jihvā of Agni, and Bahurūpā as the seventh;
[these are located] in the directions of Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara.
The six tongues, beginning with Hiraṇyā, are specified in their successive order.
"But from the middle, the multiformed [channel] goes toward the south and north.
To the question "For what purpose is the taking of the full [measure]? he says:
"(In order to complete the purificatory rites ending with the topknot)."
"Cūḍānta" refers to that which has the *cūḍā*—the ritual of the top-knot (*śikhā*)—at its end; "saṃskāra" is the rite itself.
For the sake of completing, that is, fulfilling, that [series] of rites. In this context... [p. 453]
Since the five sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and ending with *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving) have been performed,
it should be understood that [the remaining rites] from *niṣkrāmaṇa* (the first outing) up to *cūḍā* (tonsure) follow. Thus,
in the venerable *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
For the complete accomplishment of all the consecratory rites (saṃskāras), one should subsequently cause the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be offered;
as well as the rite of emergence from the womb (niṣkrāmaṇa), the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), and the binding of the sacred thread (vratabandhana).
"The account from the *cūḍā* ceremony up to the *godāna* was performed by Pūrṇā.
Now, since it was stated that "one should give the *pūrṇā*," one might ask how that is done; therefore, he says: "(tadyathā)" [as follows].

"(Sarpiṣā)" means with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). According to Amara: "Clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sacrificial oil (*ājya*), oblation (*havis*), and *sarpiḥ* [are synonyms]. "(Puṣkaropari)" [means] upon a lotus leaf.

Above the *puṣkara*, which is the lotus serving as the support for the clarified butter (*ājya*). As the venerable author of the *Mṛgendravṛtti* stated regarding the procedure for the *puṣkara*: "In this rite of the *puṣkara*, everything should be prepared up to the lotus that serves as the support for the clarified butter. (Following that,) at the tips of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

(As with the conch: "Equal to a conch. This characteristic has been stated in the description of the *mudrās* regarding the two ends—the base and the tip—of the handles of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles (p.

The *śaṅkha-mudrā* should be formed by supporting oneself with the left and right hands at the moment of completion. (*Tau*) refers to the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles. (*Ūrdhvakāyaḥ*) means with the body, head, and neck held straight.
(*Anidvignaḥ*) means undisturbed; or, it may mean one who possesses internal meditative cultivation (*antarbhāvanā*). Likewise...

"Having held [the vessel] with the right hand according to the *Śrīrāmanāthapaddhati*, and subsequently with the left hand, standing with body, head, and neck erect through internal contemplation— [one should] cast [it]. (One should cast it.)
The meaning is "he should cause to fall."
The sequence of the fire-vessel.

(20) Having divided the firewood for the purpose of chewing and so forth, and having preserved it in another place, one should offer fuel-sticks sixteen finger-breadths long with the vowels beginning with *ā* for the nourishment of the Śiva-fire.
One should offer oblations of *palāśa* wood [with the mantras beginning with] "śivāgre rāpyāya... and so forth.

(96) Now, with the passage beginning with "caru" and ending with "juhuyāt," he explains the sequence for honoring the fire prior to the invocation of Śiva for the purpose of cooking the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and other rites.
"Caru and so forth. By the word "and so forth," incense and other offerings are meant. This has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Of incense, lamps, and caru...

(272) And when this has been done, one should draw forth the fire. For the sake of nourishment and growth, [one should do so] with the vowels—meaning with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*.
Likewise, it is stated in the venerable Vātulaśuddha: "These sixteen indeed begin with *a* and end with the *visarga*."
Regarding the words "the vowels" and "the fuel": this characteristic has been stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"The fuel-sticks, however, should be uncracked, straight, with their bark intact, and sixteen finger-breadths long. Here, in the fire of Śiva, which has been consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) but in which Śiva has not yet been invoked;
Regarding "the sacrificial pap (caru), speech," and so forth: the intended meaning is that the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed once Śiva has been invoked.

Likewise, it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara: "The sacrificial pap and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) should be offered into one who has been consecrated by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras)."
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in a fire where Śiva has been invoked, not in one where Śiva has not been summoned.
Thus [it is said].
The method for praying to the Śiva-fire.
(22) Seated upon a white lotus throne, four-faced and four-armed,
with a long beard, the form of Brahmā, his crest adorned with matted locks.
His lotus-like hands are occupied with the *sruk*, the *maṇḍalu*, the staff,
and the rosary; or else he is endowed with arms, being three-eyed, red-complexioned, and possessing the weapons of Śiva along with that staff.
Having thus meditated upon Agni:
"O Agni, since you are the sovereign splendor and the supreme purifier, therefore,
having established you within the lotus of my heart, I satisfy you."
I shall satisfy him.
Having thus requested the command;

(97) (pra) now, preceded by the description of the meditation on the Śiva-fire, he explains the manner of requesting for the invocation of Śiva with the passage beginning with "white" (sita) and ending with "having requested" (prārthya).
The meaning of the verse regarding meditation is clear. "(O Agni)" is the address. "Tejas" means vigor.
According to the *Nānārtharatnamālā*, "tejas" [denotes] strength, majesty, fire, the radiance of the sun, and semen.
"(Him)" refers to Śiva. "(I satiate)" means I offer oblations. The rest is self-evident.
p. 457) The procedure for the fire-oblation preceded by the worship of Śiva in the fire.

(22) Immediately thereafter, having entered the central channel of the body of fire, one should worship, as before, the radiant Blessed One together with his throne and retinue within the heart-lotus of that [fire-body].
Having offered incense and lamps,

and having performed the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire, one emerges; then, having uttered the root mantra, [one offers] the crest of light in the form of a flame that has issued from the nostril of Śiva residing within the fire.
One should meditate on that which has taken its seat in both places— [the Śiva residing in the sacrificial fire] and the Śiva absorbed in the crest of the sacrificial Śiva— [whose form is light,

delimited by the application of the mere rays of the sacrificial crest, and undelimited by the separation from the rays absorbed in the crest of the crest]. One should meditate on it as established in both locations.

Thus, having performed the union of the channels together with the jar, the sacrifice, the fire, Śiva, and the self (ātman), and having offered the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the purpose of satiating the mantras, as well as the Brahma-aṅgas ten times that amount, one should proceed.
Having offered the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) and likewise performed the special propitiation (tarpaṇa),
one should [proceed] with the root mantra for the purpose of averting ill omens, bringing about auspicious omens, and ensuring the attainment of the desired place and time.

Having offered four hundred [oblations according to one's capacity], and having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) together with the root mantra for the sake of purification, one should offer a hundred [more] full oblations. Then—
One should perform the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) and the kindling (*dīpana*) of the mantras. Having performed the satiation with the mantra "Oṃ Hoṃ, to the head of Īśāna, svāhā," one should offer a lamp.
Then, with each successive oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta-āhuti*), beginning with "Oṃ Hoṃ, to Īśāna... and so forth.

The libation (*tarpaṇa*): *oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ [hrāṃ] īśāna-mūrddhāya huṃ phaṭ*, etc.; by means of these three oblations (*tryāhuti*), the illumination [of the fire] is performed. (98) (Pra) Now, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*) and other rites, one performs the worship of Śiva in the fire.

He first states the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the words beginning with "immediately after" and ending with "illumination. Regarding "(having entered)": the meaning is that one should recollect oneself as having entered.
"(In his heart-lotus)" means in the lotus-heart of Śiva’s fire. "(The Blessed One)": *bhaga*... [is] power (*aiśvarya*).
The Blessed One (Bhagavān) is he who possesses qualities such as sovereignty; in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa it is said:
"Sovereignty in its entirety, heroism, fame, fortune, knowledge, and dispassion—these six are declared to be 'bhaga'."

Thus it is stated in the Śruti. Here, having worshipped Śiva in the Śivāgni—from the worship of the Ādhāraśakti and other ancillaries of enjoyment up to the end of the ritual—during the occasion of the food offering (naivedya), one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa). As it has been taught:
First, having performed the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*), one should then worship Śiva as before within the heart-lotus of the fire.

At the time of the food offering (*naivedya*), having offered oblations according to one's capacity with sesame seeds and other materials using the root mantra and the Brahma-aṅga mantras for a tenth part [of the total], and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the food offering. Thus it is said.

And he will state [this] after describing the entire procedure for the fire-oblation up to its conclusion: "Immediately thereafter, having offered the food offering, water for sipping, sandalwood paste, betel, and so forth...
[referring to the mouths of Śiva and the fire].
The meaning is: [the fire] of Śiva and the upward-facing fire.

Likewise, in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*: "Having entered through the channel that fire of Śiva produced from Vāgīśī—which is stainless—one should worship the Supreme Śiva within its own heart as before."

"Having emerged with the face turned upward" and "well-joined with the upward-facing fire" refer to the sequence of the union of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*) of Śiva residing in the jar, on the sacrificial ground, and in the fire, as well as that of the Guru.
The phrase "(in both cases)" means [the union] of the two Śivas residing in the fire and established in the sacrifice.

460) He extends the stated principle to other cases as well with the word "thus" (*evam*). Regarding the phrase "together with the self" (*ātmanā saha*), the intended meaning here is that one should perform the connection of one's own channels (*nāḍī*) by means of the *kuṃbha*, *yāga*, *agni*, and *śiva* rites.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhati*:
"One should perform the conjunction of one's own channels with [the numbers] nine, four, three, and eleven.
He states the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*) (for the purpose of satiating the mantras): "(By a tenth part of that)"—of that.
"By a tenth part of the root mantra" means one [offering] for every ten [recitations].
The intended meaning here is that, in relation to the primary Śiva-mantra, this constitutes the "prescribed oblation" (kalpahoma) for the Brahmā-aṅga mantras which serve as its limbs.
As it is stated in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "One should perform oblations to the extent of one-tenth," and "having offered the limbs of Brahmā.

In this context, regarding the ritual application of Brahmā and the lords beginning with Īśāna, one should first utter the *praṇava* (OM), and subsequently utter their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).

The teachers maintain that one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) after reciting the mantras found in the middle of the *vyomavyāpin* section, beginning with "To the West," "To Īśāna," "To the Head," and so forth.
Likewise, it has been stated by the venerable Śrī Somaśambhu: "Then one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the words of the Brahma-seeds.
[This is] for the purpose of averting ill-omens regarding place, time, and action, and for securing auspicious omens.

The "bringing about of place" (*deśāpādana*) consists of the conceptualization of [the soul] as being within one or another of the five or eight fields (*kṣetra*); and the "bringing about of time" (*kālāpādana*) is the accomplishment of internal time in accordance with the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus it has been stated by the commentator on the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.

The pacification of ill omens, the removal of the defects of ill omens occurring in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, the production of auspicious omens, and likewise the accomplishment of such auspicious omens— as it is stated in the illustrious *Kālottara*:
When gods are seen in celestial palaces, that is always considered to be auspicious;
and when various flowers fall from the sky.
A rainbow is auspicious for men, especially when accompanied by gentle rain;
or if there is a shower of falling dust, that indeed is a bird-omen in the sky.
The sweet warbling of peacocks, swans, parrots, and other such birds is desired;
likewise, the falling of rain from the conjunction with the rays of the sun is auspicious.
The auspicious sound of conchs, kettledrums, clouds, and lutes,
as well as the sight of teachers, Brahmins, women, and kings.
Likewise, the sight of elephants and horses is highly commended;
it is auspicious to see donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and serpents for one observing a vow.
Speech that is praised is commendable when the path is not sought by the wicked;
