sudden quarreling is undesirable, as is a harsh sound arising from negligence.
Likewise, seeing virtuous people who resemble palaces or trees is auspicious for sacrificial rites; however, it is so for the building of a house only when the matter is auspicious, not otherwise.
"One hundred oblations are to be offered with the Aghora mantra.

This refers to the cause of those [rites], namely: the pacification of ill omens arising from place, time, or action, and the attainment of auspicious omens. He describes the sequence for performing the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the lamp-offering (*dīpa*) with the word "Then" (*tataḥ*).
The cooking of the sacrificial oblation (caru).
(23) Having prepared the *caru* oblation according to the rules;

(99) now, having described the worship of Śiva and the sequence of the *homa* sacrifice, one might wonder what should be done immediately thereafter; anticipating this doubt, [the author] states "having prepared" (*kṛtvā*) by means of the passage beginning with "according to the rules" (*vidhivat*), [instructing that] one should cook the *caru*.
Up to this point; here, regarding the preparation of the *caru*, what is to be done should be understood as it will be explained in the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
The performance of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the day [of the rite] for the purifiers (pavitra).

(24) Then, having taken up the purifiers (*pavitra*) placed in pure vessels, having brought them near the fire, and having set them down upon a *maṇḍala* with the seat of the *praṇava* made of *darbha* grass in the western part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
one should sprinkle them with the *astra-mantra*. Upon the nine threads, [one should contemplate] the *praṇava*, the moon, and the fire.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in sequence upon the knots with their respective names in the dative case, preceded by the *praṇava* and joined with a salutation— namely Brahmā, Nāga, Guha, Ravi, Sādākhya, and all the gods— one should place *prakṛti* upon the knots.
Pauruṣī, Vīrā, Aparājitā, Jayā, Vijayā, and Ajitā.
One should install (or worship) Sadāśivā, Manonmanī, and Sarvatomukhī as before, each by its own name.
One should place the sixteen digits (kalās) of Śiva and Śakti upon the *tattvapavitraka* [the two purifiers], which is the descent of the Gaṅgā.
Having placed the four mandalas together with their presiding deities upon the four purifiers (pavitra), and having worshipped them and consecrated them with the Saṃhitā-mantra,
one should cover them with a black antelope skin and other materials for the duration of a year.
Meditating upon Śiva— the witness of all actions, the imperishable, the protector, the refuge,

and the cause for the attainment of the fruits of karma— and having performed twenty-one oblations with the *saṃpāta* method using the mantra-collection (*mantra-saṃhitā*), one should protect [the site] with the *astra-mantra*.
Having enveloped [the objects] with the Kavaca mantra and rendered them immortal with the Amṛtīkaraṇa mantra, one should place them near the water-pot.

(200) Now, [the author] describes what is to be done on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the *pavitra* threads, beginning with the words "Then the *pavitra*s" and ending with "one should place."
He states the sequence for the placement of the tutelary deities of the sūtras with the words “in the nine-fold threads” (*tantunavakeṣu*).
This means: upon the threads that have been tripled three times, which constitute the purifiers (*pavitra*).
Thus it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:

"That which is woven by brahmin maidens is tripled and then tripled again. The word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of what has been mentioned [with the following]. (This is to be done) with the *praṇava* and the salutation (*namaskāra*).

The *praṇava* and the salutation (*namaskāra*), namely the word "namaḥ"— that which is joined with these two [is the mantra]. (275) That which has the dative case at its end— that is, that whose final member is the fourth case ending— is described as such.

By him—by one whose name begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and *candra* (Hāṃ), etc. Here, it should be understood that [the mantras] begin with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the *Praṇava*," and so forth. He states the sequence for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the presiding deities of the ten knots located on the *tattva-pavitraka* (sacred thread) with the words "in the knots" (*granthiṣu*). [This is to be done] "as before" (*pūrvavat*).

The meaning is: [the mantra] joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and *namaskāra* (namaḥ), ending in the dative case; [this is done] by means of one's own respective name (*svasvanāmnā*) according to its original designation (*prakṛtyādisaṃjñayā*). He describes the method for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities presiding over the eighteen knots of the purifier (*pavitra*) at Gaṅgāvatāraka, saying: "at Gaṅgāvatāraka."
The meaning is "at the knots of the Gaṅgā-avatāra.
(Dviraṣṭakakalāḥ) refers to the sixteen kalās contained within the Prāsāda mantra. Here...

Some maintain that the *prāsādakalās* should be deposited together with Śiva and Śakti; others hold that the *śaśinī* and the rest should be deposited along with those two. As it is said: "Śaśinī, Śākhinī, Lakṣmī, Kāminī, and Prabhā likewise."
Puṣpiṇī, Puṣṭibhāvā, Āmudā, and likewise Kumudā.
Āśāsī, Śāyinī, Vidyā, Mohinī, Pramohinī, Vitaklinī, Saumyā, Amṛtā, and the sixteenth digit, Kalā.
Thus it was stated by the illustrious commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*:
"(The four mandalas)" refers to the tetrad beginning with the solar mandala; "(consisting of the year)" means from the day of the *pavitrāropaṇa* rite until today, for the duration of one year.

He whose body is that Time, which consists of the year, as its locus to be presided over—[that is,] him who is the witness of all actions (*sarvakṛtyasākṣiṇam*), meaning all annual rites and every action throughout the year.

The witness of them is the observer; (an indeclinable) *akṣīṇam* means undecaying. Thus, "undecaying and imperishable" means complete. (The protector) means the guardian of the fruits of all actions. (Twenty-one times).
The meaning is "twenty-one times. Regarding the phrase "(offered with the remnants)":
he will explain this definition in the section on the preparation of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) within the ritual procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), stating:
"With the *Saṃhitā* [formula] 'svāhā' in the fire, shaking the *sruva* ladle over the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) above the person to be consecrated."
"One should cause to fall."
The preliminary ritual procedure for the offering of the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka).

(25) Then, having offered the *caru* oblation to Śiva-Sūrya, and having honored the door-keepers, Gaṇapati, and the Guru with the sacred thread (*pavitreṇa*), one should fumigate the fragrant *pavitra* together with sandalwood paste, flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), while reciting: *Oṃ*.

Having recited the invocation distinguished by the solar names beginning with "Samasta," and having offered [the oblation] with that root mantra ending in *svāhā*, [one should offer it] also to its limbs and to the planets.
Having offered [the oblations] with their respective mantras ending in *svāhā*, having rendered them supreme (*paramīkṛtya*), having performed the recitation (*japan*) and the offering (*nivedya*),

having prostrated (*namaskṛtya*) and sipped water for purification (*ācamya*), and having performed the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), [he approaches] the sacrificial hall and so forth.

Having encircled the ritual implements for worship and so forth with the *kavaca* mantra and thread, one should offer the *pavitraka* in sequence to the gatekeepers, the local deities (*vāstunātha*), and Lakṣmī, and then to Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*) together with their weapons.

One should offer incense and the sacred thread (*pavitra*) with the respective mantras for each [deity], ending with *svāhā*. Then, having recited the verse beginning with "tatassamasta... and ending with *svāhā*, one should first offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) to the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*), the weapon-pitcher (*astravardhanī*), and the [other] pitchers using the Śiva-mantra.
Having placed the fragrant *pavitra* [sacred thread], having recited the mantra and offered the oblation, and having worshipped Gaṇapati— [in the form of the Lord of the Ganas]—
and the gurus with the *pavitra*, one should approach the vicinity of the mandala,
offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and, preceded by the invocation mantra, present the fragrant *pavitra*.
One should offer [the recitation], having performed the recitation preceded by the rite of supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa), and having offered it, one should ask for forgiveness.

Now, having described the procedure for preparing the purifiers (*pavitra*), [the author] states the preliminary rites to be performed prior to the offering of the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitra*) to the Deity, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "having asked for forgiveness" (*kṣamāpya*).

469) Regarding that, he first describes the offering of the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitra*) to the Sun: "(To Śiva-Sūrya)" and "(the fragrant purifier). The characteristics of this have been stated previously and indicated; and he will state them [again] later.

"One with a single knot and few threads" refers to the mantra beginning with "Oṃ samasta... and so forth. The meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) will be explained later. Regarding the phrase "distinguished by the name of Sūrya," here, instead of the word *śambhu* in the expression "O Śambhu, in every way, at all times," one should substitute [the name] as follows: "O Sūrya, in every way, at all times, obeisance to you," and so on.

One should recite [the mantra]. (By its root: by the root-mantra of the Sun. (By their respective mantras: by the heart-mantras and so forth, and the mantras of Soma and so forth. He explains the encircling with threads of the sacrificial pavilion and other such areas, [beginning] with the words: "Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite."
"Such as the sacrificial hall (*yāgadhāma*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the location of the bull (*vṛṣabhasthāna*) and others are indicated.
This has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Due to reliance upon the sacrificial hall, the location of the bull, the temple (*prāsāda*), and the fire..."
"One should wrap the *kārakaupya* with thread and armor. Thus it is said. (p.
470) Regarding the offering of fragrant purifiers (*gandhapavitra*) for the doors and so forth, he says: "The door... and so on.

Regarding the offering of scented threads (*gandhapavitra*) to the guardians of the directions, it says "(Indrādi)". Regarding the offering of threads to the *śivakalaśa* and the *vardhanī*, it says "(Śivakuṃbha)". Regarding the offering of threads to Gaṇapati and the Gurus, it says "(Gaṇapati)".

"Having worshipped with the *pavitra*," it is said. Here, after the worship with the *pavitra*, one should pray, "By your command, may this rite be free from obstacles," and say the same to the lineage gurus (*paṅktiguravaḥ*).
He describes the offering of the *pavitra* to the Lord of the Maṇḍala with the word "Maṇḍala."

(Prefaced by the invocation mantra: "Prefaced by the invocation mantra" means that which has the mantra beginning with *oṃ samasta* and so forth, in the form of a verse (*kārikā*), as its preceding part; thus it is described. "(Having asked for forgiveness)" means having requested that [any faults] be forgiven.
The procedure for the offering of substances as part of the observance and enjoyment of Śiva’s vow.
(26) Having gone into the presence of the deity, sat down upon one's own seat, and performed worship, one should offer the preliminary components of the vow-practice.
In that regard, one should take a tooth-stick with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra in the east; ashes with the *aghora* mantra in the south; clay with the *sadyojāta* mantra in the west;
the fruit-water of the *dhātrī* tree with the *vāmadeva* mantra in the north; and [the water of the *agasti* flower] in the northeast.
[With the Īśāna-mantra] water with fruit, or water with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the Īśāna-mantra;
again, at that very spot, flowers with the Mūla-mantra or the Śiras-mantra;
yellow orpiment in the southeast with the Hṛdaya-mantra; and agarwood in the southwest.
Having brought the excellent sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron from the southwest (Nairṛta) or to the crest (Śikhā),
or having offered the remaining honorable common substances with the Armor (Kavaca) mantra, [he should offer them] in the west with the Sadyojāta mantra.

The materials for the fire sacrifice (homa) include *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth; the physical requisites consist of a staff, a rosary, a loincloth, and an alms-bowl; the components of the vow (*vrata*) are collyrium, saffron, oil, a probe, and hair-cleansing powder, all kept on the right side.
One should offer betel, a mirror, yellow pigment (rocanā), and so forth with the Vāmadeva mantra in the north;
the seat, sandals, vessel, meditation belt, and parasol with the Īśāna mantra in the northeast; and the sacrificial porridge (caru) and clarified butter in the northeast.
With the *dukampātra* and the *tapa* vessel, one should offer perfumes and so forth to the northeast (as on page 472), and food and so forth to the east. One should present these offerings.
Whatever among these is incomplete, one should mentally visualize it as perfected.

(202) Next, having described the sequence for offering perfumes and sacred threads (*pavitra*) to the pavilion and so forth, as well as to the deities presiding over the pavilion’s enclosure, [the text proceeds to describe] the substances for Śiva’s observance (*vrata*) and the ritual enjoyments (*bhoga*).
He extends the rule for the offering by means of the passage beginning with "O God" and ending with "one should arrange.

Regarding the phrase "the ancillaries of the practice of the vow and so forth": "vow-practice" refers to the performance of the vow; that which has this as its beginning is described thus, and its ancillaries are the implements such as the tooth-stick and so on. How?
Regarding the instruction "one should offer," he says: "(In that regard). This means: in those ancillaries such as the practice of the vow (*vratacaryā*).
"(The water of *dhātrī* fruit)" refers to both the *dhātrī* fruit and the water. Regarding "(or water in the northeast)":
here one should understand the distinction of location and the distinction of mantra. Thus it has been taught.
The venerable Somaśambhu’s feet have stated:
"In the northern [direction] of the God of gods, one should offer an āmalakī fruit;
and water for purification should be offered with the Vāmadeva mantra, or even upon the head."
"In the northeast, [one should offer] water with the Īśa mantra or the root mantra.
[This refers to] the Aghora mantra [for the form]. "[The offering of] perfume and so forth" [is performed in this manner].
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the rubbing of the hands, mouth-fresheners, and so forth are indicated.

[This refers to] the collection of materials useful for the observances (vrata), such as the tooth-stick, earth, ashes, water, products of the cow (gavya), substances for the fire-oblation (homa-dravya), the staff, and the rosary.

That which is to be given for the increase of the vow should be offered as an auxiliary to the vow; thus has it been determined by the illustrious commentator on the *Somaśambhupaddhati*. Now, raising the objection, "How is this to be done in the absence of substances such as saffron and the like?", he says that one should deposit that [substitute].

Furthermore, keeping in mind the venerable *Mṛgendra-śruti* which states, "once again, everything according to the extent of one's mental capacity," he says "(whatever is not available)" to indicate that one should offer whatever can be obtained.
The procedure for the offering of the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitrāropaṇakrama).
(27) Thereafter, having worshipped the deity with the eightfold offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),
one should then [offer] the portion for Śiva from the sacrificial food (*caru*), which has been consecrated with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) and enveloped by the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*).

Having worshipped with the heart-mantra (the *hrāṃ* mantra) and consecrated it as nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*), one should offer it to the Blessed One; then, as in the daily rite, having given the sacred thread (*pavitra*) to the gatekeepers, to oneself, and to Gaṇapati, Lakṣmī, and the lineage of gurus, one should afterwards offer it to Śiva.
Having offered it to the seat of Śiva,

and having taken in his joined palms the *āmantraṇa-pavitraka*— which has been perfumed with scents and the like, consists of a single knot and few threads, is fumigated with incense, and is accompanied by flowers— [he holds it].
One should recite the mantra consisting of an address, [the mantra consisting of words of excellent flowers and good counsel].
O Lord who fulfills all deficiencies in the ritual procedures regarding this sacrifice, I, whose every action is accomplished through your will, invoke you.
Grant success to that which I am sacrificing for in the realms of both the conscious and the unconscious; O Śambhu, may there be salutation to You in every way and at all times—be gracious unto me.
Or rather, O Lord of Gods, you were addressed by Sahadevī, accompanied by the lords of the Gaṇas,
the lords of mantras, the guardians of the worlds, and your retinues.
(475) "I announce to you that at dawn I shall offer the *pavitraka* and perform the ritual observance (*niyama*) by your command, O Supreme Lord."

If the consecration (*adhivāsa*) is performed immediately, one should recite "the purifier (*pavitraka*) at this very moment. Having thus addressed it, having rendered it nectar-like through exhalation (*recaka*), having uttered the root mantra up to its dissolution, having offered it to Śiva, and having offered (or recited) it for the limbs of Brahmā—
Having gratified the deity with incense, lamps, and other offerings, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) with the root mantra,
and having performed the *amṛtamudrā* and the *mahāmudrā*;
(203) [then], having proclaimed the manner of offering the preliminary components such as the observance of vows (*vratacaryā*), [one should offer] the cord to the deity.

"Having done so, one should dye it; with effort one should bind it, and with a cord one should tie knots—thus the experts know regarding the *ru* [deer-skin]," thus he clarifies the sequence for the offering of the fragrant *pavitra* with the passage beginning with "(thereafter, the deity)" and ending with "having performed. Regarding the term "(scented with fragrance)": here, by the word "fragrance" (*gandha*),...
Black agallochum and camphor are indicated. Likewise, in the venerable *Raurava*:
"Black agallochum, camphor, musk, fresh butter, nutmeg, *ghoṣa*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, and the three fruits."
Cardamom, cloves, black pepper, *ghātra*, and likewise *gorocanā*—
these are declared to be the fragrant substances (*gandhadravya*). Now, the coloring substances (*rañjanadravya*) are described.
Red ochre, the mark of caste, saffron, and likewise yellow pigment (rocanā),
combined with red sandalwood and mixed with camphor;
as well as realgar, turmeric, madder, and the wooden spoon.
It is declared that "the dyeing substance" is that which dyes the purifying thread (*pavitraka*) with a triple-stranded cord. Likewise, in the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara*:
Murā, vāṃśī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of rajanī,
musalī, and musta are known as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhigaṇa).

"Having fewer threads" means having fewer threads than the number appropriate for the specific ritual occasion according to the sacred tradition. "Consisting of words of address": here, the word *pada* denotes a characteristic mark (*lakṣma*). As Amara-datta says: "A *pada*..."
"In the objects that are the feet, characterized by the state of being established as a refuge"—this means that a mantra consists of a collection of sentences that indicate an address.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "The wise one should recite the supreme mantra consisting of the vocative form.
Now, having raised the doubt as to how it is that he should recite the vocative mantra, [the author says:]
He clarifies that mantra with "Oṃ samasta... and so forth. "Oṃ" is for the purpose of illuminating the mantra.

"(Samastavidhivicchidrapūraṇeśa)"—all rites (*samastavidhayaḥ*) were previously explained as being manifold due to the distinctions among their respective substrata, such as one's own form (*nijamūrti*) and so on.

All the modes of worship, including their primary and secondary limbs, which are divided into the categories of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*), and were performed prior to the time of the *pavitrārohaṇa*—
their deficiencies [are to be remedied] by means of obstacles.

Capable of fulfilling them—that is, capable of completing those [deficiencies] which will be described as having the characteristics of being incomplete, such as the *karaṇas*, and being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), etc. (To Makha: Regarding the sacrifice to Śiva;
(O Lord,) O Master; (the fulfiller of your desires); yours.
Having obtained the necessary implements through knowledge, I address [you]; I request permission to receive this special worship. As for that which is heard as the invocation:

"Daily, for the sake of proximity, worship, and authorization"—this refers to the accomplishment (*tatsiddhi*) of the fruit of the ritual known as the *pavitraka*. The remainder is easy to understand. [The term] *āmantraṇa*...
He states another method with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). Regarding the term "restriction" (*niyamam*): it refers to the restriction of the limit of the vow (*vratāvadherniyamam*).
The rest is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "having thus addressed" (*evamāmantrya*): the meaning is "having awakened [the deity] in this manner.
Regarding the phrase "having rendered nectar-like by means of *recaka*" (*recakeṇāmṛtīkṛtya*): here, one should render the *pavitra* held in the joined palms (*añjali*) into nectar.
The essential meaning [is as follows]. It has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Having thus addressed the Lord and rendered [the offering] immortal through the exhaling breath (*recaka*), one should recite the root mantra up to the syllable *Śiva* and present it to Śiva."
Thus [it is said]. "Up to the limit of dissolution" means up to the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space above the head).
The ritual procedure to be performed immediately after the offering of the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitrāropaṇa).
Having recited [the mantra], having offered [the oblation], and having recited and offered one-tenth of the limbs of Brahmā, one should circumambulate and prostrate with the eight limbs.

Now, having illustrated the method for offering fragrant purifiers (*gandhapavitra*) to the deity, [the author] describes the rites to be performed immediately thereafter, beginning with the words "having recited" (*japtvā*) and ending with "he should prostrate" (*praṇamet*).
p.
479) The ritual activity for the sake of Śiva has fire as its locus.

(29) Then, having offered a third portion of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to the Blessed One residing in the fire, having performed the purification with the mantra, having given [the remainder] to the limbs of Brahmā, having asked for forgiveness, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of expiation—

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, having presented the food offering (*naivedya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), sandalwood paste, betel leaves, and so forth, and having paid homage to the ashes, one should offer the *nirodhārghya* (the final offering of cessation).
[Having offered the new water for sipping, betel leaves, and so forth, one should offer the *nirodha-*]... having given [the *nirodhārghya*],...
Having restrained Śiva with the *niṣṭhuya* [or *niṣṭhurayā*] mantra, having performed the *vyāhṛti-homa*, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, and having likewise restrained the fire; (205)

Now, regarding the section on the installation of the fire (*agnyādhikaraṇa*), he describes that ritual action with the words beginning with "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "having restrained" (*niruddhya*). [The phrase] "having offered the third part of the sacrificial porridge" (*caros tṛtīyāṃśaṃ hutvā*) indicates the following sequence of performance: having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) according to the prescribed rules...

"Purified by the *saṃpātāhuti* offering, one should divide that [oblation] threefold with the *darvī* ladle according to the distinction between the deity, the fire, and oneself. Having given two portions to Śiva and the fire while protecting the portion for oneself," so it is heard in the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.
One should divide the *caru* into three parts for the sake of the gods, the fire, and the self; immediately thereafter, one should divide the portion assigned to Śiva into five parts.
Having offered [the oblation] to Śiva— who resides in the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the *karkarī* vessel, the maṇḍala, one’s own chosen *liṅga*, or the substratum—

the remainder is to be presented at the time of the observance (*vrata*) that constitutes a limb of the ritual. Likewise, having divided the portion intended for the fire into four parts, one part is for the presentation.
After making the offering immediately following the *caru*-offering, one should give the second *antarbali*;
then, having made the third offering into the fire at the time of the *pavitrāropaṇa* and having given that as well, the fourth *bali* should be offered.
Likewise, having divided one's own portion according to the number of oneself and the disciples, [one should consume it] together with them at the conclusion of the rite.
"It is to be consumed."
The performance of the bali offering.

(30) Having offered the *caru* oblation to those who eat the inner offerings— namely Brahmā and the others, Indra and the others, and Rudra and the others who eat the outer offerings— along with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*), he should offer it together with the *pavitra* blades.
Now, the procedure for the bali offering, beginning with "the enclosure" (*paridhi*) and ending with "having given" (*datvā*).
The procedure for the internal and external bali offerings has been shown previously.
The procedure for what is to be done immediately after the performance of the bali offering.

(32) Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), performed hymns of praise and veneration (*stotra-vandana*), completed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and fully worshipped both the deity residing in the mandala and that which remains from the previously offered rites; ||
Next, he describes the duties to be performed immediately thereafter, starting with the words "having sipped water" (*samācamya*) and ending with "having worshipped" (*saṃpūjya*).
The Sanskrit Purification and Protection Ritual.

(32) Having consecrated a vessel made of purified bamboo or other materials by placing the *astra*, *kavaca*, and *hṛdaya* mantras upon it, having placed the purifying substances within it with the root mantra (*mūla*), and having again placed the *hṛdaya*, *kavaca*, and *astra* mantras upon them, having arranged them according to another rite, having wound them with threads, and having worshipped them—

Having worshipped with the *saṃhitā* mantras, having entrusted [the deity] for protection to one stationed at the site of the water-pot (*kalaśa*), having made the formal request, and having honored the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) for being vigilant in guarding the sacrifice— even that which resides in the *liṅga*—
Having fully worshipped Śiva and obtained his permission, (207) p.
482) (pra) then, following the consecration of the *pavitra* sanctified by the *saṃpāta* [offering],...

And he states the protection [of the vessel] with the passage beginning with "purified" (*pūte*) and ending with "having obtained permission" (*anujñāpya*). "Purified" (*pūte*) means thoroughly cleansed. "Produced from bamboo and so forth" (*vaṃśādisaṃbhave*) means originating from bamboo and the like.
The worship of the knowledge-guru and so forth.
(33) Having offered the *pavitra* into the Siddhānta manuscript and to the Guru, and having performed the vigil for the Deity with dance, song, and so forth, one should go outside,

perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and, being pure, [place] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the tooth-stick upon three mandalas made of cow dung.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in due order, being pure, and having spread out a clean bed with *darbha* grass, one who desires to eat should perform protection by means of three enclosures of sesame seeds.

One should sleep while recollecting Śiva. One who seeks liberation should likewise sleep on a bed of ashes [or sleep on a mat]. This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the sacred thread (*pavitra*). (209) p.
Now, regarding the worship of the Guru of Knowledge (*vidyāguru-pūjā*): [the section] beginning with "the Siddhānta" and ending with "having performed" [is concluded].

Now, raising the question of what one should do immediately after that, he says [the portion] beginning with "outside" and ending with "one should sleep. The conclusion of the stated subject matter is indicated by the word "thus" (*iti*). The word "completed" (*samāpta*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Thus [ends the section].
An Explanation of the Ritual for the Consecration of the Purifier (pavitra).
272. The procedure for the preliminary rites preceding the offering of the *pavitra* on the second day of the *pavitrādhivāsa*.

(38) Then, having risen in the morning, performed his bath, and completed the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), he entered the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*). Having purified the ground and worshipped the God of gods, and without dismissing him, [he offered] the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitra*).

Having taken the purificatory materials (*pavitraka*) and the components of the vow (*vratāṅga*), excluding the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and having placed them in a pure vessel, one should set them upon a mandala in the northeast, offer eight flowers, and bid farewell to Śiva.

Having removed the floral offerings (*nirmālya*) and the like, and having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), one should perform the two daily rites (*nityāhnika*) as before on a pure ground (p.
Having performed the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) pertaining to the specific occasion and having executed the special libation (*tarpaṇa*),
and having worshipped the Sun as before, and having fully honored the doors and the door-keepers,
and having entered within by the western door as before, [one should offer] to Vāstoṣpati.
Having offered flowers, worshipped one’s own seat with the *praṇava*, and sat down,

one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Having performed the purification of the place through the prescribed internal sacrifice, oblation, and meditation, [one prepares] the materials for the special *arghya*—

Having performed the purification, the specific cleansing, the self-consecration, the mantra-purification, the Śiva-hand, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [one should worship] Vāstupati, Lakṣmī, the Śiva-vase, the weapon-mantra, and the vardhanī-vessel.

Having worshipped Vastravardhanī, the world-protectors (lokapālas), Gaṇapati, and the preceptors in sequence, and having worshipped the one situated in the maṇḍala as before, he should especially bathe and worship the one situated in the liṅga with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances.
Having approached the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having sprinkled the pit with water while reciting the Astra-mantra,
one should worship Brahmā and the other deities, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas), together with their weapons, upon the girdles, the enclosing sticks, and the sacrificial seats.

Having consecrated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*) as before, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should honor Śiva residing in the fire with perfumes and other offerings.

Having performed the general and specific propitiation of the mantras, and for the sake of pacifying bad dreams and the like— [for the pacification of [the mind's] agitation]— having offered one hundred and eight oblations as an expiation with the Astra-mantra,
having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and having prepared and accomplished the sacrificial pap (caru) as before;

[Having completed the casting], one should divide [the materials] as before. (220) (Pra) Now, having thus explained the consecration of the *pavitra* (purifying thread), he describes the rites to be performed prior to the installation of the *pavitra* on the following day with the words beginning with "atha" (now), [ending with] "vibhajet" (one should divide).

[This concludes] with the words "without even dismissing the deity. Here, the intended meaning is that one should worship Śiva with the "eight-flower offering" (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), because this is prescribed for the occasion of dismissal during the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* rite.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Having worshipped the deity with the eight flowers, one should dismiss him.
And immediately thereafter, he will say:
"Having offered the eight flowers and having dismissed Śiva..."

486) (The two daily rites: the two duties for the morning and midday. He says that one should perform the occasional twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and the special libation (*tarpaṇa*), just as on the previous day.

Regarding the term "occasion-specific" (*naimittikī*): here, the teachers maintain that at the time of offering the *pavitra* during worship, a *gandha-pavitra* (a fragrant purifier) should also be given.
The ritual procedure for the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the deities stationed in the pavilion.

(35) Then, having offered the *caru* oblation to Sūrya, and having honored his gatekeepers, Gaṇapati, and the Guru with the *pavitra*, one should recite "Kālātman" and so forth, preceded by the name of Sūrya, and [offer] the *pavitra*s with the Sūrya-mantra.

Having given [the offerings], having given the *pavitra* for the seizing of the limbs (*tadaṅgagraha*), having recited [mantras], offered the oblation, and sipped water, having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, he should give the *pavitra* to the doors of pacification and so forth,
to Nandin and the others, and to Vāstoṣpati and Mahālakṣmī.
Having given and offered the *pavitra* to the World Protectors (*lokapāla*),
and having first presented the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) to the water-jar (*kumbha*) and the ewer (*vardhanī*), one recites "Kālātma" and so forth (p.
Having recited [the mantras], having placed the *pavitra* [strainers] upon them, having offered the *pavitra* to Gaṇapati and the Gurus,
and likewise having offered the *pavitra* to the one residing in the maṇḍala— and to Gaṇapati and the Gurus for the *vardhanī* vessels— having thus given the *pavitra* to the Blessed One, [222]...
Now, [the author] explains the procedure for the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) to the deities residing in the pavilion,
beginning with the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with the word "having given" (*datvā*).
The preliminary ritual procedure for the installation of the purifier (pavitrāropaṇa) of the Deity.

(36) Having worshipped Śiva, who resides in the *liṅga*— [the *liṅga* being] the *vitrāṇi*— and having offered the ancillaries such as the observance (*vratacaryā*) according to their respective places, excluding the *pañcagavya* and the *caru*,
even the *pañcagavya* and *caru* prepared on that very day [should be offered].

Having offered the *caru* of the five-fold [oblation], one should worship, as in the daily rite, the door-keepers at the [daily] gateway, as well as Gaṇapati, Lakṣmī, and the lineage of Gurus, with the *pavitra*. (222)
Now, [the author] states the preliminary rites for the installation of the deity’s *pavitra* (sacred thread),
beginning with the words "situated in the *liṅga*" and ending with "having worshipped" (on page 488).

Having placed the tooth-stick and other items in their proper places, [the author], keeping in mind the venerable *Maya-śruti* which states "the most excellent Guru," says: "On the following day as well,
one should offer the substances that are auxiliary to the enjoyment of the vow," thus [referring to] "the limbs of the vow-practice and so forth."

"According to their respective places" means in the directions starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna. "Accomplished on that day" means performed on that very day. Here, in the offering of substances, only new water, saffron, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), betel, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be offered.
The intention, however, is that the other items are indeed the substances already offered on the previous day; as was stated previously:

"Without discarding the fragrance and the purifier (pavitra), having taken even the ancillaries of the vow—excluding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial porridge (caru)—and placed them in a pure vessel."

(268) The Ritual for the Investiture of the Purifier (Pavitrāropaṇa) of Śiva. (Kriyāpāda) (37) Having meditated upon the Lord Śiva— who is accompanied by the circle of Prakṛti, who is praised, who is not censured by the circle [of deities], and who is intent on bestowing supreme gifts— one should [proceed].
Recalling that which consists of time (kālātmaka), [one should contemplate] the year, the season, the month, the fortnight, and the day.

[I take refuge in] the Lord, the protector of the field, who is the embodiment of the *ghaṭikā*, *prāṇa*, and so forth; the sole cause for the activity of all the senses, the body, and their objects; the unique witness of performed, unperformed, and abandoned actions, as well as afflicted karma; and the guardian of the field.
With a pure mind, having taken up the purifying substances [the pure and imperishable purifiers],
and fumigating them while facing the vessel for a short time,
he should announce: "O God, by you who are the soul of Time, whatever has been seen as corrupt in my [sacrifice]."
In this rite, whatever has been done with difficulty, abandoned, performed, gathered,
or concealed— let that which was done by me be difficult or not difficult,
performed or nourished, or even unperformed.
O Śambhu, by means of this purifying [thread], through your will and with my whole being, [I am bound].

Having uttered: *oṃ pūraya pūraya makhavrataniyameśvarāya svāhā*, and having uttered up to the level of *māyā*: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ ātmatattvādhipataye śivāya svāhā*—[this being] within the *ātmatattva* which extends to the limit of *prakṛti* and is protected by the cause that is Brahman.
Having uttered [the mantra] ending in -yānta, for the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), which is pervaded by Śuddhavidyā and protected by Viṣṇu as its cause:
*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ vidyātattvādhipataye śivāya svāhā*.

Having uttered [the mantra] ending with Īśvara [ending with Śiva], and having uttered [the mantra] ending with Śiva— namely, "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva, the Lord of the Śivatattva, who pervades up to the end of Śiva and is protected by Rudra as its cause"—
one should, in due order, offer [an oblation] accompanied by dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.
One who seeks liberation (mumukṣu) should place three purifiers (pavitra) upon the head of the *liṅga*;

however, one who seeks worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should recite "Śivatattva" and so forth, and then place the three purifiers. Afterwards, over all the principles (tattvas) protected by all the causal deities, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.
Having recited "To Śiva, the Lord of all principles, svāhā" up to the point of dissolution,

having offered the Gaṅgāvatāraka [mantra] consisting of all principles, and having offered the purifiers (pavitra) to the limbs of Brahmā, one should offer a handful of flowers to Śiva with the root mantra and the Mahāmudrā.
Having rendered [the deity] supreme.
(223) Now, he extends by analogy the procedure for the investiture of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) for Śiva, beginning with the words "the deity" and ending with "having rendered supreme."
491) (The mandala with its primordial nature): This means it is accompanied by the primary mandala of Viriñca and others, and is praised by Viriñca and the rest; thus it is described.

"One should contemplate Śiva as being praised by the feet of Somaśambhu and as being pleased by Viriñca and the other [gods]. Regarding the word *prakṛti*, Yādava states: "In the context of the five elements, *prakṛti* refers to the primary cause (*pradhāna*). He explains how one should perform the petition with the words beginning with "Oṃ" and so forth.

(In the form of Time: known as the moments (truṭi), lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā, kalā, muhūrta, ghaṭikā, yāma, day-and-night (ahorātra), fortnight (pakṣa), month (māsa), season (ṛtu), solstice (ayana), year (saṃvatsara), yuga, manvantara, kalpa, and mahākalpa.
By him whose body is time consisting of eighteen components, which is to be eternally presided over; by him, in my ritual procedure— that is, in my activity—
whatever was performed with difficulty was executed incompletely, and whatever was abandoned was done through ignorance and so forth.
Any action that was left unattended, whether performed or not performed,
or which was abandoned due to necessity, either intentionally or through distraction.
Even that task which was my own responsibility has been performed. And as for that which was concealed by speech, it was done with stinginess regarding wealth.

Even a misdeed, due to the absence of expiation, was hidden out of shame. May that action, though seen somewhere, be unafflicted rather than afflicted; may that which was poorly executed become well-nourished.

By this [word], there is a collective designation for those who have been abandoned, seized, or hidden, because there is no difference among them in their state of being disregarded. "In every way" (*sarvātmanā*) means by way of having the nature of the *ātmatattva* and so forth, by virtue of pervading all things, that is to say, by filling everything. "By this" (*amunā*) refers to the purifier (*pavitra*).
Fill, fill all the gaps in my karma characterized by afflictions and so forth, for the Lord of Sacrificial Vows and Observances, svāhā! "Sacrifice" (*makha*) refers to the ritual offering;
"vow" (*vrata*) refers to the eighth day of the dark fortnight and so forth; "observance" (*niyama*) refers to non-anger and so forth, or those rules established by oneself.
Their lord; to him—*svāhā*. Here, the word *sva-* denotes one's own self.
The word *hi-* [is as follows]... (page no. 493 missing).
The intended meaning is that the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) pervades the entire path from earth up to *māyā*.
Regarding the phrase "protected by Brahmā as its cause": here, "Brahmā" is so designated because it is taught in the venerable *Kiraṇa* and other scriptures.
Some maintain that one who abides in the impure path is indeed pure and not merely *prākṛta* (material).

Because the lords of the causes are also threefold— distinguished as *aṇu*, *śakti*, and *śambhu*— just like the *mantras* and *mantreśvaras*, there is the presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Brahmā and the others.
The Gurus maintain that it is precisely those who possess specific powers (*yukta-śakti-viśeṣa*) who are designated there by such terms as "Brahmā" and so forth.

As it is stated in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*: "Or, being one, he exists in five ways through various names and forms. This refers to the "principle of the Self" (*ātmatattva*). Regarding this, some hold that the locative case here is used in the sense of a causal condition (*nimitta-artha*).

They say that the locative case here is used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*), and it should be explained by supplying the word "Śiva" as the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). This should be understood in the same way for what follows. (Having uttered up to the end of Māyā-tattva).
Here, [it refers to] the lotus of the palate (*tālu-padma*) of the one who pervades the limits of the Māyā-tattva.
p.
495) One should perform the utterance ending in the letter *ma* for that which is manifest and denotes Rudra.
He states the procedure for the second offering of the purifier (*pavitra*) with the word "pure" (*śuddha*).

"[In that which] has an extension reaching up to Pure Knowledge" (*śuddhavidyāntavyāptike*): that whose extension reaches as far as the principle of Pure Knowledge—that is, up to the principle of Īśvara—is so described. Regarding this, [it is stated] in the venerable *Mṛgendra* and other texts.

Since it is heard that the Īśvara-tattva is included within Śuddhavidyā, and because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the phrase "having uttered up to Īśvara," the word *vidyā-tattva* is intended here through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) to mean the *īśvara-tattva*. This [power] pervades half of that tattva.

The intention is that it is the *vidyā-tattva*. Having meditated upon Śiva as its presiding deity, [one should recite] "having uttered up to Īśvara. In this context, the utterance should be performed ending with the *bindu*, which denotes Īśvara, which pervades up to the *īśvara-tattva*, and which shines forth between the eyebrows.
He explains the procedure for the third bestowal of the purifier (*pavitra*) with the word "Śiva.
[The phrase] "in that which has pervasion ending in Śiva" means that its pervasion extends as far as Śiva and his Śakti; it is described thus.
That is to say, the Śiva-tattva is that which pervades the darkness [of ignorance] within the path of the Śakti-tattva.

Having meditated upon Śiva as the presiding lord therein— [as indicated by the instruction] "having uttered [the mantra] ending with Śiva"— here, [one meditates on] that which shines at the end of the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), denoting Sadāśiva.
Having recited the mantra at the end of the *nāda* accompanied by the *ardhacandra* and *nirodhi*,
one should place the sacred thread (*pavitra*) upon the top of the *liṅga*.
Anticipating the question of who should be given this purifier, he says: "(The seeker of liberation).
This means one who desires liberation, that is to say, one who possesses the lifelong initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*).
Anticipating the question of how it could be given to anyone other than such a person, he says: "(The seeker of enjoyment). This refers to the seeker of worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*).

"One who desires enjoyment" (bhuktikāmaḥ) means one who has been initiated into the material initiation (bhautikadīkṣā); it does not mean a householder. This distinction will be clarified in the discussion on initiation, and therefore it is not elaborated upon here.

In this context regarding the seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), some [hold that] the *pavitra* of the Śiva-tattva situated above [purifies] the Vidyā-tattva located below it. [Missing pages 497 and 498.]
"O Maheśvara, please complete that which is unfinished and deficient in words."
O Lord of the Gods, O Maheśāna, you are perfectly pure, the purifier, and the destroyer of sins;
by you, the entire world, both the stationary and the moving, has been purified.
O Lord, whatever vow has been broken by me through the occurrence of deficiency,
may all that become whole again, bound together by the thread of your command.

Having thus made this request, (228) he then states the subsequent duties with the passage beginning with "(with hands joined in a *puṣpāñjali*)" and ending with "having requested. Anticipating the question, "How should one make the request? [the author proceeds].
He states the mantra for requesting [the deity]: "Oṃ, you are the goal" (*tvaṃ gatiḥ*). "The goal" (*gatiḥ*) is characterized by liberation.
As it is said in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*:
"That which is the final state of a person whose seed of saṃsāra has been burnt."
That should be understood as his "going," not as remaining in another location.
Thus it is said; and in the *Śrīmatparākhyatantra* as well: "But for him, there shall be attainment and equanimity," because it is impossible for the Supreme Lord to possess a destination (p.

It should be understood that [the Lord] is denoted by the word "gati" because He is the cause thereof. "(Of all beings)" means of all creatures; according to the *Vaijayantī*, the term *bhūta* refers to a living being starting from the ether (*kha*) down to the insect. "(Moving and unmoving)" refers to the stationary and the mobile. "(Established)" is used figuratively to express faults and for the purpose of their cessation.

He is perfectly established as the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*); [by] internal movement, he is the inner witness (*antaryāmin*). He is the observer (*draṣṭṛ*), the witness of auspicious and inauspicious actions. [By] action, through bodily activity;
[by] mind, through causes such as meditation; [by] speech, in the form of praise and so forth—[such is his] course.

"You must go. This means that you alone are the object of my actions, which are accomplished through body, mind, and speech. "Unperformed" refers to that which has been omitted, such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth.
"Devoid of speech" means lacking the words for such things as the announcement of welcome. "Well-purified" [refers to one who is purified].
"Extremely pure" means exceedingly pure, that is to say, eternally stainless. "(Purifying)" means the cause of protection from falling. "(Destroyer of evil)" [means...

You alone are the substance that destroys evil, impurity, and the like; therefore, everything has been purified by you. Whatever vow I have broken or interrupted through the occurrence of deficiencies—all that has been strung together by the thread of your command, woven upon the thread of your decree.
May it become one.
The procedure for the act to be performed immediately following the request.
(39) Having offered incense, lamps, the *ārātrika* lamp, a mirror, a parasol, and chowries,

and having visualized [the deity] as satisfied while being praised by Ananta and others, one should perform the rites of *amṛtīkaraṇa* and *paramīkaraṇa*, recite the mantra, present the offering, and [perform the same] for the limbs of Brahmā.

Having recited [the mantra] ten times, one should offer it. The preceptor (ācārya) should place the purificatory thread (pavitra) upon all the deities. The practitioner (sādhaka) should likewise bestow it upon the mantra to be accomplished (sādhya-mantra).
This may be done as desired, from the beginning of the four-month period until the conclusion of the ritual.
Having undertaken the vow and observance instructed by the Guru, and having praised the Deity with hymns,
prostrated, and asked for forgiveness, he approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the sake of the Lord residing in the fire.
Having placed the purifiers (pavitra), one should offer more than a hundred oblations according to the rule for the sake of filling the gaps and ensuring stability;
then, having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra for the purpose of expiation (prāyaścitta).

Having offered a hundred oblations, having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having presented the food offering, water for sipping, sandalwood paste, betel leaves, and so forth, having applied the ash-sandalwood paste, having restrained Śiva, having offered the *vyāhṛti* mantras, and having given the purifier (*pavitra*) to Śiva.
Having extinguished the fire and offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation,
(225) (289) [he] then, having explained the manner of the request, states what is to be done immediately thereafter, beginning with the words "incense and lamp" and ending with "having offered."
"To all the gods" means to the gods stationed in the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
Some say that the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) must be performed for those gods who have been worshipped in the daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*);
this is because the practitioner has been initiated with the initiation that confers authority (*sādhikāradīkṣā*). He too—

"The practitioner should give [the mantra] of the *kāmya* [rite]," so it is said. He describes the manner of undertaking the observances for the *pavitra* [rite] with the words "for four months" (*caturmāsa*).

"(Beginning with four months and ending with the performance of the ritual). Here, the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to three months and so forth. This has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu:
"Four, three, or two months, or even half a month."
For seven days, or five nights, or three days, or even for a single day.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the phrase "until the completion of the ritual," the injunction for the four-month period and so forth is indeed limited to the duration of Viṣṇu’s sleep, because it is prescribed that [the rite] occurs while Janārdana is asleep. That limit, however, is specifically the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika; for one performs [the rite] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.

This is because of the statement, "Hari is awakening. For this very reason, it is ordained in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra* that the limit for the observance of the sacred thread (*pavitra*) is precisely the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kṛttikā, as in:
"O Bird, one should pass four months according to the rule."
Having set the Kārttikī full moon as the limit, [starting] from the ninth day of the bright fortnight itself.
Thus, for this very reason, the rule for undertaking vows such as the Cāturmāsya should be observed according to one's capacity and preference, extending at least until that specific lunar day.
And this method of observance has been taught in the venerable Pauṣkara and other scriptures, as follows:
"Having resolved upon the four months and taken up a desired place of residence, one should undertake the adoption of earth, ashes, and so forth, while remaining bound by those very observances."
"Furthermore, the Guru should avoid traveling on a path where there is fresh cutting [of trees], and likewise elsewhere.
Also, from the *Śrīmanmohaśūrottara-śruti*:
"O Thousand-eyed One, one must not go to a place that is devoid of purity."
Once he has been dismissed, one may go wherever one pleases according to one's own will.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, he states another alternative: "(as desired)" and "(or as instructed by the Guru). Here, prior to the time limit stated as the ultimate boundary, one may also adopt that time limit for the observance which has been personally indicated by the Guru himself, even if it differs from the aforementioned period.
Thus it should be understood; so has it been described by the commentator on the *Śrīmatsomaśambhupaddhati*.

He describes the procedure for the investiture of the purifier (*pavitrāropaṇa*) of the deity who is the locus of the fire (*agnyādhāra*), [beginning] with the words "near the sacrificial pit" (*kuṇḍāntikam*).
(The Purifiers: The purifiers of the principles of the self (*ātmatattva*) and so forth. As it was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Even when Śiva resides within the fire, there is likewise this fourfold set of purifiers. (Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations.)
Thus; it should be understood that here the four oblations beginning with *bhūḥ* are to be offered.
290–The ritual procedure for the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) and so forth.

(80) Having offered the *bali* with the *pavitra* to those seated upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*viṣṭara*), and having offered the inner *bali* and the outer *bali* along with the *pavitra*, and having performed the ritual of total integration (*sakalīkṛtya*) preceded by hymns of praise and salutation, one should offer the *pavitra* to the preceptor and to the books of the Siddhānta.
Having worshipped Śiva situated in the maṇḍala, having reported the ritual performance, and having asked for forgiveness,
he should worship the deity residing in the liṅga and that in the water-pot, and honor the world-protectors (lokapālas) to ensure they remain vigilant for the protection of the sacrifice. (226)
(Pr) Now, the procedure for the offering of the *bali* and so forth, beginning with "the enclosure" (*paridhi*) and ending with "having prepared" (*saṃbhāvya*) on page 506,
[is performed] "for the Guru. Here, the *pavitra* [purifier] should be offered with the *pañcabrahma-mantra*.
Likewise, in the illustrious *Suprabheda*, it is stated that the purification cord (*pavitraka*) for the preceptor is to be made with the five Brahmans;
for the disciple, however, with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*); and for others, with the heart mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Thus [it is said].
The ritual procedure for the worship of the members of the assembly.

(42) Having honored those initiated according to one's ability with food, clothing, and so forth, and having satisfied the poor, the blind, the wretched, the helpless, children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the afflicted, one should say: "May Sadāśiva be pleased by this gift. (227)

Next, he describes the worship of the *sadasyas* with the passage beginning with "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) and ending with "one should say" (*brūyāt*). "According to one's capacity" means according to one's wealth. "With food, clothing, and so forth" means with food, clothing, mental offerings, and the like. "Initiated ones" (*dīkṣitān*) refers to those who have received the Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*).
(And [the terms] "miserable," "blind," and "wretched"): "A miser (*kṛpaṇa*) is one who is poor; *kṛpaṇa*, *durvidha*, and *dīna* are synonyms," according to Amara.
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to children, the elderly, and so forth. "(May he be pleased)" means he should act kindly; "(let him speak)" means let him be spoken to.
The procedure for eating.
(Kriyā) (42) Then he should eat together with his disciples. (Pra) Now, with the words beginning with "then" and ending with "he should eat," he states what is to be done immediately thereafter.
(292) The procedure for performing [the rite] on the second day according to the one-day (ekāha) system.

(43) On the following day, having bathed, performed the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), and fetched the purificatory materials (*pavitra*) from Śiva, he placed them in a pure vessel as on the previous day; having worshipped and dismissed the Lord with the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering, and having completed the two daily routines (*nityāhnika*), [he performed] the occasional rite (*naimittika*).

Having performed the ritual beginning with the twilight worship and ending with the worship of Śiva—just as on the previous day—and having also fully worshipped [the deity] residing in the fire, one performs the libation of mantras.
Having prepared the *caru*, having cooked it, and having completed its preparation, one should offer it; then, having offered the *pavitra* ornaments to Sūrya and the other deities as before,
and having likewise offered the *pavitra* ornaments to Śiva preceded by the offering of the ritual substances (*dravya*), the rite concludes with the recitation (*japa*).
Having completed the concluding rites of the recitation (*japāntakarma*), having offered libations even to that which resides in the fire, and having presented the sacrificial oblation (*caru*),
one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra, the weapon mantra, or the Aghora mantra for the sake of expiation, and then perform the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). (229)

Now, having explained the main body of the *pavitra* rite, [the author] states the duties to be performed on the second day in the case of a one-day (*ekāha*) performance, from the words "on the following day" (*aparedyuḥ*) up to "having performed" (*vidhāya*).
Regarding the sequence [of time], such as "today," "on this day," or "on the previous day," the terms "previous" (*pūrva*), "subsequent" (*uttara*), and "later" (*apara*) are used.
Likewise, according to Amarasimha: "The words *adhara*, *anya*, *itarētara*, and *pūrvedyuḥ* [and so forth] [are used in specific senses]."
The ritual procedure for the dedication of karma.

(44) "O Blessed One, may I be one who desires enjoyment; let this vow be effective for the attainment of fruit"—thus he should offer the vow to Śiva. But he who desires liberation [should say]: "O Lord, let this karma not be mine.

"Having offered the *bandhaka*," that is, having announced the *karman*. (220) Now, he explains the procedure for the dedication of the *karman* with the passage beginning with "one who desires enjoyment" (*bhuktikāmaḥ*) and ending with "having announced" (*nivedya*). "One who desires enjoyment" (*bhuktikāmaḥ*) refers to one who seeks worldly existence (*bhautikaḥ*). "But one who desires liberation" (*muktikāmas tu*)...

The *naiṣṭhika* [is one who has reached the final goal]. (The *bandhaka*) is that which obstructs liberation. (Having offered) thus—here it should be understood that one should offer [the water] with the special *arghya* water into the hand of Śiva while granting a boon (*varada-hasta*), using the root mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*.
Likewise, in the *Śrīrāmanātha-paddhati*:
"The Praṇava, the Heart [mantra], the Root [mantra], and finally the word 'śivāya';
having uttered these along with 'svāhā' for the worship, fire-oblation, and so forth, together with the water of the arghya."
One should present the ritual action with the Udbhavā mudrā in the hand that holds the sacrificial offering (varahasta).
Thus it is said.
The sequence for the dismissal of the sacrifice.

292-(kri) (45) Having offered food, water for rinsing the mouth, sandalwood paste, and betel to the one residing in the fire, having applied ash-sandalwood [to oneself], and having entered the fire, one should offer eight flowers.
Having bowed and offered the *arghya*, one should unite the Lord residing in the fire with Śiva situated in the *maṇḍala* by means of the yoga of the channels;

then, having withdrawn the mantras of the fire, led them to the *dvādaśānta*, and emerged [from there], one should establish them within one's own heart. Having gratified the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*, that too—
One should dismiss [them].
Alternatively, at the conclusion of the Caṇḍa-worship, having worshipped that [deity] as well and offered oblations according to one's capacity,
one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). Having offered the *bali* to the deities beginning with Sūrya who were worshipped in the pavilion and seated upon the *paridhi* and *viṣṭara*,
and having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*), one should offer the *bali* again, preceded by hymns of praise and prostrations, and then perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkṛtya*).

Having united [the deity] residing in the maṇḍala with the one in the water-pot (kumbha), and having withdrawn the mantras from the water-pot (kumbha) and the *vardhanī* vessel, unite them with the Lord of the Sacrifice (yāgeśvara); then, with the words "Forgive me for my dependence," he should dismiss [the deity]. Then, having worshipped the God with the eightfold flower-offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*),...

Having dismissed the deities associated with the specific ritual context— whether they are dependent or independent— and having likewise dismissed the Sun as is appropriate, one should then dismiss the guardians of the directions, the door-keepers, and so forth, in reverse order.

511) Now, he extends by analogy the sequence for the dismissal of the sacrifice (*yāgavisarjana*) with the passage beginning with “(to the one residing in the fire)” and ending with “having dismissed. [The phrase] “having united [the deity] with Śiva residing in the mandala” refers to the specific presence (*viśeṣasannidhāna*) therein.
The meaning is "having made [the presence] possible. (Mantrān) means the *saṃhitā* mantras. (Visarjayet) means "he should dismiss.

Here, it should be understood that one should dismiss Śiva—who possesses general presence within the water-pot for the sake of one's own consecration—only after having requested his permission. As was stated previously: "In this [rite], [it lasts] until the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*)."

"Having requested, 'O Blessed One, you should remain,' he speaks of the dismissal of Śiva residing in one's own chosen *liṅga* with [the word] 'then' (*tataḥ*). [The word] 'the God' (*devam*) refers to Śiva situated in one's own chosen *liṅga*. [The word] 'as is fitting' (*yathārham*) means as is appropriate; that is to say, in accordance with the specific ritual context."

He states the sequence for the dismissal of the world-protectors and others with the word "then. Regarding the phrase "the world-protectors and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes all the deities worshipped in the pavilion. Therefore, the meaning is that one should dismiss the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and the rest without further expectation, reversing the order of worship.
p.
512) The method for the worship and dismissal of Caṇḍeśa and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
(46) Having duly procured the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) from a deity,
and having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara either in a mandala or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), [one should offer] the purificatory threads.
Having placed [the offerings] upon it and presented the floral remains (nirmālya) along with the sacred grass (pavitra), one should make this petition:
"Whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive, may that become complete for me by your command, O Caṇḍanātha. Thus.

Thereafter, having praised him and propitiated Caṇḍeśvara in the fierce fire, having offered a hundred oblations, having performed the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), having cast the floral remains (*nirmālya*) into a blind well or similar place, and having burned the purificatory threads (*pavitra*) in the fire,
[he should worship] that fire and Brahmā and the other deities, preceded by the *vyāhṛti* oblations on both sides.

One should dismiss [the deity]. Then, having purified the ground with cow dung, performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and effected the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should bathe the deity once more and worship him.

Now, having explained the sequence for the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the sacrifice, [the author] sets forth the method for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the worship of Caṇḍeśvara, and its dismissal, with the passage beginning with "from the deity" (*devāt*) and ending with "having thoroughly purified" (*saṃśodhya*). "From the deity" (*devāt*) means from Śiva, who resides in the locus of one's own chosen *liṅga*. "The purifiers" (*pavitrāṇi*)...

"Having placed [them]" means that one should wear pure and clean [cloths]. This has been stated by the venerable feet of Somaśambhu: "The excellence of the threads for Caṇḍeśa, Ravi, and Vahni is like that of Śiva. [Regarding] the *nirmālya*: having set aside the stale offering for the sake of Caṇḍa...

This refers to flower garlands and the like that have been set aside. Here, since it is established by the term *nirmālya* that even a *pavitra* (sacred thread) removed from Īśa [Śiva] is included, its separate mention is to indicate that for one who has received a fresh, pure *pavitra*,
the offering of that *nirmālya-pavitra* must certainly be performed for him as well.

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of making it known. He describes the manner of the petition to Caṇḍeśvara with the words "(whatever little... and so forth. "(Annual)" means occurring within a year. The rest is easy to understand.
And [he established] Caṇḍeśvara between the two sacrificial mounds and fire-pits.

Now, having described the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍanātha and so forth, he explains the ritual to be performed immediately thereafter with the passage beginning with "(having sipped water)" and ending with "one should worship. Regarding the phrase "(having bathed the Deity)": here, [one bathes] Śiva, who resides in his own chosen *liṅga*, for the purpose of the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).

It should be understood that because [the deity] has been worshipped and honored throughout the day, one should worship one's own chosen *liṅga* as a daily practice for the purpose of clearing away the faded flowers (*nirmālya*). This was stated by the venerable Somaśambhu: "Having bathed Śiva, one should worship Him."
298. The procedure for immediate consecration (adhivāsa).

(47) Immediately after the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), following the previously mentioned sequence for the Sun and the other deities who have been worshipped in the pavilion, one should offer a pure *pavitra* after giving the fragrant *pavitra*; likewise for the Deity, after giving the fragrant *pavitra*.

Afterwards, having offered eight flowers and having placed the pure *pavitra*s upon them, and having likewise placed the fragrant *pavitra*s and pure *pavitra*s upon the fire, [one should offer] the remaining *pavitra*s as well.
Having offered the oblation and performed [the rites] as before, one should dismiss the sacrifice as previously described.

(223) Now, with the words beginning with "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) and ending with "one should dismiss" (*visṛjet*), he explains the sequence of procedures to be performed for the immediate consecration (*adhivāsa*).
The ritual procedure for consuming the five products of the cow.
(Kriyā) (47) Thereafter, for the sake of purification, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

(Pra) Now, with the words beginning with "thereafter" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "one should cause to consume" (*prāśayet*), he states what is to be done immediately following that. At this juncture, [one should perform the rite] with the waters contained within the *śivakumbha*, the *astra*, and the *vardhanī*.
It should be understood that "the disciple is to be consecrated" [is the meaning]. Likewise, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*, at the conclusion of the *pavitra* rite, it is said:
"Then, having dismissed the sacrifice to Caṇḍa and performed the *avabhṛtha* bath, one should partake [of the ritual].
And this was stated previously as well.
One should dismiss [the guest] with the words, "Forgive me, out of consideration."
The Ritual for the Worship of the Guru.
(49) The Guru is to be worshipped like Śiva with garments, wealth, and ornaments;
when the Lord Guru is satisfied, Śaṅkara becomes satisfied.
The Supreme Lord has declared that for him with whom the Guru is fully satisfied, there is the complete and equal compendium of his entire ritual section and so forth for the year. (225)
Next, [the author] explains the worship of the guru with two verses beginning with "The Guru," etc.;
the meaning of these verses is clear.
The necessity of performing the rite of purification (pavitraka) in the presence of the Guru.
(50) Even a disciple who resides five *yojanas* away should perform the *pavitra* rite in the presence of the Guru.
(226) Now, he states that this performance of the *pavitra* must indeed be carried out in the presence of the Guru alone.
From the words beginning with "the five" up to the end of the phrase "one should bring about."
The method for performing the *pavitraka* rite in the absence of the Guru:

(Kriyā-pāda) (52). Thereafter, if [the disciple] is situated at a distance or is incapable, he should perform it together with his own lineage members, such as his elder brothers and so forth; in their absence, he should perform it himself.
(227) The rite of purification was proclaimed by that Guru known as Aghoraśiva, who is celebrated in the world as Parameśvara-aparākhya.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇavidhi*) in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.

Now, he describes the method for performing the purification (*pavitrakaraṇa*) in the absence of the Guru, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and ending with "he should accomplish" (*nirvartayet*).
Now follows the conclusion of this section on the *pavitra* with the single verse beginning with "Parameśvara. The meaning of the verse is easily understood.

Thus ends [the section] from the *Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā*, known as the *Prabhāsa*, composed by Guru Nirmalamaṇi— the son of Ācārya Tāgarāja, who was born in the lineage of the presiding deity of the illustrious Kamalālaya.
The ritual procedure for the Pavitra [offering] is completed in this commentary on the Kriyākramadyotikā.
May there be auspiciousness.
The ritual procedure for the *damanaka* flower.
Furthermore, those men who will not perform the Damana festival,
to them I have granted the fruit of merit arising from the month of Caitra.

Having heard this, and out of fear of not obtaining the meritorious fruit of worship in the month of Caitra, practitioners have faith even in the ritual procedure for the Damanaka festival prescribed in another tantra;
one should perform the sacrifice with the Pavitra [thread] for those who possess such faith. [One should take the flower] found in a garden...
Or, having gone to where the *damana* plant is located in the house, one should awaken it by sprinkling it with water using the *astra-mantra*, worshipping it with the *saṃhitā-mantras*, and saying:
"O you who have arisen from the grace of Hara, be present here!"
"You must be led away for the sake of Śiva’s work, by the command of Śiva."
Thus, having brought the *damana* plant along with its five limbs into the presence of the fire, and having performed the *saṃpātana* (sprinkling) rite,
one should offer it.
To the west of Śiva, one should take the root of the *damana* and the earth with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
In the north, the stalk is held by Vāma; the *dhātrī* fruit in the south by Rūpin;
the leaf and ashes in the east by Tatpuruṣa; and the wood for cleansing the teeth [is offered] there.

Having offered the fruit and sandalwood with the Gāyatrī mantra in the northeast, and having taken the *damanaka* flower along with its five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) in his joined palms, he should address [the deity]:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, I have been offered here by you at this very moment."
"However, by your command, the full festival shall be performed according to the means available.
Having thus joined [the deity] to the head of the Lord with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and offered eight flowers, he then recites:
*oṃ hāṃ hauṃ ātmatattvādhipataye śivāya namaḥ oṃ hāṃ hauṃ*.

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the lord of all principles (sarva-tattva).
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, fulfill, fulfill the sacrifice (makha), salutation to Śiva—thus [he worships] the God in sequence.
Having placed it upon his head and offered it, [he says]:
"O Blessed One, whether I have done too much or too little, may all that be complete for me; may this Dāmanaka festival be fulfilled."
Having made this request, and having offered the *damana* herb to Agni and the other deities, and having made the formal announcement, one should dismiss the sacrifice.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the *damanaka* flower in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*, composed by the venerable Aghoraśivācārya, whose other name is Parameśvara.

Having approached the root of the banyan tree, he who bestows grace upon those self-controlled ones by means of this [work], which is fashioned according to his own understanding and joined with the logic of the Śiva-āgamas— even if only in part— [attains success].
I shall compose a commentary on the ritual procedure for the sequence of worshiping the cords (dāma).

Now, having thus described the ritual for the offering of the *pavitra* (the sacred thread), which is an obligatory constituent of the annual rites, [the author] states the reason for performing the *damanaka* worship by means of the verse beginning with "Those who...
and ending with "...have faith. This refers to the verse beginning with "ye punar... and so forth.

The words of the Supreme Lord addressed to Damana; that is to say, [the procedure] prescribed in another Tantra (*tantrāntara*) as well as that prescribed in the *Svacchandabhairavatantra*. This has been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"Although this has been proclaimed in the *Svacchanda-bhairava-tantra*, nevertheless, because it is common [to other systems], it is also applicable here in the Siddhānta.

By this [statement], "one should not perform mixed conduct," and so forth, the expectation that "this must not be done" out of fear of such words is removed. "(Sādhakāḥ)" means those who accomplish both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), namely the teachers (*ācāryas*) and others. "(Śraddadhate)" [means they have faith].

They have faith [in this]. Here, if the Damanaka festival is not performed, the worship of the month of Caitra would belong to Bhairava in the form of Damanaka; therefore, the essential meaning is that for the sake of obtaining the fruits of the worship and other rites of that month, the worship of Damanaka must necessarily be performed.

Now he states the ritual of acceptance (*adhivāsana*) with the words beginning with "that" (*tat*) and ending with "he should sleep" (*svapet*). [The textual markers marked by these symbols are not found in the printed root-text; therefore, it is inferred that they follow the commentary. "(Those who have faith in that)" refers to those who possess faith in the festival of *damanaka*.
"Pavitravat" means equal to the *pavitra* [purification rite]. "(Yāgam)" refers to the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-pūjā*) and so forth.
The method for consecrating the *damanaka* plant is stated by the words beginning with "(udyānagatam).
"(Sapañcāṅgam)" means accompanied by the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*).
(522) The root text is of a different nature; and although we have searched for it in various manuscripts, we have not found it within this much time.
It should be understood that if anything further were to be found beyond this, it would be printed at the conclusion of the book.

The five components here are designated as the root, stalk, leaf, flower, and fruit; the meaning is that one should perform the *saṃpāta-saṃskāra* (the ritual sprinkling) of the *damanaka* plant. After these consecrations, he states what must be done next with the words "of Śiva."

He describes the sequence for offering the *damana* flower preceded by a formal request with the words "with the five limbs" (*sapañcāṅgam*). He describes the manner of placing the remaining *damana* flowers with the word "the rest" (*śeṣam*).
[The term] "in the jar" (*kumbhe*) means in Śiva who resides in the jar. [The term] "having offered" (*nivedayitvā*) means [saying] "protect [them]."
"Announce it"—the intention is that one should place [it] nearby. He states what is to be done immediately thereafter:

"The sacred thread (*pavitra*). Thus, having explained the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *damanaka* flower as a subsidiary rite (*aṅga*), he now describes the method for the primary rite (*aṅgin*), the offering of the *damanaka*, beginning with the morning duties.
From the passage beginning with "(at dawn)" (p.
523) up to the end of "having made this request," he describes the dismissal of the sacrifice with the words: "one should dismiss the sacrifice."
Now follows the conclusion (thus).

Thus ends [the section] in the *Prabhāsākhyā*, the commentary on the *Kriyākramadyotikā* known as the *Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā*, composed by Guru Nirmalamaṇi, the son of Ācārya Tāgarāja— who was born in the lineage of the presiding devotees dwelling in the illustrious Kamalālaya.
The ritual for *damanaka* is completed.
